Since the sentence has already removed the pledge from the argument, the reader is left with the second half of the choice, and the second half is a description of what the people were doing.

Think of a traveller who is told that the fine for the toll road is capped, and who drives through the barrier without paying. The cap he is relying on was never issued, and the barrier does not know his name.

---

## Verse 2:81

> But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**THE ANSWER THAT CANCELS THE CLAIM**

The claim about a limited punishment is answered with words that overturn it: ***“But no! Those who commit evil”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the answer as the refutation of the community's claim, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense. The correction is placed directly against the speech that had gone before, so that the claim is cancelled rather than answered. The phrase does not argue with what was said; it removes it, the way a correction is made to a sentence that had already been accepted as true.

The verdict then follows in a general sentence: ***“and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever”***. al-Saʿdī reads the description as a condition that sweeps past the community in the verse to everyone who meets it. He explains the phrase about being engrossed as a sin that surrounds its owner and leaves him no way out. In his reading that state is the state of unbelief, since a person who holds faith is not enclosed by his sin in that way. He notes that a group later used the verse against Muslims, and that the verse is an argument against them rather than for them.

**RESIDENTS, NOT VISITORS**

The description chosen for the people of the Fire is that of settled inhabitants, and the sentence adds that they remain there. That is exactly what the earlier claim had denied, since the community in the passage had assumed that its stay would be short and its end known. The Book states the same settlement elsewhere in a sentence about the same Fire, (2:39 — **“will be the residents of the Fire”**), and the two passages are read together as one verdict.

Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the sentence as the justice of God set against the claim of the community. He notes that the rule applies without regard to lineage, since the standard is the deed and the state of the heart rather than the people from whom a person descends. al-Ālūsī reads the answer as a refutation in a form that covers the people addressed and everyone else who meets the description, which is why the sentence is phrased as a general rule rather than as a reply to one community. Because the rule is general, the reader cannot file it away as a report about someone else.

**WHY THE VERSE SPEAKS IN GENERAL TERMS**

A rebuke aimed at one community would have let every other hearer off, and the sentence is not built that way. The reason the address stays general is that the standard it describes is not local, since a person is settled in the Fire or he is not, and the difference is not the name of his community. Since the Book had just quoted a claim built on descent, the answer removes descent from the argument in a single stroke.

The verse also keeps the account honest. The community in the passage is not told that its claim was too optimistic; it is told what the claim revealed, which is a heart that had decided how much of its own deed would be counted. That is why the answer arrives as a rule rather than as an insult, and it is why the rule can be read by anyone who hears it, in any generation, without needing a share in the story's quarrel.

Think of a tenant who tells the landlord that the notice period is ten days because that is what he remembers from his father's lease. The lease is produced, the period is different, and the memory is not a clause.

---

## Verse 2:82

> And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever

**THE OTHER SIDE OF THE SENTENCE**

The Book does not leave the verdict at the fate of the people of the Fire: ***“And those who believe”*** ***“and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the two clauses as the second half of the answer to the community's claim, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same order, with faith named before the good works that follow it. Ibn Kathīr keeps the pair together as well, with the sentence standing as the counterweight to the verse before it.

The placement is noticed by al-Ālūsī, since the people of faith are mentioned after the people of the Fire, so that the reader is given both outcomes in one frame rather than a warning alone. Ibn ʿUthaymīn explains the closing phrase as companionship with the Garden, since the word for its people implies remaining with what they have been given. He keeps the note that the Garden is what God has prepared for the mindful.

**FAITH AND WORK IN ONE CLAUSE**

The sentence binds the two halves of the description together, and it does not treat either as optional. al-Jalālayn keeps the ordering, with belief stated first and the deeds joined to it. al-Saʿdī reads the pair as the description of a life that has turned in a direction rather than as a sum of transactions. The works in the verse are not a price paid for the Garden; they are the shape that faith takes when it is real. Because the description joins belief to work in one breath, the reader is shown that a claim of faith without a change of conduct is not the state the verse is describing. The reason the deeds are named after the belief is that the root is put first and the fruit is named where it grows.

Because the two halves of the description stand in one sentence, the reader is shown that faith and work are not two accounts to be settled apart. That is why the account does not present the two outcomes as a scheme of rewards and penalties alone. The verse contrasts two kinds of residence, and it leaves the quality of the deeds with the One who sees them. Because the description of the believer is stated in general terms, the reader is invited to ask whether the description fits him rather than whether the ledger balances, and the question is left open on purpose.

**THE MEANING OF THE TWO RESIDENCES**

The two verses together form one sentence of judgement, and the Garden and the Fire are each given to the people who belong in them. The Book states the same settled life elsewhere with the same vocabulary, (18:107 — **“the Gardens of Paradise”**), and it makes the contrast between the two harvests explicit in another sūrah, (42:20 — **“the harvest of the Hereafter”**). Since the community in the story had been trading the one for the other, the reader is shown what the trade was worth.

The comfort in the verse is bound up with its severity. Because the sentence about the believers is as absolute as the sentence about the others, a person who holds faith and works is given a certainty that no claim of lineage could provide. The account closes the argument about the Fire with a promise about the Garden that stands beside it.

The case is like two brothers who are offered the same land by the same owner, one taking the deed and the other keeping the invitation letter in his pocket. Both of them had paper, and only one of them had the land.

---

## Verse 2:83

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent

**THE COVENANT AND ITS FIRST ARTICLE**

The sūrah now returns to the covenant: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none”*** ***“but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans”*** — the opening articles of a pledge taken from the community. al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as the record of that pledge, and al-Ālūsī places it as a further item in the account of the ancestors' conduct. The case against the community is drawn from the record rather than from an accusation. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the first article in its own words, with the worship of God alone declared as the foundation on which everything else in the pledge rests.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the pledge is described as taken from the children of Israel as a people, and that the few named in the closing clause as true to it were those who acted on it rather than those who carried its name. al-Saʿdī reads the articles as fundamentals of religion that God commanded in every law, because such principles carry the public interest of every time and place. He keeps the first article as the pillar on which the rest depend. The reason the pledge begins with worship is that every other article in the list takes its authority from the One who is worshipped. The duties which follow are branches of a single root.

**KINSHIP, THE POOR, AND THE TONGUE**

The covenant then turns from worship to the people who hold a claim on the community: ***“and the needy”***. The list is kept in the same order by Ibn Kathīr, with parents first and the poor brought in after the family, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sequence. The Book states the same command in another sūrah in a sentence addressed to all people (4:36 — **“associate none with Him”**). The duty to parents is recorded in a passage that names the worship of God first (17:23 — **“you worship none but Him”**).

Then comes the article that orders the community's speech: ***“speak kindly to people”***. The words chosen are not a command to tell the truth alone but a command about the manner of address, and the verse places that duty beside the duty to parents rather than in a separate class of worship. Because the sentence binds the tongue with the same authority that binds the hand, the reader is shown that a covenant with God is conducted in public as much as in private.

**PRAYER, ALMS, AND THE TURNING AWAY**

The covenant closes with the two pillars that hold a community together: ***“establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the duties inside the same sentence as the ones before them. The pair is read by al-Saʿdī as the two institutions that make the rest of the list possible. Prayer is the community's address to God, and the alms-tax is the community's address to its poor, and the pledge is not complete with one of them alone. Because the two duties are named together, the reader is shown that worship and welfare were held by one agreement, so that a community cannot be devout in one direction and careless in the other. The reason the covenant keeps circling the same list is that the failure it describes was not a rejection of the text but a refusal to be bound by it.

The verse then reports what happened to the pledge: ***“But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away”*** ***“except for a few of you”*** ***“and were indifferent”***. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the turning away as a refusal made after the pledge had been accepted. The small group of the faithful is kept in the sentence by al-Jalālayn. al-Qurṭubī collects the articles of this covenant and the reports about how each one was treated. Because the account has kept every article in view, the reader is shown a community that agreed to a list and then walked away from most of it.

The closing word describes a person who does not fight the command; he puts it aside. That is why the sentence stands after the whole covenant rather than after its first article, since the fault it names is not an argument with one duty but a settled indifference to the whole. Since the few are named as the exception, the account is careful not to write off a people for the conduct of most of them, and the verse leaves the reader with a pledge and a choice.

Think of a family that signs a written agreement about the care of an elderly parent and then moves to another town. The paper stays in the drawer, the parent stays where she is, and nobody in the family has denied the agreement out loud.

---

## Verse 2:84

> And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness

**THE PLEDGE ABOUT BLOOD AND HOMES**

The next verse records another article of the same covenant: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant”*** ***“that you would neither shed each other’s blood”*** ***“nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the two prohibitions as a covenant of the community against itself. The first clause is explained by al-Baghawī as the command that no one among them should spill the blood of another, with a reported reading that extends it to the blood of anyone at all. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the pair together and reads the second prohibition as the neighbour's right to remain where he lives. The intent is stated plainly by al-Ālūsī, which is that no one among them should touch another by killing or by driving him out.

The two clauses are worth noticing together because they name the two ways a community destroys itself from inside. Killing is the act of a hand, and expulsion is the act of an order, and both are put in one sentence and forbidden by one pledge. In the grammar of the pledge the prohibition is carried in the form of a statement, so that the community is described as a people bound to a course rather than merely warned against one.

**THE PLEDGE THAT WAS ACCEPTED**

The verse then reports the community's answer: ***“you gave your pledge”*** ***“and bore witness”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the acknowledgement in the sentence, with the covenant ratified by the people and witnessed against them, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same order. The wording is deliberately double, since the community agreed and then called itself to witness in the agreement. Because the sentence records the giving and the witnessing together, the reader is shown that the fault which follows is not a misunderstanding of the terms.

The conduct described in these verses is placed by al-Saʿdī among the people living at the time the revelation came down, with the two tribes of Madinah and their long quarrel. He keeps the covenant in view as the standard against which the conduct is judged. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the verse as the completion of the pledge described just before it, with the remaining articles stated in the community's own hearing. Since the acceptance is reported in the same breath as the pledge, the verse leaves no room for a defence built on ignorance of the terms.

**WHY THE OLD PLEDGE IS REPEATED**

A community that has already broken a pledge is not usually served by hearing it again, and the Book repeats it for a reason. The reason is that the reader of the passage is being shown the ground of the judgement that follows, and the ground was not a new demand but an old agreement. That is why the sentence about the acceptance is kept, and it is why the two crimes are named before the account of their commission.

The pledge also has a wider use. The Book states the value of a single life in another sūrah in a sentence addressed to this same people (5:32 — **“whoever takes a life”**). The corruption that follows a broken agreement is named as a mark of those who lost their way (2:27 — **“and spread corruption in the land”**). Because the agreement and the witness have been kept side by side, the reader meets the next verse already knowing the terms on which the community is judged, and that verse supplies the conduct.

Think of a neighbourhood that draws up a rule about not building over the shared well, and every household signs it at a public meeting. The signatures are on the page years later, and the wall is built over the well.

---

## Verse 2:85

> But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do

**THE CHARGE OF CONTRADICTION**

The report turns from the pledge to the practice: ***“But here you are, killing each other”*** ***“and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin”*** ***“and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as the charge laid against the community for the very deeds the covenant had forbidden. The setting is filled in by al-Ālūsī, with the tribes of Madinah and their alliances pulling the community into the quarrel that the pledge had closed. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the charge in the same sequence, with the killing, the expulsion and the help given to one side against the other.

The contradiction is stated next: ***“as captives, you still ransom them”*** ***“though expelling them was unlawful”*** ***“for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture”***. The sentence is kept by Ibn ʿUthaymīn as the exposure of a community that honoured one part of the Book and dropped the part that stood in its way. The transaction is explained by al-Saʿdī through the two sides of the record, since the ransoming was a duty the community kept while the killing and the expulsion were duties it ignored. al-Qurṭubī notes the grammar of the opening address, where the pronoun stands as the subject of the sentence, and he keeps the charge pointed at the people who were hearing it. The two customs are set side by side in the sentence for a reason, since the community was ready to pay for a captive and not ready to spare a neighbour. That is why the charge is not that the law was kept badly but that the parts of it which suited the community were the parts it chose to keep.

**WHAT THE BOOK SAID AND WHAT THE PEOPLE CHOSE**

The verse puts a question in the middle of the passage: ***“Do you believe in some of the Scripture”*** ***“and reject the rest?”***. The question is not about the contents of the Book but about the practice of a community that treated it as a set of options. Because the same book carried the duty to ransom the captive and the prohibition on spilling blood, the two customs could not both be honoured, and the community honoured the one that cost it least.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the verse as the record of a pledge broken by the people who made it, and it lists the injunctions the community had accepted and then abandoned. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the contradiction at the centre of the reading, since the same hand that paid the ransom had driven the captive's household out, and he notes that a religion treated this way is not being obeyed but used. Since the deeds have already been named, the question lands on conduct rather than on belief. It is asked in the second person, which leaves no room for the answer to be given about someone else.

**DISGRACE AND THE LONG PUNISHMENT**

The verse then states the price: ***“Is there any reward”*** ***“for those who do”*** ***“so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life”*** ***“and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment?”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as the verdict of the passage. The two stages are kept in the order given by al-Ālūsī, with the humiliation met in this life and the heavier account kept for the day of judgement. Because the community had chosen the standing it was protecting, the first instalment of its punishment is the loss of that standing.

The verse closes with the sentence that also closes other passages of the sūrah: ***“For Allah is never unaware of what you do”***. Since a community that honours part of a book in public and abandons the rest in the field relies on the parts of the record that are not watched, the line answers the assumption on which the whole contradiction rested. The Book states the same knowledge at the close of a later address in this sūrah (2:149), so that the reader understands the sentence was not written for one community alone. Since the practice described in the verse is the practice of treating a text as a list of options, the closing line is the right one. It removes the assumption that the two halves of a book can be separated without the One who revealed it noticing.

Think of a committee that votes to honour the rules about punctual payment and ignores the rules about safety on site. Two meetings, one rulebook, and the minutes read out at the end show both decisions in the same handwriting.

---

## Verse 2:86

> These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped

**THE TRADE AND THE PRICE**

The passage closes with the verdict on the people just described: ***“These are the ones”*** ***“who trade the Hereafter”*** ***“for the life of this world.”*** al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as the identification of the people whose conduct has been set out above. Al-Ālūsī explains the trade as the preference of the lower life over the higher, with the exchange made deliberately by people who were able to gain the better portion. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense of a purchase made with the wrong currency.

The verse is read by al-Saʿdī together with the events of the one before it, and the choice is explained by him as a calculation about reputation. The people feared the disgrace of abandoning their allies more than they feared the Fire, and they chose the Fire rather than the shame. That is why the sentence is phrased as a trade rather than as a lapse, because a trader knows what he is giving up, and the verse keeps the word in place of the deed. Ibn ʿUthaymīn notes that the same trade is repeated in later generations, where people hold the world tightly and treat the Hereafter as though it were nothing. He keeps the comparison as a warning rather than as an insult aimed at one community.

**THE PUNISHMENT THAT IS NOT LIGHTENED**

What the trade costs is then stated: ***“So their punishment will not be reduced”*** ***“nor will they be helped”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the two clauses in the order given. The first is read by al-Ālūsī as the refusal of any relief, whether by reduction or by abatement, and the second as the refusal of any party who could stand up for them. The note that the punishment remains at its full weight without a moment of relief is kept by Ibn ʿUthaymīn. He mentions the wish of the people of the Fire for a single day of respite, which the Book records in another sūrah (40:49).

The two clauses together answer the claim reported earlier in the passage, where the community expected a short stay. Because the sentence removes both the reduction and the helper, it closes the two doors through which a person imagines a lighter end, a shorter term or a friend at court. Because the trade is stated as a completed deal, the punishment is presented as the consequence of a transaction already made rather than as a penalty imposed at random.

**WHAT THE VERSE LEAVES WITH THE READER**

The sentence is worth reading with the Book's own words about the other harvest beside it. (42:20 — **“the harvest of the Hereafter”**) is named as the portion of those who seek what God has. (3:77 — **“no share in the Hereafter”**) is named as the state of those who sell their pledge for a price. The Book states both sentences as settled facts, and the reader is left with the choice that the passage has been building toward from its first question.

Because the passage has shown the conduct in detail, the reader is not asked to accept a verdict on trust. A person who trades one good for another usually believes he is gaining in the exchange, and the verse accepts the description of the trade and then states what it bought. The reason the Book keeps the two harvests side by side is that a reader who understands what was traded will understand what was lost. Because the account has shown the community's conduct in detail, the reader does not need to be told which side of the trade was heavier, and the sentence leaves the ledger where it stands. The passage ends with the people who lost both sides of the exchange, and the Book ends it without a further argument, since the conduct has been described and the reckoning has been named.

Think of a man who sells an orchard for the price of a week's meals because the week is in front of him and the trees are not. The meals are eaten, the weeks pass, and the orchard was never his again.

---

## Verse 2:87

> Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others

**A FAVOUR RECITED BEFORE A CHARGE**

The passage opens with a reminder of what the community had been given: ***“Indeed, We gave Moses the Book”*** ***“and sent after him successive messengers.”*** al-Ṭabarī reads the gift as the Torah, and al-Baghawī notes that it was given to Moses at once rather than in instalments. al-Saʿdī places the sentence among the favours granted to this people, since the messengers who came after Moses judged by the Book they had received, and the line keeps that succession in view. In Arabic the term for following in succession describes a train of messengers, one after another, as al-Qurṭubī explains, so that the reader sees a long history of guidance rather than a single event.

The reminder continues with the last of that line: ***“And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs”*** ***“and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the proofs as the signs that confirmed his mission, and al-Jalālayn names the spirit as the means of support given to him. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sequence, with the Book, the messengers and the son of Mary named in one sentence, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the order as it stands.

**THE CHARGE STATED IN THEIR OWN RECORD**

The account then turns from the gift to the response: ***“that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some”*** ***“and killing others”***. The sentence is a question, and the question carries the accusation inside it. Because the community is addressed as a people visited by messenger after messenger, the fault named is not a lack of information but a pattern of response, and the pattern is described with two verbs that cover words and hands.

The Book states the same pattern in another sūrah with the same two acts, (5:70 — **“they denied some and killed others”**), and the killing of the prophets is named among the reasons a people earned disgrace in a passage addressed to the same community (3:21). al-Ālūsī reads the opening of the verse as a fresh section in the record of their crimes, and the framing of the sentence carries an oath-like emphasis, so that the reader is drawn to what follows. Because the verse is not reporting a rumour, it sets out a settled record, and the record is read back to the people who made it.

**WHAT THE VERSE ASKS OF THE READER**

A reader who meets this verse is being taught how to receive a message he does not like. The verse does not describe a community that rejected everything, since some messengers were received and some were not. The fault is selectivity, and the criterion was the comfort of the message rather than the source of it. Because the same God sent them all, a message cannot be refused on the ground of its messenger, and the question leaves no other ground standing.

The mention of the holy spirit in the same sentence as the clear proofs is part of the argument. The signs had been given and the support had been given, and the community still reached for the messenger when the message was inconvenient. Since the account has already shown how the Book was handled by the same people, the reader understands that the violence of the last clause was the end of a road that began with the alteration of words.

The case is like a household that honours the letters it likes and throws away the ones that ask it to change. The postman is blamed for the second kind, and the letters were all sent from the same office.

---

## Verse 2:88

> They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!” In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief. They have but little faith

**THE EXCUSE THEY OFFERED**

The community answers the call with a claim about itself: ***“They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!”***. al-Ṭabarī records the disagreement among the readers over the form of the word, and he keeps the claim as the community's own description of its hearts. al-Qurṭubī explains the term as a cover laid over something, so that the sentence means that the hearts have wrappings around them. In Arabic the word for such a covering can be used of a container sealed at the mouth, as al-Jalālayn notes, and the claim therefore amounts to saying that nothing said to them can enter.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the claim as a boast rather than a complaint, with the community asserting that their hearts are able to absorb any knowledge and are simply not moved by this one. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān takes the sentence as sarcasm, since a people who claimed to be the keepers of a book were describing themselves as unable to hear it. al-Saʿdī reads the same words as a plea, with the community offering the covers on its hearts as an excuse for not answering the call.

**THE ANSWER TO THE EXCUSE**

The verse does not accept the excuse: ***“In fact, Allah has condemned them”*** ***“for their disbelief. They have”*** ***“but little faith”***. al-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as the rejection of the plea, since the condemnation is traced to the disbelief itself rather than to the covers the community had described. al-Ālūsī reads the clause as an explanation of the arrogance named in the verse before it, so that the claim about the hearts is shown as another form of the same refusal. Because the cause of the condemnation is stated as their own disbelief, the verse removes the covering from the argument and leaves the choice where it belongs.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the verdict in the same order, with the curse first and the smallness of their faith named after it. The Book states the same verdict on the same condition elsewhere in the sūrah, (2:7 — **“Allah has sealed their hearts”**), where the closing of the heart is traced to what the people did. Since the two passages describe one state, the reader is shown that the covering in this verse is not a barrier placed from outside but a condition that followed a decision.

**WHY THE EXCUSE FAILS**

An excuse is only as good as the thing it explains, and this one explains too much. If the hearts could not receive the message, then the message would never have been sent to them. Because the community had produced no act of obedience to match its claim, the verse treats the covering as a description of the refusal rather than a reason for it. That is why the answer does not argue about the hearts; the disbelief is named and the sentence moves on.

The verse also keeps the door open, since it accuses the community of little faith rather than none. The Book states the same smallness elsewhere with the same judgement, and the reader is left with a warning that a claim about one's own heart is not a defence. A person who says that his heart is closed has usually closed it himself, and the verse asks him to notice the difference.

Think of a man who locks his own door and then complains that the visitors cannot get in. The knocking continues, and the hand that turned the key belongs to the man inside.

---

## Verse 2:89

> Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it. So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers

**THE PRAYER THEY HAD MADE BEFORE**

The verse recalls what the community had done before the messenger arrived: ***“Although they used to pray”*** ***“for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists”***. al-Ṭabarī records the claim of victory as it was made, and al-Jalālayn explains that the community used to ask for help through the prophet who was expected. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same report, with the community telling the Arab tribes that a messenger was about to appear and that they would follow him. Because the request had been made in the open, it was remembered by the people who heard it, and that memory is the ground of the charge.

The messenger they had described arrived with what they had said they were waiting for: ***“when there came to them a Book from Allah”*** ***“which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the recognition and the rejection in one sentence, and al-Saʿdī explains that the Book came confirming what they already held and that they knew it as clearly as they knew their own concerns. Ibn Kathīr keeps the confirmation in the same place, with the Book confirming what had come before it. In the grammar of the sentence the Book is named without the definite article, which al-Ālūsī reads as a mark of its greatness in the eyes of the address. Because the Book is named in the same breath as the recognition, the reader is shown that the refusal happened in the presence of the evidence. The reason the condemnation is stated as a sentence of its own is that the fault was completed by the rejection rather than by the arrival of the messenger.

**RECOGNITION AND REJECTION IN ONE BREATH**

The verse puts recognition and rejection side by side, and the pairing is the point. The community did not fail to identify the Book; it identified it and then refused it. Because the same Book confirmed the Scripture they carried, the rejection was not a defence of the earlier text but a rejection of what that text had announced. The Book states the same recognition elsewhere in the sūrah, where the people who were given the Scripture are said to know it as they know their own children, (2:146 — **“recognize their own children”**), and the earlier announcement of a messenger is recorded in another sūrah (61:6 — **“giving good news of a messenger”**).

The closing sentence states the verdict: ***“So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the condemnation as the consequence of the rejection, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same order. Ibn Kathīr reads the sentence as the announcement of what the refusal had earned, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the note that the sentence applies to those who knew and rejected rather than to a people who never heard.

**WHAT THE VERSE SHOWS ABOUT WAITING**

A person can wait for a good thing for years and then refuse it on the day it arrives, and this verse is the record of that happening to a whole community. The reason the wait is mentioned at all is that it removes the excuse of surprise, since the shape of the expected messenger had been described by the community itself. Since the recognition is stated in the verse as a fact, the reader is shown that the refusal was a decision rather than an error of judgement.

The verse also teaches the reader how to read a promise. The community had asked for victory through the messenger, and when the messenger came, the victory they wanted was bound up with obedience to him. Because the two could not be separated, they chose the part they liked and refused the part that cost them. The Book leaves the sentence where it stands, and the reader is left to weigh his own version of the same bargain.

The case is like a merchant who spends years advertising a ship that will bring him goods, and who refuses to board it when it docks. The harbour records the arrival, and the ledger records the refusal.

---

## Verse 2:90

> Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath. And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment

**THE PRICE AND THE MERCHANDISE**

The verse states the value of the bargain: ***“Miserable is the price they have sold their souls”*** ***“for denying Allah’s revelation”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as a judgement on what the community took in exchange for themselves, and al-Ālūsī sets out the trade in its parts, with the souls standing as the goods and the denial as the price. al-Qurṭubī notes that the word of dispraise at the head of the sentence is built to carry blame in full, in the way its counterpart carries praise. Ibn ʿUthaymīn sets out the same construction as a verb of censure, and he keeps the point that the sentence is a verdict rather than a description.

The second half of the charge names the motive: ***“and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants!”***. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the resentment as a refusal to accept that prophethood is a gift rather than a position that can be earned, and it notes that the community objected to the choice rather than to the message. Because the grace had been given to a messenger outside their own line, the objection was about standing, and the verse states the objection in the same sentence as the price.

**WRATH UPON WRATH**

The sentence then reports what the bargain earned: ***“They have earned wrath upon wrath.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the two wraths as stacked, with the anger of God following the refusal after the anger that had followed the earlier offences, and al-Saʿdī reads the doubling as the accumulation of one offence on top of another. The Book states a similar accumulation about this community in the passage that records their earlier conduct, where wrath is named after wrath for a people who had made a habit of refusal (2:61).

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the note of accumulation in the clause, and Ibn Kathīr reads the wraths as the punishment added for the rejection of the final messenger. Because the trade has already been named, the wrath is presented as what the community bought rather than as what fell on it by chance. Since the account has shown the community receiving favour after favour, the doubling is the natural end of a road that the people walked deliberately. The reason the wrath is doubled rather than single is that the rejection added a new offence to a record that was already long. Because the community had been warned by the fate of those before it, the second wrath came with the first still standing, and the reader is shown what accumulation means in a life that keeps refusing.

**THE HUMILIATING END**

The verse closes with the fate that fits the trade: ***“And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the humiliation as the counterpart of the standing the community had been protecting, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same note in the closing word. The Book states the same pairing of disgrace and punishment in a later passage of the sūrah, where the community is told what its bargain will cost it. Because the punishment is described as humiliating rather than merely painful, the sentence returns to the motive named at the beginning, which was the standing the community was protecting.

A person who trades a lasting good for a position in front of others usually does not count the position as part of the price. This verse counts it, and the whole exchange is set out in one sentence. Because the account has shown the objection to be about standing rather than about truth, the punishment is described as humiliating, and the description fits the crime. The reader is left with a trade he can recognise, and the verse lets him see the price before he reaches the counter.

The case is like a man who sells a field to buy a title, and who discovers on the day of the purchase that the title was the only thing the field would have bought him.

---

## Verse 2:91

> When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,” and they deny what came afterwards, though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”

**THE ANSWER THAT SPLITS THE BOOK**

The verse reports the reply the community gives to the call: ***“When it is said to them”*** ***““Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the answer as the claim of the community, and al-Baghawī explains the second half as the claim that the Torah is enough for them. al-Ālūsī notes that the verb of the first clause is left in the passive, since the one who issues the call is not the point of the sentence. Because the claim is about what was sent to them, the verse shows a community measuring revelation by its address rather than by its author.

The sentence then names the other half of the practice: ***“and they deny what came afterwards”*** ***“though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures!”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the confirmation in the argument, since the Book they rejected was the one their own Scripture had announced. al-Saʿdī explains the fault as the separation of one part of what God sent down from another, since belief is owed to all of it, and the separation is what turns the claim into a denial. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same order, with the denial following the claim, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the note that the Book they refused was the truth they had been expecting.

**THE COUNTER-QUESTION**

The verse does not argue with the claim on its own ground; it asks a question instead: ***“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why”*** ***“then did you kill Allah’s prophets before”*** ***“if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”***. The question is aimed at the meaning of the claim, since a community that had killed the messengers sent to it cannot be described as a community that believes in what was sent down to it. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the question as a rebuke addressed to the claim, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same force in the sentence. Because the question turns on the community's own history, the answer is already in the record.

The Book states the same inconsistency in another sūrah, where the people who separate God from His messengers are described with a single sentence (4:150). Ibn Kathīr keeps the two halves of belief together, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the refusal of the later Book as evidence of what the claim about the earlier one was worth. Since the belief the community claimed was a belief in what suited it, the question in the verse exposes the claim as a cover for the refusal.

**WHO DECIDES WHAT TO BELIEVE**

The verse raises the question every reader has to answer, which is whether revelation is accepted as a whole or sorted according to preference. Because the community had a book it liked, it treated the later message as an interruption rather than as a continuation. The verse does not deny that the earlier Scripture came from God; it denies that a claim about it can be used to refuse what God sends next.

The closing question carries the same lesson into the reader's own life. A person who believes in the parts of a message that cost him nothing is not being asked to believe at all, and the verse shows the end of that road in the community it describes. That is why the question is left unanswered in the text, since the people addressed had no reply, and the reader is meant to notice the silence.

The case is like a man who signs a contract for one page of a document and calls himself a partner, while refusing every clause that asks him for work. The signature is real, and the partnership is not.

---

## Verse 2:92

> Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully

**THE PROOFS THEY HAD SEEN**

The verse returns to the record: ***“Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the proofs as the signs that established the truth of his mission, and al-Ālūsī keeps the same reading, with the proofs standing as the miracles that confirmed him. The signs that the Book names elsewhere are listed by al-Qurṭubī, with the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts and the parting of the sea among them. The same account is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, which notes that the signs had manifested themselves before the Book was given, so that the community had seen them with its own eyes. Because the proofs are stated as a fact in the verse, the account of what follows is an account of a people who knew better.

Ibn ʿUthaymīn sets out the construction of the opening, where the sentence is strengthened by an oath-like particle and an emphatic one, so that the reminder arrives with force. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the proofs as commands, prohibitions and signs, and al-Jalālayn names the staff, the hand and the parting of the sea among them.

**WHAT THEY MADE WHILE HE WAS AWAY**

The second half of the verse reports what the community did with the proofs they had seen: ***“then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the calf in the same position as the witnesses, with the worship following the signs rather than preceding them. al-Jalālayn explains the absence as the period of the appointment, when Moses had gone to receive what the community was waiting for, and the timing is part of the fault. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the note that the calf was taken as a god, and al-Baghawī keeps the same reading with the signs described as the clear demonstrations.

The Book reports the same scene in another sūrah, where the community is described taking the calf after the departure of its prophet (7:148). Because the proofs are named first and the calf second, the order is itself the charge. The reader is shown a people who traded what they had seen for something they had made. The closing word states the verdict: the act was wrongdoing, and the word is chosen for a deed done with knowledge rather than in ignorance.

**WHAT THE ORDER OF THE VERSE TEACHES**

A community is not usually judged by the worst thing it did on a bad day; it is judged by what it does after the evidence has arrived. This verse keeps the evidence in the sentence, and it keeps the lapse after it, so that the reader cannot separate the two. The reason the signs are recited before the fault is that the fault would otherwise be a mistake, and the verse is not describing a mistake.

The lesson reaches the reader in his own setting, where the proofs are the Book and the messenger. Because the community in the verse had seen more than most people see, its failure is not a comfort to anyone; it is a warning about what a heart can do with a clear sign. Since the account has already shown the community negotiating with a command, the reader understands that the calf was not an isolated moment but the end of a habit.

The case is like a man who is shown the road home by three separate travellers and then walks in the opposite direction because the way is uphill. The road was never hidden, and the hill was.

---

## Verse 2:93

> And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered, “We hear and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!”

**THE COVENANT AND THE MOUNTAIN**

The verse recalls the occasion of the pledge: ***“And when We took your covenant”*** ***“and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to”*** ***“that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”*** ***“and obey,” they answered, “We hear”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the covenant and the mountain in the same sentence, and al-Ālūsī explains that the command to hold firmly carries the sense of taking the Book seriously rather than of merely possessing it. In Arabic the term for taking something firmly carries that sense of seriousness, and the verse places it beside the command to listen.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the raising of the mountain as the sign that stood over the community at the moment of the pledge, and al-Jalālayn describes the same scene, with the mountain lifted as a threat for a people who had refused. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the verse as a refutation of the claim made in the account before it, and it keeps the mountain in the sentence as the fact that the community remembered. Because the pledge was taken under a sight that no one could forget, the account of the answer that follows cannot be treated as an oversight. The reason the mountain is mentioned in the sentence is that the pledge was not a private conversation between a prophet and his people.

**THE ANSWER THE VERSE RECORDS**

The sentence then reports what the community said, and the report is split across the verse: ***“and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the answer as it stands, with hearing named and obedience refused in the same breath, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same order. The verse does not soften the report, since the community is shown answering a command in front of a raised mountain with a refusal. Because the two words are placed side by side, the reader sees a people who knew what was being asked and declined it.

The verse then gives the reason for the refusal: ***“because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do”*** ***“if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the disbelief as the source of the answer, and al-Qurṭubī notes the same connection between the love of the calf and the refusal of the command. The Book reports the calf again in another passage, where the community is described taking it in the absence of its prophet (2:92), and the two verses are read together as one account.

**WHAT THE VERSE SAYS ABOUT A SPLIT HEART**

The love of the calf and the answer to the pledge are reported in one verse because they belong to one heart. A person cannot keep an idol in his affections and obey the command that forbids it, and the verse shows the two positions meeting in a single sentence. Because the love is described as rooted, the fault is not a mood but a settled attachment, and the verse treats it as such.

The closing question asks what the belief of such a community amounts to. The verse does not deny that a book was in their hands; it denies that the book had reached their hearts, and the calf in the middle of the sentence is the evidence. Since the command had asked for obedience and not merely for agreement, the answer recorded in the verse is the honest one, and the reader is left to ask what his own answer would be under the same mountain.

The case is like a man who signs a deed of loyalty while keeping a rival's portrait in his pocket, and who says that he heard the terms. The hearing is on the record, and the portrait is in the pocket.

---

## Verse 2:94

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!”

**THE CLAIM PUT TO THE TEST**

The verse takes the community's claim and offers to test it: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively”*** ***“for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity”***. al-Ṭabarī records the claim as the community had made it, and al-Saʿdī explains the home as the Garden, with the claim being that no one enters it except their own people. The sentence is read by al-Ālūsī as the refutation of one more claim after the refutation of the claim about belief, and he keeps the order of the passage in view. Because the claim was about a privilege that had been reserved, the verse meets it with a test that only the claimant can perform.

The claim is set by al-Qurṭubī beside the others the sūrah has reported, with the claim about the Fire standing in the same list, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same connection. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the exclusivity of the claim in the verse, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, with the Garden named as the home in question. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the challenge was public, and that a claim of this kind cannot be left standing once it is put to the test.

**THE WISH THAT WOULD PROVE IT**

The verse then states the test: ***“then wish for death”*** ***“if what you say is true!”***. The request is not a request for suicide; it is the invitation to desire the meeting that the claim presumes, since a person who is certain of an exclusive Garden should welcome the door. al-Ṭabarī keeps the wish as the proof of the claim, and al-Saʿdī explains the same point, with the certainty of the claim and the desire for the reward belonging together. The Book states the same test in another sūrah, where the challenge is issued in the same form (62:6).

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the wish in the verse as the community's own statement, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the note that the wish would cost nothing if the claim were sound. Because the community had spoken about the Hereafter with confidence, the verse asks it to put the confidence into a single sentence, and the request is the measure of the claim. That is why the words are put in the mouth of the messenger: the test is issued in public, and the whole passage is watching for the answer.

**WHY NO ONE ANSWERED**

The next verse reports the silence, and this one explains why it was expected. A person who wishes for death in public has decided that what waits for him is better than what he holds, and the community was not ready to say that. The reason the challenge is fair is that the claim itself had made the comparison, since a privilege reserved for a people implies a hope those people should be glad to reach. Since the claim was made in the hearing of others, the test was made in the same hearing, and the silence that followed belongs to the record.

The verse also teaches the reader what certainty looks like. A claim about the unseen is easy to make and hard to hold, and the Book shows the difference by asking for a sentence rather than for an argument. Because the reader has followed the claims through the passage, he can hear the emptiness of this one without being told, and the verse leaves the challenge where it put it.

The case is like a man who tells a whole street that he has a house waiting for him across the river, and who is then offered the ferry at no cost. The boat leaves, and the man watches it from the bank.

---

## Verse 2:95

> But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers

**THE WISH THEY WILL NOT MAKE**

The answer to the challenge is stated as a fact: ***“But they will never wish”*** ***“for that because of what their hands have done.”*** al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as the report of what the community will not do, and al-Baghawī explains the reason the same way, since the people know that their claim is false and that the wish would only bring the reckoning forward. al-Ālūsī keeps the clause as a fresh sentence, separate from the command to wish, so that the statement describes the community rather than instructing it. Because the reason is given in the same sentence, the reader is told that the silence came from knowledge rather than from weakness.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the deeds in the clause as what the hands have sent ahead, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense, with the consequences of their rejection named as the thing that holds them back. In the language of the Book the phrase for what the hands have sent ahead means the deeds that travel in front of a person to meet him. The phrase is used here for a record the community already knows. Since the account has shown the community's conduct in detail, the reader can supply the deeds that the sentence leaves unnamed.

**WHAT THE SILENCE REVEALS**

A refusal to make a wish is not a refusal of the reward; it is a decision about the journey. The community in the verse believed in a garden for itself, and it did not want to be told to go there yet. That is why the verse does not describe the community as doubters; it describes them as people who had read their own record. Because the deeds were known to them, the silence in the next breath is the confession the verse puts on the record.

The Book states the same test and the same failure in another sūrah, where the wish is refused with one sentence. The community's answer did not change with the setting. al-Ālūsī keeps the sentence as the announcement of what the community will do rather than as a prediction about individuals, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that no report of a single person accepting the challenge ever reached the community's own traditions. The silence was remembered as silence.

**THE KNOWLEDGE THAT CLOSES THE VERSE**

A short sentence then gives the silence its meaning: ***“And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the reason the report is exact, since the One who made it sees the hearts behind the refusal. al-Jalālayn keeps the closing word as a description of the people whose deeds have been named. Because the knowledge is stated at the end of an account of hidden motives, the reader is shown that the silence of the community was not private.

The sentence also answers a question the reader might carry, which is how the Book can speak with such certainty about a wish no one made. Since the Speaker knows the wrongdoers, the report is not a guess about behaviour but a statement about what is in the people. That is why the verse ends where it ends: the account of the claim, the test and the silence is closed by the One who knew the answer beforehand, and the reader is left with a mirror rather than a courtroom.

The case is like a man who is offered a journey home tonight and who suddenly remembers the state of his house. The offer is withdrawn, and the man is left with the reason he gave himself.

---

## Verse 2:96

> You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years. But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do

**THE GREED REPORTED AS A FACT**

The verse states what an observer will find: ***“You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the comparison as it stands, with the community described as more attached to life than the idolaters who had no expectation of a reckoning. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same comparison and notes that the community's love of the world had become its defining mark. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the clause as the description of the Jews addressed in the passage, and al-Jalālayn notes that the sentence opens with the force of an oath.

The phrase about a thousand years is the measure of the craving: longer than anyone can live, and longer than anyone can use. al-Saʿdī reads the wish as the utmost greed, since the community wished for something impossible. He keeps the note that even the wish was a sign of what they feared. Because the sentence states the wish as a fact about each one of them, the reader is shown a people whose hope had been transferred from the Hereafter to the counting of years.

**THE WISH AND ITS LIMIT**

The verse then removes the value of the wish: ***“But even if they were to live”*** ***“that long, it would not save them from the punishment.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the answer to the wish, and al-Ālūsī explains that the long life would change nothing in what waits for the community. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the same point and notes that a later generation repeats the same trade, with people gripping the world and treating the Hereafter as nothing. Because the wish is answered in the same verse, the reader is not left to wonder whether the years would have helped.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the wish as the evidence of the community's own knowledge, since a person who clings to this life so tightly has said something about what he expects afterwards. al-Saʿdī keeps the same reading, with the desire for a long life shown as the counterpart of a bad account. Since the claim about an exclusive Garden had already been tested in the verse before, the craving for years in this world is the second half of the same silence.

**THE SIGHT THAT SEES THEM**

The verse closes with the sentence that answers every hidden motive: ***“And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the closing verdict of the passage, and Ibn Kathīr reads it as the warning that the deeds behind the clinging are all observed. al-Jalālayn keeps the same note in the closing word, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sentence as a statement about the community's deeds. Because an inner wish has been described, the closing sentence is needed, since the wish itself is part of what is seen.

The passage ends here with the community's deepest attachment named and its hope of length removed. The Book does not end the account with a further argument, because the conduct has been described and the sight of God has been stated. A reader who has followed the passage from the covenant to the calf and from the claim about the Garden to the wish for a thousand years is left with a single question, which is where his own hope is placed. The reason the Book reports a wish rather than an argument is that a person's hope is a truer measure of his belief than anything he says about it.

The case is like a tenant who begs for a longer lease on a house he has already been told is condemned. The years are granted or refused, and the house comes down either way.

---

## Verse 2:97

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.”

**THE EXCUSE THE VERSE ANSWERS**

The passage answers an excuse the community had produced: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know”***. al-Ṭabarī records the agreement of the commentators that the verse was given in answer to a people who claimed that the angel of revelation was their enemy and that another angel was their friend, and he collects the reports about the occasion. The questioner is named in the report of Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Baghawī opens his commentary with the same account, in which the community asked which angel came down from heaven and then declared the answer to be the angel they counted an enemy. The excuse is set out in full by al-Qurṭubī: they said that no prophet had ever come without an angel from his Lord, so who is your companion? and when they heard the name they objected that he was the angel of war and fighting, while the other, who descends with rain and mercy, would have won their following. Because the objection was aimed at the carrier of the message, the verse answers it by describing what the carrier was sent to do.

Another report shows the same division in a different setting, and it is kept by al-Ālūsī, where the community described Gabriel as the angel of every punishment and Michael as the angel of plenty and peace. The claim is called by al-Saʿdī a contradiction and an arrogance before God, since the same angel had carried the revelation to the prophets before him and had done so by the command of the One who sent him. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the scene as one in a series, since the community kept producing fresh excuses as each of the earlier ones was answered. The reason the verse does not dispute the preference they announced is that a preference among servants of God is not a question about the message, and the answer moves past it to the message itself.

**THE WORK OF THE ANGEL AND THE HEART**

The sentence then states what the angel brought: ***“that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it”***. The revelation is kept by al-Ṭabarī as the act of God carried by the angel, and al-Jalālayn keeps the bringing down of the Qur'an upon the heart as the work of the angel named in the verse. Ibn Kathīr keeps the confirmation in the same clause and identifies what was confirmed as the Torah and the Gospel, so the new Book is shown standing on the same ground as the earlier ones. Because the Book is placed in the heart rather than only delivered to the ear, the reader is shown that the message was meant to settle where knowledge is held and decisions are made.

The mention of the will of God is the point that removes the excuse entirely. Since the sending belongs to God and the angel only carries it, an enemy of the carrier has set himself against the sender, and the sentence leaves the reader with that conclusion rather than with an argument about angels. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading of the passage, and al-Baghawī carries the report about the occasion beside the text of the verse. The Book states the same arrival and the same content in the verse that follows, where the angels are named again as a group (2:98), and the two verses are read together as a single answer.

**TWO NAMES FOR THE BOOK**

The description closes with two names for what the Book is: ***“a guide and good news”*** ***“for the believers.”*** al-Jalālayn spells the pair out as guidance away from error and good tidings of Paradise, and al-Ṭabarī keeps them as the description of what was sent down. Because a guide leads and good news steadies, the two words describe the work the Book does in a person rather than the reputation of the one who carried it, and the sentence puts that work in front of the reader.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the verse in the flow of the excuses and notes that each answer left the community with less room to object. al-Saʿdī keeps the words of the description as the summary of the Book's benefit, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading. Since the answer names the fruit of the Book instead of the identity of the carrier, the objection is shown to have been beside the point from the beginning, and the reader is invited to judge the Book by what it does.

**WHERE THE ARGUMENT LEAVES THE READER**

A person who refuses a message because of who carried it settles the message in his own mind before reading it, and this verse shows that decision for what it is. Because the content is described as a guide and good news, the reader is asked to weigh the Book by its effect, and the question of the carrier is left where it belongs.

The lesson reaches past the community in the passage. A reader who meets the Book through a teacher he dislikes, or through a community he distrusts, stands in the position of the people addressed here, and the verse leaves him with the same two words. The Book is either a guide and good news or it is not, and the answer to that question does not change with the postman.

The case is like a man who refuses a letter of pardon because he dislikes the man who brings it. The pardon is genuine, the door is open, and the carrier has gone home.

---

## Verse 2:98

> Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers

**THE LIST AND THE CONDITION**

The verse sets out the list that the excuse had tried to divide: ***“Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel”*** ***“and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the angels inside the same sentence as God and the messengers, and he reads the verse as the announcement that enmity toward the servant is enmity toward the One who sent him. al-Qurṭubī explains the construction as a condition with its answer, so that the hostility a person declares returns to him as a verdict, and he notes that the enmity of the part is followed by the enmity of God toward the whole person. Because the answer is stated as a consequence rather than as a threat, the reader is shown the road a declaration of this kind takes.

The two names at the end of the row carry a second meaning. al-Jalālayn notes that the specific names are joined to the collective word for the angels, so the two are shown to belong to the same body as the rest, and he adds that the closing word names the disbelievers rather than referring to them alone, which points at their standing rather than at their number. al-Ālūsī explains that enmity in the language belongs properly to created beings and that the hostility attributed to God is a figure for the opposition a person has placed between himself and his Lord. Because the list ends with God at the head of it, the excuse is dismantled at its root, since a quarrel with one servant has become a quarrel with the One who sent all of them.

**WHY THE ANGELS ARE NAMED**

The community in the passage had drawn a line between one angel and another, and the verse removes the line by naming both. al-Saʿdī keeps the two verses together, with the answer to the excuse resting on the plain fact that the angel carried out a command that was never his own, so that a preference among angels changes nothing about the message. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the list as it stands and reads the verse as the completion of the answer given to the excuse. The Book names the same principle in another passage, where belief in God is joined to belief in His angels and His books (2:177), and the two verses belong to one argument.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the names in the order the verse gives them, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the statement of what follows for the person who declares such a hostility. Because the sentence ends with the disbelievers rather than with the angels, the reader is shown where the fault lies, and the naming of the two angels in the middle of the list turns out to be the dismantling of the excuse rather than a digression from it.

**THE SHAPE OF THE VERDICT**

A sentence built as "whoever does this, then this follows" is not the same as a threat, and this verse is built as a statement of fact. The community had declared one angel to be an enemy; the verse tells them what such a declaration has made them. Since the sentence is put in the third person, the reader is not cornered but shown the road, and he is left to walk it or to leave it.

The lesson also covers the way a person treats the servants of God in general. Enmity that begins with one carrier of a message rarely stays there, and the verse sets the whole list out at once so that the reader can see where such a road leads. Because the answer is stated as a consequence, the verse leaves the disbelievers to their own choice and leaves the reader with the list still in front of him.

The case is like a man who quarrels with the deliverer of a summons and then discovers that the summons came from the court. The quarrel was real, and the court was never the postman.

---

## Verse 2:99

> Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious

**VERSES DESCRIBED AS CLEAR**

The verse answers a claim that had been made about the signs: ***“Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as the statement of what had been sent down, with the clarity of the verses standing as their own description, and he points to what the Book lays open of the hidden reports and the concealed matters of the earlier community. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the clear signs as the manifest tokens that set out commands and prohibitions, and al-Jalālayn keeps that sense while recording the remark that occasioned the verse. The occasion is preserved by al-Qurṭubī, who reports the claim that no clear sign had been given, and al-Ālūsī keeps the same setting and treats the verse as a story joined to the story before it.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the halves of the sentence together, with the clarity of the verses stated first and the denial named after it, so the refusal is left without an excuse. al-Saʿdī explains the purpose of clear verses as twofold, since they guide the one who seeks guidance and they establish the proof against the one who resists. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes the claim of the community that nothing recognisable had been brought to them, and the verse is read there as the removal of that claim. Because the verses are described as clear, the reader is shown that the denial is a decision about the truth rather than a failure to find it.

**THE ONE WHO DENIES**

The second half of the sentence narrows the field, and the denial is traced to a particular kind of person. In the wording of the sentence the denial is restricted to the rebellious, so that the fault is named as a departure from the boundary rather than as an intellectual conclusion. al-Saʿdī keeps that reading, with the denial presented as the act of a person who has already left the path, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same restriction in his report of the verse. Because the one who denies is described by his conduct rather than by his learning, the reader is shown that the evidence was never the obstacle.

The Book describes the same resistance in another passage, where a demand for a sign is answered as a question rather than as a proof (2:118). al-Ṭabarī keeps the clarity of the signs as the description of the message itself, and al-Baghawī keeps the same reading of the sentence. Since the clarity of the verses is stated as a fact, the reader is not invited to debate whether the sign is enough, and the verse turns the question toward the person who is doing the denying.

**WHAT CLEAR VERSES ASK OF A READER**

A clear sign does not remove the possibility of refusal; it removes the possibility of an honest excuse. The verse states the sign and then states the refusal, and it leaves the reader with the choice that stands between the two. Because the clarity of the sign is stated beside the condition of the denier, the verse teaches that the decisive question is not whether the evidence is enough but what a person has decided to do with it. Because the Book describes itself here as clear, the reader is expected to test the claim by reading rather than by waiting for a further proof.

The verse also closes the door to a particular kind of conversation, which is the search for a sign that will settle the matter without requiring anything of the searcher. The signs had been sent, and the denial is traced to a condition rather than to a shortage of evidence. Since the reader has followed the passage from the claims about the Book to the excuses about its carrier, he is shown that the argument was never about information.

The case is like a traveller who asks for a road sign at every junction and then says that no sign was ever posted. The signs stand at every turn, and the traveller is on the wrong road.

---

## Verse 2:100

> Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe

**THE PATTERN IN THE PLEDGES**

The verse states a pattern as a question: ***“Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside?”***. al-Qurṭubī sets out the construction of the opening, where a joining particle carries the question, and he keeps the sentence as a rebuke aimed at the community. The same opening is explained in the same way by al-Baghawī, who keeps the report of the man who denied that any pledge had been taken from them at all. al-Jalālayn keeps the sense of the question as an expression of astonishment rather than a request for information. Because the sentence is a question, the reader is drawn into the record before he is told what to think of it.

al-Saʿdī reads the pattern as the wonder of a people who made covenant after covenant and kept almost none of them, and he notes that the phrase for every time carries the sense of repetition, so that the failure is shown as a habit rather than as an accident. The covenant is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the pledges taken from the community and the group as the leaders who set them aside, and he records the reminder that had been given to them from their own Scripture. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the Torah itself reports the pledge, and the verse is read there as the exposure of a denial that the community's own book contradicts. Since the reminder came from the book they carried, the denial in the verse is shown to be a refusal rather than a doubt.

**THE GROUP AND THE MAJORITY**

The verse then closes with a sentence that answers the question it asked: ***“In fact, most of them do not believe”***. al-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as the reason the pattern repeats, and he notes that the breaking of the pledges followed from the state of belief rather than from a shortage of warnings. al-Ālūsī collects the reports about the pledges and about the man who denied them, and he keeps the question in its place at the head of the passage. The group that casts the covenant aside is not described as a small faction acting against the wishes of the whole, since the majority is named as sharing the condition, and the reader is shown the root of the habit rather than only its fruit.

The Book records the same pattern about the same people earlier in the sūrah, where the taking of the covenant and the turning away from it are reported together (2:83). al-Jalālayn keeps the closing words as a statement of the general case, and al-Baghawī keeps the earlier reference to the pledges in view. Because the account has already shown what the community did with the earlier agreements, the reader meets this verse with the evidence already in hand.

**WHAT A REPEATED COVENANT SAYS**

A person who makes the same promise many times is usually telling himself that the promise is new. The verse shows the pattern from the outside, where the repetition is the record of a habit rather than of a fresh beginning. Because the sentence asks why rather than whether, the reader is not invited to dispute the facts, and he is shown the instability that the facts reveal.

The verse also keeps the reader from a comfortable conclusion. The reason the failure is traced to belief is that a promise is only as firm as the ground beneath it, and the ground in this community had been worn away. Since the passage has shown the same people handling the Book and making excuses about angels, the reader is not surprised by the habit, and the question in the verse lands on his own agreements as much as on theirs.

The case is like a tenant who signs a new lease every spring and moves out every winter. The landlord keeps the file, and the file has become a record of patterns rather than of promises.

---

## Verse 2:101

> Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know

**THE CONFIRMATION AND THE RESPONSE**
