The verse records what happened when the expectation was met: ***“Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them”*** ***“confirming their own Scriptures”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the confirmation in the sentence as the description of what the messenger brought, and he names the addressees as the rabbis and scholars of the earlier community. al-Qurṭubī notes the same construction, with the description attached to the messenger, and he reports the view that what was thrown aside was the Scripture the community already held. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the confirmation as the agreement of the new message with the traits and the description that the earlier Scripture carried, so that recognition was available before the content was weighed. Because the arrival is described as the fulfilment of what the community carried, the reader is shown that the moment was an answer rather than a surprise.

al-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as the account of a messenger arriving with a great Book that agreed with what the community held, and he notes that the community had been claiming to hold fast to its own Scripture. al-Jalālayn keeps the same order, with the messenger named and the confirmation stated, and al-Baghawī records the report that they used to read their Scripture without acting on it and even adorned it while leaving its commands. Since the confirmation came from the book they had, the refusal is shown to have been aimed at two books at once.

**THE BOOK BEHIND THE BACK**

The sentence then reports the response: ***“some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs”*** ***“as if they did not know”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the throwing as the description of the community's treatment of what was sent, and al-Ālūsī reads the clause as a continuation of the rebuke that runs through the passage. The image is explained by al-Saʿdī as a discarding done out of aversion, which is a stronger form of turning away than a simple refusal to look. Because the clause names the Book of God as the thing thrown, the reader is shown that the community was not discarding a stranger's letter but its own inheritance.

The closing clause states the pretence, and the community behaved as though it had never known what it knew. al-Jalālayn keeps the sense that they did not act on what their Scripture said about the messenger, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the verse as the sequel to the habit of breaking pledges and places the scene in the same list of conduct. The same act is recorded in the passage that reports the covenant to make the Scripture known, where the people are said to have thrown it behind their backs (3:187). Because the pretence is named in the sentence, the reader is shown that the ignorance was performed for an audience, and the audience was itself.

**WHAT THE VERSE SAYS ABOUT KNOWLEDGE**

A person who knows something and pretends not to has decided that the knowledge is an inconvenience, and the verse puts that decision on the record. The community in the passage had the confirmation in its own hands and threw it away, and the sentence describes the act with a single picture. Since the Book had come confirming what they carried, what they refused was their own ground as much as the new arrival.

The verse also shows the difference between ignorance and refusal. The people who threw the Book behind them are not described as uninformed, and the clause about them reads as a measure of what the pretence cost. Because the pretence is stated in the verse, the reader understands that the community's later claims of an honest dispute have already been answered, and the record of the act stands in the middle of the account.

The case is like a student who is handed the examination paper with his own notes attached to it and who then covers the page. The notes are his, the paper is open, and the covering is the only part of the scene that was added.

---

## Verse 2:102

> They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew

**THE MAGIC AND THE NAME OF SOLOMON**

The verse states what the community took up in place of the Book: ***“They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût”***. al-Ṭabarī records the claim that the community had built around Solomon, with the accusation of sorcery answered in the same sentence, and he keeps the reports about the group who exchanged the Book for what the devils recited in the king's reign. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same account, with the community leaving the guidance of the prophets and acting on what the devils had written, and al-Jalālayn describes the books that were buried and then brought out after the king's death, when people took them up and left the Scriptures of their prophets.

The sentence clears the king in the middle of the accusation, and al-Ālūsī reads that acquittal as the point of the clause, since magic was being told in Solomon's name during his own reign. al-Saʿdī keeps the sentence in the line of the passage, where the community's exchange of the Book for a worthless craft stands beside their earlier refusals. Because the sentence lays the disbelief on the devils, the reader is shown where the choice lay, and the name of the king is cleared in the same breath that reports the crime.

**THE TWO NAMES AND WHAT THEY WERE SENT FOR**

The sentence then reaches the pair named in the middle of the story: ***“and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺”*** ***“so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.””***. The warning is kept by al-Ṭabarī as part of the report, with the pair appearing as a trial placed before people rather than as a source of the craft, and he records the early view that God never sent magic down upon them at all. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the sending as a mercy, since the two were sent to inform people of the true nature of magic and its forms so that they could tell it apart from the miracles of the prophets. Because the warning is preserved inside the verse, no one can claim that the teaching arrived without a caution, and the two angels are cleared in the same passage that names them.

The names themselves are explained by al-Baghawī as Syriac in origin and as carrying a foreign form that was left unaltered in the Arabic sentence, and he records the reading that turned the pair into two kings rather than two angels. al-Ālūsī collects the other reports, including the view that the two were men of Babylon, and he locates the city in the region known to the earliest commentators. al-Qurṭubī gives the parsing that makes the two names a substitute for the devils named in the previous clause, and he calls that reading the soundest of the views. Since the verse is read as an acquittal of both the king and the angels, the trial is shown to have been placed before people who were free to refuse it.

**THE RIFT, THE HARM, AND THE WILL OF GOD**

The account then describes the use people made of what they had learned: ***“Yet people learned ˹magic˺”*** ***“that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband”*** ***“and wife;”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the separation of a husband from his wife as the purpose for which the craft was used, and al-Ālūsī keeps the same description in the passage. The image is deliberate, since the craft is shown attacking the closest bond a household has, and the reader is shown the kind of work the community had taken up in the place of a Book.

The sentence then limits the craft's power: ***“although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them”*** ***“and did not benefit them”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the limit inside the report, so that the harm is traced back to the will of God and the craft is left without authority of its own. al-Jalālayn keeps the same note, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the harm and the lack of benefit together in one clause. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the doctrinal point out of the sentence, which is that causes do not produce their effects by themselves and that the One who made the cause is the One who makes the effect. Because the verse joins the harm to the will of God, the reader is shown that the trade was a loss before it was ever a sin.

**WHAT THEY KNEW AND WHAT THEY SOLD**

The verse then states what the people knew: ***“although they already knew”*** ***“that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable”*** ***“indeed was the price”*** ***“for which they sold their souls”*** ***“if only they knew”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the knowledge in the sentence, with the community aware of the price before it paid it, and Ibn Kathīr records the report that they knew the truth and then abandoned it and hid it, which is how the earlier clause about them is read as a pretence. al-Qurṭubī collects the reports about the sale and keeps the sentence as the closing verdict of the passage. Because the knowledge stands before the sale, the transaction is shown as deliberate rather than as an error of judgement.

The closing words weigh the price rather than the craft, and the account ends where the fault began, which is the value people placed on their own souls. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gathers the rulings that follow from the passage and keeps the prohibition of the craft in the foreground, so that the reward named in the next verse stands as the opposite of what the community bought. The same loss is stated elsewhere in the Book for those who trade revelation for a small gain (2:174), and the two sentences are read together.

**WHY THE ACCOUNT IS KEPT IN THE BOOK**

A story of this kind is kept in the Book so that a community can recognise the shape of a bad bargain long before it makes one. The verse shows people who knew the cost, chose the craft, and lost the Hereafter in exchange for a harm they could not even control. Because the account ends with the price rather than with the magic, the reader is turned from the wonder of the story toward the question of what he himself would sell his own share for.

The passage also closes the door to two opposite mistakes. One is to blame the angels for what people chose, and the verse clears them in the same sentence that names the trial. The other is to treat the craft as harmless, and the sentence states the rift it makes between a husband and his wife. Since both corrections are carried by the same sentence, the reader is left with the balance the Book intended, which is that the trial was real, the warning was given, and the choice belonged to the people who heard it.

The case is like a man who sells his share of a household to buy a key that breaks the doors of the same household. The key works, the doors are broken, and the share is gone.

---

## Verse 2:103

> If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew

**THE CONDITION THAT WAS NOT MET**

The verse states what would have been: ***“If only they were faithful”*** ***“and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement of what the community would have received, and he identifies the people in view as those who were learning the craft from the two angels. The mindfulness named in the sentence is directed by al-Qurṭubī at the craft the previous verse described, so that the condition is a turning away from what they had taken up. The faith in the sentence is read by Ibn ʿAbbās as belief in the messenger and the Book, and he adds the turning away from sorcery that the community had chosen instead. Because the condition is placed after the account of the craft, the reader is shown the road the community did not take.

The same reading is kept by al-Jalālayn, with the condition stated in its two parts and the answer supplied by the words that follow it, and al-Ālūsī explains that the construction was changed from a plain verb into a noun so that the reward is shown as something fixed rather than as something that might pass. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān treats the two verses together and keeps the lesson on the use of magic in the foreground, so that the reward named here stands as the opposite of the price paid there. Since the passage has shown the trade the community made, the better offer is left to the reader to weigh.

**THE REWARD THAT WOULD HAVE BEEN**

The sentence states the reward as a fact about a road not taken, and the wording carries the sense of something returned. The term for the reward carries the sense of a return, as al-Qurṭubī notes, so the sentence describes a repayment rather than a prize handed out at random. Because the return is described as better, the comparison is left to the reader, who has just seen what the craft paid to the people who bought it.

The closing phrase, ***“if only they knew”***, returns to knowledge, since the community knew what the craft would cost and did not weigh the value of what it refused. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps that reading of the clause, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense of a knowledge that would have changed the choice. The Book joins faith and good work to a reward from the Lord in another passage (2:277), and the two sentences are read together as one offer made at different moments. Because the sentence is put as a wish rather than as a command, the reader is left with the regret that the community would not feel, and the verse asks him to feel it instead.

**WHAT THE VERSE ASKS ABOUT REWARD**

A person who compares a craft with a reward is already weighing the two, and the verse assumes that the reader has seen the comparison. Because the loss in the previous verse was described as a sale, the gain that was available is described in the same terms, and the two sentences stand on either side of one choice. That is why the verse is short; it does not need to argue with a case that the passage has already made.

The verse also keeps the reader from measuring the reward by what he can see in this world. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the reward as the thing that would have followed, and The sentence is kept by al-Ālūsī as the answer to a condition that was never met. Since the reward is left unnamed and the loss was spelled out, the reader is shown where the Book places its weight, and the closing word about knowledge leaves him with the question of what he himself knows.

The case is like a farmer who sells a standing crop for a handful of coins and then complains about the price of bread. The coins were counted, the crop was not, and the market did the rest.

---

## Verse 2:104

> O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment

**THE WORD THE BELIEVERS WERE ASKED TO LEAVE**

The verse turns to the believers with an instruction about speech: ***“O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!]”*** ***“But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!]”***. al-Ṭabarī records the disagreement among the readers over how the first word was understood and the reports that some took it as an instruction to avoid any word of disagreement at all, and al-Qurṭubī sets out the same material in order. al-Saʿdī explains that the believers used the first expression intending a sound meaning, and that the other community seized on it as an opening for an insult, which is why the believers were given another word that could not be turned. Because the instruction is about a manner of address, the verse shows how careful the Book is about the words a community uses.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the pair of expressions as they are given, with the first forbidden and the second prescribed, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the note that the verse was addressed to the believers about the vocabulary the other community had used. The first expression is explained by al-Ālūsī as belonging to a family of words for watching over another's interest, and al-Baghawī records the sense of lending an ear along with what the expression signified in the other community's language. Since the change is from one word to another with a similar sense, the reader is shown that the Book was closing a door rather than forbidding a question.

**WHY SPEECH IS REGULATED**

A word can be sound in itself and still become a handle for mockery, and the verse closes the handle without conceding the meaning. The reason the instruction is given to the believers rather than to the mockers is that the believers are the ones who can act on it, and the Book does not leave their speech in the hands of their opponents. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the scene as one of the mischiefs the other community invented, and it keeps the instruction as the answer to it.

The sentence then adds a command that governs the whole exchange: ***“and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the listening as the duty that accompanies the change of words, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair, with the first expression traced to a form of request and the second given as its replacement. Because the command to listen comes after the command about speech, the reader is shown that the issue was never the sound of a word but the attention behind it.

**THE WARNING AT THE END**

The verse closes with the punishment of those who refused, and the warning is placed after an instruction to the believers for a reason. Because the mockery had been aimed at the messenger, the sentence names the consequence of that mockery rather than the consequence of the believers' mistake. al-Baghawī keeps the note that the warning is aimed at the disbelievers rather than at the community being addressed, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading. Since the instruction had been given to the believers, the reader is shown that the danger in the verse belongs to a different group.

The Book makes the manner of speech with the messenger part of a duty in another passage, where the believers are forbidden to raise their voices above his (49:2). al-Saʿdī keeps the ruling that a permitted thing may be left when it turns into a road to something forbidden, which is the principle the instruction rests on. Because the verse regulates words without forbidding questions, the reader is shown that a community may ask and still be careful, and the command to listen is given so that the care does not become fear.

The case is like a household that stops using a nickname because a neighbour has turned it into an insult. The nickname was harmless, the neighbour was not, and the household chose a better word.

---

## Verse 2:105

> The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty

**THE WISH AGAINST THE BLESSING**

The verse states the position of the two groups: ***“The disbelievers from the People of the Book”*** ***“and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the wish as the refusal of the good that had come to the believers, and he notes that the two groups are joined in one sentence so that the wish is shared. The same sense is kept by al-Qurṭubī, who reads the verb as a wish rather than an action, and he notes that the clause about the polytheists follows the same construction as the first. Ibn ʿAbbās names a leading figure of the community and his companions among those addressed, and al-Jalālayn keeps the two groups in the same sentence with the second joined to the first as a specification. Because the two groups are joined in one wish, the reader is shown that the opposition was not a dispute about doctrine.

al-Ālūsī explains the verb as the love of a thing together with the wish for it to happen, so that the sentence describes an inner refusal rather than an attack, and he notes that the negation of such a wish is a figure for hatred. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the verse as the record of how the two communities regarded the believers, and it places the sentence in the flow of the passage. Because the wish is stated rather than the deed, the reader is shown how far the objection had gone, since even the good that reached the believers was resented.

**THE SELECTION AND THE BOUNTY**

The verse then states the ground of the blessing: ***“but Allah selects whoever He wills”*** ***“for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the selection as the act of God, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, with the choice resting on the will of the One who gives. al-Jalālayn adds that the selection is for the office of prophethood in particular, so that the sentence names the favour that the two groups most resented. Because the blessing is traced to a choice rather than to a claim, the reader is shown that the objection of the two groups was aimed at the Giver.

The bounty is kept by al-Qurṭubī as the description of God rather than of the recipients, and the sentence ends with the attribute that answers the wish. The Book states the same selection in the passage that answered the objection about the messenger, where the community resented the grace granted to whom God willed (2:90), and the two verses are read together as one answer to the same resentment. Because the closing words describe the Lord rather than the believers, the reader is left with the source of the good rather than with the quarrel about it.

**WHAT THE WISH REVEALS**

A person who resents the good that reaches someone else has admitted that the good is real, and the sentence builds its argument on that admission. The two groups in the sentence did not deny the blessing; they refused to see it reach the believers, and the Book states the refusal as the mark of their position. Because the sentence puts both communities in one line, the reader is shown that the fault is a state of the heart rather than a school of thought.

The verse also teaches the reader where to look when a blessing arrives with opposition attached. Since the bounty belongs to God, the blessing is not diminished by the resentment it produces, and the sentence leaves the reader with the attribute rather than with the argument. The passage has shown the same opposition in several forms, and the verse gathers them into a single wish and a single answer.

The case is like neighbours who refuse to look at a garden because it belongs to a household they dislike. The garden grows anyway, and the season does not consult the street.

---

## Verse 2:106

> If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE CLAIM ABOUT ABROGATION**

The verse answers an objection that had been raised about the Book: ***“If We ever abrogate a verse”*** ***“or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better”*** ***“or similar one. Do you not know”***. al-Ṭabarī explains the abrogation as the transfer of a ruling from one verse to another, and he keeps the sentence as the statement of God's freedom in what He sends, with the change confined to commands and prohibitions rather than to reports. al-Baghawī records the taunt that the community raised, in which they claimed that the messenger was speaking from himself and changing his own instructions. al-Qurṭubī collects the questions raised about the verse, including the readings of its words, and he keeps the sentence as the answer to those who denied the possibility. Because the sentence is put as a condition, the reader is shown that the practice is stated as a fact about revelation rather than as a change of mind.

The objection is preserved by al-Ālūsī, who reports the claim that the Book contradicted itself and that its words were the words of a man, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same setting in which the mockery began. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the pair of acts in the verse, with the abrogation and the causing to be forgotten named together, and he reports the claim of the community that the messenger commanded a thing one day and forbade it the next. Since the objection and the answer are kept side by side, the reader is shown what the passage is doing, which is answering a taunt rather than announcing a new rule.

**THE REPLACEMENT AND ITS MEASURE**

The sentence then states what follows: the replacement is a better verse or one like it. Ibn ʿUthaymīn sets out the readings of the two verbs, showing how the reciters differed over the shape of the second act, and he keeps the sentence as a statement of what God does with what He has sent. al-Saʿdī explains that the community had denied the practice altogether and argued that it could not happen, and he keeps the sentence as the refutation of that denial, with the replacement described as more beneficial than what it replaced. Because the replacement is described as better or equal, the reader is shown that nothing was lost in the change.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gives the clearest case in the sūrah, which is the change of the direction of prayer from the earlier sanctuary to the House in Mecca, and it notes that the change gave the objectors their opportunity to taunt. al-Ṭabarī keeps the comparison as the description of the replacement, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading of the two words. Because the sentence names both the removal and the replacement, the practice is shown as a single act of care rather than as two disconnected events.

**THE QUESTION THAT CLOSES THE VERSE**

The verse ends with a question: ***“that Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. The question is aimed at the assumption behind the objection, which is that the Book should follow the expectations of the people who were asked to receive it. al-Saʿdī keeps the closing words as the ground of the whole answer, since the One who governs what is sent is able to replace it with what serves the people better. The same attribute stands at the close of the passage that reports the envy of the People of the Book (2:109), and the two sentences are read together as one answer. Because the closing sentence names capability, the reader is shown that the issue was never about possibility but about surrender.

The passage has now answered several objections, about the carrier of the revelation, about the Book, and about the change of rulings, and the answers have one shape, which is the naming of the One who sent the message. Since the verse is placed among the instructions to the believers, the reader is shown that the objections of others were being used to steady the community that had accepted the Book, and the closing question leaves that community with an attribute to hold rather than an argument to win.

The case is like a household that follows the builder's plan and is told by a neighbour that the plan was revised. The revision came from the same builder, the house stands, and the neighbour was never the client.

---

## Verse 2:107

> Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah

**THE QUESTION THAT AFFIRMS**

The verse answers the objection about abrogation with a question that assumes the answer: ***“Do you not know”*** ***“that the kingdom of the heavens”***. al-Qurṭubī notes that the question form here does not seek information, since the addressee already knows what is being put to him, and he explains the kingdom as the act of creating and originating rather than as a claim of rank. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same phrase as the stores of the heavens and the earth, and he notes that the One who owns them commands His servants with what He wills because He knows what is good for them. Because the question is put to a person who already knows the answer, the verse turns the objection back on the one who raised it.

The ownership described in the sentence is not a distant title, and al-Saʿdī draws out what follows from it for the passage. If the Lord owns the servants and disposes of them as a merciful owner disposes of what is his, then no objection stands against the rulings He lays down, and the servant is shown as one who is managed rather than as one who manages. The same ownership is explained by Ibn ʿUthaymīn through the placing of the words, since the fronting of what would normally come later marks the ownership as exclusive, and he adds that the ownership covers both what is held and what is done with it. Because the sentence joins the kingdom to the rulings, the reader is shown why the change of a ruling is not a defect in the rule of God.

**THE GUARDIAN AND THE HELPER**

The verse then states what the reader lacks: ***“and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian”*** ***“or helper besides Allah”***. al-Baghawī explains that the question is an affirmation, so the sentence means that the addressee knows this already, and he gives the guardian as a near friend and the helper as the one who manages affairs in his favour. al-Jalālayn keeps the pair as the protector who safeguards and the helper who keeps harm away when it comes, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense of a protector and an ally. Because the sentence names both, the reader is shown that the person who has no guardian and no helper is being asked to rely on the One who owns everything.

al-Ālūsī reads the ownership of the two horizons as the ownership of all the earth, and he notes that the sentence secures the whole field of directions rather than one point in it. Ibn Kathīr keeps the verse as the statement that the creatures have no ally and no helper besides their Lord, and he keeps it in the flow of the answers given to the objections about the Book. Since the passage has just answered the claim about the change of rulings, the reader is shown that the same Lord who owns the heavens also owns the right to decide what is recited and what is replaced.

**WHY THE ANSWER IS A QUESTION**

A question can be the shortest way of closing an argument, and the sentence is put as a question because the objector's premise had already conceded the point. If the kingdom belongs to God, then the objection is not a request for explanation but a claim of authority that no creature holds. Because the sentence names the two directions and then names the two supports that are missing, the reader is left without a third option, and the verse ends there rather than adding a warning.

The lesson also reaches the reader who comes to the Book with conditions of his own. A person who accepts the message while reserving the right to approve its rulings has placed himself where the guardian and the helper would stand, and the verse quietly removes both seats. The Book states the same ownership in another passage, where whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth is said to belong to Him (42:4). Since the verse is addressed to the believers, the correction is offered as a reminder rather than as a rebuke, and the reader is shown that the same knowledge that answers an objection also settles a heart.

The case is like a guest who is told that the house belongs to his host and then argues with the seating plan. The house is not his, the meal is not his, and the host has been generous all evening.

---

## Verse 2:108

> Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way

**THE QUESTION PUT TO THE BELIEVERS**

The verse turns from the objectors to the believers: ***“Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger”*** ***“as Moses was asked before?”***. al-Ṭabarī records the reports about the occasion and keeps the sentence as a rebuke aimed at a way of asking rather than at asking itself. The opening is explained by al-Qurṭubī as a break from what preceded it, with the sense of a correction, and he keeps the question as a reproach rather than as an inquiry. al-Jalālayn records the demands that were put to the Prophet, including the request that the valley be widened and that gold be given to him, and he keeps the comparison with the earlier community in the same sentence. Because the comparison is with a people who had asked for signs rather than for guidance, the reader is shown what kind of question the verse is forbidding.

Ibn Kathīr records the demand that had been made of Moses to show God openly, and as-Saʿdī keeps the same point, that the questions in view are the questions of stubbornness and objection rather than the questions of learning. The sense kept by Ibn ʿAbbās is that the earlier community asked to see their Lord, to hear His speech, and to have other such demands met. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the community was always making insolent demands, and it places the verse as a warning to the believers against taking the same road. Since the demand in both cases was for a proof that would settle the matter without requiring obedience, the reader is shown that the fault lay in the purpose of the asking.

**THE TRADE AND THE ROAD**

The sentence then names the consequence: ***“But whoever trades belief”*** ***“for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the trade as the exchange of one thing for another, with the believer who leaves his faith for a doubt shown as a person who has made a bad bargain. al-Ālūsī keeps the same sense and treats the sentence as a statement about the end of such a road rather than as a threat, and al-Jalālayn keeps the figure of the path in the closing words. Because the sentence speaks of trading, the reader is shown that the loss is chosen rather than suffered, and the verse leaves him with the two sides of the exchange in view.

The Book records the same demand in another passage, where the People of the Book ask for a revelation in writing and are reminded that their ancestors asked Moses for something greater (4:153). Ibn Kathīr keeps the closing phrase as the description of a person who has left the path altogether, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading. Because the sentence ends with the road rather than with the demand, the reader is shown where the question was leading, and the verse turns a request for evidence into a question about direction.

**WHAT THE VERSE TEACHES ABOUT QUESTIONS**

A question can be a door to knowledge or a way of postponing what is already known, and the verse separates the two by the company the question keeps. Because the earlier community's asking began a habit of testing the messenger, the verse warns the believers that a question can be a first step away from the path. The earlier community asked for what they had no business asking, and the sentence shows that the habit itself was the beginning of a trade. Because the verse addresses the believers, the reader is taught that faith does not exempt a person from this danger; it only gives him more to lose.

The lesson also protects the reader from measuring his faith by the size of the sign he waits for. Moses was asked for a sign by his own people, and that demand is named as the model of a question that leads away from the path rather than along it. Since the trade is named before the straying, the reader learns that a fault of the will precedes a fault of the mind, and the closing words describe the end of a road rather than the size of a mistake. The reason the trade is named before the straying is that a person chooses the exchange while he is still standing on the road, and the wandering comes after the choice rather than instead of it.

The case is like a traveller who asks the guide for the map of the whole country before he will take a single step. The guide has pointed at the road, and the traveller is still standing at the gate.

---

## Verse 2:109

> Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE WISH AND ITS CAUSE**

The verse states what the community wanted: ***“Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief”*** ***“because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the wish as a longing rather than as an act, and he places the sentence among the addresses given to the believers in this part of the sūrah. The verb is explained by al-Qurṭubī as wishing, and he notes that the cause named in the sentence is envy, so that the wish is traced to a fault in the speakers rather than to a fault in the message. Ibn ʿAbbās names leading figures of the community and their companions among those in view, and he keeps the note that the truth had already become clear to them. Because the sentence names the envy rather than the argument, the reader is shown that the opposition was not the fruit of study.

The report about a group who came to two companions after a setback is recorded by al-Baghawī, in which they were told that if they were on the truth they would not have been defeated, which shows how the wish was worked into advice. al-Ālūsī keeps the same report and the same setting, and al-Jalālayn keeps the wish and the envy in one sentence with the knowledge of the truth stated after them. Because the truth had been made clear before the wish was formed, the reader is shown that the community's problem was not a lack of evidence but a refusal to follow it.

**THE ORDER TO PARDON AND BEAR**

The sentence then gives the believers an instruction: ***“and bear with them”*** ***“until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the pardon as the forbearance of the believers and the patience as the waiting that accompanies it, and he keeps the decision in the hands of God. al-Qurṭubī keeps the pair as one instruction with the waiting attached to it, so that the believers are told what to do with their own hands while the matter is left to God. Ibn Kathīr keeps the instruction in the same order, with the pardon first and the patience after it, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the verse as the warning the believers needed against the stratagems of the other community. Because the instruction is given before the outcome is named, the reader is shown that the believers were asked for a manner rather than for a victory.

The instruction is kept by al-Saʿdī as part of the mercy shown to the believers, since it stops them from spending their strength on enemies who were working in secret. The Book names the same envy in another passage, where the question is asked whether the people resent others for the bounty God has given (4:54). Since the verse closes with the attribute of capability, the reader is shown that the delay in the decision is a matter of timing rather than of power.

**WHY THE ANSWER IS PATIENCE**

A wish that cannot be fulfilled is still a danger, because it shapes the advice a person gives and the company he keeps. The verse tells the believers where the wish comes from and then tells them to bear with the people who hold it. Because the instruction is patience rather than silence, the reader is shown that forbearance is not the same as agreement, and the believers are left with their own clear knowledge of the truth while the decision waits.

The lesson also gives the reader a way of reading opposition. A community that argues from the text and a community that argues from envy may use the same words, and the verse teaches the reader to look at the ground of the argument rather than at its surface. Since the verse ends with the attribute of capability, the reader is shown that no plan against the truth can outlast the One who holds the decision.

The case is like a household that is advised by a neighbour to move out of a house he has been trying to buy. The advice is patient, the house is sound, and the neighbour's interest is not the household's.

---

## Verse 2:110

> Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**THE TWO DUTIES AND THE ANSWER TO ENVY**

The verse answers the envy of the previous passage with an instruction: ***“Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth”***. al-Ṭabarī explains the establishing of the prayer as the performance of it with its limits and its obligations, and he keeps the two duties together as the worship of the body and of wealth. The sense of the sending forth is given by al-Baghawī as what a person advances for himself, and he keeps the good as obedience and righteous work. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the prayer as the five daily prayers and the alms as what is due from wealth, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading of the pair. Because the instruction follows an account of envy, the reader is shown that the cure for a poisoned atmosphere is not argument but worship.

The command to occupy the present time with the prayer, the alms, and every act of nearness to God is drawn by al-Saʿdī, who notes that the promise attached to it covers whatever good a person sends ahead. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the same instruction in the setting of a community waiting for a change of law, and it keeps the note that a deed performed before the change loses nothing of its reward. Since the passage had just described a people who wanted the believers to turn back, the reader is shown that the answer to the wish is a life of steady worship rather than a debate.

**THE REWARD THAT IS FOUND**

The sentence then states what will come of it: ***“for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the finding as the presence of the reward with God, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the sentence as the assurance that nothing sent ahead is lost. al-Ālūsī reads the two duties as the worship that defends the believers against what they fear, so that the instruction is a shield as well as a duty, and he keeps the closing attribute as the ground of the promise. Because the reward is described as found rather than as given, the reader is shown that it is kept for him and returned to him whole.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sending as the good a person stores for his own soul, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the closing words as the statement that God sees what the believers do and will repay it. The Book gives the same instruction earlier in the sūrah, where prayer and alms are commanded with the bowing of those who bow (2:43). Since the sentence names both what is done and who sees it, the reader is taught that worship is a deposit rather than a loss.

**WHAT WORSHIP DOES WITH ENVY**

Envy is usually answered in kind, and the verse answers it with two duties that have nothing to do with the envious. The prayer turns a person toward God and the alms turns him toward people, so that the two duties close both doors through which envy enters. Because the instruction is given while the other community is still scheming, the reader is shown that the believers were not asked to wait for the danger to pass before serving, and the reward is placed with God rather than with the community's mood.

The lesson also reaches a reader who measures his religion by the respect it earns. The verse does not promise that the neighbours will change their wish, and it promises instead that what is sent ahead will be found. Since the closing words name the One who sees, the reader is left with an audience that never looks away, and the envy of the passage loses its power to set the agenda.

The case is like a farmer whose neighbour resents his field and who answers by planting a second one. The neighbour's grudge keeps its shape, and the harvest doubles.

---

## Verse 2:111

> The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”

**THE CLAIM AND THE DESIRES**

The verse states the claim that each community made: ***“The Jews and Christians each claim”*** ***“that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the claim as the speech of both communities and notes the difficulty in the wording, since the verse gathers them together although each group made the claim for itself. al-Qurṭubī explains the sentence in the same way, with each community claiming the Garden for its own members and denying it to the rest. Ibn ʿAbbās records the same claim from both sides, and al-Baghawī explains the grammatical form of the word used for the Jewish claim. Because the two claims cancel each other out, the reader is shown that neither rests on evidence.

The sentence then names what the claims are: ***“These are their desires”***. al-Saʿdī explains that each group judged the Garden for itself alone, and he calls the claim a wish that cannot be accepted without proof, which is why the verse asks for the proof immediately after. al-Jalālayn keeps the note that the two communities made these claims when they disputed in the presence of the Prophet, each party claiming Paradise for itself. Because the claims are called desires rather than doctrines, the reader is shown that the argument belongs to the appetite rather than to the text.

**THE DEMAND FOR PROOF**

The closing words put a condition on the claim: ***“if what you say is true.””***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the demand as the request for evidence, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the answer given to the two communities in the same words. al-Ālūsī reads the verse as a challenge that carries its own judgement, since the proof demanded is of a kind that no wish can supply. Because the request is addressed to the Prophet but aimed at the claimants, the reader is shown that the verse is establishing a rule for everyone who makes a claim about the next world.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the two communities had forgotten the substance of religion and kept only the name, and it keeps the verse as the exposure of a claim that had no ground. al-Saʿdī draws the general rule out of the sentence, which is that every claim needs its proof, and he applies it to anyone who claims a share of the Garden on the strength of a wish. Because the demand comes at the end of the sentence, the reader is left holding the claim and the empty hand of the one who made it.

**WHAT A CLAIM NEEDS**

A claim about the next world cannot be tested by inspection, and the verse meets such a claim by asking for its proof. The communities named in the sentence recited their Scriptures and still made a claim that their own books did not carry, and the request for proof is a reminder of what a book is for. Because the verse answers a claim of privilege, the reader is taught that the question is not which community a person belongs to but what his Scripture has actually established.

The verse also instructs the reader about the wish itself. The Book names the claim a desire because a person who has no proof and no practice may still want the outcome, and desire is not enough to change the terms. Since the proof was demanded before the reply to the claim is given, the reader is shown that the Book answers argument with the standard of argument, and the comfort of the claimants is left where it belongs, with themselves. The Book names the same rule in another passage, where the wishes of the communities are set aside and the outcome is tied to what a person has earned (4:123).

The case is like a man who is invited to sit at a table by another guest who had no authority to invite him. The seat may be given, the door is not opened that way, and the host has not been consulted.

---

## Verse 2:112

> But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**THE CORRECTION OF THE CLAIM**

The verse opens with a correction: ***“But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the opening word as the denial of what the two communities had claimed, and he explains the submitting of the self as the surrender of the person with his intent. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, with the surrender taken as making one's religion sincere for God and working for Him. al-Ālūsī reads the opening as a rejection of the claim and a statement of the true condition, and al-Jalālayn explains the mention of the self as the placing of one's purpose under the command of God. Because the answer replaces the claim about ancestry with a condition about conduct, the reader is shown that the question was never about which community a person was born into.

The verse then completes the condition: ***“and does good will have their reward with their Lord.”*** al-Saʿdī explains the pair as sincerity for God together with good work, and he notes that the reward named in the sentence is the Garden with everything it holds. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same pair, with the reward placed with the Lord, so that the outcome is tied to the acceptance of the deed rather than to the claim of the doer. Because the condition has two halves, the reader is shown that intention without practice and practice without intention both fall short of the sentence.

**THE FEAR AND THE GRIEF**

The sentence then closes with a promise: ***“And there will be no fear”*** ***“for them, nor will they grieve”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the pair as the removal of what is feared and what is regretted, and he notes that the people described are those whose condition has been met. al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense, with the fear belonging to the future and the grief to the past. Because the two words cover both directions of time, the reader is shown that the promise answers the two things that sour a person's comfort, and it does so by removing them rather than by distracting from them.

The Book makes the same promise to the people described in an earlier passage, where the believers, the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians who believe in God and do good are named with the same two words (2:62). Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the reward as the Garden and keeps the two promises in the same order as the verse, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the verse as the standard that cuts across the claims of the communities named in the passage. Since the claim of privilege has already been answered, the promise at the end is left open to everyone who meets the condition.

**WHAT SETTLES A RELIGION**

A religion measured by membership asks what a person is; the verse asks what a person does with what he is. The two halves of the condition are joined because a person can surrender his purpose without working, and he can work without surrendering his purpose. Because the verse places the reward with the Lord, the reader is shown that the outcome is not administered by the communities who had made the claims, and the sentence leaves the question where the Book leaves it.

The closing promise also removes the two motives that keep people from obeying. Fear of what may come keeps a person from stepping forward, and grief over what has passed keeps him looking back, and the verse promises the people of this condition that neither will have the last word over them. Since the sentence is put as a statement rather than as a hope, the reader is given a promise to stand on, and the claim of the earlier verse is left behind with the desires that produced it.

The case is like a household that is judged by what it does at the table rather than by the name on the door. The door has a name, the table has food, and the guests are known by how they behave at both.

---

## Verse 2:113

> The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures. And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute

**THE TWO CLAIMS AGAINST EACH OTHER**

The verse reports the exchange between the two communities: ***“The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on””*** ***“and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,””***. al-Ṭabarī records the setting of a dispute that took place in the presence of the messenger, where the two parties argued and each declared the other to be on nothing. al-Ālūsī keeps the same scene, with the delegation from the Christians of Najrān and the Jews of Medina trading accusations, and he notes that each side rejected the prophet of the other. al-Qurṭubī explains the claim as the assertion that the other community has no ground to stand on and no share in the mercy of God. Because the claim is put in the mouths of both communities, the reader is shown a quarrel in which each side uses the same argument.

The sentence then states what both sides had in common: ***“although both recite the Scriptures.”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the note that the two communities recited their books while rejecting the prophets the books named, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same point about the two Scriptures. al-Saʿdī reads the passage as the account of a rivalry carried so far that each group declared the other to be in error, and he notes that the same pattern appeared among the idolaters who had no book at all. Because the two sides recited what they claimed to stand on, the reader is shown that the quarrel was not about the texts but about the reading of them.

**THE THIRD GROUP AND THE JUDGEMENT**

The verse then widens the frame: ***“And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute”***. al-Qurṭubī keeps the group as those who have no knowledge, and he notes that their speech follows the same pattern as the speech of the two communities, so the reader is shown that the habit is not tied to learning. al-Ṭabarī keeps the closing sentence as the statement that the judgement belongs to God alone, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the verse as the record of a hostility that had become mutual between the two communities. Because the quarrel is left to the judgement of God, the reader is shown that the believers were not asked to settle it with a claim of their own.

The Book states the same theme in another passage, where the earlier communities differed out of mutual envy after knowledge had come to them, and their Lord is named as the one who will judge between them (45:17). Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the closing sentence as the promise that God will judge what they differed over, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the passage in the flow of the argument against the claims of the two communities. Since the sentence about judgement comes last, the reader is shown that the argument is closed not by a victory but by a court.

**WHAT THE QUARREL TEACHES**

Two communities can recite the same kind of book and still accuse each other of standing on nothing, and the verse shows how such a quarrel works. Each side uses the book it has as a possession rather than as a guide, and the accusation grows from the wish to keep the truth for oneself. Because the sentence mentions the recitation of the Scriptures in the middle of the claims, the reader is shown that the texts had become arguments for the claimants rather than judges over them.

The verse also gives the reader a way to hold a disagreement. The believers are shown a quarrel they are not asked to join, and the judgement is left to the day when no claim will be of use. Since the closing sentence names the Judge rather than the verdict, the reader is taught that the truth is not in doubt but the timing is, and the verse leaves him with a patience that the parties in the quarrel had lost. Because each side had a book it could recite, the verse shows that the quarrel was carried on with borrowed authority, and the reason the judgement is deferred is that a claim made in the heat of a dispute is rarely the claim its holder would make before God. The point of mentioning the pagans in the same sentence is that the habit grows without learning, since a person with no book at all can still dismiss everyone who has one.

The case is like two travellers quarrelling over which of them holds the only map, while both stand at the same fork in the road. The map belongs to the road, and the road has not moved.

---

## Verse 2:114

> Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear. For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter

**THE WORST OF WRONGS**

The verse opens with a question that has no addressee: ***“Who does more wrong than those”*** ***“who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship”***. al-Ṭabarī explains the wrong as the placing of a thing outside its proper place, so that the act described is shown as a disorder rather than only as an offence. al-Qurṭubī reads the question as the statement that no one is more wrong than such a person, and he sets out the grammatical construction that makes the sentence decisive. Ibn ʿAbbās names the king who destroyed the sanctuary and led the campaign against the earlier community, and al-Baghawī records the same account. Because the question is put in the absolute, the reader is shown that the act is measured against the whole scale of wrong rather than against other acts of its kind.

The sentence then adds the second part of the act: ***“and strive to destroy them?”***. al-Saʿdī explains the striving as the exertion of every effort, and he divides the destruction into the physical ruin of the buildings and the moral ruin of driving people away from them, so that the reader sees the two ways the same crime is committed. al-Jalālayn keeps the ruin as the destruction of the places and the hindering of those who would pray in them. Because the sentence pairs the prevention of worship with the destruction of its home, the reader is shown that the target is the mention of God's name itself.

**THE FEAR AND THE TWO ENDS**

The verse then states the consequence for those who act in this way: ***“Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that such people have no claim on the sanctuaries and should enter them, if at all, in fear. al-Ālūsī keeps the same reading and treats the sentence as the fitting answer to a claim of guardianship, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the words as the description of what such people deserve. Because the sentence measures the act against the house of worship rather than against the worshippers, the reader is shown that the wrong belongs to the place as much as to the people.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the rulings out of the verse and begins with the equal respect owed to every house of worship, and it keeps the passage as a warning against desecration in any form. The sentence then closes with the two ends of the wrong: ***“For them is disgrace in this world”*** ***“and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter”***. al-Saʿdī keeps the pair as the disgrace of this life and the punishment of the next, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading of the two. The Book records the same theme in another passage, where the destruction of monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques is placed beside the reason the places stand, which is the mention of God's name (22:40). Because the closing sentence names both worlds, the reader is shown that no ruin of a sanctuary escapes the reckoning.

**WHAT THE VERSE PROTECTS**

A place of worship is not a building with a name on it; it is a space set aside for the mention of God, and the verse protects the purpose rather than the walls. The crime described is committed by a person who wants the name of God to stop being heard in a particular place, and the verse answers with the two ends that such a person will meet. Because the question at the head of the verse is left open, the reader is invited to answer it himself, and the answer is that no one does more wrong.

The passage also warns the reader against a subtler form of the same act. A community can leave a sanctuary standing and still empty it, by making the mention of God unwelcome inside it or by keeping the people away from it, and the striving to destroy is named as part of the same crime. Since the closing sentence names the world and the Hereafter together, the reader is taught that the place of worship is a trust, and the verse leaves him with the duty of keeping it in use.

The case is like a man who locks a well that serves a whole village and keeps the key in his pocket. The water is still there, the village is thirsty, and the lock is his only achievement.

---

## Verse 2:115

> To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing

**THE TWO DIRECTIONS AND THEIR OWNER**

The verse states the ownership of the directions: ***“To Allah belong the east”*** ***“and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing”***. al-Ṭabarī explains the sentence as the statement that the two directions and everything between them belong to God, so that the ownership of the horizons carries the ownership of all the earth. al-Qurṭubī keeps the sense of the naming of the two directions as the places of rising and setting, and he notes that what lies between them is included in the same claim. al-Ālūsī reads the naming of the two as a figure for the whole earth, and he records the view that the roundness of the earth does not affect the claim, since the two named directions stand for every point. Because the ownership is stated before the permission, the reader is shown that the turning is allowed because the earth is not held by anyone else.

The permission then follows from the ownership: ***“and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah”***. al-Jalālayn records the two occasions given for the verse, one being the criticism of the change in the direction of prayer and the other being the prayers offered on a journey, and he keeps the permission as the sense of the sentence. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the verse as the direction for a person who does not know the correct direction, and al-Baghawī records the report about the companions who prayed in the wrong direction on a journey before the change of the qiblah. Because the sentence is put as a general permission, the reader is shown that a worshipper whose intention is to face God is not cut off by geography.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The sentence ends with two attributes: ***“Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the first as the breadth that holds everything and the second as the knowledge that misses nothing, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same pair with the servant's intention in view. al-Saʿdī explains the naming of the two horizons as the naming of the places where the great signs of the rising and the setting are seen, so that the One who owns them owns all the directions. Since the closing names knowledge, the reader is shown that the permission rests on what God knows of the heart rather than on the precision of the compass.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the verse in the setting of the other passages in this part of the sūrah, where the three hostile groups are answered in turn, and the permission is read there as part of the mercy shown to the community. Ibn Kathīr keeps the closing pair as the assurance that nothing is hidden from the One who accepts the turning, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading. Because the two attributes are named after the permission, the reader is shown that the allowance is not a concession to carelessness but a mercy that sees the intent.

**WHAT THE PERMISSION TEACHES**

A worshipper can be precise about a direction and absent in his heart, and the verse puts the two attributes of breadth and knowledge at the end so that both are weighed together. The Book states the change of the direction of prayer in another passage, where the turning toward the Sacred Mosque is commanded and the purpose of the change is named (2:144). Because the verse before that change is a permission for the traveller and the uncertain, the reader is shown that the community was being led rather than tested by geography.

The lesson also reaches a reader who fears that a mistake in form cancels his worship. The two attributes at the close say that God encompasses the earth and knows the heart, and the permission in the middle says that the turning counts when the intention is right. Since the two directions are named as belonging to God, the reader is left without a direction that is outside His kingdom, and the sentence ends where the worshipper's confidence belongs.

The case is like a servant who is told by his master that every room in the house is his and that a knock at any door will be heard. The house is not rented, the doors are all his, and the master is listening.

---

## Verse 2:116

> They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will

**THE CLAIM AND ITS ANSWER**

The verse reports a claim: ***“They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him!”*** al-Qurṭubī records the reports that the claim came from a group among the People of the Book in the case of one figure and from others in the case of another, and he keeps the claim as the attribution of a son to God. al-Ālūsī gathers the same reports and shows how the claim was made by different communities about different figures, so that the sentence covers the case as a whole. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading of the claim, naming the two figures the communities attached to God, and al-Jalālayn notes the reading of the verse in which the words are reported either as their speech or as a statement about them. Because the claim is reported before it is answered, the reader is shown that the Book lets the words stand on the record.

The answer comes immediately: ***“Glory be to Him!”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the phrase as the declaration that God is above what they attribute to Him, and he reads it as the exaltation that closes the claim. al-Saʿdī explains the phrase as the declaration of God's freedom from any likeness and any partner, so that the sentence clears the ground before the argument begins. Because the answer is given as an exaltation rather than as a refutation, the reader is shown that the claim is dismissed on the level of what God is before it is examined as a statement.

**THE OWNERSHIP AND THE SUBMISSION**

The sentence then supplies the argument: ***“In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens”*** ***“and the earth”*** ***“all are subject to His Will”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the ownership as the ground of the answer, since what belongs to God cannot be a partner to Him, and he collects the reports about the meaning of the closing word. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the submission as the obedience of everything to the will of its Lord, and he notes that the whole of creation is included. al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense, with everything in the two realms owned by God, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the closing words as the statement that all creation is subject to His command. Because the argument rests on ownership, the reader is shown that the claim collapses before it can even be discussed.

al-Saʿdī reads the passage as the statement that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God and stands under His will, and he notes how patient the sentence is with the people who made the claim. The Book answers the same claim in another passage, where the claim of offspring is met with the question of how He could have a child when He has no mate and has created everything (6:101). Since the verse ends with the submission of the creation, the reader is shown that the claim about a son misunderstands what it means to be a creature.

**WHAT THE CLAIM GETS WRONG**

A person who gives God a son has reasoned by analogy from his own household, and the verse answers the analogy with the ownership that holds the whole creation. The claim is not only an error about God; it also misplaces the creatures, since a son would be a partner rather than a servant. Because the submission of everything is named in the sentence, the reader is shown that the whole creation, high and low, has already been placed in the position the claim denies.

The verse also teaches a manner of speaking about God. The exaltation comes before the argument, and the argument then rests on what belongs to God rather than on what people prefer to say. Since the sentence closes with the subjection of the creation, the reader is left with a settled order rather than with a debate, and the claim is answered by the shape of the world rather than by a contest of words.

The case is like a man who presents himself at a workshop as the owner's son and is shown the door by the foreman. The machines are running, the roster is on the wall, and the son's name is not on it.

---

## Verse 2:117

> ˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth! When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is

**THE MAKER WITH NO PRECEDENT**

The verse answers the claim about offspring with the act of creation itself: ***“˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens”*** ***“and the earth!”***. al-Ṭabarī explains the word as the One who brings the heavens and the earth into being, and he notes the turn in the Arabic form, since the word carries the sense of the one who originates rather than the thing originated. The same explanation is kept by al-Qurṭubī, who adds that the sentence describes an act performed without any model to copy, and who notes the grammatical weight of the word as an intensive description rather than a plain adjective. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sense that the two realms were brought into being when they were nothing before, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading with the addition that the making had no exemplary precedent.

The purpose of the sentence is drawn out by Ibn ʿUthaymīn, who asks what the verse is answering and then answers his own question: the One able to originate the heavens and the earth without a model is able to create a child without a father, so the claim reported in the previous verse is answered by what the reader sees above him. The same link is kept by Ibn Kathīr, who reads this verse and the ones after it as the refutation of the claim of a son, and by as-Saʿdī, who notes that the pair were made with a perfecting skill rather than from a prior pattern. Because the action named here is the making of the whole world, the reader is shown that the smaller claim collapses under the larger fact.

**THE DECREE AND THE WORD**

The sentence then states how the making works: ***“When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!””***. al-Ṭabarī explains the decree as the fixing of the matter, and al-Baghawī keeps the same sense, giving the determining of a thing as the meaning of the clause. al-Ālūsī keeps the reading of the sentence as the statement of what happens when God wills a thing to exist, and he records the discussion of the form of the expression used for decree. Because the sentence moves from the making of the world to the making of any single thing, the reader is shown that no gap stands between the will and the event.

The closing words state the result: ***“And it is”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sentence as the instant answer to the command, and he applies it to the creation of a child without a father, showing that the case of such a birth is no harder for God than the case of Adam, who had neither father nor mother. as-Saʿdī notes that nothing resists the command and nothing holds it back, so the sentence is the strongest form of the answer to the claim. The Book states the same pattern in another passage, where the making of a thing is described as a word and the result follows at once (36:82), and the two sentences are read together.

**WHY THE ANSWER IS CREATION**

An argument about offspring is an argument about what God can do, and the verse answers it by pointing at what God has already done. Because the heavens and the earth stand without a model, the reader is shown that the ordinary rules a person knows do not bind their Maker. That is why the claim of the previous verse is answered here rather than argued with; the sentence replaces the disputed picture with the fact of creation.

The lesson also steadies a reader who measures God by what he has seen. A household, a body, a family and a child all follow patterns that a person takes for granted, and the sentence names the One who set those patterns and stands outside them. Because the answer is given as creation rather than as argument, the reader is shown that the claim about a son was never a question about possibility. Since the sentence closes on the result rather than on the command, the reader is left with an act rather than with a discussion, and the verse ends the question by opening the world.

The case is like a man who argues about whether a carpenter can make a chair without a photograph and then looks at the house the carpenter built. The photograph was never the point, and the house is standing.

---

## Verse 2:118

> Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!” The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike. Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith

**THE DEMAND FOR A VOICE FROM ABOVE**

The verse reports the demand of the ignorant: ***“Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us”*** ***“or a sign would come to us!””***. al-Ṭabarī collects the reports about who is meant here, whether the Christians, the Jews, or the polytheists of the Arabs, and he keeps the demand itself as the subject of the verse. The same reports are set in order by al-Qurṭubī, with a companion's view that the Jews are meant and another view that the Christians are, and he notes the form of the demand as a wish that carries a challenge. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the reading that the speakers did not know the oneness of God, and he explains the demand as a request for a sign that the prophethood might be confirmed. Because the sentence describes the speakers by what they lack rather than by what they hold, the reader is shown that the demand came from ignorance rather than from learning.

The demand itself is explained by Ibn ʿUthaymīn as the request that God speak to them directly, so that the message would come with a voice they could hear, and by as-Saʿdī as a proposal of the kind of sign the speakers thought would settle the matter. The same sense is kept by al-Jalālayn, with the disbelievers asking why God does not speak to them or send them a sign of the kind they had chosen. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the demands as absurd, and it notes that they were made in order to feel triumphant in their refusal. Since the sign asked for is one that the askers had picked, the reader is shown that the request was a way of keeping control of the terms.

**THE HEARTS THAT MATCH**

The verse then widens the frame: ***“The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the closing clause as the statement that the later speakers resemble the earlier ones in their hearts rather than in their wording. al-Ālūsī notes the place of the verse in the passage, since the earlier sentences answered a claim about God and this one answers a claim about the messenger, and the two are shown to belong to one rebellion. The same reading is kept by Ibn Kathīr, who places the demand beside the demands of the earlier communities, so that the reader sees a habit rather than an incident. Because the sentence compares the hearts rather than the words, the reader is shown that the fault was older than the wording.

The comparison is also a caution, since the hearts are said to be alike rather than the people. as-Saʿdī explains that the demands were the products of minds that thought they could improve on what had been sent, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading. The Book records a similar demand in another passage, where a people asked for something greater from Moses (4:153), and the account here is read as the same request in another age.

**THE SIGNS AND THOSE WHO ARE SURE**

The verse closes with what had already been given: ***“Indeed, We have made the signs clear”*** ***“for people of sure faith”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that the signs were made plain, with the certainty named as the reception they find. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading and notes that the clarity is not withheld from anyone but meets the people who are prepared to receive it. Ibn ʿUthaymīn notes that the signs were already clear to those who looked, so the demand for a new one says something about the demander rather than about the evidence. Because the sentence names certainty rather than cleverness, the reader is shown that the door was never locked by the difficulty of the proofs.

The lesson reaches a reader who waits for a personal sign before obeying. The verse shows the demand of the earlier speakers and then states that the signs are already clear, and the two sentences together leave the reader with what he has rather than with what he wants. Since the passage has answered the claim about God and the demand about the messenger, the reader is shown that both objections came from the same place, and the verse ends with the people who had settled the question.

The case is like a man who asks the harbour master for a second lighthouse and stands on the pier while the first one is sweeping the bay. The light is doing its work, and the man is doing something else.

---

## Verse 2:119

> We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire

**THE TRUTH THE MESSENGER WAS SENT WITH**

The verse states the commission: ***“We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the assurance that the messenger had delivered what he was sent with, and he reads the connection with the sentence that follows, where the task of conveying is separated from the outcome in the hearts of the listeners. The same reading is kept by al-Qurṭubī, who notes the form of the two descriptions that come next, since they are states of the messenger rather than separate messages. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the truth as the Qur'an and the declaration of the oneness of God, and al-Jalālayn keeps the sense of guidance as the content of what was sent.
