Because the sentence places the truth in the message rather than in the response to it, the reader is shown that the messenger's success is not measured by the number of those who accept.

The several explanations of the truth, whether truthfulness, the Qur'an, or the religion with its rulings, are recorded by al-Baghawī, and al-Ālūsī keeps the general sense as the stronger of them. as-Saʿdī gathers the three things the commission rests on: the sending itself, the life and conduct of the one sent, and the message he brought. Because the sentence names the truth as the thing carried, the reader is shown that the message stands on its own feet, and the refusal of the hearers does not bend it.

**THE TWO OFFICES**

The verse then names the two offices: ***“as a deliverer of good news”*** ***“and a warner.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the pair as the two forms the message takes, one for those who respond and one for those who turn away, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading with the Garden named for the one and the Fire for the other. The pair is kept by Ibn Kathīr in the same order, with the good news for those who accept what was brought and the warning for those who refuse it. Because the two offices are joined in one sentence, the reader is shown that mercy and warning are not two missions but one, and the messenger carries both in the same words.

The pair is stated in the same terms in another passage, where the sending is described with the same two words (35:24). The Book uses them of the messengers as a group in a further passage, where the prophets are named as deliverers of good news and as warners (2:213). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the verse as the answer to a heavy thought, since the refusal of an obstinate people could make the messenger fear that his work had failed. The sentence tells him what his work was. Since the offices are named in the order of hope first, the reader is shown that the message comes looking for acceptance before it announces a warning.

**WHAT THE MESSENGER IS NOT ASKED**

The sentence then draws the line: ***“And you will not be accountable”*** ***“for the residents of the Hellfire”***. al-Ṭabarī notes the reading of the majority, in which the sentence is a statement to the messenger that his duty was the conveying and the warning, and that he is not questioned about those who refused. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, and Ibn Kathīr keeps it as the statement that the messenger is not asked about the dwellers of the Fire. Because the sentence follows the two offices, the reader is shown where the messenger's work ends and where the outcome belongs.

The lesson reaches every reader who carries a message to others, whether a parent, a teacher or a friend. The verse shows the messenger released from the responsibility of the answer, and it leaves that responsibility with the person who heard. Since the passage had just reported a demand for signs, the sentence quietly answers the exhaustion that such a demand produces, and the messenger is left with the work he was given rather than with the result he had hoped for.

The case is like a postman who delivers a court notice and is then asked why the recipient did not appear. The notice was delivered, the date was printed, and the appearance was never the postman's business.

---

## Verse 2:120

> Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah

**THE PLEASURE THAT WILL NOT COME**

The verse states the position of the two communities: ***“Never will the Jews”*** ***“or Christians be pleased with you”*** ***“until you follow their faith.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that the two communities will not be satisfied with anything short of agreement, and he notes that the demand of the previous verse was never the real aim. al-Qurṭubī explains that their purpose was not the signs they asked for but the wish that the messenger adopt what they held. al-Baghawī records the report that they used to ask for a truce while holding out the hope that they would follow, and he keeps the verse as the answer to that hope. Because the sentence names the condition they set, the reader is shown that the argument was about authority rather than about evidence.

Ibn ʿAbbās names the Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najrān as the two parties in view, and al-Ālūsī reads the sentence as the description of how deep the hostility of the two communities ran, since the repetition of the negation is a stronger form than a single denial. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading, with the following of their religion named as the price of their satisfaction. Because the sentence puts the condition in the future and denies it, the reader is shown that no concession short of the whole faith would have satisfied them, and the verse closes that door for the messenger.

**THE GUIDANCE THAT IS GUIDANCE**

The answer comes as a sentence to be spoken: ***“Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.””***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the declaration that the guidance of God is the guidance, with everything else shown to be straying. as-Saʿdī explains that the two communities called people to what they held and claimed it was guidance, and that the answer names the one guidance while what the others hold is desire. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading of the sentence and treats the two claims as mutually exclusive. Because the answer is put in the mouth of the messenger rather than stated about him, the reader is shown that the sentence is a public declaration rather than a private reflection.

The Book reports the same claim from the other side in another passage, where the community is warned not to believe anyone who does not follow their religion (3:73). Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the guidance as the religion of God, and Ibn ʿUthaymīn notes that the sentence names the guidance in the absolute, so that every other road is shown to be its opposite. Since the sentence is placed between the condition and the warning, the reader is shown that the declaration is the boundary that the messenger was not to cross.

**THE WARNING ABOUT DESIRES**

The verse then states what would follow: ***“And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge”*** ***“that has come to you, there would be none to protect”*** ***“or help you against Allah”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that no ally would stand for the messenger if he followed them, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading with the knowledge named as the thing that makes such a turn impossible. as-Saʿdī notes that the sentence is addressed to the messenger while the lesson belongs to the community, since the one who knows and then follows a desire loses his protection. The warning is placed in the mouth of a prophet so that no reader may think himself beyond it. Because the sentence names knowledge as what had already come, the reader is shown that the danger is not ignorance but betrayal of what a person knows.

The same warning appears in another passage, where the command is to judge by what has been revealed and not to follow the desires of others (5:48). al-Ālūsī keeps the closing words as the removal of every support, so that the sentence describes a person standing alone, and Ibn Kathīr keeps it as the strongest form of the caution. Since the verse ends with the absence of help, the reader is left with the two roads in front of him, and the sentence shows what waits at the end of the one the messenger was told to leave.

The case is like a man who is offered a seat at a table on condition that he denies his own father. The table is set, the host is smiling, and the man walks home.

---

## Verse 2:121

> Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers

**THOSE WHO FOLLOW THE BOOK**

The verse turns to a different group: ***“Those We have given the Book follow it”*** ***“as it should be followed. It is they”***. al-Ṭabarī collects the reports about those named here, whether the believers from among the companions or those from the earlier community who accepted the message, and he keeps the sentence as the description of a people whose reading of the Book produced action. al-Qurṭubī sets the views side by side, with one report naming the companions and the Book as the Qur'an and another naming those who submitted from the Children of Israel, and he keeps both readings open. al-Baghawī records the report about the group who came by sea with the envoy from the king of Abyssinia, forty men, thirty-two of whom were from that land. Because the sentence describes a following rather than a reciting, the reader is shown that the Book's own measure of its readers is what they do with it.

The following described in the sentence is drawn out by as-Saʿdī, who explains that the reading here means the following of the Book, so that its lawful becomes lawful for the reader and its unlawful becomes unlawful, and its clear commands are carried out. al-Jalālayn keeps the same point, with the reading as it was revealed named as the state of the people described. Ibn ʿUthaymīn sets out the construction of the sentence and notes how the two statements inside it relate, which keeps the reader's attention on the people rather than on a formula. Because the sentence joins the giving of the Book to the following of it, the reader is shown that a gift unopened is not yet a gift received.

**WHO BELIEVES IN IT**

The verse then names the result: ***“who ˹truly˺ believe in it.”***. al-Ālūsī reads the sentence as the statement of the believers among the People of the Book, placed after the account of those who refused, so that the two groups are shown in contrast. Ibn ʿAbbās names the believers from the earlier community, among them a learned man and his companions and a monk, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the reports about those who are meant. Because the sentence ties belief to the following of the Book, the reader is shown that faith here is described by its fruit rather than by its label.

The Book names the same people in another passage, where the believers, the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians who believe in God and do good are promised their reward (2:62), and the two sentences are read together. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the passage turns to the honest among the People of the Book after dealing with those whose denial was hopeless, and the verse is read as the other side of the same account. Since the sentence arrives after the refusal of the previous verses, the reader is shown that the Book keeps a place open for whoever follows what he has been given.

**THE LOSERS**

The verse closes with the opposite case: ***“As for those who reject it, it is they”*** ***“who are the losers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that those who deny the Book have lost the share they were given, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading of the two halves of the verse. al-Ālūsī treats the closing sentence as the counterpart of the opening one, so that the reader sees one Book and two responses with their two ends. Because the sentence does not name a punishment but a loss, the reader is shown that the fault is measured first against what was in the person's own hand.

The lesson also reaches the reader who holds a book he does not follow. The verse describes the following of the Book as the mark of belief and the rejection of it as a loss, and it leaves the middle ground unnamed. Since the passage has dealt with the claims of the two communities, the reader is shown that the question was never which Book a person claimed but what he did with the one he had, and the sentence ends with the loss rather than with an accusation.

The case is like a patient who is given a prescription and puts it in a drawer beside the medicine. The prescription is correct, the drawer is full, and the illness is not impressed.

---

## Verse 2:122

> O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others

**THE REMINDER AT THE TURN**

The verse returns to the opening address of the sūrah: ***“O Children of Israel!”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as an admonition given to the community present at the time of the messenger, and he keeps it as the reminder of favours rather than as a reproach, so that the reader is shown the kindness before the account of the failures. The address is explained by Ibn ʿAbbās as the call to the descendants of Jacob, and he keeps the same note of a favour recalled rather than a debt demanded. Ibn ʿUthaymīn explains that the figure named here is Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham, and he notes that the address covers all who trace their descent to him rather than the men alone. Because the verse begins with a call to a whole people, the reader is shown that the account which follows is addressed to a community rather than to a crowd.

The long section of the sūrah dealing with the conduct of this people ends where it began, as Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes, and the two verses stand as the frame of the account. The pair of verses is kept together by Ibn Kathīr with the warning that follows, so that the reminder and the caution stand in one place. Because the address is repeated at the close of a long account, the reader is shown that the reminder is not new information but a summons to attention.

**THE FAVOURS REMEMBERED**

The sentence states what is to be remembered: ***“Remember My favours upon you”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the favours as the gifts already recounted in the sūrah, and Ibn ʿAbbās names the deliverance of the forefathers from the tyrant as the first of them. al-Jalālayn keeps the sentence as the reminder of the same favours named earlier in the sūrah, so that the reader meets the repetition as a summary rather than as a new claim. Because the favours are named as belonging to God rather than to the people, the reader is shown that the memory being asked for is a memory of the Giver.

The Book states the same reminder twice in the sūrah, once in the opening address and once here, and the two are read as one frame (2:40). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the account in view as the long middle of the section. Since the verse asks for a remembrance rather than for a response, the reader is shown that the ground of the account is gratitude, and the failures that follow are measured against it.

**THE HONOUR AND ITS MEANING**

The sentence then names the distinction: ***“and how I honoured you above the others”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the honour as the preference given to that people in their own time, and al-Ālūsī notes that the verse stands in the same block as the warning that follows it, so that the honour is named beside the responsibility. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sense of a preference given to the forefathers, and Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the same reading of the two halves of the sentence. Because the honour is stated as something given rather than earned, the reader is shown that the distinction carried no claim of its own.

The lesson also reaches a community that inherits a distinction. The sentence names the favour and the honour, and it does not name a privilege that passes down without the conduct that the rest of the sūrah describes. Since the address is followed immediately by the warning about a day on which no one will help another, the reader is shown that the credit of the past is not the currency of that day.

The case is like a family that keeps the founder's medal on the wall and forgets the trade he practised. The medal is genuine, the workshop is closed, and the name is still signed on nothing.

---

## Verse 2:123

> And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given

**THE WARNING ATTACHED TO THE REMINDER**

The verse follows the reminder with a caution: ***“And guard yourselves against the Day”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as the warning given to the people who had just been reminded of their favours, and he keeps the guarding as the taking of protection from what that Day holds. Ibn ʿUthaymīn explains the same instruction as the taking of a shield against the punishment, so that the sentence is a shelter offered rather than a threat announced. al-Ālūsī notes that the verse repeats a warning already given earlier in the sūrah, and he treats the repetition as a reinforcement for a people who had been addressed so often. Because the caution comes directly after the mention of favours, the reader is shown that a gift and a reckoning can be remembered in the same breath.

The Book states the same warning in the earlier address with the same terms, and the two passages are read as one (2:48). Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sentence as the command to fear the torment of that Day, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading of the opening. Since the verse is addressed to the people who had received the favours, the reader is shown that the more a person has been given, the more the day of accounting concerns him.

**NO SOUL HELPS ANOTHER**

The sentence then states what that Day will be like: ***“when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the clause as the statement that no person will settle anything for another, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, with the repayment named as the thing that no soul performs on behalf of another. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sense that even the closest help will fail there, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the three denials in their order. Because the sentence begins with the closest bond a person knows, the reader is shown that the failure is not of willingness but of power.

The three denials that follow are each explained with the same plainness. al-Ṭabarī keeps the ransom as the price that will not be accepted, the intercession as the plea that will not carry, and ***“and no help will be given”*** as the aid that will not arrive, and al-Ālūsī keeps the same three in the same order. The Book records the same three denials with the same words in the earlier passage, where no intercession is accepted and no ransom taken (2:48). Because the sentence lists what will not be taken, the reader is shown that the Day is not a market in which standing or wealth can be exchanged. The reason the three denials are named rather than described is that each one removes a hope a person may be carrying, and the reader is left with none of them.

**WHAT THE VERSE LEAVES THE READER**

A person who is told that no one can help him on a particular day has been told where to place his reliance now. The verse does not describe the Day so much as it empties it of the supports people carry, and it leaves the reader with the work he can still do. Because the sentence names no intercessor and no price, the reader is shown that preparation is the only currency that survives the journey.

The lesson also reaches a reader who trusts in the standing of his family or community. The verse names a day on which no soul helps another, and it places that day immediately after a reminder of inherited favours, which is where such trust is usually placed. Since the sentence ends with the absence of help, the reader is left facing what he has done rather than who he knows, and the verse closes with a silence that has to be answered before the Day arrives.

The case is like a traveller who arrives at a border crossing with letters of introduction and no passport. The letters are impressive, the officers are polite, and the gate does not open.

---

## Verse 2:124

> ˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”

**THE TESTING AND THE FULFILMENT**

The verse opens a new account: ***“˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments”*** ***“which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model”***. al-Ṭabarī explains the testing as the trial of the servant, and he keeps the words as the commands and prohibitions with which the prophet was charged, and he notes that the sentence reports a fulfilment rather than a discussion. al-Qurṭubī notes that the mention of the House and the direction of prayer led into this account, since Abraham was the one who built the House, and he keeps the many questions that follow in his commentary. The report that the commands were ten traits, five concerning the head and five concerning the body, is recorded by Ibn ʿAbbās, and the fulfilment is kept as compliance with them all. Because the sentence names the trial and the fulfilment in one breath, the reader is shown that the man was tested and passed before he was honoured.

The testing is explained by as-Saʿdī as the way God deals with His servants, so that the false is shown from the true, and he notes that the account of Abraham is placed here because every community among the People of the Book claimed him. al-Jalālayn keeps the words as the commands and prohibitions, and he mentions the rites of the pilgrimage among what they included. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the passage as the answer to a claim of inherited leadership, since the account shows what the leadership was built on rather than who was descended from whom. Because the sentence puts the fulfilment before the promise, the reader is shown the order in which the honour came.

**THE ROLE MODEL AND THE OFFSPRING**

The sentence then reports the question and the answer: ***“for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the question as the request of a father for his descendants, and he keeps the answer as the statement that the covenant does not reach those who do wrong. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the promise of leadership for the people and the limitation that follows it, and al-Ālūsī keeps the attachment of the account to the verses around it. Because the question is asked by a prophet who had just been honoured, the reader is shown that the concern was for others rather than for himself.

The answer is the hinge of the passage: ***“Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.””***. al-Jalālayn keeps the sentence as the exclusion of the unjust from the promise, so that the honour is tied to conduct rather than to descent. as-Saʿdī keeps the same reading and notes that the trial came first so that the answer would rest on what had been shown. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the covenant as the promise of leadership, and he notes that the wrongdoers are shut out of it. Because the answer does not cancel the promise but limits those who inherit it, the reader is shown that a line of descent is not a claim on God.

**WHAT THE PASSAGE ANSWERS**

The community addressed in the previous verses had claimed a place because of their ancestor, and the verse answers that claim with the ancestor's own story. Abraham was tested, fulfilled, and then given the leadership, and the covenant was not extended to the wrongdoers among his descendants. Because the verse places the condition inside the promise, the reader is shown that the leadership of Abraham is a standard rather than a birthright.

The Book names Abraham in another passage as a model of devotion and uprightness (16:120), and the same word for the role model is used there of the man himself. al-Ṭabarī keeps the promise as the leadership that others follow, which is the sense the sentence carries at its close. Since the passage has just closed the account of the earlier community's failures, the reader is shown why the Book turns here, and the verse leaves the claim of descent answered by the conduct of the ancestor.

The case is like a company that is proud of its founder and cannot name a single practice he would recognise. The founder's portrait hangs in the lobby, his standards are on paper, and the work on the floor is someone else's.

---

## Verse 2:125

> And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺

**A PLACE OF RETURN AND OF SAFETY**

The account continues with the House: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre”*** ***“and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham”*** ***“as a site of prayer.””***. al-Ṭabarī explains the centre as the place to which people return, and he keeps the sanctuary as the safety granted at the House, and he notes the attachment of this account to the testing of Abraham before it. al-Baghawī gives the same sense of the centre as a place of return, and he records the reports of the early commentators that people come to it from every direction. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the House as the resort to which people turn, and he keeps the command to take the standing-place as a place of prayer. Because the sentence names both a gathering and a safety, the reader is shown that the House was given two gifts at once, one for the body and one for the fear that troubles it.

The sanctuary is described by as-Saʿdī as a safety that extended to everything within the sacred area, so that even animals and trees were left in peace there, and he notes how the people honoured it before the coming of the message. al-Jalālayn keeps the sense of the sanctuary as a place where no blood is shed and no wrong is done, and he keeps the standing-place in the same sentence. al-Ālūsī notes that the name used in the verse is the familiar designation of the House, and he collects the reports about the station of Abraham. Because the safety is named as a gift of God rather than as an achievement of the people, the reader is shown that the peace of the sanctuary rested on its Owner rather than on its guards.

**THE TWO WHO WERE ENTRUSTED**

The sentence then names the two servants given the task: ***“And We entrusted Abraham”*** ***“and Ishmael to purify My House”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the purification as the cleansing of the House from what does not belong in it, and he keeps the two names together as the recipients of the charge. The command to purify the House for the worshippers is kept by Ibn Kathīr, who names the four states of worship that the verse lists. The question that the pairing raises is noted by Ibn ʿUthaymīn, since the father was the builder, and the answer is kept from the following passage, where the two are shown raising the foundations together. Because the charge is given to two rather than to one, the reader is shown that the service of the House was shared from the beginning.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān opens its account of the House in the course of the story of Abraham, and the passage is read there as part of the answer to the community who denied the messenger while claiming the legacy of the House. The purification described in the verse is kept by al-Jalālayn as the removal of what defiles the House, whether the idols or the words that do not belong there. Since the task is named as a purification and not as a construction, the reader is shown that the honour lay in keeping the House fit for its purpose.

**THE PEOPLE THE HOUSE IS FOR**

The verse then names those for whom the House is prepared: ***“for those who circle it”*** ***“who meditate in it”*** ***“and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the four states of worship as the description of those who belong in the House, and he keeps the order of the sentence. al-Baghawī keeps the same reading of the circling and the standing and the bowing and the prostration, and as-Saʿdī keeps the note that the House is a place of return for the religious and worldly interests of the people. Because the worshippers are named rather than the guardians, the reader is shown what the House is for, and the standing-place of Abraham is placed inside the same sentence as a place of prayer.

The Book names the same House in another passage, where the site is assigned to Abraham with the command to purify it (22:26), and the two verses are read as one charge. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the standing-place among the signs of the House in the passage that lists them (3:97). Since the verse ends with the worshippers, the reader is left with the purpose of the building rather than with the honour of the builders, and the account turns the reader toward the prayer.

The case is like a house that a family builds for guests and then argues about who owns the gate. The guests are arriving, the gate is open, and the argument is not about them.

---

## Verse 2:126

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”

**THE PRAYER FOR SECURITY AND PROVISION**

The verse reports the prayer: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure”*** ***“and provide fruits to its people”*** ***“those among them who believe in Allah”*** ***“and the Last Day.””***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the prayer as it is reported, with the Prophet asking for safety for the place and provision for its people, and he notes the sense of the request as it stands in the sentence. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading and notes that the prayer asked for security and a wide provision for the descendants and for others, and al-Baghawī explains that the place was a valley with no cultivation, which is why the provision of fruits had to be asked for. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same pair of requests and notes that the second was restricted to the believers. Because the two requests cover safety and food, the reader is shown a prayer that reaches for the two things a household cannot provide for itself.

The restriction in the prayer is explained by as-Saʿdī as an act of courtesy before God, since the first request had been made without qualification and the second was tied to the believers. al-Jalālayn keeps the sense of the security granted, with the city made a sanctuary where lives are protected, and he keeps the provision in the same sentence. al-Ālūsī notes that the place referred to was the barren valley, and he keeps the prayer in the setting of the account of the House. Because the prayer names the believers while the answer widens the field, the reader is shown that the bounty of God is not confined to the terms of the request.

**THE ANSWER ABOUT THE DISBELIEVERS**

The verse then reports the answer: ***“He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves”*** ***“for a little while”*** ***“then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!””***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the answer as the statement that the disbelievers receive their share in this world, and he keeps the closing words as the verdict on their end. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading and notes that the enjoyment granted is brief by comparison with what follows it, and Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the answer in the flow of the account. Because the duration of the enjoyment is named before its end, the reader is shown that the delay is a mercy that has a limit.

The pair of worlds in the sentence is drawn out by as-Saʿdī, who keeps the blessed end for the believers and the return to the Fire for those who refuse, so that the two requests of the prayer are answered in the same sentence. al-Jalālayn keeps the closing description of the destination, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the verse among the prayers of Abraham, keeping his readiness to carry out what was commanded. The Book uses the same closing phrase of a destination in another passage, where it follows the description of those who earn wrath (3:162), and the two sentences are read together. Since the verse ends with the destination rather than with the enjoyment, the reader is shown where the weight of the sentence lies.

**WHAT THE PASSAGE LEAVES WITH THE READER**

A prayer for a place and its people is answered in a way that runs past the praying prophet, and the verse keeps both halves of the answer in front of the reader. The security was granted, the provision was granted, and the reckoning of the next life was left where it belongs. Because the answer mentions the disbelievers directly, the reader is shown that no community is exempt from the account, and the prayer of a prophet did not spare them.

The passage has moved from the House and its purification to the prayer that was made beside it, and the reader is left with a picture of worship and provision joined in one place. The Book reports the same prayer in another passage, where Abraham settles part of his offspring in the barren valley and asks that they may be provided for (14:37). Since the verse closes with the destination rather than with the city, the reader is shown that the safety of a place is a mercy for a time, while the account of its people reaches further than any wall.

The case is like a man who plants a garden in a valley and prays for rain and a fence, and who is told that the fence will hold for a season while the harvest is weighed in another year. The rain came, the fence stands, and the weighing is still ahead.

---

## Verse 2:127

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE FOUNDATIONS RAISED**

The verse returns to the two builders and their work: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord!”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the raising of the foundations as the work of the two together, and he explains the foundations as the base on which the walls were then set. al-Qurṭubī collects the reports on that term, with one view naming the base of the building and another naming the walls, and he notes that the well-known reading is the first. The account itself is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān as a further mark of the prophet's obedience. He had left a fertile land and settled his wife and child in a barren desert, and now he took up the labour of the House with his own hands. Because the sentence shows the two working rather than the result they obtained, the reader is shown the kind of service that built the House.

The mention of the memory is explained by al-Ālūsī through the turn in the wording. The scene is kept in the present so that people may imitate the pair in carrying out hard acts of worship while praying at the same time. The pair's inner state is described by as-Saʿdī, who keeps the two in a condition of fear and hope, working with their hands and asking acceptance with their words. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the report that they built and then prayed that the work on the House be accepted, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same order of building and asking. Since the request comes while the work is still going on, the reader is shown that the praise was not the point of the building, and acceptance was.

**THE PRAYER FOR ACCEPTANCE**

The sentence reports the prayer itself: ***“Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are”*** ***“indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the request as the asking that the deed be received, and he keeps the two names at the close as the ground of the petition, since the One who hears the prayer knows the intention behind the work. as-Saʿdī draws out the purpose of the request, which is that the building should carry a benefit that reaches others, so the pair asked for more than a completed wall. al-Jalālayn keeps the two names in the same order, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps them as the reason the request could be made at all. Because the pair ask after doing the work rather than before it, the reader is shown that prayer and labour belonged together in the account of the House.

The Book reports the same labour elsewhere in the story of Abraham, where he settles part of his offspring in the barren valley and asks that the hearts of people be drawn to them (14:37). Ibn Kathīr keeps the raising of the House among the marks of the prophet's rank, and the Book names the House as the first sanctuary established for humanity in another passage (3:96). Since the verse closes on the two names, the reader is left with a God who hears what was asked and knows what was meant, which is the comfort the two builders needed as they worked.

**WHAT THE TWO BUILDERS TEACH**

A person who works for a cause can begin to look at his own hands, and the verse shows the two builders looking higher at the end of the work than at the beginning. Because the request is for acceptance, the reader is shown that the value of a deed is not settled by its size or its finish. That is why the account of the House is interrupted by a prayer, and the interruption is the lesson.

The lesson also reaches a reader who works without asking. The pair in the verse built, then asked, and the order of the two acts shows that effort is not a substitute for dependence. Since the request is put in the first person plural of two men who were father and son, the work and the prayer are shown as shared. The sentence leaves a picture of two pairs of hands lifted from the same stones.

The case is like two craftsmen who finish a bridge and stand at its middle asking that no one be hurt on it. The bridge is sound, the traffic is coming, and the prayer continues over the traffic.

---

## Verse 2:128

> Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**THE SUBMISSION ASKED FOR**

The prayer continues with a request for the two of them: ***“Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the request for continuance in the state the two already held, so that the prayer asks for a firmness rather than for a beginning. al-Qurṭubī notes that the two prophets asked for constancy and permanence, and he explains the submission here as covering faith and deeds together rather than a single act. al-Baghawī gathers the descriptions attached to the request, with the pair asking to be ones who affirm the oneness of God, obey Him, act sincerely and humble themselves before Him. Because the request comes from men already submitted, the reader is shown that the state itself needs to be asked for and kept.

al-Ālūsī sets out two ways of taking this submission, one from the yielding of the self and the other from making the self sincere, and he keeps the request for constancy in the words of the prayer. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense of obedience and sincerity, with the pair asking to worship God without associating anything with Him, and al-Jalālayn keeps the first half of the prayer in the same order. Since the sentence asks for what the two already practised, the reader is shown that no rank in the account makes the next step a formality.

**THE NATION FROM THE DESCENDANTS**

The prayer then widens to those who would come after: ***“and from our descendants a nation”*** ***“that will submit to you. Show us our rituals”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the nation as a body of people rather than an individual, and he keeps the request for the rituals as the asking for the forms of worship to be shown. al-Baghawī explains the nation as a community that follows the prophets, and he keeps the request for the rites in the same sentence. as-Saʿdī notes that the pair prayed for themselves first and for their offspring after, so the reader sees the order of concern in the prayer. Because the request moves from the two to a whole people, the reader is shown the reach of the hope that stood beside the new walls.

The rites named in the prayer are explained by al-Qurṭubī as the places and forms of the pilgrimage, and he keeps the reports about the showing of them. al-Jalālayn notes that the mention of the descendants is partitive, so the prayer asks for a portion of the line rather than for all of it, which keeps the request within what God had promised. The Book commands the pilgrimage in another passage, where the call goes out to all people to come on foot and on every lean camel (22:27). The same rites are named in the passage that praises the way of the forefather (22:78). Since the prayer asks to be shown, the reader is shown that worship in this account was taught rather than invented.

**THE TURNING IN GRACE**

The prayer closes with a request and a description: ***“and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the turning as the acceptance of the two back into favour, and he keeps the two names at the close as the ground of the request. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading of the pair of names, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the whole prayer proceeds from the same sense of awe and knowledge that marked the prophet throughout his life. Because the request for grace comes after the requests for work and for descendants, the reader is shown that the pair did not trust in the labour of their hands or in the future of their line.

The lesson reaches a reader who prays for outcomes and forgets forgiveness. The two in the verse ask for a nation, for rites, and for grace in the same breath. The order places the mercy last but not smallest, since it covers whatever fell short in everything asked before it. al-Ālūsī keeps the two names as the fitting close of a prayer made by two servants rather than by two equals. Since the sentence ends on mercy, the reader is left with the two names as an answer rather than as a title, and the verse closes where a person's fear most needs to close.

The case is like a farmer who asks for rain, for seed, and for machinery, and then asks that the year be forgiven for whatever he gets wrong. The requests are real, the tools are ordered, and the last request is the one he repeats most often.

---

## Verse 2:129

> Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”

**THE PRAYER FOR A MESSENGER**

The prayer turns to the line of the descendants: ***“Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger”***. al-Ṭabarī reads this request as the prayer of the two prophets for the messenger who would come at the end, and he records the saying that the messenger described himself as the answer to the prayer of his father Abraham and the glad tidings of Jesus. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same identification and records the reading which has the request made for the last of the people rather than their first, and he reports the search for the man who could tell the companions whose prayer had been answered. al-Baghawī keeps the sense that the messenger came from the believing people who descended from the two, and he notes the report of the scholar who said he had been waiting for the answer to this prayer. Because the sentence asks for one to be raised from among the descendants, the reader is shown that the prayer looked forward across centuries.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the messenger as one raised from the offspring of Ishmael, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading under the heading that the prophet's coming was the answer to this request. al-Jalālayn notes that the petition was granted with the sending of the messenger who came to the people of the House. Because the request is placed in the mouth of a father praying with his son beside him, the reader is shown the kind of hope that was standing on the foundations of the House as they were laid.

**THE WORK OF THE MESSENGER**

The sentence lists the tasks: ***“who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book”*** ***“and wisdom, and purify them.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the reciting first, then the teaching, then the purification, and he explains the purification as the cleansing of the people from what defiles them. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same order and notes that the Book and the wisdom are named together so that the reading is not separated from understanding. al-Ālūsī reads the request for a messenger from among the people as part of the mercy of the prayer, since one from their own number would care for them and they would understand him. Because the list moves from the recitation to the teaching and then to the cleansing, the reader is shown that the message was meant to reach the ear, the mind and the character in that order.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gives its attention to the opening task in the list, and it keeps the recognition that the recitation is the first work of the messenger. Because the recitation is placed before the teaching, the reader is shown that the words were meant to be heard before they were explained. The same three tasks are named in the Book for the messenger who was sent in another passage. The reciting of the revelations and the purification of the people are named there with the teaching of the Book and the wisdom (62:2). Ibn Kathīr keeps the verse as the prayer of Abraham and Ishmael for the one who would carry those tasks, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the list in the same order. Since the request names the work rather than the person, the reader is shown what the messenger was sent to do, and the answer to the prayer is measured by that list.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The prayer ends with the two names: ***“Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.””***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the pair as the ground of what was asked, with the power that can raise a messenger from the line and the wisdom that can time his coming. al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair, and the Book uses the same two names of the sender in the passage that lists the same tasks for the messenger of the community (3:164). Because the names come at the end of a request for something that had not yet happened, the reader is shown that the two who prayed were relying on power and wisdom rather than on probability.

The lesson also reaches a reader who prays for a future he may not see. The two in the verse asked for a messenger who would come long after them, and the answer was granted to a people they never met. al-Baghawī keeps the report about the scholar who had been waiting for the fulfilment, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same hope in the material around the verse. Since the prayer ends with the two names, the reader is left with a request that was answered outside the lifetime of the askers, and the verse shows what such a prayer can reach.

The case is like a farmer who plants a row of slow-growing trees at the edge of a field he will not harvest. The trees are for a house he will never live in, and the shade arrives anyway.

---

## Verse 2:130

> And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous

**THE QUESTION THAT HAS ONE ANSWER**

The verse puts a question with no open answer: ***“And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool!”***. al-Ṭabarī reads the sentence as the question that narrows to a single class of person, since no one with a sound mind would leave the way of the prophet once its worth had been recognised. al-Qurṭubī sets out the construction, with the question standing in the place of a declaration, and he keeps the sense that the turning away is the act of a person who has cheated himself. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the fool as the one who has ruined himself and lost his own share, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense of a person who has cheapened his own soul. Because the sentence asks who would do such a thing, the reader is shown that the question is answered in the asking, and the act is described as a self-inflicted loss.

The occasion of the verse is recorded by al-Baghawī, where a learned man among the people of the Book called his two nephews to the faith and reminded them of what their own Scripture said about the prophet, and one of them accepted while the other hung back. al-Ālūsī keeps the reading of the sentence as a denial and a wonder that any sound mind would turn away from a way so clear, and he keeps that sense through the verse. Because the fault is traced to the judgement of the person rather than to any defect in the way, the reader is shown where the loss falls.

**THE CHOICE IN THIS LIFE**

The verse then states what was given to the prophet: ***“We certainly chose him in this life”*** ***“and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the choosing as the selection made in this world, and he keeps the promise of the next life as the confirmation of the choice. as-Saʿdī explains the same contrast, with the chosen man shown first in the world he lived in and then in the world to come, so that the reader sees both halves of the honour. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the choosing as the selection for the friendship of God, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading of the two halves. Because the sentence names both lives in one breath, the reader is shown that the honour given to this prophet was not limited to a reputation among people.

The same position is stated in the Book for the prophet in another passage, where he is named as one who submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist (3:67), and the Book asks in a further passage who could be better in faith than one who submits and follows his way (4:125). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as the refutation of the claims made by the two communities about their own standing, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the verse as the statement of the choice and the promise. Since the two lives are named together, the reader is shown that the fool who turns away loses a share in both.

**WHAT THE VERSE PUTS IN FRONT OF THE READER**

A question with one answer is a way of letting the reader supply it himself, and that form keeps the reader from arguing with a statement. The man named in the verse gave up ownership of a religion, a lineage and a promise, and the sentence shows the trade as a loss rather than as a choice. Because the question is asked about the faith rather than about the man, the reader is shown that the way itself was never in question.

The lesson also reaches a reader who inherits the name of a tradition without its content. The sentence names the prophet, the choice and the promise, and it places the turning away in the same sentence. Since the passage has dealt with the advice of the prophet to his children, the reader is shown what the advice was for, and the verse leaves the question with him rather than with the fool it describes.

The case is like a man who inherits a house with an orchard and lets it go for the price of the gate. The gate was solid, the orchard was bearing, and the buyer was laughing all the way home.

---

## Verse 2:131

> When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”

**THE ORDER GIVEN**

The verse reports the exchange that stood behind the honour: ***“When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.””***. al-Ṭabarī explains the order as the call to make worship sincere for God and to bow to Him in obedience, and he keeps the answer as the acceptance that followed at once. al-Qurṭubī notes the occasion reported for the order, which some place at the time when the prophet was shown the star, the moon and the sun and reasoned his way past them, and he keeps the answer as the submission of the man to the Lord of everything. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, with the order given after the prophet came out of the fire, and he keeps the answer as the declaration that God is one. Because the sentence reports both halves of the exchange, the reader is shown that the word was given and returned in the same moment.

The order itself is explained by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān as the basic principle of the prophet's religion, since the call to submit was answered by a man who agreed willingly rather than under pressure. Ibn Kathīr keeps the exchange as the evidence of the prophet's readiness to obey, and al-Jalālayn keeps the answer in the same words with nothing added. Because the answer names the Lord of all worlds rather than the command alone, the reader is shown that the prophet placed himself among the whole creation that answers to God, and the sentence gives the reason the call was so easily met.

**THE ANSWER GIVEN**

A command that arrives with an offer of honour is still a command, and the verse shows the prophet answering the rank with obedience rather than with a question. al-Ālūsī keeps the construction of the sentence, where the moment of the order is the moment that the choosing in the previous verse is attached to, so that the honour and the obedience are shown to belong to one scene. as-Saʿdī keeps the same connection, with the submission of the prophet shown as the content of the praise given to him. Because the sentence has no pause between the order and the answer, the reader is shown that no hesitation stood between them.

The Book records the same readiness in another passage, where the prophet is named as one who submitted in all uprightness (3:67), and the answer given here is read as the history of that description. al-Ṭabarī keeps the answer as the model for the reader, since the submission asked of the prophet is the submission asked of the community. Since the passage is addressed to a people who argued about inherited claims, the reader is shown that the ancestor's religion was settled by one sentence, and the verse leaves it at that.

**WHAT THE VERSE SHOWS ABOUT SURRENDER**

Surrender that is asked for and given in the same breath is not the absence of a self; it is the placing of a self under the right authority. The verse shows the prophet setting his own answer in the largest possible frame, which is the Lordship that holds every world at once. Because the answer names all the worlds, the reader is shown that the call to submit was not a withdrawal from life but an entry into the widest order there is.

The lesson also reaches a reader who treats obedience as a loss of standing. The verse follows a passage about being chosen and honoured, and it puts the command to submit at the centre of that honour rather than beside it. Since the exchange is reported without commentary, the reader is left with the two sentences themselves, and the verse lets the smallest dialogue in the passage speak for the largest claim.

The case is like a craftsman who is offered a partnership and answers by asking what the work requires. The partnership is real, the tools are ready, and the first order is the proof of the answer.

---

## Verse 2:132

> This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”

**THE ADVICE AND THE TWO WHO GAVE IT**

The verse records what the two fathers left to their children: ***“This was the advice of Abraham”*** ***“as well as Jacob”*** ***“to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen”***. al-Ṭabarī explains that the advice carried the very word the prophet had spoken, which was the declaration of submission to the Lord of the worlds, and he keeps the two fathers as the givers of the same counsel. al-Qurṭubī sets out the two views on what was bequeathed, whether the religion or the word the prophet had just spoken, and he prefers the second because the word stands closest in the passage, so that the children were told to repeat it. al-Baghawī keeps the readings of the verb in the sentence and treats the two forms as two ways of saying the same thing. Because the advice is given by two prophets to their own households, the reader is shown that the religion of the passage was passed on as an inheritance of words and not only of blood.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the report that the prophet's counsel to his sons was the declaration that there is no god but God, and that he gave it while dying, and that Jacob gave the same counsel to his children. al-Ālūsī reads the sentence as a praise of the prophet for bringing others to the perfection he had reached himself, which is a second rank after his own excellence. Because the sentence names both fathers in one line, the reader is shown that the counsel was not the habit of one household, and the advice of the two is placed side by side as one inheritance.

**THE CHOICE AND THE CHARGE**

The advice itself is reported in the sentence: ***“for you this faith”*** ***“so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.””***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the choosing as the act of God, and he keeps the charge at the close as the command to hold the state until the end of life. al-Jalālayn keeps the same pairing, with the faith named as the thing chosen for the children and the closing charge as the concern that they remain in it. The counsel is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān as the religion handed on within the household so that it outlives the one who carried it. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, with the chosen faith named as the religion of submission. Because the charge speaks of dying rather than of living, the reader is shown that the concern of the two fathers was for the end of the road, which is the part no one can see in advance.

The same charge is given to the community in another passage, where the believers are told to be mindful of God and not to die except in a state of full submission (3:102). al-Baghawī keeps the choice of the faith as the mark of favour, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the advice as a word the children could carry. The Book names the same way in the passage that praises the forefather, and the two sentences are read together as one counsel given at two different times. Since the charge is issued by a father to his children, the reader is shown that the most valuable thing a household can pass on is the way it holds at the end.

**WHAT A HOUSEHOLD PASSES ON**

An inheritance of property is divided among heirs, and an inheritance of counsel is not divided at all; the verse shows the second kind being given to children by name. Because the advice is short, the reader is shown that the whole religion can be carried in a sentence, and the sentence is the one the prophet had answered his Lord with. That is why the two fathers repeated it rather than writing a longer message, since the thing they wanted kept was a direction rather than a set of details.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is a parent or a guardian. The verse shows advice given while the fathers were still living and repeated near the end, and the concern in it is not for the children's comfort but for their finish. Since the passage has dealt with the claims of two communities about their ancestors, the reader is shown what the ancestors themselves were busy with. It was making sure the next generation submitted, and the verse leaves that as the work of a household.

The case is like a father who is leaving a house and a business to his children and is worried about the one thing on the door: whether they will keep the sign above it. The house is paid for, the business is running, and the sign is the inheritance he keeps mentioning.

---

## Verse 2:133

> Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”

**THE QUESTION PUT TO THE LISTENERS**

The verse begins with a challenge: ***“Or did you witness”*** ***“when death came to Jacob?”***. al-Ṭabarī explains the opening as a new question put to the people being addressed, and he keeps the sense that they were not present at the scene they were claiming to judge. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading and names the addressees as the two communities who disputed with the believers, so that the question is aimed at a claim rather than at a fact. al-Baghawī records the occasion reported for the verse, in which the Jews told the prophet that Jacob had charged his sons with their own religion on the day of his death, and the sentence answers them from their own story. Because the question asks about their presence, the reader is shown that the claim rested on a scene none of them had seen.

The scene itself is kept by al-Jalālayn as the setting in which the patriarch charged his sons, and by al-Ālūsī with the report that the reason for the revelation was exactly the claim just described. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the question and the answer as the content of the verse, with the people of the Book addressed as a body. Because the verse turns a claim about a deathbed into a question about witnesses, the reader is shown that the argument was answered on its own ground, and the account of the patriarch is placed where the claim had been made.

**THE QUESTION AND THE ANSWER**

The verse then reports the scene: ***“He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?””*** ***“They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the question as the concern of a father at the end of his life, and he keeps the answer as the pledge the children gave as one body. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same exchange in the account, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the answer as the children's declaration of the worship of the God of their forefathers. The scene is kept by as-Saʿdī as proof that the household of the forefather was one household in worship, since the children answered their father with a creed rather than with a claim. Because the question is about worship rather than about property, the reader is shown what the dying man thought worth asking about, and the answer shows that the household was ready with it.

The answer names the line: ***“Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac”***, and then gathers all of them into one: ***“the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.””***. al-Ālūsī keeps the reading of the names as the ancestors of the line, and he keeps the closing declaration as the pledge of the children. al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense, with the God of the forefathers named and the submission declared. Because the sentence gathers three generations into a single object of worship, the reader is shown that the line itself was never the point, and the closing words place the children with the whole creation that answers to God.

**WHAT THE SCENE SETTLES**

A claim about a deathbed is easy to make and impossible to check, and the verse settles this one by producing the conversation the claimants had not witnessed. Because the answer of the children is a pledge of worship rather than a claim of privilege, the reader is shown what the patriarch's household was built on. That is why the passage does not argue about the claim at length; it sets the scene in front of the claimants and lets the words do the rest.

The lesson also reaches a reader who inherits a story about a great ancestor. The verse shows the ancestor asking one question at the end, and the answer has nothing to do with the standing of the family. Since the passage has just recorded the advice given by two fathers, the same concern is shown to have run through the household. The verse leaves the reader with the question and the answer that mattered, which is the worship of the One God.

The case is like a family that gathers at a bedside to hear about a will and is asked a different question instead. The papers are ready, the notary is waiting, and the question that is being asked is the one that settles the estate.

---

## Verse 2:134

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

**THE COMMUNITY THAT HAS GONE**

The verse states the distance between the generations: ***“That was a community”*** ***“that had already gone before.”***. al-Ṭabarī names the community as the prophets and their households who had passed, and he keeps the sentence as the statement that the earlier generation has left the field. al-Qurṭubī sets out the construction of the opening sentence, and he keeps the sense that the people named have finished their course. al-Ālūsī explains the reference as the forefather and his sons, and he collects the senses the description carries, since the description covers a body of people gathered by one purpose. Because the sentence closes an account of one household's history, the reader is shown that the story is now addressed to those who came after it.

al-Jalālayn keeps the same reference, with the forefather and his sons named as the community that has passed, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sentence as the statement that the group has perished and left its record behind. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the practical point out of the two verses, which is that the good deeds of ancestors do not carry a person, and the misdeeds of ancestors do not burden him. Because the verse marks the passing of a generation, the reader is shown where the claims of descent lose their force, and the account moves from a family to its readers.

**WHAT EACH GENERATION EARNS**

The verse then states the rule: ***“For them is what they earned”*** ***“and for you is what you have earned.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the pairing as the statement that each body of people has what its own hands produced, and he keeps the two halves side by side. The first half is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the good the earlier people earned, and the second as what the later people earn. Because the sentence repeats the same verb for both groups, the reader is shown that the measure is the same for a prophet's household and for those who followed it, and no one is credited with the work of another.

The same rule is stated in the Book for every soul, where no one reaps except what he sows and no burdened soul carries the burden of another (6:164). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the two sides of the rule in view, and the Book states the same sentence about the same community in the passage that closes the account of the children of Israel (2:141). Since the verse puts the two earnings beside each other, the reader is shown that the ledger is personal, and the sentence leaves him with his own page rather than with the names on the cover.

**WHAT THE VERSE FREES THE READER FROM**

A reader who is told that he will not be asked about the dead has been freed from an argument and given a task. The verse removes the weight of a family's record in both directions, since neither the glories nor the failures of the earlier community are charged to the one who came later. The closing words, ***“And you will not be accountable”*** ***“for what they have done”***, remove the last support a person may lean on. That statement is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the assurance that the later people will not be questioned about the deeds of the earlier ones. Because the sentence mentions what each group earned, the reader is shown that the account is kept for the living rather than for the famous dead.

The lesson also reaches a reader who leans on a name. The verse names a community that had gone before, gives it its own earnings, and then turns to the listener with the second half of the same rule. Since the sentence ends with the removal of the question about the ancestors, the reader is left with the question about himself, and the passage closes the account of the household on that note.

The case is like a man who inherits his grandfather's ledgers with every page filled in. The figures are real, the debts are settled, and the new book on the desk has his own name on the cover.

---

## Verse 2:135

> The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”

**THE INVITATION AND ITS ANSWER**

The verse reports the invitation: ***“The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No!”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the call of each community to what it held, with the guidance held out as the reward for agreeing. al-Qurṭubī notes that each group invited the believers to what it practised, so that the sentence records two invitations rather than one, and he keeps the answer as the rejection of both. al-Baghawī records the occasion in which the leaders of the Jewish community in Medina were the speakers in view, and al-Jalālayn keeps the sense that the first of the two claims belonged to the Jews of Medina and the second to the Christians of another town. Because the invitation speaks of guidance, the reader is shown that the claim was about the outcome rather than about the contents, and the answer refuses the premise rather than the wording.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading of the dispute between the two communities and the believers, and al-Ālūsī reads the sentence as the answer to their call after the answer to their claim about their ancestors, so that the two objections are dealt with in order. Because the answer opens with a single word of refusal, the reader is shown that the invitation was declined at the door rather than discussed inside.

**THE FAITH OF THE FOREFATHER**

The answer then states the position: ***“We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright”*** ***“who was not a polytheist.””***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the answer as the statement that the believers follow the way of the prophet whose uprightness was pure, and he notes that the rejection of polytheism is part of the description. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same sense and notes that each of the two communities had been invited to what the other held, so the answer names the one way that preceded both. as-Saʿdī explains the description as the turning of the person toward God and away from everything else, so that the way named is a direction of the heart before it is a list of rules. Because the sentence names the prophet rather than a school, the reader is shown that the argument was settled by history rather than by preference.

The same way is named in the Book in another passage, where the prophet is told to follow the faith of Abraham, the upright (16:123), and the Book states in a further passage that he was neither a Jew nor a Christian but one who submitted in all uprightness (3:67). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as the answer to the two communities who claimed him for themselves while departing from his way, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the verse as the declaration of the way the believers follow. Since the prophet is named as the upright one, the reader is shown that a claim to his legacy is tested by his way rather than by a family tree.

**WHAT THE VERSE DECIDES**

Two communities invited the believers to their own guidance, and the answer named a way that belonged to neither of them. Because the answer is put in the mouth of the messenger, the reader is shown that the position was a declaration rather than a preference, and the sentence gives the reason for the refusal at the same time as the refusal itself. That is why the passage does not weigh the two invitations against each other; it points to the root from which both had grown away.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is asked to join a group for the sake of certainty. The verse shows the invitation made with guidance as the price, and it answers with a way whose definition is a man's life rather than a community's claim. Since the sentence ends with the refusal of polytheism, the reader is left with the boundary the answer drew, and the verse closes the argument where the two communities had left the road.

The case is like two houses inviting a traveller to their tables and naming their courtyards as the destination. The traveller names the road they both left, and the table is set somewhere else.

---

## Verse 2:136

> Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us; and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”

**THE CREED SET OUT**

The verse gives the believers their statement: ***“Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah”*** ***“and what has been revealed to us”*** ***“and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the instruction to the community to declare what it holds, and he lists the contents in the order the sentence gives them, with the revelation to the community placed first and the earlier books after it. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading and records the report about the People of the Book who used to read their Scripture in one language and explain it in another when the Muslims came to them. al-Ālūsī notes that the address here is to the believers rather than to the two communities, since the sentence is a declaration of what they hold instead of an argument with those who refused. Because the sentence begins with the name of God and then lists what was sent, the reader is shown the order of the creed, and the sentence keeps the community inside the line of the prophets rather than outside it.

The verse is read by as-Saʿdī as gathering everything that must be believed, with the heart's assent that carries the acts of the limbs along with it. The whole religion, he notes, is contained in the sentence. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the instruction as the teaching given to the believers so that they would have a clear statement of what the oneness of God means, and al-Jalālayn keeps the list of the earlier prophets with the scrolls given to the first of them named. Because the sentence names the earlier prophets one by one, the reader is shown that the new community was not asked to begin a new history.

**THE LINE OF THE PROPHETS**

The sentence continues the list: ***“and his descendants”*** ***“and what was given to Moses, Jesus”*** ***“and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the descendants as the tribes of the people of Israel, and he keeps the list of the prophets with Moses and Jesus named in it, and he explains the closing clause as the refusal to accept some and reject others. Ibn Kathīr keeps the list and the closing clause in the same order, and al-Jalālayn keeps the prophets from the Lord as the source of all that was given. Because the sentence names many messengers and then states that no difference is made among them, the reader is shown that the community's faith was in the sending rather than in a favourite.

The same creed is stated in the Book for the messenger and the believers in another passage, where the angels, the books and the messengers are named, and the same refusal to distinguish between them is declared (2:285). The sentence in this verse repeats the same clause with the same words as a further passage (3:84). as-Saʿdī keeps the clause as the mark that separates the community's creed from the practice of the two who accepted some prophets and rejected others. Since the sentence lists the messengers as one body, the reader is shown that the community's faith was never a choice among messengers, and the clause closes the door on that choice.

**THE SUBMISSION AT THE END**

The sentence closes with a declaration: ***“And to Allah we all submit.””***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the closing words as the statement that the community hands itself over to God, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading of the declaration. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the verse as the summary of the faith the earlier passages had defined, and al-Ālūsī keeps the closing words as the fitting end of a creed that began with belief. Because the sentence begins with what is believed and ends with what is done with the self, the reader is shown that the creed of the passage is not a list to be recited but a position to be held.

The lesson reaches a reader who holds a list of beliefs and stops there. The verse puts the declaration of submission in the same sentence as the belief in God and the books, and the closing words place the person inside the faith rather than beside it. Since the passage has answered the invitations of the two communities, the reader is shown what the answer looks like when it is spelled out, and the verse leaves the community with a sentence it can say about itself.

The case is like a household that answers a survey about its faith by naming every room in the house and then the door it lives behind. The rooms are all listed, the survey is complete, and the answer is the address.

---

## Verse 2:137

> So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺. But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE CONDITION AND ITS ANSWER**

The verse puts the two communities before a single test: ***“So if they believe in what you believe”*** ***“then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the comparison as one between two acts of belief rather than between two objects. He notes that the wording came down using the clearer of the two Arabic constructions. al-Qurṭubī keeps the address as one made to the messenger and his community together, and he notes that a reader among the earliest reported the sentence in the form ***“in what you believe”*** without the added particle, which settles the sense further. Because the sentence sets one condition for both groups, the reader is shown that the road is a single road, and the answer is a single answer.

The teachers read the two halves as one statement about guidance. al-Baghawī keeps the reading of the earliest commentator in the form that names the thing believed rather than its likeness. He keeps the further reading in which the likeness stands for the whole of the faith. as-Saʿdī draws the point out: guidance lies in this belief and nowhere else, and the claim that it lay in one of the two inherited systems was the very claim being answered. Because the sentence follows the creed the believers had just been taught, the reader is shown that the standard had been stated before the test was set.

**THE TURNING AWAY**

The second half states what follows a refusal: ***“But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the turning away as a refusal to believe with that same belief. He explains the closing description as the state of people who have split off from the body of the believers. al-Jalālayn keeps the sense of open conflict with the religion, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the description as conflict with the truth itself. al-Ālūsī reads the first half as a manner of drawing the opponent out so that he is confounded by the answer, since the offer is put in his own terms before it is set aside. Because the refusal is described as opposition rather than as a simple mistake, the reader is shown that the sentence is about a position taken and not about an error of information.
