The promise that follows is kept by al-Ṭabarī as the assurance that the messenger would be shielded from the harm of those who turned away, and al-Jalālayn records how that promise was fulfilled in the dealings of the first community in Medina. as-Saʿdī keeps the same reading, with the two openings of the sentence turned toward the hearer. Because the promise is given without a condition, the reader is shown that the outcome of the encounter did not rest on the response of the opponents.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The sentence ends with the ground of both halves: ***“But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the two names as the reason the warning can be trusted, since the One who hears what is said knows what is intended. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading, with the guarding placed in the hands of the One who hears and knows. The Book promises the same guarding in another passage, where the messenger is told that God is enough for him. The question of guidance is answered in the same terms, (2:272 — **“it is Allah who guides whoever He wills”**). Because the two names come last, the reader is shown that the sentence closes on knowledge rather than on the dispute.

The belief asked for here is placed by Ibn ʿUthaymīn within the wider account of faith, since assent of the heart is what the tongue states and what the limbs then carry out. That is why the verse can reduce a long argument to one condition, since the matter turns on what a person holds and not on what he inherits. Since the passage has just set out the creed of the believers, the reader is shown where the line was drawn.

The case is like a race where two runners are told the course and then asked to run it. The road is marked, the finish is fixed, and the difference afterwards is only in who moves.

---

## Verse 2:138

> This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way? And we worship ˹none but˺ Him

**THE IMAGE OF THE DYE**

The verse answers the two communities with a picture taken from their own practice: ***“This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah.”***. al-Ṭabarī records that the Christians used to dip their children in water and claim a consecration for them. He keeps the answer as the statement that the dye of God is submission to Him. al-Qurṭubī keeps the first words as standing in place of the faith named in the verse before it, and he records the report that the two communities dyed their children into their own systems, while the dye of God is the religion He sent. Because the sentence uses an image from the ceremonial of the objectors, the reader is shown that the answer is aimed at their confidence rather than at their words.

al-Baghawī gathers what the teachers said about the image, and he keeps the reading that the religion leaves its mark on a person as dye marks cloth. The same passage keeps the further reading that the religion clings to the one who carries it and does not leave him. The image is drawn out further by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, since a colour is seen at once by anyone looking, and the signs of a pure faith should show in a face, in movements and in habits. Because the sentence gives the faith a visible mark, the reader is shown that the religion of the passage was never meant to stay hidden in the mind.

**THE QUESTION PUT TO THE CLAIMANTS**

The middle of the verse asks a question that closes the argument: ***“And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way?”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the question as the statement that no dye is finer or purer than this one. It is the religion God sent with Noah and with the prophets after him. as-Saʿdī reads the question as one of wonder, since a sound mind at once sees the answer and no alternative is left standing. The question is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās with the answer already folded into it. Because the question is put after the image has been explained, the reader is shown that the beauty of the dye is not a matter of taste.

al-Jalālayn notes that the first words of the verse reach back to the declaration of belief in the verse before, so that the dye and the creed are one thing named twice. al-Ālūsī keeps the image as one of purification, since the mark of the faith works through the person as the dye works through the cloth. Because the verse answers by describing a process rather than by listing rules, the reader is shown how the faith was meant to change a person rather than to sit beside him.

**THE WORSHIP AT THE CLOSE**

The sentence ends with a declaration: ***“And we worship ˹none but˺ Him”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the closing words as the statement that the community worships God alone. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense, with the declaration of oneness following at once. as-Saʿdī keeps the two parts of the religion in the sentence: a heart that is sincere for God alone, and a following of what He sent, since worship is the whole of what He loves in speech and deed. The natural way of the heart is named in the Book in a further passage: (30:30 — **“the natural Way of Allah”**). Because the verse ends on worship rather than on the dye, the reader is shown that the mark was never the aim and the service was.

The image also reaches a reader who carries a label without its content. A cloth keeps its colour only while the dye holds, and the verse shows the same rule worked into a person. Since the question in the middle offers no alternative to the dye of God, the reader is left with the plainest possible answer to the claims of the two communities.

The case is like a woman who dyes a bolt of cloth and then leaves it in the rain. The colour was true, the cloth was good, and the visible mark depended on what came after the dipping.

---

## Verse 2:139

> Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺

**THE DISPUTE**

The verse turns the argument over: ***“Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah”*** ***“while He is our Lord”*** ***“and your Lord?”***. al-Qurṭubī records the reports that the dispute was the claim of the older communities to a rank above the believers. They held that they were nearer to God through their fathers, their books and their freedom from idol worship. as-Saʿdī sets out what such a dispute should be at its best, since a discussion over a difference is meant to bring the mistaken back by the nearest road, to establish the proof against the stubborn and to make the true and the false plain. Because the sentence names the shared Lordship in the middle of the dispute, the reader is shown that the claim being answered was one of ownership.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the question as one about the religion of God, with the shared Lordship placed at its centre. al-Jalālayn keeps the reading in which the point objected to was the raising of a messenger from among the Arabs. al-Ālūsī notes that the address turns to the messenger alone because the duty of the answer belonged to him first. Because the question is put to people of two systems with one Lord, the reader is shown that neither group could own what both had received.

**THE TWO LEDGERS**

The verse then puts a distance between two sets of records: ***“We are accountable for our deeds”*** ***“and you for yours.”***. The answer is kept by Ibn Kathīr as a complete renunciation on both sides. He keeps the same position from a further passage where the messenger is told to say: (10:41 — **“My deeds are mine and your deeds are yours”**). as-Saʿdī draws the consequence out: a Lord who is Lord of all does not owe honour to one group over another, and the differences among people are settled by what each has done. Because each side is left with its own ledger, the reader is shown that the argument about standing was never a matter of lineage.

al-Ṭabarī keeps the same two halves as the statement that the account of each community is kept for itself, and al-Jalālayn notes that the sentence leaves open the possibility that good deeds on one side would deserve honour. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the three verses as the close of the section in which the claims of the two communities were answered. The community is now taught to declare that it worships God alone and has kept its religion clear of association. Because the verse ends the section with a declaration, the reader is shown that the answer was meant to be said as much as understood.

**THE DEVOTION NAMED**

The sentence closes on the direction of worship: ***“And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺”***. The closing words are kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the acknowledgement that God alone is worshipped. al-Jalālayn keeps them as the statement that the service is sincere in religion and in deed, with the contrast to the other side implied. The Book gives the same sharing of Lordship in another passage: (42:15 — **“Allah is our Lord and your Lord”**). Because the closing words state devotion rather than victory, the reader is shown what the community was asked to hand over: not an argument but itself.

The lesson also reaches a reader who argues about rank. One Lord is named for both sides, one ledger for each, and one devotion for the community that answers. Since the question stands in the middle of the sentence, the reader is shown that the dispute is settled by the two clauses that surround it, which give God to both parties and the account to each.

The case is like two brothers in a courtyard arguing over which of them the house belongs to, while both live off the same orchard. The land is one, the fruit is shared, and the argument will end when someone opens the ledger.

---

## Verse 2:140

> Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?” Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah? And Allah is never unaware of what you do

**THE CLAIM PUT TO THEM**

The verse takes the argument to its root: ***“Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?”*** ***“Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?”***. al-Ṭabarī sets out the two readings of the opening and keeps the sense that the question is joined to the question before it, so that the whole passage puts one challenge after another to the same people. al-Qurṭubī keeps the readings of the last part of the sentence where some reciters read it with the second person and others with the third, and he keeps the sense in both forms. Because the opening names the forefathers by name, the reader is shown that the claim was about the family of the prophet and not about an abstract point.

as-Saʿdī reads the verse as another claim from the same people, since they held that they were nearer to those prophets than the believers, and he keeps the answer as a choice that leaves them no room, since either they are the ones who know or God is. al-Jalālayn keeps the same choice, and he keeps the passage from the Book in which the forefather is described as neither of the two, since the Book says of him: (3:67 — **“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian”**). Because the sentence offers the claimants a choice of knowers, the reader is shown that the answer depended on nothing but their own claim about themselves.

**THE HIDING OF THE TESTIMONY**

The verse then names the offence: ***“Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah?”***. The description is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the concealment itself, with the sentence carrying the sense of insolence and daring as well as of disbelief. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading, and he notes that the community had been given the knowledge and then let it lie unused. The Book warns against the same act in a further passage, where the people of the Book are told: (2:42 — **“Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly”**). Because the verse asks who could be worse, the reader is shown that the concealment was set among the gravest of acts rather than among small ones.

al-Baghawī keeps the reports on what was hidden and on the men who were asked about it, and al-Ālūsī keeps the sentence as a charge against the scholars who knew. Because the wrong named in the sentence is an act done to knowledge, the reader is shown that the fault lay in the will rather than in the understanding.

**THE CLOSE OF THE ARGUMENT**

The sentence ends with a reminder: ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you do”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the closing words as the warning that nothing of the concealment is lost, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense with the deed named as a thing seen. Because the passage has just asked who could be worse than the hider of testimony, the reader is shown that the question was never open, and the sentence closes the case with the knowledge of God.

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps quiet about what he knows. The knowledge is named first and the concealment after, so that the fault is the gap between the two. Since the claim about the forefathers had been repeated for several verses, the reader is shown that the argument was not finally about history, and the last words place the whole dispute under the eye of the One who knows.

The case is like a witness who stands in a courtroom holding the paper in his hand and then says he has nothing to add. The paper is in his pocket, the court is waiting, and his silence is the offence.

---

## Verse 2:141

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

**THE SENTENCE REPEATED**

The verse brings back a sentence already given: ***“That was a community”*** ***“that had already gone before.”***. al-Ṭabarī names the community as the forefather and his sons with the tribes of Israel, and he keeps the sentence as the statement that they have finished their course. The same reading is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās, with the group described as one that perished and left its record behind. Because the same words had already closed the earlier section, the reader is shown that this sentence is a fixed boundary and not a passing remark.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reason for the repetition, since the sentence carried a threat and a warning: if those prophets were repaid by what they earned, then those who came after are more fit to be repaid in the same way. al-Ālūsī keeps the repetition as emphasis against what has settled into people's natures, that is, the pride in fathers and the reliance on them, and he keeps the further reading that the sentence is a confirmation of the warning. Because the sentence is repeated and not reworded, the reader is shown that no argument afterwards can reopen the matter.

**WHAT EACH ONE EARNS**

The middle of the verse states the rule: ***“For them is what they earned”*** ***“and for you is what you have earned.”***. The first half is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the good the earlier people gathered, and the second as what those who come later gather, with al-Jalālayn keeping the same pairing without adding to it. as-Saʿdī draws the reason for the repetition out: attachment to created beings had to be cut off, and what counts is what a person himself is described by, not the deeds of his forebears. Because the two halves use the same verb, the reader is shown that the ledger is one ledger for everybody.

The same rule is stated in the Book for every soul, (53:39 — **“each person will only have what they endeavoured”**), and Ibn ʿUthaymīn notes that the benefits of this sentence were set out earlier in the passage and refers his reader back to them. Because the verse gives the earlier people what they earned and the later ones what they earn, the reader is shown that no share of another person's work is transferred by name or by blood.

**THE WEIGHT LIFTED**

The closing words remove a burden: ***“And you will not be accountable”*** ***“for what they have done”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sentence as the assurance that those who came later will not be questioned about the deeds of the earlier ones, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same sense with the warning already noted. Because the sentence was repeated at the point where the two communities had rested their case on their ancestors, the reader is shown exactly where the claim was cut.

The lesson also reaches a reader who leans on a family name. The verse gives the ancestors their record and the hearer his own, and it closes the question about the two. Since the passage has answered the claims of the two communities about their forefathers, the reader is shown that the reply ends with a sentence about himself, and the verse leaves him holding only his own page.

The case is like a man who keeps a chest of his grandfather's medals in the hallway. The medals are real, the chest is polished, and none of them will answer for him on the day the ledger is opened.

---

## Verse 2:142

> The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”

**THE QUESTION FORESEEN**

The verse announces an objection before it is made: ***“The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?””***. al-Ṭabarī explains the description as the mark of people who were foolish about the truth itself. He names the objectors as the scholars of the Jews and the people of hypocrisy. al-Jalālayn notes that the opening verb is put in the future to inform of what had not yet happened, which is one of the signs of the unseen in the passage. Because the objection is reported before it is raised, the reader is shown that the answer was prepared for it and not invented afterwards.

al-Ālūsī gathers the reports on who the description covers, since some teachers kept it to one of the three groups and others kept it wide enough to include all who objected. He keeps the sense that the description fitted those who had taken their position by imitation rather than by reflection. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the question as the objection of the ignorant among the Jews and the idol worshippers. as-Saʿdī keeps the report that the community had faced the earlier sanctuary while it was in Mecca and for a period after the migration. The change raised a wonder among those who were watching. Because the question is about a change rather than about a rule, the reader is shown that the matter was about obedience and not about geography.

**THE SHARED OWNERSHIP**

The answer is given at once: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the answer as the statement that every direction belongs to God and no quarter of the earth has a claim of its own. The One who owns both sides may turn His servants where He wills. as-Saʿdī notes that the objection is answered with a short statement rather than with a long defence, and the Book states the same ownership in another passage: (2:115 — **“To Allah belong the east and the west”**). Because the answer begins with ownership, the reader is shown that the question about direction had been answered before it was asked.

The same reading is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās, with the House named as the place the community was turned towards. In the material that opens this passage, Ibn ʿUthaymīn notes that the opening verb carries the sense of what is still to come, so that the news of the objection is given as news of the unseen. The wider point is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, since a servant turns to God in worship and God is not held by any direction. The direction is a command to be obeyed and not a place where He is confined. Because the verse follows the change of direction with the ownership of the earth, the reader is shown that the command was never about the earth.

**THE GUIDANCE GIVEN**

The sentence closes on guidance: ***“He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the closing words as the statement that the road is reached by God's favour and not by ancestry. He keeps the connection to the earlier passage in which guidance was named for those who held the belief of the community. Because the answer to a question about direction turns into a statement about guidance, the reader is shown that the passage is about obedience as a whole and not about a change of place.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is unsettled by a change he did not expect. The verse reports the objection, answers it with ownership, and then names the Straight Path, so that the reader's attention is moved from the earth to the road. Since the questioners are described as foolish, the reader is shown what the description was based on: not on the question itself but on the position from which it came.

The case is like a guest who asks the family why the table was moved from one room to another. The house belongs to the host, the meal is the same, and the guest has been fed in both rooms.

---

## Verse 2:143

> And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah. And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity

**THE UPRIGHT COMMUNITY**

The verse states the rank given to the community: ***“And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the community as a generation singled out and placed above the other religious bodies. He keeps the description as the mark of a people set in the middle. al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports in which the middle position is explained as justice, and notes that the community is placed below the prophets and above the nations. Because the sentence names a position between two others, the reader is shown that the rank was given for a purpose and not for display.

The same rank is named in the Book in a further passage, where the community is called to strive for the cause of God. The passage states that this community was chosen and eased in its religion: (22:78 — **“and laid upon you no hardship in the religion”**). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the plain sense of the description as moderation and balance, and keeps the report in which the position was explained as justice and excellence. Because the verse states the purpose before the test that follows, the reader is shown that the community's standing was tied to a duty.

**THE TEST IN THE CHANGE**

The verse then explains the change: ***“We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the change as the means by which the loyal and the wavering were separated. The earlier direction was the one the community had faced before the command came. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, with the messenger as the one whose command was the test. Because a change of practice can be followed for many reasons, the reader is shown that the test lay in obedience to a command rather than in the act itself.

al-Ālūsī keeps the sentence as an interjection placed between two connected speeches. He keeps the reading that it confirms the answer to the objectors, since the community whose testimony is accepted is the one fit to be followed. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the change as the means by which those who followed the messenger were shown from those who turned back on their heels. Because the separation was made by a small command, the reader is shown what kind of loyalty was being measured.

**THE FAITH NOT LOST**

The sentence then gives comfort: ***“It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the difficulty as the weight the change placed on the community. The exception is the ease given to those whom God steadied. as-Saʿdī keeps the same reading, with the test made light for the ones whose hearts had been guided. Because the exception is named at once, the reader is shown that the weight of the command was measured as well.

The verse closes with a promise: ***“And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith.”*** and ***“Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the promise as the assurance that the worship performed towards the earlier direction was not lost. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense, with the reward kept whole. The two names at the close are read by al-Jalālayn as the ground of the promise, since the One who is gracious does not let the work of His servants fall. Because the passage ends on mercy after naming a hard test, the reader is shown where the difficulty of the command was finally placed.

The lesson also reaches a reader who fears that a change has wasted what he did before. The test, the faithful and the reward are named in the same breath. Since the community was set in the middle to bear witness, the reader is shown that the honour was carried by those who held their ground, and the promise at the close covers the ground already walked.

The case is like a caravan asked to change its route in the middle of the desert. The water skins are already filled, the road is different, and the guide promises that the distance covered will still count.

---

## Verse 2:144

> Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺—wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what they do

**THE FACE LIFTED**

The verse opens with a scene of waiting: ***“Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the movement as a turning of the face upwards. The messenger used to raise his gaze before the change came. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, with the look directed upward in hope of the revelation and in longing for the command. Because the sentence describes a repeated act rather than a single moment, the reader is shown how long the wish had been carried.

al-Ālūsī keeps the reports on what stood behind the wish, since the change of direction would remove an argument from the other side and would turn the community towards the sanctuary of the forefather. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the reading in which the gaze was raised in expectation of the angel coming with the command. Because the messenger's wish is reported without reproof, the reader is shown that the scene is one of nearness rather than of fault.

**THE ANSWER GIVEN**

The answer follows immediately: ***“that will please you.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the promise as a mark of honour, since God is described as hastening to the pleasure of His messenger. The face is named rather than the sight because the concern was greater than the look. Ibn ʿUthaymīn notes that the sentence is confirmed by an oath, a particle and a heavy ending, and that the plural form of the verb is used for majesty, so that the promise is stated in the strongest form the language carries. Because the promise is put in that form, the reader is shown that the wish was answered with more than it asked.

The command is then given: ***“So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺”*** ***“wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the command as the institution of the direction that would remain, and he keeps the sense of the setting of the face towards a thing. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading with the House named as the direction. Because the command is given to the messenger and then to all who are with him, the reader is shown that the address moved from one person to a community within a single breath.

**THE WITNESS OF THE SCRIPTURE**

The verse then notes what the other side knew, since the earlier books had told them what the change would be. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that the people of the earlier books recognised the command as coming from God. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, with knowledge standing against their denial. Because the verse records their knowledge and their conduct together, the reader is shown that the denial to come was made in full knowledge.

The closing words are kept by al-Ṭabarī as the warning that nothing of the denial is hidden: ***“And Allah is never unaware of what they do”***. The Book repeats the command in a further passage, and it states there: (2:149 — **“This is certainly the truth from your Lord”**). Because the sentence ends on the knowledge of God, the reader is shown that the truth of the command did not depend on the recognition of the others.

The lesson also reaches a reader who waits for an answer to a wish he has not spoken. The verse shows the wish seen, the answer given and the command published in three steps. Since the closing words name the knowledge of God, the reader is left with the scene of a face lifted to the sky and an answer already on its way.

The case is like a child who keeps looking at the door while the family is deciding about a trip. The decision is already being made inside, and the child's watching is the only visible part of it.

---

## Verse 2:145

> Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺, nor would you accept theirs; nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another. And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers

**THE PROOFS THAT DO NOT HELP**

The verse states what no evidence can change: ***“Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that the refusal was settled before the proof arrived. The argument was being used as an excuse rather than as a search. al-Jalālayn keeps the opening as an oath followed by a condition, so that the sentence is one of the strongest forms of denial. Because the verse speaks of every possible proof, the reader is shown that the matter had passed beyond evidence.

al-Baghawī records the request the communities had made for a sign. He keeps the answer as the statement that the signs would not bring them to the direction of the community. as-Saʿdī keeps the reading in which the messenger's concern for their guidance had reached its limit, and keeps the note that their refusal came from stubbornness rather than from ignorance. Because the proofs and the refusal are named together, the reader is shown where the responsibility of the messenger ended.

**THE DIRECTIONS THAT DO NOT MEET**

The middle of the verse sets out three separations: ***“nor would you accept theirs”*** ***“nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that the lines would not meet. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, with the two communities facing places different from one another. The three denials are kept by Ibn Kathīr in the order given, so that the refusal runs in every direction at once. Because the communities are separated from each other as well as from the believers, the reader is shown that the division was not made by the new command.

al-Ālūsī keeps the sense that the mention of the people of the earlier books in the full form of the description adds weight to the rebuke, since knowledge had reached them and changed nothing. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same point, since the fault named in the verse is not a lack of proof but a refusal to give assent. Because the verse lists three refusals rather than one, the reader is shown how far the separation reached.

**THE WARNING AT THE CLOSE**

The sentence ends with a warning: ***“And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you”*** ***“then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the warning as one addressed to the messenger while intended for the community. Following their wishes meant returning to their direction. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, with the sentence framed as a prohibition that carries a threat. Because the warning is put in the second person to the one least likely to fall, the reader is shown how heavy the matter was held.

The Book keeps the same warning in a further passage, where the messenger is told: (5:49 — **“do not follow their desires”**). A further passage states that obedience to the majority of those on earth would lead away from the path: (6:116 — **“they would lead you away from Allah's Way”**). Because the closing words name the wrongdoers, the reader is shown that the danger described was not a small slip but a wrong done to the self.

The lesson also reaches a reader who hopes to satisfy everyone. The verse shows a refusal that no proof would move, a division that already existed, and a warning against following the other side for the sake of peace. Since the passage has just settled the direction, the reader is shown that the way forward was to hold it.

The case is like a man who offers to change the position of his house so that a neighbour will be pleased. The neighbour is unmoved, the house is where it was built, and the offer has cost the owner his own doorway.

---

## Verse 2:146

> Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly

**THE RECOGNITION**

The verse sets out what the other side already knew: ***“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺”*** ***“as they recognize their own children.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the recognition as the knowledge of the scholars among the two communities, who knew where the command of God had settled, and he keeps the comparison as one of plain recognition without confusion. al-Baghawī keeps the reports on the believers among the people of the earlier books, and keeps the exchange in which one of the companions was asked about this recognition and answered that he knew the messenger as he knew his own son. Because the sentence compares recognition of a person to recognition of a child, the reader is shown that the knowledge in view needed no proof.

al-Jalālayn keeps the same comparison and records the saying of the scholar who held that his recognition of the messenger was stronger than his recognition of his own son, since no doubt could attach to it. al-Ālūsī notes that the scholars are the ones intended, since recognition belongs to them by right, and he keeps the reading in which the sentence stands as a state of the earlier people. Because the sentence names the knowledge so plainly, the reader is shown that the hiding which follows was done with open eyes.

**THE HIDING OF THE TRUTH**

The verse then names the act: ***“Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly”***. The description is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the concealment of what stood written about the messenger in their own books, and the same reading is kept by as-Saʿdī, with the group described as the greater number of those who disbelieved. Because the verse adds knowledge to the concealment, the reader is shown that the fault lay in the will and not in the understanding.

The comfort and the warning are drawn out of the sentence together by as-Saʿdī: the report consoles the messenger and the believers, and it warns them against the harm that such people could do. The Book states the same act as one forbidden in an earlier passage, where the people of the Book are told: (2:42 — **“Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly”**). Because the sentence names a group rather than a whole people, the reader is shown that the description was drawn with care.

**THE KNOWLEDGE IN COMMON**

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps these verses as the completion of the account of the two communities, since the earlier passage had shown them denying in public what they knew in private, and the present verse shows the same conduct towards the messenger. al-Baghawī keeps the same sense through his reports, and The Book names the same people in a further passage: (6:20 — **“Those to whom We gave the Scripture”**). Because the verse places recognition and concealment in the same sentence, the reader is shown that the knowledge of the earlier books was never in question.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is handed a truth and does nothing with it. The gift is named first, then the recognition, then the hiding, so that the fault is shown as a series of steps. Since the passage has answered every claim of the two communities, the reader is shown what remained after the arguments had run out, which was a page kept closed on purpose.

The case is like a man who keeps a map in his pocket while insisting he cannot find the road. The road is drawn in full, the signs are up, and the map is the only thing that has been folded away.

---

## Verse 2:147

> ˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord, so do not ever be one of those who doubt

**THE TRUTH NAMED**

The verse states where the matter stands: ***“˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord”*** ***“so do not ever be one of those who doubt”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that the truth is what God taught His messenger. He adds that the direction the messenger had been turned towards was the House. Because the sentence follows the account of the concealers, the reader is shown that the doubt it warns against was being planted by others.

The reference of the truth is kept by al-Qurṭubī as the facing of the House rather than what the other side reported about its own direction. He records one of the early reciters reading the opening in the accusative with the verb of knowing. al-Ālūsī reads the sentence as a fresh statement aimed at the people who hid what they knew. Because the sentence names the source of the truth, the reader is shown that the matter did not rest on the reports of either community.

**THE WARNING TO THE MESSENGER**

The second half speaks to the messenger himself: ***“so do not ever be one of those who doubt”***. al-Jalālayn notes that the form warns against the disposition of doubting rather than against a single act. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense, that the doubters are those who waver over what they know. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the opening as a sentence that settles what came before, so that the concealment of the others would not shake the messenger's certainty. Because the warning is given to the one least likely to fall, the reader is shown how heavy the matter was held.

The Book repeats the same two-part sentence in another passage, (3:60 — **“This is the truth from your Lord, so do not be one of those who doubt”**). Ibn Kathīr keeps the report that the people of the earlier books knew the truth of what the messenger brought. Because the verse pairs truth with a warning, the reader is shown that knowledge alone does not settle a person.

**WHAT THE VERSE FIXES**

A doubt that arrives after knowledge is not the same as a search for evidence, and the verse marks the difference. That is why the source of the truth is named before the danger of wavering. Since the passage has just dealt with people who hid what they knew, the reader is shown what their concealment was meant to produce.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is shaken by the confidence of others. The verse does not argue with the doubters; it addresses the messenger and names the truth he holds. Since the warning is put in the strongest form the language carries, the reader is left with the sense that the ground under the community was already settled.

The case is like a man who has seen the deed of a house with his own eyes and then hears a neighbour dispute the boundary. The deed is in his hand, the neighbour is guessing, and the doubt would cost him nothing but his footing.

---

## Verse 2:148

> Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good. Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE DIRECTIONS OF THE NATIONS**

The verse accounts for the differences among people: ***“Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the opening as a statement about each community of a religious system, with the possessors of the system understood in the sentence. He keeps the report of the earliest commentator that it means every owner of a community. al-Ālūsī collects the readings, with one sense covering the nations and another covering the sides of the House for the community itself. Because the sentence allows every group its own direction, the reader is shown that the difference was never a defect in the command.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the two reports, one naming the direction each group chose and the other naming the House as the direction given to the prophets. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the observed fact behind the sentence, since every community with a tradition has had an orientation of its own. Because the sentence states the situation plainly, the reader is shown that the real question was never the direction but the obedience.

**THE RACE IN GOOD WORKS**

The verse then turns from the difference to a command: ***“So compete with one another in doing good.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the command as the call to hasten to what is right, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps it as the call to the community to outdo the other nations in obedience. as-Saʿdī draws the point out, since the honour lies in obeying God and seeking nearness to Him, which is agreed upon in every revealed law. Because the command is given directly after the mention of differing directions, the reader is shown where the rivalry was meant to run.

The Book repeats the command in the account of the earlier books, (5:48 — **“So compete with one another in doing good”**). al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense and adds that the gathering promised in the next sentence is the gathering of the Day of Resurrection. Because the sentence turns the competition towards deeds rather than towards positions, the reader is shown what could be compared between one group and another.

**THE GATHERING AND THE POWER**

The verse closes with the promise of the return: ***“Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺.”*** and ***“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the gathering as the assembly in which each person is repaid for what he did. as-Saʿdī keeps the whole verse as a consolation to the community and a warning to those who disputed. Because the gathering is promised to everyone everywhere, the reader is shown that no direction on earth could take a person out of the account.

The lesson also reaches a reader who measures himself against others instead of against the command. The verse leaves the directions where they are and moves the competition to good works. Since the last words name power over everything, the reader is left with an account that no distance escapes.

The case is like runners on different tracks who are told to keep their own lanes and to run their fastest. The lanes are parallel, the finish line is shared, and the only thing compared at the end is the distance covered.

---

## Verse 2:149

> Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. This is certainly the truth from your Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do

**THE COMMAND REPEATED**

The verse restates the command for every place: ***“Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the opening as a statement about every place a person may set out from, and he keeps the turning of the face as the facing of the House. al-Qurṭubī keeps the repetition as a confirmation of the command and as a mark of care for it, since the change had been very hard on the community. Because the repetition covers travel and residence alike, the reader is shown that the direction did not depend on where a person stood.

al-Jalālayn notes the same purpose in the repetition, since it shows that the rule applies on a journey and at home. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the House named as the direction of the forefather, and he keeps the closing warning as the statement that nothing hidden about the matter is lost. Because the command is repeated for the messenger after being given to the community, the reader is shown that the two addresses carry one ruling.

**THE TRUTH RESTATED**

The middle of the verse attaches the command to its source: ***“This is certainly the truth from your Lord.”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the emphasis in the sentence, since the particles were brought together so that no one would hold the slightest doubt and so that no one would take the matter as a preference rather than as an obligation. al-Ṭabarī keeps the same reading, with the command resting on the word of God rather than on the habit of a people. Because the sentence names the truth again, the reader is shown that the change was not a concession to any group in the city.

The command is given again in the previous passage, (2:144 — **“wherever you are, turn your faces towards it”**). Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the closing words as a warning about what the other side concealed, and al-Ālūsī keeps the sentence as one joined to the command to compete in good works. Because the truth is stated in the middle of a command, the reader is shown that the order and its ground were given together.

**THE WARNING AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a reminder: ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the closing words as the statement that God watches His servants in every state, so that they should mind their conduct and obey His commands. al-Ṭabarī keeps the same sense, with the deeds of people kept in view. Because the sentence finishes a passage about people who argued over a direction, the reader is shown that the argument had an audience greater than either side.

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps a rule in public and forgets it in private. The direction, the truth and the knowledge of God are named in one breath. Since the closing words cover everything done, the reader is left with a command that was never only about the place where he stands.

The case is like a servant who is told to face the door of the house wherever he works. The house is fixed, the instructions are plain, and the master can see the yard from every window.

---

## Verse 2:150

> Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it, so that people will have no argument against you, except the wrongdoers among them. Do not fear them; fear Me, so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided

**THE COMMAND FOR ALL**

The verse extends the command from the messenger to the community: ***“Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the two halves as one ruling for the messenger and for the believers after him, and he keeps the sense that the direction follows a person wherever he goes. al-Baghawī keeps the repetition as the confirmation of the change of practice, since a new ruling needed to be settled in the minds of the community. Because the two addresses stand together, the reader is shown that no member of the community stood outside the command.

Ibn ʿUthaymīn notes that the sentence had been given before in this passage and was repeated here for emphasis and as a preparation for what follows. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, with the repetition removing any ground for dispute about the change. Because the verse repeats what was already known, the reader is shown that the matter was important enough to be fixed twice.

**THE ARGUMENT SILENCED**

The verse then states the purpose: ***“so that people will have no argument against you, except the wrongdoers among them.”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the argument as the objection of the people of the earlier books, who knew from their own writings where the House stood. al-Baghawī gathers the reports on what the exception covers, with one reading limiting it to those who persist in the objection. Because the purpose named is the silencing of an argument, the reader is shown that the command was also a public answer.

al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that the objectors would be left without a case, and al-Ālūsī keeps the construction of the verse, where the sentence is joined to the whole passage rather than to the clause before it. Because the exception names the wrongdoers, the reader is shown that the argument was never made in good faith by all who raised it.

**THE FEAR AND THE FAVOUR**

The verse turns to the inner state: ***“Do not fear them; fear Me”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the two commands as the instruction to fear God rather than the talk of people, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading. Because the command is given after the mention of the wrongdoers, the reader is shown that the fear of people was the pressure the verse was removing.

The verse closes on the purpose of the whole passage: ***“so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the favour as the completion of the blessing by the appointment of the direction, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense with the guidance named at the end. The Book names the same completion in the passage of the final ordinances, (5:3 — **“completed My favour upon you”**). Because the sentence ends on favour and guidance, the reader is shown that the change of direction was a gift rather than a burden.

The lesson also reaches a reader who fears the opinion of a crowd more than the judgement of God. The argument, the fear and the favour are named in order. Since the favour is completed by the very command that raised the objection, the reader is left with the sense that the pressure was the last thing to be feared.

The case is like a family that moves its house to the right side of a plot and is told by neighbours that the old side was better. The plot is theirs, the door is fixed, and the neighbours were never the ones to please.

---

## Verse 2:151

> Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves—reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you never knew—

**THE MESSENGER FROM THEM**

The verse sets out the favour that outranks the rest: ***“Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the completion of the favour already named, and he keeps the messenger as one raised from the community itself. al-Qurṭubī keeps the readings on the opening particle, which stands for a dropped clause of comparison, so that the sense is that God completed the favour as He sent the messenger. Because the messenger came from the people, the reader is shown that the gift was close enough to be recognised.

The same sense of a messenger from their own line is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ālūsī notes in the same place that the sending is placed where the favour is meant. The Book describes the same coming in a further passage, (9:128 — **“a messenger from among yourselves”**). Because the verse ties the messenger to the community, the reader is shown that the favour was measured by the closeness of the one who brought it.

**THE TASKS THAT FOLLOW**

The verse then lists what the messenger does: ***“reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom”*** ***“and teaching you what you never knew”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the reciting first, then the cleansing, then the teaching, and he keeps the last clause as the instruction in what the community had no way of reaching. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the list as the answer to the prayer of the forefather, since the request for a messenger from the descendants was made at the building of the House. Because the list begins with recitation, the reader is shown that the words were heard before they were explained.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reciting as covering everything recited to the community, and he keeps the purification as the cleansing from what defiles a person. al-Jalālayn keeps the same order and names the wisdom as the ordinances the community was taught. Because the list ends with what the community could never have known, the reader is shown that the teaching was a gift rather than a discovery.

**THE PRAYER ANSWERED**

The Book names the same tasks for the messenger in another passage, (62:2 — **“reciting to them His revelations, purifying them”**). Ibn Kathīr keeps the verse as the statement that the favour was completed by the sending, and al-Baghawī keeps the reports in which the coming of the messenger is traced back to the prayer of the forefather. Because the same three tasks appear in two places, the reader is shown that the work of the messenger was fixed from the first building of the House.

The lesson also reaches a reader who receives a teacher without receiving the teaching. The recitation, the cleansing and the instruction are given as one work. Since the verse follows the account of the direction, the reader is shown that the community was given more than a place to face.

The case is like a village that asks for a doctor and receives one born in its own street. The man knows the wells and the winters, and the medicine arrives in a familiar voice.

---

## Verse 2:152

> remember Me; I will remember you. And thank Me, and never be ungrateful

**THE COMMAND AND ITS ANSWER**

The verse gives the community a short command with a promise: ***“remember Me; I will remember you.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the remembrance as obedience to what God commanded and avoided. The answer is kept as mercy and forgiveness. al-Baghawī keeps the report of the earliest commentator, that the remembrance is obedience and the answer is forgiveness. Because the two halves stand side by side, the reader is shown that the command and its reward were given together.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, with the remembrance bringing forgiveness. He keeps a further report in which the remembrance of ease is answered in hardship. al-Qurṭubī notes that the two clauses form a command and its answer, and that the answer carries the sense of repayment. Because the sentence is so brief, the reader is shown that the whole exchange between a servant and his Lord can be put in a few words.

**THE REMEMBRANCE OF THE HEART**

The verse asks for more than words: ***“remember Me”***. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the remembrance as a matter of the heart first, with the tongue as its interpreter. Spoken remembrance counts only when the heart is present. al-Ālūsī keeps the three kinds the teachers named, the remembrance of the tongue, of the heart and of the limbs. Because the command is addressed to the whole person, the reader is shown that the answer to it could not be a phrase alone.

al-Jalālayn keeps the practice of remembrance as prayer and praise. He keeps the report in which God promises to remember a servant who remembers Him within himself. al-Bukhārī keeps the same promise in the sound report, where the servant who remembers God in himself is remembered in Himself. Because the promise answers a hidden act with a hidden act, the reader is shown that the remembrance was never for an audience.

**THE THANKS AND ITS OPPOSITE**

The verse closes by naming the counterpart: ***“And thank Me, and never be ungrateful”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the thanks as the acknowledgement of the blessings given. He keeps the warning as the prohibition of turning away from that thanks. al-Ṭabarī keeps the same reading, with the ungrateful person described as one who stops giving thanks for what he received. Because the closing words name the opposite of thanks rather than a punishment, the reader is shown that the fault was a failure to see the gift.

The Book names the reward of thanks in another passage, (14:7 — **“If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more”**). as-Saʿdī keeps both halves of the verse as the root of the servant's relation with his Lord. The remembrance keeps the heart awake, and the thanks keeps the blessing visible, since the two together hold a person before his Lord. Because the verse puts remembrance before thanks, the reader is shown the order of the two.

The lesson also reaches a reader whose blessings have become invisible through habit. The verse gives him two short commands and one promise. Since the promise is attached to a private act, the reader is left with a practice that costs no one else anything and cannot be taken from him.

The case is like a man who is given a house and writes the giver's name above the door. The house is his to use, the name is small, and the writing takes a minute every morning.

---

## Verse 2:153

> O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient

**THE HELP TO BE SOUGHT**

The verse sets out the two supports of the community: ***“O believers! Seek comfort in patience”*** ***“and prayer. Allah is truly with those”*** ***“who are patient”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the command as the urging to bear what is heavy on bodies and on wealth, and he keeps the two supports as the means of carrying out obedience. as-Saʿdī keeps patience as the restraining of the self over what it dislikes, and he divides it into patience in obedience, patience against disobedience and patience under painful decrees. Because the verse gives two supports rather than one, the reader is shown that the community was not asked to endure by its own strength alone.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the patience as the steadfastness that carries out obligations and holds back from what is forbidden, and he keeps the prayer as the giving of extra prayer by night and day. al-Ālūsī keeps the sense of a companionship of help and victory in the closing words, since God is with the patient by aiding them. Because the sentence is addressed to the believers as a body, the reader is shown that the help was given to a community and not only to individuals.

**THE PRAYER AND ITS PLACE**

Prayer is named beside patience and given the later place in the list. al-Jalālayn notes that prayer is singled out from the other acts of worship because of how often it returns and how great it is. al-Ālūsī keeps the same view, since prayer is the root of nearness to God. Because the two commands are put together, the reader is shown that the endurance of the passage was tied to the turning towards God in worship.

The Book gives the same pair of supports in an earlier passage, (2:45 — **“Seek help through patience and prayer”**), and it adds there that the practice is heavy for all but the humble (2:45). Ibn Kathīr keeps the verse as the command that follows the call to remember God, and he keeps the pair in the same order. Because the verse came before the account of trials, the reader is shown that the support was given ahead of the need.

**THE COMPANIONSHIP NAMED**

The sentence closes on a promise: ***“Allah is truly with those who are patient”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the companionship as the help given to those who hold their ground, and he keeps the same sense of support through the passage. as-Saʿdī keeps the promise as the greatest support a worker can be given, since the one who has God with him is not alone in what he carries. Because the sentence names the patient rather than the strong, the reader is shown what kind of person the promise was given to.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is looking for a way through a hard season. The verse gives him a companion, a practice and a promise. Since the two supports are things he already has, the reader is left with a command that does not depend on better circumstances.

The case is like a man crossing a long plain with a friend and a water skin. The plain does not shorten, the friend does not tire, and the water skin is refilled at every stop.

---

## Verse 2:154

> Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead—in fact, they are alive! But you do not perceive it

**THE SAYING FORBIDDEN**

The verse corrects the talk of the community about its dead: ***“Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead”***. al-Baghawī records that the sentence came down about the men killed at the first great battle of the community, and he keeps the report that their number and their two groups were known at the time. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the report of what was being said about them by the people of the city, since the words of the objectors are part of the account. Because the verse forbids a way of speaking rather than a belief alone, the reader is shown that words about the dead were part of the matter.

The correction is kept by al-Ṭabarī as the statement that the dead are those whose life has been taken from them, while the one killed in God's way is not among them. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the prohibition as covering the speech of the tongue and the belief of the heart together, with the tongue saying that they died and the heart holding that they are dead. Because the verse is addressed to the community after a loss, the reader is shown that it speaks to grief as well as to language.

**THE LIFE THAT CONTINUES**

The verse states the contrary: ***“in fact, they are alive!”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that God has kept them in life with Him and provided for them. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading and records the report that the spirits of such people are given a life that moves freely. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sentence as the answer to those who spoke of loss. Because the verse states life rather than memory, the reader is shown that the honour of the killed was not merely a status among the living.

The same sentence is kept by Ibn Kathīr with the note that the killed in the way of God are alive and provided for. as-Saʿdī keeps the whole passage as the highest example of patience, since the community was asked to hold its ground even where life itself was at stake. Because the cause of God is named rather than the community, the reader is shown that the ruling rested on what the person died for.

**THE SIGHT THAT FAILS**

The verse closes on the limits of the observer: ***“But you do not perceive it”***. al-Ālūsī keeps the closing words as the statement that the state of the killed is beyond what the eye can reach, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading. The Book states the same ruling in another passage, (3:169 — **“Never think of those martyred in the cause of Allah as dead”**), and it adds there that they are alive with their Lord and provided for. Because the verse ends on perception rather than on doubt, the reader is shown that the life of the killed is a matter of news and not of observation.

The lesson also reaches a reader who measures everything by what he can see. The verse forbids a sentence, states a fact and then names the limit of his sight. Since the passage has just urged patience under trial, the reader is left with the case that patience reaches furthest.

The case is like people watching a boat pass behind a hill and calling it gone. The boat is on the water, the hill is between the two, and only the observer has lost sight of it.

---

## Verse 2:155

> We will certainly test you with a touch of fear and famine and loss of property, life, and crops. Give good news to those who patiently endure—

**THE TEST ANNOUNCED**

The verse announces what lies ahead for the community: ***“We will certainly test you with a touch of fear”*** ***“and famine and loss of property, life”*** ***“and crops. Give good news to those who patiently endure”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the news that the community would be tried with hard matters so that it would be seen who followed the messenger and who turned back. al-Baghawī keeps the reports on what each item covers, with the fear explained as the fear of an enemy and the famine as the years of drought. Because the list begins with a small measure, the reader is shown how the trials were described to a community that was told to expect them.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the items in the same order, with the loss of life explained as killing, disease and death, and the loss of crops as the failure of the harvest. al-Jalālayn keeps the same list and draws the purpose out, which is that the patience of the community be shown. Because the sentence names the loss of property as well as the loss of life, the reader is shown that the trial was described in the terms of ordinary living.

**THE MEANING OF THE TEST**

The verse states the reason for such news: ***“We will certainly test you”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the testing as the means by which the truthful is told from the liar and the patient from the impatient, and he keeps the note that this is God's established way with His servants. al-Ālūsī keeps the same sense, with the trial described as the treatment of one who is being examined rather than as a matter of God learning something new. Because the verse tells the community what to expect, the reader is shown that the trials were part of the road rather than a sign of abandonment.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the readings and the grammatical notes on the opening, and he keeps the sense that the trial may come as ease or as hardship. The Book states the same method in another passage, (47:31 — **“until We prove those of you who ˹truly˺ struggle”**), and the Book names hardship and ease together as a trial in a further passage, (21:35 — **“as a trial”**). Because the test is named before the bearers, the reader is shown that the burden was measured for those who would carry it.

**THE GOOD NEWS**

The verse then turns to those who hold their ground. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the news of reward held out to those who endure under the trial. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, with the news described as the gardens promised to the patient. Because the good news is given before the trial is described in detail, the reader is shown that the comfort was attached to the endurance and not to the relief.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is waiting for calm before he becomes patient. The trials are named, then the patience, then the good news. Since the passage has already given the community its two supports, the reader is left with a list of troubles that is shorter than the promise attached to it.

The case is like a family warned that the winter will be hard and given a warm house before the first frost. The cold is coming, the house is built, and the warning and the gift arrive in the same letter.

---

## Verse 2:156

> who, when faced with a disaster, say, “Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.”

**THE SAYING OF THE PATIENT**

The verse gives the words that mark its people: ***“who, when faced with a disaster, say, “Surely to Allah we belong”*** ***“and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the words as the acknowledgement of service and of the return, and he keeps the patient as those who know that whatever they have is a favour from their Lord. al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports on what a disaster covers, with the sense that it takes in whatever harms a person in himself, in his wealth or in his household. Because the verse ties the words to the moment of the blow, the reader is shown where patience was said to begin.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same point and records the report that patience belongs to the one who holds it at the first shock. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the words as the statement of a servant who knows that he is owned and that he is returning, and he keeps the further note that a person who is not pleased with the decree cannot expect his own work to be accepted. Because the verse gives the words rather than a mood, the reader is shown that patience was given a language.

**THE OWNERSHIP AND THE RETURN**

The two halves of the saying answer each other: ***“Surely to Allah we belong”*** ***“and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first half as the acknowledgement that the servant is God's possession and that God does with him what He wills, and the second as the return in the Hereafter where the account is settled. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading, with the saying placed in the mouth of those who are struck and who then wait for the reward. Because the saying begins with belonging and ends with returning, the reader is shown that loss and ownership were held in one sentence.

The Book states what follows for these people in the next passage, (2:157 — **“who will receive Allah's blessings and mercy”**), and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as the teaching of the way to make hardship bearable, since the pain is eased by a truth known beforehand. Because the verse reports the words rather than commanding them, the reader is shown that the saying was already the habit of the people described.

**WHAT THE VERSE TEACHES**

A person who owns nothing cannot be robbed of anything in the same way, and the saying places the whole of a life in the hand of God. That is why the verse does not ask for a display of strength at the moment of loss. Since the words name the return as well as the ownership, the reader is shown that the loss was measured against a destination rather than against what was held.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been given bad news and has no words for it. The verse supplies the words and names the people who use them. Since the passage has promised good news to the patient, the reader is left with a sentence that can be said at the worst moment.

The case is like a traveller whose bag is taken at a station while his ticket is in his hand. The bag is gone, the train is on time, and the destination was never inside the bag.

---

## Verse 2:157

> They are the ones who will receive Allah’s blessings and mercy. And it is they who are ˹rightly˺ guided

**THE REWARD NAMED**

The passage closes by naming what the patient receive: ***“They are the ones”*** ***“who will receive Allah’s blessings”*** ***“and mercy. And it is they”*** ***“who are ˹rightly˺ guided”***. The sentence is kept by al-Ṭabarī as a return to the people described just before, the ones who said the words of belonging and return at the moment of loss. He keeps the blessings as the forgiveness of God for His servants. Because the sentence gathers the four phrases into one promise, the reader is shown that the words of the patient were answered before they were finished.

**WHAT THE TWO NOUNS COVER**

The two nouns are unpacked by Ibn ʿAbbās as a division between this life and the next. The blessings cover forgiveness here, and the mercy covers the relief from punishment there. al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense, with the two nouns resting on the patient from their Lord, and the last sentence naming them as the rightly guided. Because the promise is split across two lives, the reader is shown that the reward began before the grave.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports in which the two nouns are matched with the pair named in the passage before, so that the blessings answer the prayer and the mercy answers the patience. He keeps a further reading in which the guidance is toward deserving the reward, and another in which it is toward the lightening of the loss. Because the sentence explains itself in stages, the reader is shown that no part of the saying went unanswered.

**THE GUIDANCE AT THE END**

The closing words are kept by al-Ālūsī as guidance that carries others along, since the patient are made a means by which people find the way. He keeps the final name as the arrival at God after the self has been left behind. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the statement that the reward of the patient is settled and their path is sound. The same promise closes the earlier passage about the humble, (2:5 — **“It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord”**). Because the last word of the passage is guidance, the reader is shown that patience is a road and not only a burden.

**THE WORDS THAT COME FIRST**

The order of the passage is kept by as-Saʿdī as a settling of the heart before the blow falls. A person who has been told beforehand what loss means will find it lighter when it comes, and the contrast between the patient and the loud complainer is the contrast between two ends. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the words of return as a training in virtue, since the saying relieves sorrow and consoles the grieving heart. Because the words are given before the troubles are described in full, the reader is shown that the community was taught the answer in advance.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has lost something he cannot recover. The passage gives him a sentence for the moment, a promise for afterwards, and a name for his road. Since the promise covers what has not yet happened, the reader is left with a loss that is already being repaid.

The case is like a man who is told by his doctor what the treatment will feel like before it starts. The pain is the same pain, the instruction is in his hand, and the waiting is shorter than it was.

---

## Verse 2:158

> Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever performs the pilgrimage or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺. And whoever does good willingly, Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing

**THE TWO HILLS AMONG THE SYMBOLS**

The verse turns from patience to the rites of the journey: ***“Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa”*** ***“and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the turn as a fitting one, since the passage has just spoken of struggle, and the pilgrimage carries both the hardship of the body and the spending of wealth. al-Baghawī keeps the reports on the two hills themselves, with one described as the smooth hard rock and the other as the softer stone, and both named as the two well-known rises by the town. Because the two hills are named as marks set up by God rather than as local customs, the reader is shown that walking between them was given a rank before any objection was raised.

**THE WALK AND THE BLAME REMOVED**

The verse then removes a worry: ***“So whoever performs the pilgrimage or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺.”*** The background is kept by al-Qurṭubī from the report of a companion who was asked about the two hills and answered that people had counted them a practice of the age before Islam and had stayed away from them, until the verse came down. al-Ṭabarī keeps a report in which the reluctance came from idols placed on the hills, and the sentence cleared the walk of any blame. Because the sentence removes a fear rather than imposing a duty, the reader is shown that the community was being released from an old scruple.

**THE MARKS OF THE RELIGION**

The sense of the marks is kept by as-Saʿdī as the visible signs of the religion, since some acts of worship are hidden between a servant and his Lord while others are set up in the open for people to see. He keeps the honour paid to such marks as a matter of the heart's piety, and he draws from it that the walk between the hills is required in the pilgrimage. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the opening particle as marking that the two hills are part of the marks rather than the whole of them. The Book praises the honour given to the same marks in a further passage, (22:32 — **“whoever honours the symbols of Allah”**), and the rites of the journey are named among the things not to be violated (5:2). Because the two hills are named as public signs, the reader is shown why their mention is followed by a promise.

**THE GOOD DONE WILLINGLY**

The verse closes on the willing doer: ***“And whoever does good willingly, Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the whole sentence as the naming of the pilgrimage and the visitation, with the two names drawn from aiming at a place and visiting it. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the walk between the hills as one of the rites commanded in the Book. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as the continuation of the account of the House, which had been opened much earlier in the chapter. Because the closing sentence speaks of what is done willingly beyond the duty, the reader is shown that the road allows for more than the minimum.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is asked to perform a rite that his family once avoided. The verse gives him the rite, the reason and the promise. Since the two hills were named as marks of God before the walk was commanded, the reader is left with an act that carries no trace of the older custom.

The case is like a man who refuses to enter a room because of a story his grandfather told. The door is opened for him, the room is used for the household's work, and the story has no bearing on the floor.

---

## Verse 2:159

> Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed—after We made it clear for humanity in the Book—will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn

**THE CONCEALMENT NAMED**

The offence that runs through the passage is named at the start: ***“Those who hide the clear proofs”*** ***“and guidance that We have revealed”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the concealers as the learned of the two earlier communities, who kept back the matter of the messenger after they had found it written. al-Baghawī keeps the report that the sentence came down about the learned of the Jews who hid the description of the messenger, the ruling on stoning and other matters that stood in the Torah. Because the sentence names what was hidden and who hid it, the reader is shown that the fault belonged to people who knew the value of what they held. Since the Book is named as the place where the truth was made plain, the reader is shown that the concealment was a refusal rather than a doubt.

**THE CLARITY THAT PRECEDED**

The middle of the sentence sets out the time and the audience: ***“after We made it clear”*** ***“for humanity in the Book”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the clarity as the showing of the matter in the earlier Scripture, with the description of the messenger and the ruling on stoning among the things made plain. as-Saʿdī keeps the ruling of the sentence as general for everyone who hides what God sent down, since God took a pledge from people of knowledge to make the Book known and not to bury it. Because the clarity came before the concealment, the reader is shown that the offence was not a mistake in understanding.

**THE CURSE FROM TWO SIDES**

The verse closes on the curse: ***“will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the curse of God as the punishment in the grave, and the curse of the angels and of the people as the calling down of harm upon them. al-Ālūsī keeps the revealed proofs as taking in what was sent to the earlier prophets concerning the matter of the messenger, and he keeps the guidance as what leads to sound conduct. The Book records the pledge in another passage, where the people of the Scripture were bound to make it known (3:187 — **“and not hide it”**).
