Because the curse comes from God and from the created together, the reader is shown that the concealment cost its owner more than a reputation.

**THE PATTERN OF THE PASSAGE**

The theme is kept by al-Qurṭubī as one that is not confined to a single group, since a wider reading makes the sentence cover everyone who hides a truth he was given. Ibn Kathīr keeps the exception that follows in the next verse, where the door is opened again for those who turn back and make the truth known. Because the sentence is followed immediately by a way out, the reader is shown that the warning was meant to correct rather than only to condemn.

The lesson also reaches a reader who holds a document that would settle a dispute and leaves it in a drawer. The harm done by the one who hides what he was given is what the sentence measures. Since the Book was named as the place where the truth was made clear, the reader is left with the knowledge that the drawer has a witness.

The case is like a surveyor who finds the original boundary stone and leaves it under the soil. The stone settles the dispute at once, the field is already claimed, and the neighbours will build their wall in the wrong place.

---

## Verse 2:160

> As for those who repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known, they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺, for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**THE DOOR OPENED**

The verse follows the curse with an exception: ***“As for those who repent, mend their ways”*** ***“and let the truth be known, they are the ones to”*** ***“whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the turning back as the return from concealment to belief and to the acknowledgement of the messenger, with the deed set right afterwards. al-Qurṭubī keeps a rule on what repentance must produce, since a claim of regret that leaves the conduct unchanged is not accepted by the teachers, and the one who was hiding must bring the hidden thing into the open. Because the sentence names three acts in order, the reader is shown that the return had a body and not only a word.

**THE THREE STEPS**

The three steps are kept by al-Ālūsī as a return from the concealment and from everything else that needs a return, a repairing of what was spoiled, and a making known of what had been hidden. He keeps the removal of the object in the first step as a widening of the sense, so that the turning back is not limited to the one fault. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the steps as leaving the older religion, worshipping God alone, and showing the description that had been kept back. Because the verse puts the making known last, the reader is shown that the hidden thing had to be produced.

**THE TURNING OF GOD TO THE SERVANT**

The answer is named in the same sentence: ***“they are the ones to”*** ***“whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the turn of God as the acceptance of the repentance, and he keeps the two closing names as mercy towards those who return. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sentence and adds that the repentance of such people is accepted because they declared what they had concealed. The Book records the same acceptance in the account of the first father, (2:37 — **“He accepted his repentance”**). Because the verse answers the repentance with a turn from God, the reader is shown that the exchange is not one-sided.

**THE NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends on two names: ***“for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”***. The same names appear in the Book where the acceptance of the servants is named as God's own act (9:104). as-Saʿdī keeps the two names as the reason the door stays open, since the one who accepts the return of His servants does so out of mercy and not out of need. Because the sentence moves from the servant's acts to the names of God, the reader is shown where the power to be forgiven lies.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the first name as the acceptance of those who return and the second as mercy for the one who dies in that state. The Book names the same acceptance of repentance among the acts of God alone (9:104). Because the verse is placed directly after a curse, the reader is shown that no fault was beyond repair while life remained.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has kept quiet about something for years. The verse gives him three steps and two names. Since the last step is the making known of what he hid, the reader is left with a repair that has to be done in public.

The case is like a man who buried a neighbour's marker while clearing his own land. The marker can be lifted, the field can be measured again, and the man who does it is not the same as the man who buried it.

---

## Verse 2:161

> Surely those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity

**THE CONDITION NAMED**

The verse returns to the curse and states its condition: ***“Surely those who disbelieve”*** ***“and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah, the angels”*** ***“and all of humanity”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the disbelievers as those who rejected the prophethood of the messenger among the two earlier communities, the other religious groups and the idolaters, and he keeps the second clause as the state in which they died. Because the sentence joins disbelief to death in the same state, the reader is shown that the matter was not closed while life continued.

**THE THREE WHO CURSE**

The curse is kept by al-Baghawī from the report of one of the earliest teachers, who described the disbeliever standing on the Day of Resurrection while God curses him, then the angels, then the people. al-Jalālayn keeps the curse as deserved in this life and in the next, and he keeps the mention of the people as covering either all people or the believers alone. Because the curse is shared between the creator and the created, the reader is shown how heavy the sentence was.

**THE CAUTION OF THE TEACHERS**

A caution is kept by al-Qurṭubī from the teachers, that a named person whose end is unknown should not be cursed, since the state of a person at death is hidden from others. He keeps the wording of the verse as the condition that makes the curse certain, which is dying in disbelief. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same rule and adds that the expressions of cursing take the ruling of the curse itself, whatever their shade or language. Because the judgement is spoken over a state that no human eye can see, the reader is shown why the teachers warned against cursing a named person. Because the sentence ties the curse to the final state, the reader is shown why the teachers held their tongues over particular people.

**THE CONTINUANCE OF THE CURSE**

The continuance of the curse is kept by al-Ālūsī as the point of the sentence, since the earlier mention of the curse in the passage described its arrival and this one describes its staying. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the curse of God as punishment, the curse of the angels as their calling down of harm, and the curse of the people as the curses of the believers landing on the disbelievers. The Book states the same sentence over the same people in another passage, where their reward is described in identical terms (3:87). Because the closing words name all of humanity, the reader is shown that the judgement is public.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is quick to call down harm on a person who has wronged him. The verse restricts that call to a state that no human eye can see. Since the sentence names the angels and all of humanity beside God, the reader is left with a sober view of who has the right to pronounce.

The case is like a courtroom where the verdict is read out and every person in the gallery stands up to repeat it. The reading is God's, the gallery agrees, and no member of the gallery could have written the verdict himself.

---

## Verse 2:162

> They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺

**THE STAY THAT DOES NOT END**

The verse describes what follows the curse: ***“They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened”*** ***“nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the opening word as a state attached to the people just named, so that the curse rests on them while they remain in it. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same construction and adds that the stay in the curse means that the curse is fixed on them for good. Because the sentence names both the place and the duration, the reader is shown that nothing in the judgement was left open.

**THE MERCY THAT DOES NOT REACH**

The second sentence is kept by al-Jalālayn as the statement that the punishment is not eased even for the blink of an eye, and that no delay is granted for a return or an excuse. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the punishment as neither lifted nor reduced, and he keeps the last words as the refusal to postpone the torment. Because the sentence names two ways of relief and denies both, the reader is shown the completeness of the sentence.

**THE WORD BEFORE THE NAME**

The order of the sentence is kept by al-Ālūsī as a mark of care, since the pronoun is used before the name of the fire is mentioned, which shows that the matter was present in the mind of the speaker. He keeps the reports in which the stay is understood as resting in the curse, with the fire following as its consequence. The Book states the same sentence over the same people in another passage (3:88). Because the fire is named late in the sentence, the reader is shown that the judgement was already settled before the place was described.

**WHAT THE SENTENCE CLOSES**

The pair of verses is kept by as-Saʿdī as the naming of the two ends that face each other: reward and punishment, guidance and loss, patience and complaint. Because the two verses stand side by side, the reader is shown which of the two ends is described as open and which as closed. He keeps the difference between the two groups as the largest difference that can be drawn. The Book names the stay in the fire as a matter of long duration in the passage of the table spread, where the state of the disbelievers is described with the same refusal of relief (5:37). Because the sentence follows a curse, the reader is shown that the punishment named is the second stage of one judgement.

The lesson also reaches a reader who assumes that a hard word spoken over him today will be softened later. The verse closes both doors in one breath. Since the sentence is spoken of people who died in their refusal, the reader is left with a warning about the state in which a life ends.

The case is like a debt that is written into a ledger with no date for payment and no clause for reduction. The sum stands, the page is closed, and the only variable left is who owes it.

---

## Verse 2:163

> Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

**THE ONE GOD NAMED**

The verse states the foundation of everything before it: ***“Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the statement that the one who deserves obedience and worship is one Lord, and he keeps it as the ground from which the other commands of the passage take their force. al-Ālūsī keeps the report that the sentence came down when the idolaters asked the messenger to describe his Lord, and he keeps the address as general for everyone who can be addressed. Because the sentence follows a passage about concealment and curse, the reader is shown what the concealment had been hiding.

**THE UNITY THAT HAS NO PARTNER**

The meaning of the unity is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as one God without a son and without a partner. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sense, that the One has no rivals and no equals. as-Saʿdī keeps the unity as standing alone in essence, names, qualities and acts, with no partner in His being, no equal to His name, and no creator or arranger beside Him. Because the sentence denies every kind of plurality, the reader is shown that the claim of the other side was not a detail of doctrine.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends on two names: ***“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the pair as the description of mercy that has no equal among creatures, since it reaches every living thing. al-Jalālayn keeps the sentence as the answer given when the messenger was asked to describe his Lord. The Book names the same two names together in the passage of the gathering, where the One is described as knowing the seen and the unseen (59:22). Because the names arrive after the denial of rivals, the reader is shown that the mercy stands on strength and not on need.

**WHERE THE PROOF LEADS**

The verse is kept by al-Qurṭubī as the point where the passage turns from a warning to a proof. He keeps the order of the sentences, with the warning against concealment first, then the statement of unity, then the call to look at the wonders of creation. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the surprise of the idolaters when they heard the sentence, since one object of worship for the whole world seemed impossible to them, and he keeps the proof as compressed into the verses that follow. The Book states what belongs to the One in an earlier passage, where nothing is compared to Him (42:11 — **“There is nothing like Him”**). Because the proof is placed after the claim, the reader is shown that the argument was made to fit the question.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has divided his trust among many hands. The verse gathers the whole of it into one name and adds two names of mercy. Since the proof of the One is offered in the creation itself, the reader is left with a claim that can be tested by looking up.

The case is like a household with a single key for a single door and a crowd of people claiming a share in it. The door opens for one owner, the key was never cut in two, and the crowd was arguing about a lock that never had a second half.

---

## Verse 2:164

> Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth; the alternation of the day and the night; the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of humanity; the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death; the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout; the shifting of the winds; and the clouds drifting between the heavens and the earth—˹in all of this˺ are surely signs for people of understanding

**THE SIGNS LISTED**

The claim of the previous sentence is answered here by pointing at the world: ***“Indeed, in the creation of the heavens”*** ***“and the earth”*** ***“the alternation of the day”*** ***“and the night”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the opening as the turn from the statement of unity to the evidence for it, so that a thoughtful reader may reach the unity of the maker by looking at what was made. al-Baghawī keeps the note that the heavens come as several since each is of a different kind, while the earth is given as one whole since its substance is dust, and he keeps the sign in the height of the sky without pillars. Because the sentence begins with the largest of the created things, the reader is shown the order in which the argument was laid out.

**THE SHIPS, THE RAIN AND THE WINDS**

The list continues: ***“the ships that sail the sea”*** ***“for the benefit of humanity”*** ***“the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death”*** ***“the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout”*** ***“the shifting of the winds”*** ***“and the clouds drifting between the heavens”*** ***“and the earth”*** — ***“˹in all of this˺ are surely signs”*** ***“for people of understanding”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the ships as a sign in that they run on the water without cracking or sinking while carrying what profits people. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the order of the list with the increase and decrease in the length of the day and the night. Because the items move from the sky to the sea to the fields, the reader is shown that the proof was spread over everything a person uses.

**THE OCCASION OF THE SENTENCE**

The occasion is kept by al-Qurṭubī from the report that the idolaters asked how a single god could suffice for all people, and the verses of the creation followed. al-Ālūsī keeps the report of the many idols set up around the House, and the wonder of the people when they heard this passage, followed by their demand for a sign. Because the sentence lists what everyone could see, the reader is shown that the demand for a sign had been answered in advance.

**WHAT THE SIGNS ARE FOR**

The purpose of the list is kept by as-Saʿdī as the measure of the mind that is used on it. The created things are proofs of the unity of the maker, of His lordship and of His mercy, and a person benefits from them according to the understanding God has given him. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same list as it appears in the sentence. The Book gives the same list with the same conclusion in a further passage (3:190), where the turn of the night and day is named among the signs and the people of reason are said to see them. Because the closing words name the people of understanding, the reader is shown that the signs were not hidden but the readers were.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the series as signs that the learned and the unlettered can grasp alike, since the wonder of the sky and the turn of night and day need no training to see. The verse ends by naming those who understand rather than those who are learned. Because the list is plain, the reader is shown that the argument was made for everyone.

The lesson also reaches a reader who looks at the world and sees only weather. The verse turns the same sky into a page of signs. Since the closing words make understanding the condition, the reader is left with the knowledge that the proof is available and the attention is his to give.

The case is like a man who walks past a working clock every morning and never wonders who winds it. The hands move, the bell rings, and the answer is standing in the middle of the street.

---

## Verse 2:165

> Still there are some who take others as Allah’s equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more. If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment

**THE EQUALS SET UP**

The verse names a group that turned away from the proof: ***“Still there are some”*** ***“who take others as Allah’s equal”*** ***“they love them as they should love Allah”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the equals as the rivals set up beside God, whose worship was given to something created. al-Baghawī keeps the same sense with the idols named, and he keeps the report that their love for their objects was measured against the love the believers hold for God. Because the sentence is placed straight after the signs, the reader is shown that the proof did not force the choice.

**THE LOVE THAT DIFFERS**

The next clause draws the difference: ***“but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the comparison as one between two loves, since the believers hold to God through ease and hardship while the others abandon their objects when trouble comes. al-Ālūsī keeps the sentence as the report of how the idolaters stood after the proofs had been set out in the passage before. Because the comparison is put in terms of love, the reader is shown where the real fault lay.

**THE SIGHT THAT IS MISSING**

The verse then turns to what the wrongdoers cannot see: ***“If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize”*** ***“that all power belongs to Allah”*** ***“and that Allah is”*** ***“indeed severe in punishment”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the verse as the report of the love the idolaters held for their objects in this life, and of how they disown one another in the next. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading, with the sight of the punishment put as the thing that would change their judgement. Because the sentence speaks of seeing rather than of hearing, the reader is shown that the argument had reached its limit in words.

**THE POWER THAT BELONGS TO ONE**

The closing words are kept by Ibn ʿUthaymīn as the statement that the strength which the idolaters hoped for from their objects belongs to God alone. as-Saʿdī keeps the whole verse as the naming of the state of the two groups after the proof was made plain, and he keeps the love of the believers as the fruit of knowing God. The Book names the sign of that love in another passage, where love is answered by following the messenger (3:31 — **“then follow me”**). Because the sentence ends on the severity of the punishment, the reader is shown that power and mercy were never in conflict.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as the pointing out of an error, since those who set up partners thought their objects were caretakers of their needs, and their attachment reached the measure of the love owed to God alone. Because the objection is answered with the peace of the next life rather than with an argument, the reader is shown how the two groups are finally separated.

The lesson also reaches a reader who gives his best affection to something that cannot answer him. The verse leaves him the sentence of the believers and the picture of the wrongdoers. Since the two loves are named side by side, the reader is left with a choice that is measured indoors.

The case is like two men walking with lamps: one lights his from the main supply, and the other fills his with water to make it last. Both lamps look alike at noon, and only one of them is lit at midnight.

---

## Verse 2:166

> ˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off

**THE DAY NAMED**

The verse opens a scene in the next life: ***“˹Consider the Day˺ when those”*** ***“who misled others will disown their followers”*** ***“when they face the torment”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the leaders as the ones who were followed, disowning those who followed them in rejection. al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that name the leaders and the chiefs, and he keeps the further report that the misleading spirits disown the people they led. Because the sentence names the moment of the torment, the reader is shown that the separation happened when it could no longer help anyone.

**THE BONDS CUT**

What falls with the separation is named at the close: ***“and the bonds that united them will be cut off”***. al-Baghawī keeps the bonds as the ties of affection and family that held between them on earth. al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense, with the leaders denying that they had misled the others, and the cords of kinship and love cut away. Because the sentence names ties rather than arguments, the reader is shown that what was lost was not only a case but a company.

**THE SCENE HELD UP FOR THE READER**

The scene is kept by Ibn ʿUthaymīn as a reminder set before people, with the time-phrase attached to a verb that is left out, so that the sentence reads as a call to remember. He keeps the note that the reminder is meant to be carried to others as well. al-Ālūsī keeps the construction in which the time-phrase stands in place of the one before it, and he keeps a further reading in which it belongs with the call to remember. Because the sentence is addressed to a reader who is still in this life, the reader is shown that the scene was shown for a purpose.

**WHAT THE FOLLOWERS LEARN**

The scene is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the leaders disowning the lowly, with their pledges and their friendship collapsing with them. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same picture, with the leaders and those who followed them separated when the punishment is seen. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the verse as the unfolding of the severity that the passage before it had named in a single sentence. The Book states the same end for friendship in another passage, where close friends become enemies on that Day, (43:67 — **“friends will be enemies to one another”**). Because the ties are cut in the next life, the reader is shown where a friendship built on the wrong ground ends.

as-Saʿdī keeps the passage as one of the fairest connections in the Book, since the proof of God's unity was followed by the state of those who set up rivals to Him, and the next verses show how the two groups meet. The verse ends with the bonds cut and the followers left with nothing they had relied on. Because the last words are about ties rather than about punishment, the reader is shown that the loss named is a loss of company.

The lesson also reaches a reader who follows a person rather than a path. The verse shows him the end of that arrangement in the plainest terms. Since the ties are cut at the moment they are needed most, the reader is left with the sense that the leader was never the ground.

The case is like two men crossing a bridge that one of them described as solid and never built. The description was confident, the planks were absent, and only one of them is standing at the far end.

---

## Verse 2:167

> The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.” And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds. And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire

**THE CRY OF THE FOLLOWERS**

The scene opened in the verse before is carried a step further: ***“The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the speakers as the followers of the men they had set up beside God, obeying them in disobedience to their Lord, and he keeps the wish as a longing for the return to the world. al-Ālūsī keeps the wish as a matched repayment, since the followers had been put in the same distress the leaders had given them, and the disowning is held back until this moment so that the pain of it might be felt. Because the sentence gives the followers a voice, the reader is shown what the leaders' refusal had bought them. Since the two groups are heard together in one scene, the reader sees that the loss was shared.

**THE DISOWNING TURNED BACK**

The wish names the turning of the tables: ***“as they disowned us.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the disowning as a cutting off, with the followers declaring themselves free of the leaders as the leaders had declared themselves free of them. The same reading is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās, with the followers disowning in the next life the very leaders they had followed in this one. Because the two disownings are set side by side, the reader is shown that the company was broken from both ends.

**THE DEEDS SHOWN AS GRIEF**

The verse then states what God does with this cry: ***“And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the showing of their works to them in the form of regret, so that the sight of what they did becomes a torment of its own. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading and adds that the deeds are shown as regrets to them in the Hereafter. al-Jalālayn keeps the word for that regret as a state the people are folded into while they look at what they lost. Because the sentence names the deeds rather than the punishment, the reader is shown how the account was presented.

**THE DOOR THAT DOES NOT OPEN**

The verse closes on the wish answered with a refusal: ***“And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the closing words as the statement that the leaders and the led alike do not come out of it. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the whole scene as the unfolding of the severity named a verse earlier, and he compares the leaders' escape from blame to the way partners in a crime turn on each other once they are caught. Because the wish for a return is answered with a closed door, the reader is shown that the time for the wish is this life alone.

The lesson also reaches a reader who follows a person he trusts more than he trusts the command. The scene gives him the end of that transfer of responsibility. Since the door closes on the wish itself, the reader is left with the knowledge that a return is offered only while he is still able to take it.

The case is like two men who agree to rob a house and are caught inside it. One of them names the other at once, the door is locked from the outside, and the plan they made together has become a quarrel.

---

## Verse 2:168

> O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy

**THE CALL TO ALL PEOPLE**

The verse turns from the scenes of the Hereafter to the table: ***“O humanity! Eat from what is lawful”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the command as the permission to eat what God made lawful, and he names the four things made unlawful in the verse that follows as the only exclusions. al-Ālūsī keeps the report that the sentence came down about the idolaters who had forbidden to themselves the kinds of cattle they had named, and he keeps the further report that it concerned people who gave up the camel's flesh because it was forbidden in the religion of the Jews. Because the address is to all people and not to one group, the reader is shown that the earth's produce was never marked off for a chosen few.

**THE LAWFUL AND THE GOOD**

The command continues with a second quality: The quality translated here as good carries the sense of what is pleasant and wholesome. The command continues with its second word: ***“and good on the earth”***. al-Baghawī keeps the reports that the audience was from several tribes who had forbidden to themselves the cultivated land and the kinds of cattle, and he keeps the sense of the good as what the law has made lawful and wholesome. al-Qurṭubī keeps the two reports on that quality, one making it a reinforcement of the lawful and one making it a second condition, so that an unclean animal is excluded even though it be owned. as-Saʿdī keeps the lawful as what is taken without seizure and without a forbidden way of earning, and the good as what is not filth, naming carrion, blood and swine among the things excluded. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the first of the two qualities as the opening of a knot, so that what is made lawful has had a restriction lifted from it. Because the two words stand together, the reader is shown that the permission was never a licence for the foul.

**THE STEPS AND THE ENMITY**

The verse closes with a warning: ***“and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the steps as the ways the enemy invites people into, and he keeps the enmity as one already made plain, since the refusal to bow before the first man and the deception of the garden had shown it. al-Baghawī keeps the reports that the steps are his traces and his slips, and a further report that they are the small offences that people count as nothing. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the steps as his whispering about what had been cultivated and what had been made unlawful. Because the sentence joins a light word to a heavy one, the reader is shown how a small step ends.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been taught to fear a food that God never forbade. The verse gives him the earth, two qualities for what he eats, and a warning about the walking rather than the plate. Since the enemy is named as an enemy in the same breath, the reader is left with the sense that the prohibition came from a known quarter.

The case is like a man who is told by a passer-by that the fruit in his own garden is poisoned, and who then stands outside his own wall while the fruit rots. The garden is his, the old rule has been lifted, and the passer-by has been an enemy from the first day.

---

## Verse 2:169

> He only incites you to commit evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know

**THE TWO EVILS NAMED**

The verse explains what the footsteps lead to: ***“He only incites you to commit evil”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the evil as the sin a person earns, and he keeps the speaker of the sentence as the enemy named before it. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the evil as the lesser offences, and he notes that the opening particle of the verse carries a restriction, so that nothing but these things is being attributed to him. as-Saʿdī keeps the same restriction as the whole point of the sentence, since a servant who knows what the enemy orders will not mistake his voice for good counsel. Because the orders are named rather than the tempter, the reader is shown what the walking after him actually produces.

**THE INDECENCY THAT FOLLOWS**

The second charge is graver than the first: ***“and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know”***. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the indecency as the major offences, naming the worst of them and the withholding of the obligatory alms among them. al-Qurṭubī keeps a note on the first of the two, that it is named so since it makes its doer sorrowful in the end. al-Jalālayn keeps the pair as what is hateful to the law, followed by the speaking about God without knowledge, such as forbidding what He never forbade. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the sense of the opening as the dropping of a suggestion into the heart rather than a plain command, and he keeps the first word as whatever troubles a sound mind. Because the sentence climbs from the lesser to the greater, the reader is shown where the road ends.

**THE CLAIM MADE WITHOUT KNOWLEDGE**

The last of the three is the one that costs the most, since it puts a word in the mouth of God. The Book records the same gravity in an earlier sentence, where the community is forbidden to hide the truth knowingly (2:42). al-Baghawī keeps the whole sentence as the answer to those who had made their own rules about food, since the forbidding of what God made lawful is itself a claim about God. Because the sentence ties the temptation to a statement about God, the reader is shown that the enemy's work is done as much with doctrine as with desire. The third charge is kept by al-Jalālayn as the forbidding of what God made lawful and the permitting of what He forbade, which is the form such a claim usually takes. Since a statement is placed beside the worst of the deeds, the reader is shown that a wrong idea can cost as much as a wrong act.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is certain about a rule he has never checked. Three things are named as the enemy's orders, and the last is the making of such rules. Since the speaking about God is placed beside the worst of the offences, the reader is left with a caution about his own certainties.

The case is like a man who signs a contract on behalf of a business he does not own. The signature looks like a formality, the paper is filed, and the debt arrives with the first post.

---

## Verse 2:170

> When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance

**THE INVITATION AND THE REFUSAL**

The verse reports an exchange: ***“When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No!”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the people addressed as those named earlier in the passage who had set up equals beside God, and he keeps the two possible references of the pronoun, one to them and one to a group of the people of the earlier books. al-Baghawī keeps the report that the messenger invited the Jews to the faith and that two of their leaders answered that they would rather follow what they had found their fathers upon. al-Qurṭubī keeps both reports, one naming the idolaters of the Arabs and one naming the Jews. Because the refusal is put in the form of a preference rather than an argument, the reader is shown that the case was never weighed.

**THE PRACTICE OF THE FATHERS**

The refusal gives its reason: ***“We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the turning of the address to a third person as a sign that the people were not fit to be spoken to directly, and he keeps the sense that the sentence was left for the thoughtful to hear. Ibn Kathīr keeps the practice as the worship of the idols and the false deities. The Book records the same answer from another people, (5:104 — **“We found our forefathers”**). Because the reply rests on what was found rather than on what was proved, the reader is shown the whole weight of the habit.

**THE QUESTION THAT CANNOT BE ANSWERED**

The verse closes with a question: ***“˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the question as the putting of the case at its worst, since following a practice is one thing and following it where the teachers were without understanding is another. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same point in plainer terms, that the fathers had little grasp of the faith and were not guided by their Lord, so the imitation could not be defended on its own terms. Because the question is left unanswered, the reader is shown that the silence was the answer. Since the practice was inherited rather than examined, the reader is shown why the invitation was refused before it was weighed.

The Book gives the likeness of those who follow such a call in the verse that follows, where they are compared to animals that hear a call and nothing more (2:171). Because the refusal is set within a passage about what God made lawful, the reader is shown that the quarrel was over the table and not only over doctrine.

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps a practice because it came from his family. The verse gives him the practice, the invitation, and the question about the teachers. Since the question is about understanding and guidance rather than about loyalty, the reader is left with the duty of asking what his forefathers actually knew.

The case is like sailors who steer by a chart drawn by a man who had never seen the coast. The chart is old, the coast is real, and the question is not whether the man was sincere but whether he had ever been there.

---

## Verse 2:171

> The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding

**THE LIKENESS AND ITS TWO SIDES**

The likeness of the people described before is set out here: The three states translated here as deaf, dumb and blind describe a closing of every door of knowledge: ***“The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the likeness as the beast that hears the sound when it is driven and does not grasp what is said to it, and he keeps the reports that name a camel or a donkey, and a sheep, as the animal in view. al-Qurṭubī keeps the note of a leading student of the language, that the people were likened to the flock being called and not to the caller. Because the likeness is drawn from the field rather than from the school, the reader is shown that the point was comprehension and not eloquence. Since the cry is described as a sound rather than a message, the reader is shown where the failure lay.

**THE CRY THAT CARRIES NOTHING**

The likeness is completed: ***“and cries of the shepherd.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps a dropped word in the sentence, whether on the side of the people or on the side of the flock, and he keeps the sense in both cases as the same: the people were buried in imitation and did not turn their minds to what was recited to them. al-Jalālayn keeps the flock as hearing a call and a cry, that is, a sound without meaning. Because the cry is named as a sound rather than as a message, the reader is shown where the failure lay.

**THE THREE SENSES CLOSED**

The verse then names the state in plain words: ***“˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb”*** ***“and blind so they have no understanding”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the three as the wilful closing of the ear to the truth, of the tongue to the truth, and of the eye to guidance, so that they made themselves as the cattle are. as-Saʿdī keeps the same list and draws out the cause: they heard only the sound that established the proof against them, and since they had no sound mind left, they lost the use of hearing, sight and speech together. The Book names the same three states over another people, (8:22 — **“deaf and dumb”**). Because the verse ends by naming understanding, the reader is shown that the fault was in the mind rather than in the ear.

The Book gives the same likeness in a further passage, where the heedless are compared to cattle and said to be further astray (25:44 — **“They are only like cattle”**). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as the refutation of the position that a way inherited from the fathers must be followed in every condition, since the disbelievers only heard a cry that was not meant to correct them. Because the likeness is repeated elsewhere in the Book, the reader is shown that the image was a settled one.

The lesson also reaches a reader who hears a great deal and takes in nothing. The verse gives him the flock, the shepherd and the three closed doors. Since the closing words name understanding as the missing thing, the reader is left with the duty of listening with the mind that answers.

The case is like a man standing in a station while announcements are read in a language he has never learned. The voice is loud, the platform is right, and the train he needs leaves while he waits for a word he knows.

---

## Verse 2:172

> O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺

**THE CALL TO THE BELIEVERS**

The verse narrows the earlier address to a particular community: ***“O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided”*** ***“for you.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the command as the instruction to eat of the lawful provision God had made wholesome for them, and he keeps the last part of the sentence as the rebuke of the invented prohibitions. al-Qurṭubī keeps the sentence as a reinforcement of the command given to all people, with the believers singled out afterwards as an honour and as a preparation for the request for thanks. as-Saʿdī keeps the same reading and adds that the good is mentioned here on its own, since the believer has been given it free of any blame, and since his faith holds him back from what is not his. Because the address is repeated after the general one, the reader is shown that the community was being given its own charge.

**THE THANKS ASKED WITH THE MEAL**

The command is followed by a second: ***“And give thanks to Allah”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the thanks as the praise of God with what is due to Him for the provisions He gave and made wholesome. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the closing condition as the statement that the one who worships God should not call His lawful things unlawful. as-Saʿdī keeps thanks as righteous action in the sense the verse carries, so that gratitude is not a phrase but a life, and he keeps the promise that eating what is good is itself a cause of good work being accepted. Because the thanks is joined to the table, the reader is shown that the smallest act of the day belongs to the account. Since the address names the believers by their faith, the reader is shown that the meal itself was made part of the service.

**THE CONDITION AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a condition: ***“if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺”***. al-Ālūsī keeps the sentence as the reason for the request, since a people who give their worship to God alone want a worship that suits His greatness, and that worship is not completed without thanks. as-Saʿdī draws the same conclusion from the other side, that whoever does not thank God has not worshipped Him alone. al-Baghawī keeps the report in which the same order was given to the messengers, and in which a traveller raises his hands in supplication while his food and drink are unlawful, and finds no answer. The Book gives the same report of answered supplication in another passage, (40:60 — **“I will respond to you”**). Because the condition stands at the end, the reader is shown what the thanks proves about the one who gives it.

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps his worship clean and his earnings careless. The verse puts the meal and the worship in one sentence. Since the thanks is the mark of worship that is given to God alone, the reader is left with the knowledge that the table is part of the service.

The case is like a guest who praises the host and then complains about the food to the other guests at the same table. The praise was loud, the table was set by the host, and the complaint was heard in the same room.

---

## Verse 2:173

> He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**THE FOUR THINGS FORBIDDEN**

The verse turns from the permission to its limit: ***“He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the opening particle as a word of restriction, so that the prohibited is confined to what is named and everything else remains as it was. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same construction and draws the rule from it, that nothing forbidden stands outside this sentence, and he notes that a further passage also came down on the same point. as-Saʿdī keeps carrion as what died without the lawful manner of slaughter, and he keeps the reason that such a thing is foul and harmful in itself. Because the sentence begins with a restriction, the reader is shown that inventing prohibitions was as serious as inventing permissions.

**THE ANIMAL DEDICATED ELSEWHERE**

The list closes with a fourth item: ***“and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the raising of the voice at the sacrifice as the act in view, since that is what the idolaters did for their gods. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, with the offering made to an idol named plainly. al-Ālūsī keeps the reports in which things separated from a living animal are joined to carrion, and he keeps the exception made for fish and locusts. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the restriction as a guard in both directions, since the forbidden must stay forbidden and the lawful must not be turned into a prohibition. Because the fourth item names a dedication rather than a substance, the reader is shown that the matter of food was tied to worship.

**THE ONE WHO IS FORCED**

The verse then lifts the fault from the one who is driven to it: ***“But if someone is compelled by necessity”*** ***“neither driven by desire”*** ***“nor exceeding immediate need”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the relief as the removal of blame from a person forced by hunger, and he keeps the two limits that keep the relief from becoming a licence. The same reading is kept by Ibn Kathīr with the note that the one who is driven to it without rebellion and without going beyond his need carries no sin. Because the relief is fenced by two conditions, the reader is shown how narrowly it was drawn.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends on forgiveness: ***“they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the closing names as the reason the concession was given at all. as-Saʿdī keeps the whole passage as a movement from the permission of the good to the forbidding of the foul, and he keeps the note that the foul is named as foul because of the harm it carries. The Book names the same prohibition in a further passage, (5:3 — **“Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and swine”**). Because the sentence ends with mercy, the reader is shown that the door was left open for the weak.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is starving and fears that any mouthful will damn him. His case is named in the sentence and the guilt is taken from him. Since the names of forgiveness are attached to the concession, the reader is left with a religion whose limits bend for necessity and nowhere else.

The case is like a traveller whose food has spoiled on a long road, and who is told that he may eat what he finds rather than go hungry, so long as he is travelling and not simply greedy.

---

## Verse 2:174

> Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment

**THE HIDING NAMED**

The verse returns to a theme of the passage: ***“Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them”*** ***“for a fleeting gain consume nothing”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the concealers as the people of the earlier books who hid what was said about the messenger, taking a bribe and turning the meanings of the verses aside. al-Baghawī keeps the report that the sentence came down about the leaders of the Jews, who used to draw gifts and food from those below them, and who feared the loss of their position when the messenger came from another people. al-Ālūsī keeps the same report and adds that they had hoped the messenger would be one of their own. Because the sentence names a trade, the reader is shown how the concealment was measured.

**THE FIRE IN THE BELLY**

The verse states what the trade produces: ***“but fire into their bellies.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the sentence as the statement that what they swallow is fire, since the price they took was gained by the worst of earnings. as-Saʿdī keeps the same point and draws the rule from it, that the repayment matches the deed, since the gain was taken by the foulest of means and the greatest of the forbidden. The names of three men of the city to whom the sentence was addressed are kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. Because the sentence speaks of the belly rather than of the purse, the reader is shown that the harm was done to the one who swallowed.

**THE SILENCE AND THE CLEANSING**

The verse then names what will be withheld: ***“Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment”*** ***“nor will He purify them.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the silence as the expression of anger and of turning away, which is a heavier thing for them than the fire itself, and he keeps the cleansing as the removal of the vices of character and the giving of deeds that deserve praise. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the statement that no word of comfort will come to them and no purification will reach them. Because the two gifts that are withheld are named here, the reader is shown what the concealer lost beside his rank. Since the sentence speaks of what is not spoken and what is not cleansed, the reader is shown that the account keeps a place for silence as well as for words.

**THE PAIN THAT FOLLOWS**

The verse closes with the sentence they earned: ***“And they will suffer a painful punishment”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the closing words as the completion of the sentence passed on those who hid what they knew. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as a warning to the scholars of the community that they should not fall into the practice of giving verdicts for gain, since what is collected for concealing the Book of God is simply fire. The Book records the same hiding and its curse in an earlier sentence of this chapter (2:159). Because the passage names the scholars as those addressed, the reader is shown that knowledge raises the weight of the fault rather than lowering it.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is paid, in standing or in comfort, to keep quiet about something true. The verse gives him the trade, the price and the meal. Since the price is named as fleeting and the meal as fire, the reader is left with a bargain that nobody would sign if he saw both sides of it.

The case is like a watchman paid by thieves to leave a gate unlocked. The coin is in his pocket, the gate is open, and the house behind it is his own village.

---

## Verse 2:175

> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire

**THE TWO TRADES**

The verse gathers the fault into a single sentence: ***“They are the ones”*** ***“who trade guidance for misguidance”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the trade as taking error and leaving guidance, and taking what brings the punishment while leaving what brings forgiveness. al-Ālūsī keeps the sentence as the answer to an unasked question, since the weight of the warning needed a reason, and the reason is the exchange they made in this life and the next. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the same figure and notes that the buyer is a willing seeker, so that the people are described as eager for what they bought. The Book states the same exchange over another group in an earlier passage, (2:16 — **“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance”**). Because the sentence names a bargain rather than a mistake, the reader is shown how deliberately the loss was taken.

**THE SECOND HALF OF THE PRICE**

The trade has two articles on each side: ***“and forgiveness for punishment.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the exchange as disbelief chosen for the price of faith, and he keeps a further reading in which the choice was the road that leads to the fire instead of the road that leads to the garden. al-Qurṭubī keeps a note on the construction, that the two consequences follow the two choices as their proper ends. Because the sentence pairs a thing lost here with a thing lost there, the reader is shown the full size of the price.

**THE QUESTION AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a question that carries a rebuke: ***“How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the question as one of wonder at how bold they were in the works that bring a person near the fire. al-Baghawī records two readings of the sentence: one, that the question asks what has made them endure the fire, and another, that they have no patience with it at all, and the wonder is at their boldness in the deeds of its people. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sense in his rendering, that the question measures their boldness for the works that push them there. Because the verse ends on a question, the reader is shown that no answer was expected from the people addressed.

The passage is carried one step further in the verse that follows, where the reason for the heavy warning is given (2:176). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the whole passage as the warning to those who take money for verdicts, since the loss described is not accidental but contracted. Because the closing question names persistence, the reader is shown that the fault was repeated until it became a habit.

The lesson also reaches a reader who says he would never make such a trade, while making it daily in small instalments. The verse gives him the ledger with both columns visible. Since the question asks how long he can keep at it, the reader is left with the knowledge that the answer is not a matter of courage but of time.

The case is like a man who trades a field for a handful of coins because the coins are bright. The field is measured in acres, the coins fit in a palm, and the seller walks away pleased for a season.

---

## Verse 2:176

> That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition

**THE REASON STATED**

The verse gives the ground of the warning that came before: ***“That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the reason their conduct was what it was, since the Book that they hid had been sent down with truth and had told of them beforehand. al-Baghawī keeps the same reading, that the punishment followed because they rejected a Book sent down with truth. al-Qurṭubī keeps the notes on what the Book refers to here, with one report naming the Qur'an and another naming the Torah, and he keeps the sense of truth as the opposite of falsehood. Because the reason is placed after the sentence about their deeds, the reader is shown that the loss was measured against what they had received.

**THE DISAGREEMENT NAMED**

The verse then names another mark of the same people: ***“And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the disagreement as one over the kind of the Book, with some of it believed and some rejected, or as a departure from the road of truth it laid down. al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that name the two earlier communities, with the Christians claiming a description of Jesus in the Torah while the Jews denied it, and he keeps a further report naming the idolaters of the city and their differing labels for the Qur'an. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading and names the labels they used, poetry, sorcery and soothsaying. Because the sentence names disagreement rather than ignorance, the reader is shown that the Book itself was the thing they quarrelled over.

**THE DISTANCE IN THE WORD**

The verse closes with a measure of the division itself: it is a parting that runs to the far end. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sentence as the statement that those who contravened what stood in the Book about the messenger, and then hid it, were far inside a break. as-Saʿdī keeps the whole verse as the naming of the two causes behind the loss, the closing of the road by their own choice and the justice of God in repaying it. The Book names the same parting over another people, (45:17 — **“they differed”**), where the difference came after knowledge had reached them. Because the last word names distance rather than doubt, the reader is shown that the quarrel was far from the text. Since the Book is named as the thing they argued over, the reader is shown that the fight was carried on with the very text in hand. The Book names the same parting of a people after knowledge had reached them in a further passage (45:17), and it warns the community against the same division (3:105). Because the verse gives the ground of the warning that came before, the reader is shown that the sentence was reasoned and not announced.

The lesson also reaches a reader who reads the Book by choosing what suits him and setting the rest aside. The two operations are named in order, the exchange and the quarrel. Since the parting is described as a distance, the reader is left with the sense that it widens with each piece of the Book he keeps.

The case is like a man who buys a map and then argues with everyone about the shape of the county. The map is on the table, the roads are drawn, and the argument grows with every mile he refuses to walk.

---

## Verse 2:177

> Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺

**THE CLAIM ABOUT THE DIRECTIONS**

The verse takes up the argument that had run through the passage: ***“Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east”*** ***“or the west. Rather, the righteous are those”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the correction of a view that made the prayer alone the whole of right conduct, and he keeps a report from the earliest teacher that the pious person is the one in whose heart obedience to God has settled. al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that the address concerned the two earlier communities, each of which faced its own quarter and claimed that its direction was the whole of the religion, and he keeps the report of the man who asked the messenger about right conduct and received this verse. al-Ālūsī keeps the same setting, since the two communities had disputed over the direction and each had confined the whole of right conduct to its own practice. Because the sentence takes the dispute away from the compass, the reader is shown where the argument had been misplaced.

**THE BELIEFS THAT COME FIRST**

The quality translated here as righteousness covers the whole of good conduct. The verse then names what the righteous person is: ***“who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books”*** ***“and the prophets”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the belief in God as the belief in one Lord described by every quality of perfection and free of every lack, and he keeps the belief in the Last Day as the acceptance of everything told about what comes after death. The Books are kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as all that was revealed and the prophets as all who were sent. Because the list begins with belief, the reader is shown that the deeds that follow grow from a living ground instead of standing alone.

**THE WEALTH GIVEN WHILE LOVED**

The verse then turns to money: ***“who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars”*** ***“and for freeing captives”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the giving as what is handed over despite the love of it, and he keeps the freeing of captives as covering both the prisoner and the one buying his own freedom by contract. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense, that what is given is given while the giver wants it and holds only a little. al-Qurṭubī keeps the order of the recipients and the rule that the gift is made in the way of charity rather than under compulsion. Because the sentence names the relatives first, the reader is shown where the duty begins.

**THE PRAYER, THE ALMS AND THE PLEDGE**

The list continues: ***“who establish prayer, pay alms-tax”*** ***“and keep the pledges they make”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the prayer as the keeping of its appointed times with its conditions, and the alms as the obligatory share. as-Saʿdī keeps the pledge as the covenant a person binds himself to, whether with God or with people. The Book names the keeping of agreements among the marks of the community in another passage, (5:2 — **“Cooperate with one another in goodness and righteousness”**). Because the pledge is placed after the two acts of worship, the reader is shown that honesty between people belongs to the same list.

**THE PATIENCE UNDER STRAIN**

The verse adds the last quality: ***“and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity”*** ***“and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the first as the patience of poverty and of illness, and the second as the patience of the battlefield when the lines meet. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same three, since need, sickness and the clash of arms cover what a person fears most. The Book sets patience and prayer together as the two supports of the community, (2:45 — **“Seek help through patience and prayer”**). Because the list ends where hardship begins, the reader is shown that all the qualities before it were being measured under pressure.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends by naming the people twice: ***“who are true ˹in faith˺”*** ***“and it is they”*** ***“who are mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the first as the truthfulness that matches the words to the deed, and the second as the fear that keeps a person inside the limits. Ibn Kathīr keeps the closing as the naming of the people of truth and of piety together. Because the sentence closes a list and not a rule, the reader is shown what the whole of right conduct amounts to.

**THE TREE AND ITS FRUIT**

The passage is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān as the point where the sūrah turns from the disputes of the earlier communities to the duties that belong to a life. He keeps the note that the address to the community begins here as the chapter reaches its half. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the two readings of the opening word and the sense that the wide good is not tied to a direction, since the change of the direction had disturbed some people when it came. Because the verse gathers belief, money, worship and endurance in one sentence, the reader is shown that no single item was allowed to stand for the whole.

The Book gathers the same qualities where it describes what a person must do to reach the good, (2:148 — **“So compete with one another in doing good”**), and it invites the same haste in a further passage, (3:133 — **“And hasten towards forgiveness from your Lord”**). Because the competition is named over deeds rather than over directions, the reader is shown where the rivalry was meant to run.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is careful about the form of his prayer and careless about the money in his hand. The verse gives him a list that begins with belief and ends with a battlefield. Since the list is read as one thing, the reader is left with a standard that cannot be met in parts.

The case is like a house whose foundations, walls, roof and door are all needed before anyone lives in it. Each part is finished on its own day, the frame stands only when the last is set, and a stranger can tell from the street whether the door is on.

---

## Verse 2:178

> O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder—a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment

**THE LAW LAID DOWN**

The verse opens a series of ordinances: ***“O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set”*** ***“for you in cases of murder”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the duty that the killer is answered for, with the sense that the punishment belongs to the killer alone and must not be carried past him to his people. al-Ālūsī keeps the same note, that the obligation is fixed with the holders of the right in view, and that the possibility of pardon does not remove it. al-Baghawī keeps the reports that the verse came down over two clans of the Arabs who had fought before the coming of the faith and had left killings and wounds unsettled between them. Because the law is stated as equality rather than as vengeance, the reader is shown what the sentence was drawn to stop.

**THE THREE PAIRS**

The pairs are named in the sentence: ***“a free man for a free man, a slave”*** ***“for a slave, and a female”*** ***“for a female. But”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the pairs as the equality of the killer and the killed, and he keeps the note that a male may be killed for a female and a free man for a slave according to the practice of the messenger. as-Saʿdī keeps the wording as taking in the man with the man and the woman with the woman, and he keeps the note that a parent is not killed for a child. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps a report that the verse concerned two clans and that the rule of an equal life stands in a further passage. The Book names that rule in the account of the table spread, (5:45 — **“a life for a life”**). Because the pairs are named so precisely, the reader is shown how the old claims of rank were being dismantled.

**THE PARDON AND THE BLOOD MONEY**

The verse opens the door of pardon: ***“if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian”*** ***“then blood-money should be decided fairly”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the pardon as the waiving of the killing in exchange for the payment. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps it as the taking of the blood money instead, and he keeps the instruction that the claimant asks according to the custom and that the payer hands it over with good grace. al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports on how the payment is arranged in stages according to its size. Because both sides of the arrangement are named, the reader is shown that the agreement had duties for the one who receives as well as for the one who pays. Since the pardon is a choice offered to the guardian, the reader is shown that the community was not pushed into revenge. Since the pardon is allowed while the law stands, the reader is shown that the right belonged to the guardian and not to the state. The Book lays the same duty of fair dealing on the one who claims a right in a further passage (2:194). Because the payment is described as courteous as well as fair, the reader is shown that the manner of the giving was part of the settlement.

**THE RELIEF AND THE WARNING**

The verse then names the arrangement for what it is: ***“and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession”*** ***“and a mercy from your Lord.”*** ***“But whoever transgresses after”*** ***“that will suffer a painful punishment”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the relief as the lightening of a rule that had been heavier for the communities before, and the warning as the case of a person who takes the payment and then turns on the killer. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same reading and adds that the blood money is fixed, paid fairly and paid promptly. Because the sentence follows the concession with a warning, the reader is shown that the softness of the rule did not soften its limit.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been wronged in a way he cannot forgive. The verse gives him his right, the shape of it, and a way to step back from it. Since the pardon is placed beside the law rather than under it, the reader is left with a door that he may open and a limit he may not cross.

The case is like a debt that the lender may write off and the borrower must pay in full if he does not. The sum is fixed, the paper is signed, and the kindness is neither owed nor lost.

---

## Verse 2:179

> There is ˹security of˺ life for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason, so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺

**THE LIFE INSIDE THE LAW**

What the law protects is named at the start: ***“There is ˹security of˺ life”*** ***“for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the law keeps people alive, since the one who intends a killing holds back when he knows the price, and both the killer and the one he meant to kill are preserved. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading and adds the tribal habit that followed a single killing with a war between two clans, from which a great number of deaths could come, until the law confined the matter to the one who was guilty. al-Jalālayn keeps the sentence as the great length of days that the rule gives. Because the sentence places life inside a rule about death, the reader is shown how the Book measures a punishment by what it prevents.

**THE WORD THAT WAS BETTER THAN THEIR PROVERB**

The verse is held up among the most compact sentences in the language. al-Ālūsī keeps the saying of the Arabs that killing is what ends killing, and he lists the reasons the verse is preferred to it: it is shorter, it holds in every case of the law, since a killing done unjustly brings more killing in its train, and it carries a promise of life rather than the bare statement that one death removes another. al-Baghawī keeps a further reading of the word for life, that the one who is punished here is kept from the punishment of the next life. Because the verse does not merely forbid a thing but promises a gain by it, the reader is shown how the law was presented to a people who counted honour above safety.

**THE MIND AND THE RESTRAINT**

The verse closes by naming the faculty it addresses: ***“so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the ending as the sense that the rule was laid down in order to bring killing to an end. al-Baghawī keeps the same reading, that the people addressed would hold back from killing for fear of the penalty. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the closing words as the warding off of one another by the fear of the law. Because the sentence ends on restraint rather than on revenge, the reader is shown what the rule was meant to produce in the heart. as-Saʿdī keeps the whole passage as the setting of the people's affairs on a fair footing, since the law takes the life of the killer and no more.

The Book sets the ruling inside the account of the pardon and the blood money, and it treats the payment of a life as a matter of fairness on both sides (2:178). Because the same law is described in the two verses as equal and as merciful together, the reader is shown that justice and ease were given as one package.

The lesson also reaches a reader who thinks a harsh rule can only make a harsh society. The sentence says the opposite in four words. Since the promise is life, the reader is left with the sense that a limit firmly drawn is one of the ways a city is kept standing.

The case is like a cliff path with a wall along the outer side. The wall is a restriction, the drop beside it is real, and the walkers who complain about the wall are the ones it keeps alive.

---

## Verse 2:180

> It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you—if they leave something of value—a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺

**THE DUTY AT THE APPROACH OF DEATH**

The verse lays down a second ordinance: ***“It is prescribed that”*** ***“when death approaches any of you”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the obligation to make a bequest for the parents and the near relatives in a fair manner. al-Baghawī keeps the sense of the approach of death as the coming of its causes and its signs in illness and disease. al-Ālūsī keeps the same reading and keeps the note that the sentence was not opened with the address used for the harsher duties, because this one was not hard on the people. Because the duty is tied to the moment when a person can no longer benefit himself, the reader is shown that the last act of a life was still counted as part of it.

**THE WEALTH THAT IS LEFT**

The condition is named next: ***“if they leave something of value”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the word as material possessions, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense of an estate that is worth passing on. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the report that this mention of good carries the sense of wealth among the Arabs, and he keeps the practice of the early community, when the shares of the heirs had not yet been fixed and a person disposed of what he owned by bequest. as-Saʿdī keeps the report that the bequest was aimed at the parents and the near relatives, with the shares of those who inherit settled afterwards by the verses of inheritance. Because the sentence measures the duty by what is left, the reader is shown that the obligation did not fall on a person with nothing to give.

**THE ORDER OF THE KIN**

The recipients are named after it: ***“a will should be made in favour of parents”*** ***“and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those”*** ***“who are mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the fairness as the giving of what is due by custom, without waste and without turning to the distant relatives while the near are left out, and he keeps the ranking of the kin by nearness and by need. Ibn Kathīr keeps the report that the sentence was later abrogated for those who inherit, since their shares were fixed. Because the duty is closed with a name for the God-fearing, the reader is shown what kind of person was expected to carry it out. Since the wasiyyah belonged to the days before the shares of the heirs were fixed, the reader is shown that the passage preserves an early stage of the law.

The Book names the bequest among the matters that must be settled before an estate is divided, and it places the shares of the heirs after it (4:11). Because the sentence names the parents before the rest of the family, the reader is shown where the first claim on a life's earnings lies.

The lesson also reaches a reader who means to set his affairs in order but keeps putting it off. The verse gives him the moment, the people and the manner. Since the moment named is the approach of death, the reader is left with the knowledge that a will written in health is itself an act of piety.

The case is like a man who leaves a farm to his children without a line written about who gets which field. The land is good, the heirs are many, and the quarrel at the gate begins before the funeral is over.

---

## Verse 2:181

> But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE CHANGE MADE AFTER HEARING**

The verse fences the duty of the verse before it: ***“But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those”*** ***“who made the change.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the change as the altering of what the dying person set out, and he keeps the sense that the fault rests on the one who alters and not on the one who made the will. al-Baghawī keeps the reports that name the trustee, the guardian and the witness among those who may alter it, whether by denying the will or by cutting it down. al-Qurṭubī keeps the construction of the sentence, that the change is known to have been heard and understood before it counts against him. Because the hearing is named first, the reader is shown that the fault was deliberate. Since the change could be made by a trustee, a guardian or a witness, the reader is shown how many hands the document passes through. The Book records the same care for what a dying person has set down in the passage of the testifying witnesses (5:106). Because the fault is laid on the one who acts, the reader is shown that no one else's silence was being blamed.

**THE FAULT LAID ON THE RIGHT PERSON**

The verse singles out the guilty: ***“who made the change.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the same reading and adds that the alteration may be by denying the bequest altogether, by reducing it, or by changing its terms, and he keeps the report of the teachers that a trustee appointed for one specific thing is not to be treated as a trustee for the rest. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sentence as the statement that the one who changes the will bears its burden and that the dead person is free of it. Because the fault is placed on the living hand, the reader is shown that the record is kept against the one who acts. Since the verse concerns a document that has been heard and understood, the reader is shown that a change made in ignorance was treated differently from one made with knowledge.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends on the knowledge of God: ***“Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the two names as the statement that what was said by the dying person is heard and that what the changer intends is known. al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense, with the hearing of the bequest and the knowledge of the change. Because the sentence closes on the two names, the reader is shown that an alteration made in a room with one witness has a second witness who never leaves. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the will as the last order a person gives, and he keeps the duty of carrying it out as it was set down.

The Book carries the same care for the property of people in the account of the orphans, where the taking of their wealth is named among the grave faults. Because the sentence stands between the duty of the will and the permission that follows for a fair settlement, the reader is shown that the passage protects the dying person from both the dishonest and the careless.
