The lesson also reaches a reader who is made an executor by a neighbour or a parent. The verse gives him the document and the two names above it. Since the fault is named as his own and not as theirs, the reader is left with a task that unites his interest and his honesty.

The case is like a man asked to hold the key to a storeroom while the owner lies ill. The goods are counted, the list is read aloud to him, and he knows exactly how much he will have to explain afterwards.

---

## Verse 2:182

> Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**THE FEAR OF A WRONG**

The verse returns with a limit of its own: ***“Whoever suspects an error”*** ***“or an injustice in the will”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the first word as the mistake made without intent, so that the testator turns from what is right by error, and the second as a deliberate wrong. al-Baghawī keeps the sense of the word as knowing rather than fearing, since the verse is about a case that has actually happened. al-Qurṭubī keeps a note on the language of the sentence and a report that the word for error covers a departure from what is right. Because two kinds of fault are named, the reader is shown that the harm to be corrected could come from the dying person as well as from the heirs. Since the settlement is left to the one who sees the wrong, the reader is shown that the passage puts the repair in the hands of the bystander. The Book orders the same repairing of what has gone wrong between people in a further passage, where the settling of a dispute is placed beside belief and patience (49:9). Because the permission is given before the wrong is done, the reader is shown that the passage expected trouble and made room for it.

**THE SETTLEMENT MADE BETWEEN THEM**

The verse then permits the correction: ***“and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the settlement as the reconciling of the testator with his heirs by turning him back to fairness in his bequest, and by preventing the heirs from blocking what the law has allowed him. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same picture, with the will carried out before the next verse came down and the settlement standing afterwards. Because the verse leaves the settlement open to the person on the spot, the reader is shown that the document was not allowed to become a trap.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The closing names are kept by as-Saʿdī as the assurance that a person who steps in to put a matter right does so under a mercy that covers his own slips as well. Because the sentence places forgiveness beside the work of a mediator, the reader is shown that the one who arranges peace is not held to a higher book than others. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the message that there is no fault in the settlement. The Book orders the same repairing of what has gone wrong between people elsewhere, giving the one who adjusts between two sides a share of the matter (2:182). Because the verse ends with the two names, the reader is shown that the correction of a wrong was itself an act of piety.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is asked to witness a document he can see is unfair. The verse gives him room to speak and to rearrange. Since the permission comes with the names of forgiveness attached, the reader is left with the knowledge that the person who fixes the paper is not the one who wrote it.

The case is like a man who is handed a set of scales with the weights hidden under the pan. The brass is polished, the merchant is honest in other matters, and the hand that unbolts the pan has done more for the trade than any praise of it.

---

## Verse 2:183

> O believers! Fasting is prescribed for you—as it was for those before you—so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺

**THE DUTY ANNOUNCED**

The verse opens the account of the fast: ***“O believers! Fasting is prescribed”*** ***“for you as it was”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the obligation of the fast laid on the community, and he keeps the sense of the opening address as the call to a people who had already believed. al-Ālūsī keeps the address itself as the mark of care, and he notes that the word for fasting carries the sense of holding back, so that even silence is sometimes named by it because it holds the tongue. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the fast here as the holding back from food, drink and intimacy from the beginning of the duty, and he keeps the note that the number of the days was later fixed. Because the command is given as an obligation and not as a counsel, the reader is shown what kind of duty this was.

**THE COMMUNITIES THAT CAME BEFORE**

The sentence reaches back before the community: ***“for those before you”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the earlier communities as sharing the duty, since the fast is one of the laws that serves people in every age, and he keeps the note that the command was placed as an encouragement to outdo them rather than as a burden laid on a single generation. al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense, that the fast had been prescribed for the communities that came before, and he keeps the point that the fast curbs the desires which lead to disobedience. Because the duty is shared with the past, the reader is shown that he is not being singled out to carry something new.

**THE PURPOSE AT THE CLOSE**

The aim is named at the close: ***“so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the ending as the warding off of disobedience, and al-Ṭabarī keeps the same sense of the fear that holds a person inside the limits. as-Saʿdī keeps the whole verse as the same message as the one before it, that the laws are for the good of the people who keep them, and that the fast in particular is not among the heavy things that crush a soul. The Book attaches the same purpose to the fast in the passage that follows, where the days of the month are named and the guidance is given its full shape (2:185). Because the closing words name restraint and not hunger, the reader is shown what the fast was for.

The Book describes the fast among the days of a month whose nights carry a command of their own, so that the duty and its ease are read together (2:187). Because the verse starts with belief and ends with God-consciousness, the reader is shown that the fast was set between the two.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has gone without food before for the sake of a body he wants to shrink. The verse gives him a fast with a purpose outside the body. Since the closing word names the fear of God rather than the loss of weight, the reader is left with an act whose measure is inward.

The case is like a man who is asked to guard a house for a month by sitting outside its door. The sitting is not the point, the house is, and the house is not his to keep unless he stays awake.

---

## Verse 2:184

> ˹Fast a˺ prescribed number of days. But whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. For those who can only fast with extreme difficulty, compensation can be made by feeding a needy person ˹for every day not fasted˺. But whoever volunteers to give more, it is better for them. And to fast is better for you, if only you knew

**THE FEW DAYS NAMED**

The verse fixes the length: ***“˹Fast a˺ prescribed number of days.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the days as a set number named in the sentence, so that the duty would be known in advance. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the days as the month that is named later in the passage. al-Ālūsī keeps the number as a small count that is easy to reckon, and he keeps the report that a counted number in this Book is always short of forty. Because the sentence gives the number first, the reader is shown how the duty was made manageable before its rules were unfolded.

**THE SICK AND THE TRAVELLER**

The first concession follows: ***“But whoever of you is ill”*** ***“or on a journey”*** ***“then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the two cases as the dropping of the duty from a person who cannot carry it, with the same number owed on other days. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading, that the sick and the travelling person fast later the number of days they missed, and he keeps the early practice that a ransom was allowed for those who could afford it before the rule was settled. The same concession is kept by Ibn Kathīr as it stands. Because the two cases are named before the alternative, the reader is shown that the relief was planned into the duty rather than added after trouble came. Since the ransom is granted to the one who cannot manage the fast at all, the reader is shown that the law measured the body and not the will. Because the closing sentence names knowledge as the missing thing, the reader is shown that the preference for the fast was an argument and not a command.

**THE RANSOM FOR THE UNABLE**

The verse then addresses those who cannot manage it at all: ***“For those who can only fast with extreme difficulty, compensation can be made by feeding a needy person ˹for every day not fasted˺.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the feeding as the ransom of a person who can afford the food but not the fast. al-Baghawī keeps the reports on the early days of the community, when the fast of a few days in every month and the day of the tenth were binding until the month was named and the rule was settled. as-Saʿdī keeps the whole passage as the measure of ease in the law. Because the verse names a substitute rather than a punishment, the reader is shown what kind of obligation this was.

**THE BETTER CHOICE AND THE BETTER CHOICE**

The verse closes with two preferences: ***“But whoever volunteers to give more, it is better”*** ***“for them. And to fast is better”*** ***“for you, if only you knew”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the giving beyond the required share, and the second as the fast itself, which is better for the one who is able. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the closing as the statement that the hardship of the fast is outweighed by its reward for the person who understands. Because the last sentence names knowledge as the missing thing, the reader is shown why the two preferences needed to be stated at all.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is ill and keeps the fast out of pride, or well and breaks it out of slackness. The verse gives him the licence, the substitute and the preference. Since the law names a way through every case, the reader is left with the knowledge that the difficulty was expected before the month began.

The case is like a mountain path with a tunnel cut beside it. The tunnels are not for the strong, the climb is not for the weak, and both reach the same valley by nightfall.

---

## Verse 2:185

> Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity with clear proofs of guidance and the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺. So whoever is present this month, let them fast. But whoever is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. Allah intends ease for you, not hardship, so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful

**THE MONTH NAMED**

The month and its honour open the sentence: ***“Ramaḍân is the month in”*** ***“which the Quran was revealed”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the naming of the month as tied to what is publicly known, since a month is a span marked out and recognised. al-Baghawī keeps the reports that the month was named so before the coming of the community, and he keeps the report that the whole Book was brought down to the lowest heaven in that month and then sent in portions. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same report, that the Book came down to the heaven of this world in the month and was then given to the messenger in instalments. The Book names the descent itself in a further passage, (44:3 — **“We sent it down on a blessed night”**). Because the month is honoured by what came down in it, the reader is shown why the fast was attached to those days.

**THE GUIDANCE THE BOOK CARRIES**

The verse describes what came down: ***“as a guide for humanity with clear proofs of guidance”*** ***“and the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the guidance as a state belonging to the Book itself, leading people away from error, and the clear proofs as the signs that make the way plain, and the standard as what separates truth from falsehood. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same three as they stand in the sentence. The Book describes its own work in the same terms in a further passage, (17:9 — **“This Quran guides to what is most upright”**). Because the Book is named as a guide for all people, the reader is shown that the month's honour did not belong to one community alone.

**THE FAST OF THE MONTH AND ITS RELIEF**

The command follows: ***“So whoever is present this month, let them fast. But whoever is ill”*** ***“or on a journey”*** ***“then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the presence in the month as the proof of fitness other than illness and journeys, and he keeps the same two concessions as in the sentence before. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the presence as being at home and able. Because the command repeats what was already given, the reader is shown that the rule was settled for the community once and for all.

**THE EASE INTENDED**

The verse then names the will behind the law: ***“Allah intends ease”*** ***“for you, not hardship”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the purpose of the concessions: ease rather than burden, and the completion of the days rather than their loss. al-Ālūsī keeps the same reading and keeps the sense that the count is finished so that nobody is left with days owed by accident. Because the sentence names the intention behind the relief, the reader is shown what the law was reaching for.

**THE COMPLETION AND THE GREATNESS**

The verse continues: ***“so that you may complete the prescribed period”*** ***“and proclaim the greatness of Allah”*** ***“for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the completion as the finishing of the days and the greatness as the naming of God over the end of the fast. as-Saʿdī keeps gratitude as the mark that ties the whole passage to the one before, where the fast itself was commanded for the sake of restraint and thanks. The Book tells the same community that its Lord answers the call of the one who prays (40:60 — **“I will respond to you”**), and the verse that follows this one carries that promise in its own words. Because the passage ends with thanks, the reader is shown that the aim of the month was a heart turned towards the giver.

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps a duty without knowing why its exceptions exist. The verse gives him the truth with the month, the rules with the relief, and the aim with the rules. Since the aim named is ease and the end named is thanks, the reader is left with a law that was built to be kept.

The case is like a host who sets a table for a whole village and lays out different dishes for the young, the old and the sick. The table is one, the day is one, and nobody is asked to eat what would harm him.

---

## Verse 2:186

> When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near. I respond to one’s prayer when they call upon Me. So let them respond ˹with obedience˺ to Me and believe in Me, perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺

**THE QUESTION ABOUT GOD**

The verse answers a question that had not been written down: ***“When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the question as one about where God is, and he keeps the answer as the nearness of the Lord to the one who calls. al-Baghawī keeps the report that the people of the city asked the messenger how their Lord hears their prayers if He is far away, and he keeps the report that a group of the companions asked whether they should speak quietly or raise their voices. as-Saʿdī keeps the same report, with the question being whether the Lord is near enough to be whispered to or far enough for a shout. Because the question was about nearness, the reader is shown that the answer was placed where the question would be asked.

**THE NEARNESS NAMED**

The answer is immediate: ***“I am truly near. I respond to one’s prayer”*** ***“when they call upon Me.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the shift in the sentence as an honour given to the messenger, since the servants are named as belonging to God and the answer is given without an intermediary. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the nearness as closeness in answering, and he keeps the report that the audience for the verse included the people of the earlier books. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the statement that the answer comes without a mediator or an intercessor. Because the answer is in the first person, the reader is shown how directly the matter was put.

**THE RESPONSE ASKED IN RETURN**

The verse then turns the sentence around: ***“So let them respond ˹with obedience˺ to Me”*** ***“and believe in Me, perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the first as the answering of the call of God with obedience, and he keeps the promise of guidance as the fruit of it. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, that the servants are asked to answer God as He answers them. The Book asks the same of the community in an earlier passage of this chapter, (2:45 — **“Seek help through patience and prayer”**). Because the verse closes on guidance rather than on the request, the reader is shown what the answer was for.

**THE PLACE OF THE VERSE**

The passage is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān as a brief sentence set in the middle of the rules of the fast, which he explains as a sign that the month was never only about food. He keeps the note that the sentence about answering is repeated in full in the Book elsewhere, and that the nearness named here is the nearness of the one who hears. Because the verse stands among the fasting verses, the reader is shown that the supplication of the fasting person was being answered while the rules were still being given.

Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the address as going through the messenger, who was the channel by which the answer reached the people, and he keeps the closing promise as the guidance that follows belief. The Book names the same bond in another passage, where the servants are told that their Lord says to call on Him and that He will answer (40:60 — **“I will respond to you”**). Because the messenger is named in the opening and God in the answer, the reader is shown that the question was answered by the one who was asked about. Since the answer is given in the first person, the reader is shown that the nearness was declared rather than argued.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been told that his Lord is distant and that access to Him must be earned. The verse answers with a first-person promise and a reversal: he is asked to answer God. Since the promise stands in the middle of a passage about hunger and thirst, the reader is left with the knowledge that the month of fasting was also a month of nearness.

The case is like a child who is told that his father is away on a long journey, and who then hears the father's voice say clearly that he is in the next room. The journey was real, the errand was long, and the voice was closer than the rumour.

---

## Verse 2:187

> It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺

**THE NIGHT THAT WAS OPENED**

The verse opens by declaring lawful what had been barred before it: ***“It has”*** ***“been made permissible”*** ***“for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast.”*** al-Ṭabarī records that the opening words carry the sense of a thing loosed and set free. The same report adds that the word used for intimacy is a covering expression for the marital act, chosen because the Quran prefers the veil to the plain word.

The earlier rule is described in the reports. al-Jalālayn keeps the first phase of the community's practice as one in which food, drink and intimacy were barred once a person had slept or had prayed the night prayer. The same reading takes this verse as the lifting of that bar. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same account from a narration of al-Bukhārī: whoever broke the fast and then slept before eating was held to the fast until the next evening. A nap after the meal thus became a wall. al-Ālūsī keeps the report of the Companion who found his wife asleep, woke her, and lay with her, and the report of a second man who did the same. The same report notes that the strain fell on the community until the verse came down.

**THE GARMENT OF THE TWO SPOUSES**

The next sentence gives the reason for the easing in an image: ***“Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the garment as a rest and a covering, so that each spouse is the other's shelter from exposure and from want. al-Jalālayn keeps the image as a figure for the embrace and for the need each has of the other. The same reading notes that the sentence works in both directions at once.

The image explains why the permission is given without embarrassment. Because a garment belongs to the body that wears it and moves with it, the sentence places the two spouses in one covering rather than in two separate claims. The reader is shown a relation in which the nearness is the point of the command rather than an exception to it.

**THE SECRET KEPT AND THE PARDON**

The verse then names what the community had been doing: ***“Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the deceit as one practised against the self. The one who takes what he was told to leave harms no one more than he harms himself. al-Ṭabarī's reading in the older reports keeps the same sense: the people were betraying their own share by doing in secret what they had been forbidden openly.

Then comes the mercy: ***“So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the acceptance as a turning that came before any formal request. The widening of the rule removed the ground of the sin altogether. al-Jalālayn keeps the same note, that the relenting was granted before the people turned to ask, and that the pardon covered what had already passed. Because the fault is described as a wrong done to oneself, the pardon restores what the wrong had damaged. And the reader is shown that the road back is short.

**WHAT IS SOUGHT AND WHAT IS EATEN**

The permission is then restated with a purpose added: ***“So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās keeps what is sought as a righteous child, and as-Saʿdī keeps it wider: the intention of drawing near to God in the act itself, together with the offspring, the chastity and the purposes of marriage. He adds that among what is written for the community in those nights is the night of decree, so that a night of rest should not be spent away from its seeking.

The verse then lays down the timetable of the fast: ***“˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night”*** ***“then complete the fast until nightfall.”*** Ibn Kathīr keeps the dawn as the moment the white thread is distinguished from the black. The same reading notes that the verse fixes the bound by sight rather than by guess, so that a person eats while he still sees the two threads apart. The completion is kept as the finishing of the day's fast at the coming of night, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same limit. Because the two ends of the fast are named by what the eye finds rather than by a clock, the rule is left within the reach of the simplest reader.

**THE RETREAT AND THE LIMITS**

One place is carved out of the permission: ***“Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques.”*** Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the state described here as the retreat kept in the mosque. The same section notes that the prohibition belongs to the days and nights of the retreat rather than to the fast alone. The verse thus marks the one station in which the permission is set aside, and marks it by the place and the practice together.

The section closes with a warning and a summary: ***“These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them.”*** The word for limits is kept by al-Qurʾān's commentators in the sense of boundary stones set between the permitted and the forbidden. as-Saʿdī keeps the closing phrase as a statement that the commands themselves are the boundary, so that the one who keeps them stays inside and the one who stretches them has left. Because the limits are named as God's own, the reader is shown that the ruling is not a cultural arrangement that a community may renegotiate.

**THE CLEARING AT THE CLOSE**

The last sentence names the method of the whole passage: ***“This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people”*** ***“so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺”*** The clearing is kept by al-Ṭabarī as the explaining of the lawful and the unlawful so that no confusion remains. the closing purpose is kept by al-Jalālayn as the guarding of the self from the forbidden.

Because the verse began with a mistake and a pardon and ends with a rule plainly stated, the reader is shown how the Quran trains a community: the fault is named without being buried, the relief is given, and a boundary is left that can be remembered.

The Book gives the same relief as a stated aim rather than as an exception. And it does so in the verse that frames the whole month, (2:185 — **“Allah intends ease for you, not hardship”**), where the same hand that commands the fast is named as the one that wishes the burden light. A further passage puts the ease inside the religion itself, (22:78), so that the reader does not take severity for piety.

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps the fast but treats his nights as a field for everything he wants, on the assumption that the hours after sunset are outside the law. The verse gives him a timetable with two ends and a boundary around the whole day, so that the fast becomes a full circle rather than a gap. Since the community in the passage needed a rule and a pardon at the same time, the reader learns to expect both from the same Lord. Because the door is named in the same breath as the wall, the mercy of the verse is not a hole in the law but part of it.

The case is like a shepherd who first shuts the gate at nightfall and finds the flock pressing against it. and then opens it at the hour the pasture can bear, keeping only the fence at the far end. The flock walks out without fear, the fence still stands, and the one who opened the gate is thanked rather than blamed.

---

## Verse 2:188

> Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property, knowing that it is a sin

**THE WEALTH OF THE HOUSEHOLD**

The verse follows the fasting commands with a prohibition about money: ***“Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the address as words to one community about their own property, so that the wealth of each is described as the wealth of all the others, in the same manner as the Book says that no one should defame his own people or kill his own selves. Because the ownership is turned outward in that way, the prohibition carries a heavier weight than a simple ban on theft.

as-Saʿdī keeps the same reading and draws out its reach. He keeps the reason for the shared phrasing as the wish that a Muslim love for his brother what he loves for himself and guard his brother's property as his own, adding that the wrongdoer's example is contagious. The one who eats another's wealth gives others leave to eat his own. He then lists what the prohibition covers: seizure by force, theft, breach of trust over a deposit or a loan, and gain through contracts that are themselves forbidden, such as interest and every form of gambling. He adds cheating in sale, hire and labour, the withholding of wages. and wages taken for work not done.

**THE GIFTS TAKEN TO THE JUDGE**

The second half of the verse names a subtler route: ***“nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the words as the casting of a case towards the rulers with money in hand, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same sense with the note that the address covers the whole community.

A story is kept in the sources for the occasion of the verse. al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī both report a dispute over land between a man of Kindah and a man of the south, brought before the Prophet ﷺ, in which the claimant had no proof and the defendant was offered an oath. The report continues that when the oath was about to be taken over property unjustly, the Prophet ﷺ had given the warning that the one who swears to a lie to take a Muslim's right will meet God with His face turned away. The verse came down over that matter. al-Jalālayn keeps the offence in the same light: the money is offered to the judges so that by their ruling a share of the people's property may be eaten.

**THE KNOWLEDGE THAT MAKES IT A SIN**

The verse ends with a condition that removes the excuse of ignorance: ***“knowing that it is a sin”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps a reading from Ibn ʿAbbās in which the verse concerns a debtor who denies a loan that has no written proof, so that the matter goes to the authorities and he takes what he knows is not his. The verse thus names the inner state, since the wrong is the clearer when the man knows that the paper he holds is another's.

Because the knowledge is named at the close rather than at the open, the reader is shown that the sin is not in the legal appearance but in the fact known to the one who pleads. A court may be deceived, but the One who wrote the deed is not. The man who deceived it stands before Him.

**THE PLACE OF THE VERSE**

The position of the sentence is kept by al-Ālūsī and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān as a deliberate pairing with the fast that precedes it. The fast trains the person to leave what is lawful for a set number of hours, so that leaving what is unlawful becomes lighter for him; the verse that follows extends the training to property. Because the two commands stand side by side, the reader is shown that a month of restraint is not a private exercise but a schooling for the dealings of the rest of the year.

The Book states the same claim about truth in speech and fairness in dealing where it addresses a community that had the text in its hands, (2:42 — **“do not mix truth with falsehood”**). . The two offences are kept together there: money taken by a false claim and truth hidden by a false mixture.

The lesson also reaches a reader who would never steal but who signs for a friend's debt without the intention of paying it, or who lets a cousin sit on his land because the papers are confusing. The verse gives him a mirror in which the small dishonesty and the large one stand side by side, and it asks him which of the two he would defend out loud.

The case is like a man who borrows his neighbour's lamp for an hour and, when he is asked for it, says the hour has not come. The lamp is small, the room is dark, and he has now made himself the owner of the daylight as well as of the night.

---

## Verse 2:189

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. Say, “They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage.” Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors. Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺. So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors, and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful

**THE QUESTION ABOUT THE CRESCENTS**

The verse opens with a question put to the Prophet ﷺ: ***“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the questioners as a group of the People of the Book pressing the community with the question. The same report has one of the Companions asking on their behalf why the crescent shows thin, swells to fullness and returns to thinness. al-Ālūsī notes the weakness of one report on the occasion and keeps the substance, that the community and its questioners wanted to know why the moon is made to run through those states.

Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the point that the question was about the wisdom rather than the mechanics. The same reading grounds it in the shape of the answer itself, since the reply names a benefit and not a cause. The further detail is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān: a Jewish group was testing the Prophet ﷺ with such questions, so that the occasion belongs to the disputation of the city rather than to private curiosity.

**THE TIMES THEY MEASURE**

The answer names the use of the moon: ***“Say, “They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage.””*** al-Ṭabarī records a reading of the verse in which the fasts of the Muslims, their breaking of the fast, their rites, their pilgrimage, the waiting periods of their women and the terms of their debts were all measured by the crescent. as-Saʿdī keeps the same list and adds the wisdom of the choice: a reckoning that a child and a shepherd and a scholar can all read from the sky, whereas a solar reckoning would be known only to those trained in it.

Because the moon is named as a public calendar rather than a private sign, the reader is shown that the rites of the religion are tied to something anyone may see. Ibn Kathīr keeps the phrase as marks of fixed periods for mankind and for the pilgrimage, and the mention of the pilgrimage at the close of the answer shows which of the uses the passage will next unfold.

**THE DOORS AND THE OLD CUSTOM**

The verse then turns from the moon to a practice that had grown up around the pilgrimage: ***“Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors.”*** The point of the correction is the inside of the man and not the wall he climbs: ***“Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺.”*** The instruction then follows in plain words: ***“So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors”***. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the custom as one of the days before Islam, in which a person entering the state of pilgrimage would refuse to enter his house by its door, even to the point of cutting a hole in the wall. The same section keeps the note that the answer corrects the assumption that such a hardship is itself devotion.

The same correction is kept by Ibn Kathīr, with the reading that the door of a house and the door of a tent are alike meant to be used as they are, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the verse as a rebuke of the men of the city who had made a burden of their own invention. Because the correction is placed after the calendar, the reader is shown that the times are made for the people and not the people for the times.

**THE CLOSE ON SUCCESS**

The verse ends with a promise attached to the command: ***“and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful”***. as-Saʿdī keeps success as the reaching of what is hoped for and the safety from what is feared. The same reading keeps its condition as mindfulness, so that the closing word gathers both this life and the next.

The Book sets the same concern in the passage where the sacred months and their number are laid out, (9:36 — **“the number of months ordained by Allah is twelve”**). . The reader is shown there that the calendar of the rites is not a custom of a nation but a measure set in the order of the heavens.

The lesson also reaches a reader who turns a rule of worship into a burden for others, insisting on a form of austerity that the religion never asked for and treating his own scruple as the standard of everyone else's piety. The verse gives him the example of a man who would climb in through a hole rather than use his own door. And it asks him which of the two entrances was the act of obedience.

The case is like a traveller who, told to set out at dawn, spends the night outside the city wall rather than sleep in his own bed, afraid that comfort will spoil the journey. The road is waiting for him either way, and the night he passed on the stones was not part of the route.

---

## Verse 2:190

> Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Allah does not like transgressors

**THE FIRST COMMAND TO FIGHT**

The verse opens the passage on fighting: ***“Fight in the cause of Allah”***. al-Baghawī keeps the report that the community was held back from fighting at the beginning of Islam. The command came after the migration to the city. So that the verse marks a new stage in the affairs of the community rather than a permanent posture. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same sequence and lists the earlier verses that told the believers to repel evil with what is better and to forgive, noting that the hand was stayed in Mecca and loosed after the migration.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the agreement of the community on that sequence. The same entry adds a report from the Companion Abū Bakr in which the verse is remembered as the first revealed on the subject. Because the command comes in a passage about fasting, pilgrimage and money, the reader is shown that the affairs of the community are gathered in one frame: worship, dealings and the defence of the whole.

**THE ROAD NAMED AS HIS**

The first words name the purpose before they name the enemy: ***“Fight in the cause of Allah”***. al-Ālūsī keeps the path as a figure for God's religion and His word, so that the sense is the fight for the honour of the religion and not spoil or a tribe. as-Saʿdī keeps the specification as a call to sincerity and a prohibition of fighting in the disputes that rise between Muslims themselves.

Because those words stand at the head of the sentence, the reader is shown that the intention is part of the command and not an ornament on it. A man may carry a weapon for a hundred reasons, and only one of them makes the act obedience.

**THOSE WHO BEGIN**

The enemy is then limited by a description: ***“˹only˺ against those who wage war against you”***. The older reports keep the sense as those who take the initiative in fighting. as-Saʿdī keeps them as the able men who are prepared for war, excluding the old who have no part in the decision and no strength for the field.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same phrase as an answer to the question of place as well as of person, so that the fight is against those who begin it, wherever they begin it. Because the description is attached to the command itself, the community is not left to decide for itself where the fight may be carried. And the reader is shown that the limit belongs to the law rather than to the general's judgement.

**THE LIMIT THAT IS NOT CROSSED**

The sentence then adds its own fence: ***“but do not exceed the limits. Allah does not like transgressors”***. as-Saʿdī draws the list from the phrase: no killing of women, children or the insane, no killing of monks and those who have withdrawn from the fight, no mutilation of the dead, no killing of animals and no felling of trees where the community gains nothing by it. and no fighting of those who have accepted the protection of the tax and paid it. He keeps the warning at the close as a sign that the excess itself is the offence, even when it is done to an enemy.

The two names at the end are kept by al-Baghawī and Ibn ʿAbbās in the same sense: God does not love those who begin hostilities or those who stretch the fighting past what they were told. Because the verse ends on the disposal of the Lord rather than on the punishment of the enemy, the reader is shown that the danger in war sits on the side of the one who holds the weapon.

The Book gives the same command with the same limit in the passage that addresses the sacred months, (9:36 — **“And together fight the polytheists as they fight against you together”**). . Each side of the encounter is measured there against what the other has brought. A further verse states the aim more plainly still, (2:193), where the fighting is to last only until the persecution ends.

The lesson also reaches a reader who takes a good cause as a licence for any method, arguing that the end he serves is noble enough to excuse the means he uses. The verse gives him a command with a fence built into it. And it shows him that the limit is not a weakness of the cause but part of its claim to be in God's path.

The case is like a doctor who is called to cut out a growth and takes the whole limb because the knife is in his hand. The operation is remembered for the arm that was lost, and the patient never asks about the growth.

---

## Verse 2:191

> Kill them wherever you come upon them and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out. For persecution is far worse than killing. And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there. If they do so, then fight them—that is the reward of the disbelievers

**THE WORD THAT MEANS FINDING**

The command continues with a phrase of wide reach: ***“Kill them wherever you come upon them”***. al-Baghawī keeps the root of the word as skill and clear sight in a matter. The same entry takes the phrase as a permission to fight where the strength of the enemy is in view and the chance is in reach. al-Ṭabarī keeps the same sense: wherever you find their fighting positions and are able to reach them.

al-Ālūsī keeps the report of the question put to Ibn ʿAbbās by a man of the Kharijite tribe about the meaning of the phrase. The report keeps the reply that it belonged to a time and a place and had been explained by what followed. Because the verse itself goes on to name a place where the permission does not run, the reader is shown that the wide phrase is to be read with the sentence that follows rather than apart from it.

**THE RETURN OF THE DISPOSSESSED**

The verse then names the second duty: ***“and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the words addressed to those who had been expelled from their homes. The same reading keeps the sense that the same road should run in the other direction: as they drove you out, drive them out. al-Jalālayn keeps the place as Mecca. The same reading keeps the note that the return was carried out after the conquest.

Because the command is shaped as a return rather than as an advance, the reader is shown that the verse does not open a country but restores a road. Since the comparison turns on what a community stands to lose rather than on what it spends, the reader is shown where the weight of the sentence lies. The symmetry is the argument: the community is told to do exactly what was done to it and to stop where the balance ends.

**THE HARM THE WEIGHT NAMES**

Then comes the sentence that weighs the two harms: ***“For persecution is far worse than killing.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the persecution as the testing of a believer in his religion until he turns from it. The same reading takes the phrase as the claim that being pushed back into idolatry after faith is worse for a man than dying on what he believes. He keeps the report of Mujāhid that the return of a believer to the idols is heavier than the loss of his life.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading, with the note that the association of partners with God is what the sentence describes. Because the comparison is between two harms rather than between a harm and a good, the reader is shown why the fight was pressed: not because blood is cheap. The fight was pressed instead because a community left without protection loses the thing that makes its life worth keeping.

**THE MOSQUE AND THE FIRST BLOW**

The next sentence names the single place where the permission is suspended: ***“And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there. If they do so, then fight them”***. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the occasion in the year of the treaty, when the community came for the lesser pilgrimage in a sacred month and had to decide whether to fight inside the inviolable precinct. The same entry keeps the note that a small quarrel was kept from growing inside the sanctuary.

al-Jalālayn keeps the same restraint and the same exception, so that the inviolability of the place holds until the enemy breaks it. Because the exception is named in the same sentence as the prohibition, the reader is shown that the law protects even the ground on which the enemy stands, until the enemy uses it as a position.

**THE RECOMPENSE NAMED**

The verse closes with a statement of what awaits them: ***“that is the reward of the disbelievers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the announcement that the one who falls in such a fight falls within the sentence he had earned, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same plain sense.

The Book puts the same encounter in a fuller statement elsewhere, (2:217 — **“And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith”**), where the reader is shown that the hostile side had a settled aim and would not stop at a border. A further passage gives the other side of the balance, (2:190), where the excess is forbidden to the believers.

The lesson also reaches a reader who is wronged and then, once the wrong is at his door, decides to settle every quarrel in the street. The verse gives him a permission bounded by place and by cause, and it asks him whether the fight he is planning is a return or a raid. Because the persecuted are told to press only to the point of release, the reader is taught to measure his own grievance against what he proposes to do.

The case is like a man whose neighbour floods his field by breaking the ditch bank, and who then breaks the bank on the other side as well. The second gap lets the water through at both ends, and the field he was defending is under water from the pair.

---

## Verse 2:192

> But if they cease, then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**THE STOPPING NAMED**

The verse hangs the whole settlement on one verb: ***“But if they cease”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the ceasing as the abandonment of both the fighting and the denial, together with the return to God. The same reading notes that the sentence was revealed about a people whose hostility had been open and whose change would therefore be visible.

al-Ālūsī keeps two readings of what is left behind. In the first, they stop the denial by turning back from it, as one report keeps the words. in the second, they stop both the denial and the fighting. The verse had just named the two matters in a single command. He keeps the second reading as the stronger, because the mention of both in the preceding sentence gives the pronoun both for its content.

**THE DOOR THAT IS LEFT OPEN**

The sentence then names what they will find: ***“then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the first name as the pardon granted to those who embrace the faith and the second as the mercy kept for those who die within it. al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair with the note that both names are given to the ones who desist.

Because the passage has just been commanding the fight, the reader is shown that the command was never aimed at a people as a tribe but at a state of hostility. The verse places the door beside the wall: as soon as the enemy lays down the cause of the fighting, the names of mercy are spoken over him. The door is not a reward for a strong side that has earned it, since it is the rule of the Lord who accepts the turning of the one who turns. Maʿārif al-Qurʾan keeps the passage as the placing of the fight within limits, so that the ceasing of the enemy closes the matter without a further price. Since the community is being trained to fight while keeping its own hand off the excess, the closing names are its protection against the belief that war ends only when a people ends.

The Book gives the same open door in a later address to those who have gone to the far end of their own ruin, (39:53 — **“Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins”**). The same breadth is put in a verse of the city period, (17:9), where the reader is told what the Book guides towards.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been injured by a group and then treats every member of it as the injury itself, refusing a hand that has been offered. The verse gives him a rule for the day his enemy stops, and it asks him whether he keeps the quarrel alive after the cause of it is gone. Because the pardon is named by God and not as a favour from the victors, the reader is shown that the settlement belongs to the Lord rather than to the side that happens to be standing. Since the sentence follows a command to fight, the reader is taught that the aim of the command was never the destruction of the other side.

The case is like a man who has bolted his door against a neighbour's dog and keeps the bolt drawn long after the animal has been taken away. The house is safe either way, and the only person still living behind the bar is the man himself.

---

## Verse 2:193

> Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution, and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺. If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors

**THE GOAL OF THE FIGHT**

The verse sets the end towards which the fighting is allowed to run: ***“Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the persecution as the association of partners with God. The same reading takes the sentence as the command to fight until no worship of anything besides God remains in the land and no believer is turned from his faith by force. al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense in a shorter form: until no testing of the believers remains.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the further note that the fight was restricted in its place in the earlier verse and is widened here for those who take up arms, whether inside the sanctuary or outside it. Because the aim is given as the removal of a condition rather than the defeat of a people, the reader is shown what kind of fight this is: it stops when the cause of it stops. It does not run on until the stronger side has finished.

**THE DEVOTION NAMED**

The next words state the positive aim: ***“and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the phrase as the religion being entirely for God, with none worshipped alongside Him. The same reading takes the two halves as the removal of one thing and the establishment of another.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the debate among the earlier readers over whether the verse was cancelled by the later command to fight the association of partners everywhere. The same entry notes that those who read it as standing keep it as the statement of the aim. Because the devotion is tied to the ending of the persecution, the reader is shown that the aim of the fight is worship made safe rather than a province gained.

**THE STOPPING AND THE HOSTILITY**

The verse then returns to the condition of the enemy: ***“If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as the closing of the file: the one who gives up the persecution has no claim against him. The enmity that remains attaches only to those who keep attacking.

The phrase is kept by al-Ṭabarī in the same narrow sense, so that the exception is the aggressor and not the people. Because the last word of the verse is the aggressor rather than the enemy, the reader is shown that the community is given a cause to fight and not a nation to hate. Since the sentence stands at the end of the passage, it functions as the seal on the limits named before it. Because the limit is named as the aggressor and not as the nation, the reader is shown that the fight is a matter of conduct rather than of blood.

The Book states the aim in a single sentence elsewhere, (8:39 — **“Fight against them until there is no more persecution”**). The reader of the two passages together is shown that the words of this verse were not a local arrangement. A further passage repeats the limit on the other side, (2:190), where the believers are told not to exceed it.

The lesson also reaches a reader in the middle of a quarrel who keeps the fight going because the ending would feel like a loss. The verse gives him a definition of victory that is not the other side's defeat but the stopping of the harm. And it asks him what he is still fighting for once the harm has stopped. Because the hostility is limited to the aggressor, the reader is taught to separate the person from the act, and to keep the road open for the day he lays the act down.

The case is like a household that blocks a shared stair against a neighbour who has been pushing his way up it. When the neighbour stops pushing, the barrier stays where it is. And the two families pass each other for years beside a plank neither of them needs.

---

## Verse 2:194

> ˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month, and all violations will bring about retaliation. So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner. ˹But˺ be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺

**THE MONTH FOR THE MONTH**

The verse opens with a sentence that answers a doubt about the calendar of the fight: ***“˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the months named here as the month of the treaty and the month of the return. The same entry keeps the early reports that the association of partners had turned the Prophet ﷺ and his companions away from the House in a sacred month. God brought him back into Mecca in the same month of the following year. The offence and its answer thus fell in like months.

al-Baghawī keeps the fuller narrative: the Prophet ﷺ set out for the lesser pilgrimage in the sacred month, the people of Mecca barred the way. The two sides agreed on a treaty that allowed the community to return the next year, when the city would be emptied for them for three days. Because the return was arranged in the same month as the barring, the balance is exact.

**THE VIOLATIONS AND THE SCALE**

The sentence then widens the rule: ***“and all violations will bring about retaliation”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the word as the plural of a holy thing. The same reading takes the phrase as the claim that every inviolable right carries a like answer when it is broken. as-Saʿdī keeps two possible readings of the whole opening. On one, the first phrase concerns the specific return: the community enters the city as it had been kept out of it. On the other, the sentence is a general law of equity, so that the breaking of any sacred limit may be answered in its own measure.

Because the rule is stated as a scale, the reader is shown that retaliation is not revenge. The one who returns a blow in a like measure keeps the matter inside the ledger. the one who takes more has moved the matter to his own account. The verse that follows names the manner of the answer, not its size in general.

**THE SAME MANNER**

The verse then gives the rule of the exchange: ***“So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the phrase in the plain reading of a like response. The same entry keeps a report in which the community had pledged not to turn their backs and to answer in kind. al-Ālūsī keeps the same sense and notes that the phrase was the answer to the worry of the community that fighting in the inviolable place and the sacred month would itself be a crime.

The rule thus keeps a symmetry that the community could apply on the field. Because the measure is the same manner and not the same injury, the verse also limits what may be done with a captured advantage. Since the sentence follows the naming of the months, the reader is shown that the sanctity of the time is answered for the offender and observed by the wronged.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a command and a promise: ***“˹But˺ be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the nearness named here as the help and the guidance granted in the field itself, so that the community is reminded of the presence of the One who sees the intention behind the retaliation.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the note that the passage has already named the four sacred months in the wider frame of the religion, so that the reader knows which months the sentence concerns, and keeps the warning that the inviolability of a place or a time does not suspend the right of the wronged. Because the close of the verse ties the fighting to mindfulness, the reader is shown that the temper of the man holding the sword is part of the law's business.

The same question is put to the Prophet ﷺ in a later verse that the community would hear, (2:217 — **“Fighting during these months is a great sin”**), where the answer measures the offence of the fight against the offence of driving believers from the sanctuary. The reader sees the ledger set out plainly.

The lesson also reaches a reader wronged in a time or a place that is held sacred, who is afraid to press his right for fear that the pressing is itself an offence. The verse gives him the balance of the months in one sentence and the manner of the answer in another, so that he knows where his right ends. Because it closes with the nearness of God, the reader is shown that the one who measures his answer carefully is not the weaker party in the dispute.

The case is like two households who share a well and a festival. When one of them fouls the water during the days of the feast, the other does not foul it in return. it brings the matter to the elders, draws its water. And keeps the feast. The well survives both of them, and the season is remembered as the one in which nobody went thirsty.

---

## Verse 2:195

> Spend in the cause of Allah and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺. And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers

**THE CALL TO SPEND**

The verse returns to a command already given in the passage and states it plainly: ***“Spend in the cause of Allah”***. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the sentence as one of the injunctions gathered under the theme of righteousness that begins earlier in the sūrah. The same entry keeps the note that the command was addressed to a community preparing for an expedition, so that the treasury of the weak and the strong mattered together.

as-Saʿdī keeps the paths of God wide: every road that leads to Him, whether a gift to a poor man, support to a relative, or the upkeep of those whose maintenance is a duty. He keeps the fighting of the cause as the greatest of them and the first to be included. He adds that the spending there is a form of struggle for the one who gives.

**THE HAND AND THE DESTRUCTION**

The second command is the one the commentators laboured over: ***“and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺”***. al-Ṭabarī gathers a cluster of reports on the phrase. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps it as the command to spend even when a man owns no more than an arrow, since the hand he is warned about is the hand that holds back. Another report from him keeps the sense in the plainest form: the destruction is not to be killed in the path of God, but to hold back from spending on it.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the narration of al-Bukhārī that the verse came down about the funds spent in the cause, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same tradition. Because the verse was read over a collection gathered for an expedition, the reader is shown that the warning was aimed at a community with a field to supply. The opposite reading is kept by al-Ālūsī from a later reader, that the destruction is excessive spending, so that the verse forbids waste after it commands giving.

Because the two readings stand on the same words, the reader is shown that the verse guards both doors: the hand that keeps the wealth, and the hand that scatters it. The first empties the community's strength in the field; the second empties the household at home. Since the warning is against a hand that throws its owner, the verse keeps the responsibility with the spender himself.

**THE GOOD AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a command whose reward is named: ***“And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the good-doers as those whose giving reaches beyond the duty. The same reading keeps the love of God for them as the aim that makes a giver generous without measure. al-Jalālayn keeps the phrase as the joining of the obligatory gift with the voluntary good.

The Book gives the same promise to those who stand up for the cause of God, (47:7 — **“If you stand up for Allah, He will help you and make your steps firm”**). And the same love of God for the generous is named in another passage, (3:134), where the reader is shown that the quality sought here is not a single payment but a settled character.

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps his savings intact through a season when his own community is in need, telling himself that prudence is a virtue. The verse gives him the image of a hand that throws its owner, and it asks him what he imagines he is saving for. Because the command is joined to the statement of a person God loves, the reader is shown that the giving is not a loss taken from a balance but a way of becoming the kind of person the Lord loves. Since the warning and the promise stand in one verse, the reader is shown that the purse and the character are judged together.

The case is like a man who owns the only boat in a flooded village and keeps it tied to his own door for fear the current will take it. The water takes it in the night, and he spends the morning watching his neighbours cross on a raft they built from his fence.

---

## Verse 2:196

> Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah. But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination. But if any of you is ill or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺, then compensate either by fasting, charity, or a sacrificial offering. In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford. Whoever cannot afford that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺—completing ten. These offerings are for those who do not live near the Sacred House. And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment

**THE DUTY TO COMPLETE**

The verse opens with an order about the two journeys: ***“Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah.”*** al-Ṭabarī sets out the two positions held among the early readers. On one, the pilgrimage is the obligation and the lesser journey is a voluntary act, with the verse requiring only that a person finish what he has begun. the proof for the pilgrimage itself is then taken from the verse of the House in the family of ʿImrān. On the other, both are named as obligations and the verse carries the duty of each. He keeps the reports of Ibn Masʿūd and others on the first side. The reading of Ibn Masʿūd is kept as well, in which the words run as the pilgrimage and the visitation to the House.

Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the word for completion as the ending of a thing and the making of it whole, so that the command is about finishing what the servant has entered upon rather than about the beginning. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same distinction and adds a report from Jābir in which the Prophet ﷺ answered a question about the lesser journey by saying that it is not a duty but that to perform it is better.

**THE PREVENTED AND THE OFFERING**

The verse then provides for the case of a journey that cannot be finished: ***“But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination.”*** Ibn Kathīr keeps the occasion of the sentence in the year of the treaty, when the association of partners barred the Prophet ﷺ and his companions from reaching the House and the community had already entered the state of the journey. He keeps too the allowance that followed: the animals were offered where the travellers were held. and the heads were shaved.

al-Jalālayn keeps the offering as a sheep and keeps the withholding of the razor as the sign that the state is still held. as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as proof that the journey, once begun, becomes a duty to finish. Such a traveller finishes the journey through the offering instead. Because the shaving is delayed until the animal arrives, the reader is shown that the visible mark of the completed journey may not be taken before the journey's substitute has done its work.

**THE ILLNESS AND THE HEAD**

The verse then makes an allowance inside the journey itself: ***“But if any of you is ill or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺, then compensate either by fasting, charity, or a sacrificial offering.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the three options as the ransom allowed to the one who shaves before the proper time. The same entry keeps the reports that name the measure of each: a fast of days, a gift of food to the poor, or an animal.

Because the ransom stands in the place of the mark that was taken early, the reader is shown that the law does not leave a man between illness and the rules of the journey. al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense in a single line: whoever shaves because of a complaint pays for the shaving. Since the verse names three ways to pay, it also teaches that a remedy is not a licence but a debt with a schedule.

**THE TWO RITES COMBINED AND THE TEN DAYS**

The verse then names a second way of performing the journey: ***“In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford. Whoever cannot afford that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺—completing ten.”*** as-Saʿdī draws from the passage the duty of finishing both rites, the obligation of the offering for the one who combines them, and the substitution of the fast for the one who cannot find an animal.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reckoning of the days exactly as the verse states it, three within the days of the journey and seven after the return home, so that the number ten is complete. Ibn ʿUthaymīn keeps the note that the fast is spread over the two periods and is not gathered in one. Because the substitution is named for the one who is short of money, the reader is shown that the law takes account of a purse as well as a calendar.

**THE PEOPLE NEAR THE HOUSE**

The sentence about the offering is then limited: ***“These offerings are for those who do not live near the Sacred House.”*** Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the ruling as one for the traveller who brings the two rites together, excluding the people of the sanctuary whose home is beside it.

Because the limit is named at the end of the passage rather than at its beginning, the reader is shown that the general command is read together with the local exception. A law stated in wide terms may carry a boundary within the same breath. It also shows that the journey is measured by the distance it costs.

**THE CLOSE ON MINDFULNESS**

The verse ends with a pair: ***“And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the first as the keeping of the commands that have just been listed and the second as the warning for the one who lets the rites fall. Because the passage has been a long list of remedies and allowances, the reader is shown that the closing warning is not a threat over the details but a reminder of who owns the journey.

The Book gathers the concession and the same closing note in a later verse, (2:203 — **“Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful”**), where the reader sees that the relief of the journey was meant to be used and not to be watched for other people's slips. A further passage keeps the duty of the House in the plainest terms, (3:97 — **“Pilgrimage to this House is an obligation by Allah upon whoever is able among the people”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has made a promise of worship and then let it drop because the circumstances changed, telling himself that the intention was enough. The verse gives him the rule for a journey stopped by force and the rule for a journey spoiled by illness, so that he has a way to finish what he began even when he cannot finish it as he planned. Because the provision is always a substitute and never an abolition, the reader is shown that a broken practice is repaired rather than forgotten.

The case is like a man who sets out to walk to a distant town and finds the road closed by a flood. He does not tear up the map or claim he has arrived. he finds the nearest crossing, pays what it costs, and reaches the town by the other bank, later than he planned and no less there.

---

## Verse 2:197

> ˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months. Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage, let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language, and arguments during pilgrimage. Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it. Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness. And be mindful of Me, O people of reason

**THE MONTHS THAT WERE ALREADY KNOWN**

The verse fixes the season of the journey: ***“˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the months as the festival month of breaking the fast, the month after it and the first ten days of the pilgrimage month, and traces the reading back to the earliest teachers of the community. He notes that the sentence works as a claim about the time rather than as a list of names, so the reader is left to take the season from the verses that follow.

al-Baghawī keeps the small difference among the early readers over the last of the months. One group counts ten days of the final month and another counts nine, and he settles the two by noting that the one counts the nights and the other the days, so that both end at the day of ʿArafah. as-Saʿdī keeps a reason for the vagueness: the time of the journey had come down from the religion of the Friend and had never been lost among the peoples, so it needed no fresh fixing as the month of fasting had needed one.

**THE COMMITMENT THAT BINDS**

The condition of the season is stated next: ***“Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the committing as the entering of the state, which makes the journey a duty for the one who had begun it even when he had begun it freely. He takes the point further in the verse of the passage before this one, where the command was to finish what had been started.

The contrast between the two journeys is kept by al-Qurṭubī. The lesser journey may be entered at any time of the year, so its state has no season to wait for; the greater journey falls once in the year and only within these months. Because the difference is named here, the reader is shown why the next commands speak to the one who has already begun.

**THE THREE THINGS SET ASIDE**

The verse then names what the state forbids: ***“let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language, and arguments during pilgrimage.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the three as lewd speech, wicked conduct and quarrelling, and notes that the last of them is sharpened into an argument rather than a difference of opinion. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the middle term as abuse and name-calling between one pilgrim and another.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the same three and notes that the prohibition is attached to the days of the journey, so that the one who has left his house for the House of God is not to arrive with the temper he left. Because the commands are aimed at the tongue as much as at the body, the reader is shown that the season is spoiled more often by a quarrel than by a missed station.

**THE GOOD KNOWN AND THE PROVISION TAKEN**

A short sentence follows with the widest reach: ***“Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as a comfort for the pilgrim whose effort is unseen by any but God. Since the journey scatters the travellers across a plain and a valley, the verse reminds them that no step of theirs is lost.

The next command answers a practice of the community: ***“Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps a report in which a group of the travellers had decided to rely on trust and set out with nothing, so that they became a burden on the others, and the verse came down over the matter. Because the command stands in the middle of a passage about worship, the reader is shown that a plain piece of good sense can belong to the religion itself.

**THE BEST PROVISION AND THE MIND**

The verse then corrects the valuation of the traveller: ***“surely the best provision is righteousness.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as a comparison between two things that both travel: food that is eaten and a guard that stays. He keeps the closing address as the reason attached to the advice: the one who weighs a journey's needs is the one who thinks.

al-Ṭabarī keeps the same sense in a shorter form, that the provision which does not run out is the fear of God. The verse then ends with the call that has run through the passage: ***“And be mindful of Me, O people of reason”***. Because the closing address is directed to the mind rather than to the crowd, the reader is shown that the whole passage is addressed to people who can judge a bargain.

The Book makes the duty of the journey plain in the verse that precedes this one, (2:196 — **“Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage”**), so that the reader sees the season and the duty as two halves of one command. A second passage states the aim of the Book itself, (17:9), and the pilgrim who reads the two together is shown that the journey is a school of the same guidance.

The lesson also reaches a reader who plans a journey of worship to the last meal and the last coin but gives no thought to the state of his own temper. The verse gives him a list of provisions in which the last item is the character he carries, and it asks him what he expects to bring back from a place he arrived at in a quarrel.

The case is like a family that loads a car for a long drive and checks the water, the fuel and the tyres, then leaves the arguing driver in the seat. The car runs perfectly and the holiday is lost at the first junction.

---

## Verse 2:198

> There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺. When you return from ’Arafât, praise Allah near the sacred place and praise Him for having guided you, for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray

**THE TRADE THE COMMUNITY FEARED**

The verse lifts a scruple about money: ***“There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the occasion in a report of al-Bukhārī from Ibn ʿAbbās: the markets of the season stood in the days before Islam, and the community held back from trading in the season of the journey, thinking that buying and selling in those days would spoil the worship.

al-Ṭabarī keeps the word for blame as a constraint, and keeps the reports that the buying and selling are permitted before the state and after it. al-Qurṭubī keeps the order of the passage as the point: the worship was first cleared of lewdness and wrangling, and the concession for trade came after, so that the gain was allowed without the corruption.

**THE GAIN REFERRED TO THE GIVER**

The permission is kept by as-Saʿdī with two conditions. The earning must not crowd out the purpose of the journey, and the gain must be referred to the bounty of God rather than to the skill of the man. He keeps the warning that a trader who trusts his own cleverness and forgets the Giver has fallen into the very constraint the verse removed.

Because the gain is called a bounty from the Lord, the reader is shown that the permission is not a licence to make the season a market. The man who travels for God and earns on the road keeps both; the man who travels for the market has lost the road he came for.

**THE RETURN FROM THE PLAIN**

The verse then turns to the station of the journey: ***“When you return from ’Arafât, praise Allah near the sacred place”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the return as the pressing on from ʿArafah towards Muzdalifah, and keeps the sacred place as the waymark there, where the pilgrims spend the night and where the call to God is raised.

Two points are drawn from the sentence by as-Saʿdī. The first is that the standing at ʿArafah was a pillar of the journey, since the return is named from it and no return happens before a standing. The second is that the remembering at the sacred place was a station known to the community, so that the verse confirms a practice rather than inventing one.

**THE GUIDANCE REMEMBERED**

The sentence then explains why the praise is owed: ***“and praise Him for having guided you, for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the closing phrase as the reason the community should be loud with gratitude, since the road they walked had been dark until the Book came.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same note and adds that the places named in the sentence are the places of the days before Islam, so that the reader is shown a plain and a valley where the same nations had walked without the light of the guidance. Because the verse moves from trade to praise and ends with guidance, the reader is shown what the journey is for: the profit of the road is a heart that has learned who to thank.

The Book puts the same praise in the verse that follows, (2:200 — **“praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers”**), so that the reader sees the thanksgiving of the pilgrim measured against the loudest speech of the days before Islam. A second passage keeps the calendar of the rites in the hands of the One who made the months, (9:36), so that no season is credited to a tribe.

The lesson also reaches a reader who returns from a journey of worship with photographs and no benefit, having argued his way through the airports and forgotten the purpose in the packing. The verse gives him the order of the way: earn without forgetting, return from the plain, and let the road end in thanks for a guidance he did not invent.

The case is like a man who spends a season travelling to a master to learn a craft, and comes home able to describe the roads perfectly. He knows every turn of the route and has learned nothing of the work, and the journey repeats the following year.

---

## Verse 2:199
