> Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims. And seek Allah’s forgiveness. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**THE CUSTOM OF THE ḤUMS**

The verse treats the community as one body of travellers: ***“Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the occasion in the practice of the people of the sanctuary and those born among them, who stood at Muzdalifah instead of joining the rest of the pilgrims at ʿArafah. al-Baghawī keeps their reasoning as it was reported: they were the people of God and the residents of His sanctuary, so they would not leave the sacred ground for the open plain.

al-Ālūsī keeps a report in the two collections of sound tradition, in which the people of the sanctuary and those who followed their religion stood at Muzdalifah and the rest of the Arabs stood at ʿArafah, and the community was ordered to go forth with the many. al-Qurṭubī keeps the note that the group honoured the sanctuary and thought it wrong to honour what lay outside it, even though they knew the standing place of the Friend.

**THE ORDER THAT GATHERED THEM**

The command gathers the privilege into the crowd: ***“go forth with the rest of the pilgrims”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the order to stand at ʿArafah with the whole body of the pilgrims, and notes that the rank of a family does not excuse a man from the station the rest of the community keeps.

Because the correction is aimed at an honour held for centuries, the reader is shown that the religion sorts a community by its obedience rather than by its ancestry. Because the privilege was the very thing the group prized, the reader is shown that the correction cost them more than a change of place. The man who stands where the Book sends him stands with the merchants, the shepherds and the scholars.

**THE FORGIVENESS ASKED AND GIVEN**

The verse then joins the rites to a request: ***“And seek Allah's forgiveness.”*** Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the sentence as the seeking of pardon after the great devotions, and notes that the community was taught to end its worship with a plea rather than with a boast. The pilgrim has finished the standing and the night and the walk, and he is sent back to the mercy of his Lord.

Then come the two names: ***“Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the first name as the pardon for the one who turns and the second as the mercy kept for the one who dies within it. Because the names follow the order to ask, the reader is shown that the plea is not a risk but an appointment. Since the rites are finished before the request is made, the reader is shown that the plea belongs to the completed work rather than to its beginning.

The Book states the same appointment in a later passage, (4:110 — **“then seeks Allah’s forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”**), where the reader sees the two names used as an answer to the same request. The verse of the passage before this one keeps the same pair over the whole journey, (2:198), so that the rites begin and end under the same mercy. Because the two names are used of the Lord rather than of the pilgrim, the reader is taught that the standing of a man rests on the mercy he is given and not on the distance he has walked. Since the command to seek pardon is given to everyone in the caravan, the reader is shown that no rank among the travellers is high enough to go without the request.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has made his group into his rank, holding a place in the mosque or in the community that the rest of the people do not share. The verse gives him an order to stand with the many, and it asks him whether his dignity rests on a station he keeps or on a Lord he asks.

The case is like a man who insists on entering the stadium through a gate reserved for the players because his father once played. The game starts, the players are on the field, and he spends the afternoon explaining the door to the stewards.

---

## Verse 2:200

> When you have fulfilled your sacred rites, praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers ˹before Islam˺, or even more passionately. There are some who say, “Our Lord! Grant us ˹Your bounties˺ in this world,” but they will have no share in the Hereafter

**THE RITES FINISHED**

The verse opens with the completion of the journey: ***“When you have fulfilled your sacred rites”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the rites as the sacrifices and the stations that belong to the season, and keeps the sense of the verb as the finishing of a work. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same word with the report in which the Prophet ﷺ gave the community the instruction to take their rites from him, so that the acts named here are the ones the community had seen him perform.

al-Jalālayn keeps the setting of the sentence at the end of the season, after the casting of the pebbles at the great pillar, the circuit of the House and the stay in the valley of Minā. Because the verse is placed at the end of the rites, the reader is shown that the praise is not a substitute for the acts but their crown.

**THE PRAISE MEASURED AGAINST LINEAGE**

The next sentence turns a familiar custom towards God: ***“praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers ˹before Islam˺, or even more passionately.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the report of Ibn ʿAbbās in which the people of the days before Islam would sit after the journey and recite the days of their fathers and count their noble descent, so that the whole day was given to ancestry. The verse takes the same energy and sends it to the Giver instead of the family.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the correction of that custom and notes the phrase that lifts the new speech above the old: the praise of God is to be louder than the boasting that had come before. Because the comparison is kept in the sentence itself, the reader is shown that the religion does not forbid enthusiasm but redirects it.

**THE FIRST OF THE TWO ASKERS**

The verse then names one kind of traveller: ***“There are some who say, “Our Lord! Grant us ˹Your bounties˺ in this world,””***. The man whose prayer has no horizon beyond the present life is kept by Ibn Kathīr, so that his request is for a share he can spend. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, that the man asks for the world and forgets what follows it.

The sentence then states his end: ***“but they will have no share in the Hereafter”***. al-Qurṭubī keeps the two parties set side by side in the passage, the one who asks for the world and the one who asks for both, so that the reader weighs the two prayers against their answers.

**THE VOCABULARY OF A PRAYER**

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the wording of the first prayer as the key to the whole contrast. The man names no measure of good and no standard of judgement; he asks for a grant, and the grant is what he has asked for. Because the next verse supplies the word that is missing here, the reader is shown that a prayer can be corrected by a single noun.

The Book sets the two prayers together in the verses of the season, (2:201 — **“Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter”**), so that the difference between the two askers is visible in a single line. The verse that follows states the answer, (2:202), and the reader is shown that the shorter prayer and the longer one are settled by the same Lord.

The lesson also reaches a reader who asks God for a job, a house and a health report, and never once for the state of his own soul. The verse gives him the example of a traveller who stood in the plain and asked for the things he could have asked for at home, and it asks him what he thinks the journey was for.

The case is like a guest invited to a banquet who asks the host for a sandwich to take away. He is fed, he is given the sandwich, and he walks home with his meal and without having met the host.

---

## Verse 2:201

> Yet there are others who say, “Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter, and protect us from the torment of the Fire.”

**THE PRAYER THAT NAMES BOTH WORLDS**

The verse sets the second asker beside the first: ***“Yet there are others who say,”*** ***“Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter,”*** ***“and protect us from the torment of the Fire.”***. al-Ālūsī gathers the reports on what the good of this world means. One of the early teachers keeps it as health and sufficiency, another keeps it as a righteous spouse, another as knowledge and worship, another as sound wealth, another as dutiful children, and another as a good name among the people.

The same breadth is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās without narrowing it, so that the expression takes in whatever a man may receive in the world and call good. Because the verse leaves the good unnamed, the reader is shown that the request is for a quality rather than for an item.

**THE WORD THAT IS THE WHOLE DIFFERENCE**

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the single word of this prayer as the mark of the second asker. The first man asks for a grant without measure; this man asks for what is good in both worlds, and he trusts the Giver to judge what is good. The difference between the two prayers is not their length but their standard.

Because the standard is named, the reader is shown why a request may be refused while its wording is honoured. A parent may decline a child's request for a knife and still be giving him what is good, and the man who prays with the word good leaves the judgement where it belongs.

**THE FIRE NAMED AT THE CLOSE**

The prayer ends in a plea for safety: ***“and protect us from the torment of the Fire.”*** Ibn Kathīr keeps the same pairing of the two worlds in the request of the believer, and keeps the shelter from the fire as the first of the good things asked for, since the reward of the next life cannot be enjoyed beside a punishment.

al-Jalālayn keeps the three parts of the prayer in the order the verse states them: the good of this world, the good of the next, and the safety from the fire. Because the last part is attached to the first two, the reader is shown that a hope of reward and a fear of loss belong in one breath.

**THE ASKER WHO TAKES THE LONGER ROAD**

as-Saʿdī keeps the prayer as the shape a servant's request should take, since it takes in the whole of what the servant needs and leaves nothing outside it. He keeps the note that a man who asks only for the world has made his share small by his own choice, and that the man who asks for both has left the measure of good with God.

Because the verse stands between the warning against the first man and the promise to the second, the reader is shown that the road to the reward is not a secret. The Book states the outcome in the sentence that follows, (2:202 — **“reward for the good they have done”**), so that the reader has the answer of both prayers in order.

A further passage keeps the same balance in a prayer the community was taught to repeat, (2:286), where the request for help and mercy follows the confession of weakness. The reader of the three passages together is shown that the words of a prayer may be taught as surely as the acts of a rite.

The lesson also reaches a reader who prays for a promotion with his whole heart and cannot remember when he last asked for protection from anything but a rival. The verse gives him a prayer that starts with a good beyond his judgement and ends with a fire he does not want to see, and it asks him whether his own order of requests makes sense.

The case is like a patient who asks the surgeon for the operation he saw in a video and names the exact stitches. The surgeon who agrees would be doing a favour to the request and an injury to the patient, and the man who leaves the method to the surgeon is the one who walks out healed.

---

## Verse 2:202

> It is they who will receive a ˹heavenly˺ reward for the good they have done. Surely Allah is swift in reckoning

**THE SHARE OF WHAT WAS EARNED**

The verse states the outcome of the longer prayer: ***“It is they who will receive”*** ***“a ˹heavenly˺ reward for the good they have done.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the pronoun as the ones who asked for good in both worlds, and keeps their portion as the reward of the journey with all its stations. He notes that the verse sets them apart from the man whose request had no horizon beyond the present life.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading and adds that the reward covers the prayer itself, because the request of a believer is an act of worship. He also keeps a second reading in which the pronoun covers both parties at once, so that the believer is repaid for his work and the denier is answered for his narrow view, and he finds the same pattern in the verse of the Book where every group is repaid for what it did.

**THE DEMONSTRATIVE THAT CONCLUDES**

The opening is kept by al-Ālūsī as a conclusion rather than a fresh sentence, and he notes that the demonstrative carries the sense of a distance because of the height of the rank it points to. Because the sentence stands without a conjunction, the reader is shown that what follows is the fruit of what came before and not another item in a list.

The same demonstrative is pointed by Ibn Kathīr at the second group alone. The two readings of the pronoun are therefore kept side by side in the sources, and the reader who takes either one finds that the reward belongs to those who asked for a good beyond their own judgement.

**THE RECKONING THAT DOES NOT WAIT**

The verse closes with a name that measures time: ***“Surely Allah is swift in reckoning”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the swiftness as the speed with which the account is settled when it is taken, so that no fair claim waits for a hearing. al-Jalālayn keeps the reports that the whole creation is reckoned in half a day of this world, and notes that the reckoning is not slow but the world has not finished.

Because the sentence is placed after the reward, the reader is shown that the swiftness cuts both ways. The man who spent his season in a quarrel with the pilgrims and the man who served them in the plain are both settled by the same ledger, and neither has to wait for the other's case.

**THE ANSWER TO THE TWO PRAYERS**

as-Saʿdī keeps the passage as the answer to the two requests of the season: the share of the first man is what he asked for, and the share of the second is what he asked for and more. Because the answers are stated in the order of the prayers, the reader is shown that the reward of the longer request is not an accident of wealth or of birth but the fruit of the wording of a request.

The Book sets out the words of the longer prayer in the verse before this one, (2:201 — **“Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter”**), so that the reader can trace the answer back to the request. A further passage keeps the same promise for those who act on what they know, (2:200), and the reader is shown that the season of the journey is one of the fields in which the seed is sown.

The lesson also reaches a reader who measures a season by what he brought home: the photographs, the receipts, the list of people he met. The verse gives him a reckoning that is already running and asks what he asked for while he stood in the plain. Because the reply is swift rather than delayed, the reader is shown that a request is a serious act with an answer attached.

The case is like a man who stands in a queue for a licence and passes the time complaining about the clerk. The clerk stamps the form and hands it over, and the man leaves with the paper and without a friend in the office.

---

## Verse 2:203

> And remember Allah during ˹these˺ appointed days. Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, neither are those who stay behind ˹till the third—seeking additional reward˺, so long as they are mindful ˹of their Lord˺. And be mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered

**THE NUMBERED DAYS**

The verse adds a station after the stay in the valley: ***“And remember Allah during ˹these˺ appointed days.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the days as the days of casting the pebbles, and keeps the remembering as the praise of God at the casting and after the prayers. al-Baghawī keeps the same days as the days of Minā, and notes that they are named as few because of their number rather than their worth.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the agreement of the scholars that the days intended here are the days of the stay in Minā, and notes the small grammatical point kept by the early readers over the form of the word: the plural may mean few or many, and the days are few in number and heavy in reward. Because the command is attached to the days of rest, the reader is shown that the worship of the season is not finished when the standing ends.

**WHAT THE DAYS WERE MADE FOR**

The honour given to those days is kept by as-Saʿdī, with the reason for it: the last rites of the journey are performed in them, the people are guests of God in them, and the fast is barred in them so that they may be days of eating, drinking and remembrance. He keeps the report in which the Prophet ﷺ described those days in exactly those three words.

Because the days are named as days of remembrance, the reader is shown that a festivity can be worship when the heart is awake in it. The community is not told to leave the cooking and the visiting; it is told what the cooking and the visiting are for.

**THE TWO DEPARTURES**

The verse then permits the whole range of practice: ***“Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful,”*** ***“neither are those who stay behind ˹till the third—seeking additional reward˺, so long as they are mindful ˹of their Lord˺.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the first departure as the leaving of Minā on the second day of the stay, after the pebbles have been cast, and keeps the second as the staying until the third.

The two options are kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as they are stated, so that each pilgrim has a choice and neither choice carries a fault. Because the sentence links both choices to mindfulness of the Lord, the reader is shown that the permission is not an invitation to carelessness, and the reason for the choice stays with the one who makes it.

**THE GATHERING AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a command and a warning: ***“And be mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered”***. The gathering is kept by Ibn Kathīr as the return to the account, so that the crowd leaving the valley is sent home with the thought of another gathering. al-Ṭabarī keeps the same sense in the plain reading of the sentence.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as the correction of the practices of the days before Islam and as the closing of the rules of the journey, so that the rites end with the thought of the meeting with the Lord. Because the last word of the verse looks past the valley, the reader is shown what the journey has been training him to remember.

The Book keeps the same easing of the rites in a later passage, (22:78 — **“laid upon you no hardship in the religion”**), so that the reader sees the two departures as one instance of a rule that runs through the religion. The verse of the season before this one ends in the same command, (2:200), and the two closes together show the pilgrim what he is meant to carry home.

The lesson also reaches a reader who performs the obligations of a season and treats the days that follow them as a holiday from God. The verse gives him days named for remembrance in the middle of the rest, and it asks him what he is resting for. Because the choice of departure is left open, the reader is shown that the law is concerned with the state of the heart rather than with the timetable of the road.

The case is like a wedding at which the guests stay on for the dancing and forget the couple. The couple are married either way, and the guests go home praising themselves for the food.

---

## Verse 2:204

> There are some ˹hypocrites˺ who impress you with their views regarding worldly affairs and openly call upon Allah to witness what is in their hearts, yet they are your worst adversaries

**THE SPEECH THAT PLEASES**

The verse turns from the travellers to a kind of man among them: ***“There are some ˹hypocrites˺ who impress you with their views regarding worldly affairs”***. al-Baghawī keeps the report that the verse came down about a man of eloquence in the city, and keeps the description of him: sweet of speech, pleasing to look at, and welcome in the company of the Prophet ﷺ.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same man and the same point, that his words were smooth and his character was not, and notes that the passage names the two kinds of people who make requests in the season, the sincere and the insincere. Because the man is described by his speech rather than by his deeds, the reader is shown that the danger named here begins with something pleasant.

**THE WITNESS HE CALLS**

The verse then reports the oath: ***“and openly call upon Allah to witness what is in their hearts”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the man as one who adds an oath to his claim, swearing that God knows his heart to agree with his tongue. He notes that the oath is false in the very act of taking it, because the conduct of the man gives the lie to his speech.

al-Ṭabarī keeps the same sense and notes that the appeal to God as a witness makes the offence heavier rather than lighter. Because the man uses the name of God as a piece of rhetoric, the reader is shown how far a gift of speech can carry a man from the truth.

**THE ADVERSARY NAMED**

The sentence then names him: ***“yet they are your worst adversaries”***. The expression is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the sharpest of opponents in a dispute, so that the man who sweetens his words is the hardest to answer when the matter turns serious. The same reading is kept by Ibn Kathīr, and the sense of a man who argues with a vengeance is kept by al-Jalālayn.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the note that the expression carries the sense of a quarrel driven to its end, so that the verse describes a person who fights the truth with the whole of his wit. Because the description is placed after the oath, the reader is shown that the adversary is not a man with a different opinion but a man with a hidden purpose.

**THE COST OF A GOOD TONGUE**

Because the verse ends with the hidden purpose rather than the pleasant speech, the reader is shown where the danger lies in his own circle. The man who agrees with everyone has no quarrel to settle and no position to defend, and the passage says that his friendship is the one to fear most.

The Book describes the same people in a later chapter, (63:1 — **“We bear witness that you are certainly the Messenger of Allah”**), where a witness is spoken with the tongue and denied by the heart. The verse before this one gives the answer of such a man, (2:202), so that a reader can compare the reward of the sincere with the end of the smooth speaker.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has learned to be agreeable in every gathering and cannot remember the last time he disagreed with anyone at cost to himself. The verse gives him a portrait of the most popular man in the room and asks what he is protecting. Because the harm is named as an adversary rather than as a fool, the reader is taught that charm is not innocence.

The case is like a man who sells a house by showing the garden and the light, never mentioning the crack in the wall behind the wardrobe. The buyer signs, the smell of the garden stays in his mind, and the crack opens in the first winter.

---

## Verse 2:205

> And when they leave ˹you˺, they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it and destroy crops and cattle. Allah does not like mischief

**THE TURNING AWAY**

The verse follows the speaker out of the room: ***“And when they leave ˹you˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the leaving as the departure of the man from the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, and keeps the picture of a person who changes the moment he is out of sight. al-Ālūsī keeps two readings of the verb: one in which he turns his back and leaves, and one in which he gains the upper hand and takes charge of affairs.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the two as actions of the heart and of the body. On the first reading he turns away in anger and pride; on the second he walks out of the gathering and sets about his work. Because the verse does not name which of the two is meant, the reader is shown that both readings describe the same man at different hours.

**THE STRIVING FOR MISCHIEF**

The sentence then names his occupation: ***“they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the mischief as the committing of forbidden things, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same plain sense. as-Saʿdī keeps the man as one whose speech repairs and whose acts destroy, so that his promise and his conduct are two different persons in one body.

Because the striving is described as a work rather than a mood, the reader is shown that the harm is deliberate. Since the labour of the man is spent on damage, the reader is shown that the mischief is chosen rather than accidental. The man who walks out of the assembly has already decided what the streets will be like when the meetings are over.

**THE CROPS AND THE CATTLE**

The harm is then given its victims: ***“and destroy crops and cattle”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the crops as the gathered stands of grain that are burned and the cattle as the animals that are killed. al-Ālūsī keeps a wider reading in which the destruction belongs to the men of power, whose injustice holds back the rain and leaves a district without harvest.

Because the two words name the food of a village rather than the persons in it, the reader is shown what mischief costs in the end. Since the crops and the cattle belong to the community and not to the man, the reader is shown that the offence reaches past the two people in the quarrel. A quarrel in a courtyard is answered by a hungry winter, and the ones who pay are not the ones who argued.

**THE DISLIKE NAMED**

The verse closes with a sentence that reaches beyond the man: ***“Allah does not like mischief”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same short judgment and notes that the dislike is stated of the act itself, and not only of the man who performs it. Because the sentence is unqualified, the reader is shown that no cause makes the destruction of a neighbour's field a service to God.

The Book states the same rule in the words of the people of the city, (2:11 — **“Do not spread corruption in the land”**), where the correction is answered with a claim of peace-making. The account of the man in this passage is closed in the verse that follows, (2:206), and the two together show what becomes of the speaker who was so pleasant at the table.

The lesson also reaches a reader who behaves with care in the gatherings of his community and lets his dealings at home run as they will. The verse gives him a second half of a life, the one he lives when the visitors have gone, and it asks him what he is building in the street behind him. Because the judgment falls on the mischief rather than on the man's reputation, the reader is taught where the real record is kept.

The case is like a man who keeps the front room of his shop spotless and stores the rubbish in the yard the customers never see. The front room is admired for a year, the drain is blocked by the winter, and the smell arrives at the front door by spring.

---

## Verse 2:206

> When it is said to them, “Fear Allah,” pride carries them off to sin. Hell will be their proper place. What an evil place to rest

**THE ADVICE THAT WAS REFUSED**

The verse records the answer to a plain word: ***“When it is said to them, “Fear Allah,””***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the address as a word to the man described in the verses before, that he should fear God in his corruption of the land and in the harm he does to the wealth of the community. al-Qurṭubī keeps a report of advice and an answer, in which the man who is reminded tells his brother to mind himself instead.

Because the counsel is a single short phrase, the reader is shown how little it takes to expose a man. The words that were refused here were not a ruling or a rebuke but the same mindfulness the whole passage has been asking of every pilgrim.

**THE PRIDE THAT CARRIES HIM OFF**

The sentence then names the mover: ***“pride carries them off to sin.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the sense that pride seizes him entirely, so that he is carried as a thing is carried, and keeps the added note that the burden of his sin comes with him. The pride is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the taking of offence at the advice, which turns a small word into an insult.

al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair of feelings under one word: the vanity and the heat of temper that follow a rebuke. Because the advice is answered with anger rather than with argument, the reader is shown that the trouble was not in the counsel but in the ear that heard it.

**THE PLACE THAT WILL HOLD HIM**

The verse then states the outcome: ***“Hell will be their proper place. What an evil place to rest”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the first sentence as the answer to the man's account, that his destination will be the fire, and the second as the naming of its evil. al-Jalālayn keeps the last term as the cradle or the resting place, so that the sentence names the place where he will settle.

Because the last word of the verse is a resting place, the reader is shown the bitter irony of the picture. The man who refused the counsel so that nothing would disturb his comfort is given a comfort that lasts, and the verse lets him keep it.

**WHAT THE THREE VERSES DESCRIBE**

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the three verses as the portrait of the insincere man in the season of the journey, set against the portrait of the sincere one in the passage before. The reader is shown the two kinds of company he will meet in the same caravan and the two ends that wait for them.

as-Saʿdī keeps the same contrast and adds the warning that the use of a good tongue is not a proof of a good heart. Because the passage has been speaking of the rites of the journey, the reader is shown that a season of worship does not by itself sort the travellers, and that the sorting is left to the One who hears the answer to a single sentence.

The Book puts a warning against the same man in the words of the worshippers of the calf, (2:205 — **“Allah does not like mischief”**), so that the reader sees the end of the one who destroys while claiming to build. A further passage keeps the portrait of the same men in the later chapter, (63:1), where the speech and the heart are shown apart, and the reader is left to guard his own.

The lesson also reaches a reader who takes correction as an insult and answers every reminder with the state of the other man's house. The verse gives him the picture of a man carried off by his own dignity, and it asks him what he is defending when he refuses a word that would have saved him. Because the verse ends with the resting place rather than the argument, the reader is shown what the quarrel was worth.

The case is like a man who refuses to turn off the road at a sign because the sign was not written politely. The road bends, the sign is behind him, and the destination is exactly the one it named.

---

## Verse 2:207

> And there are those who would dedicate their lives to Allah’s pleasure. And Allah is Ever Gracious to ˹His˺ servants

**THE LIFE THAT WAS GIVEN AWAY**

The verse turns from the speaker to another man: ***“And there are those who”*** ***“would dedicate their lives to Allah’s pleasure.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the order of the passage as its own comment, since the verses before it described the conduct of the insincere and this sentence describes the conduct of the sincere.

The giving of the life is kept by al-Ṭabarī as a sale, and he supports the reading from the verse where God names the price: the believers have sold their lives and their wealth and the exchange is the garden. as-Saʿdī keeps the same image and notes that the sale is not a loss, because the buyer is faithful to the bargain and the price is beyond measure.

**THE MAN WHO LEFT HIS WEALTH**

The reports place the sentence in a particular life. al-Jalālayn keeps the man who left his fortune with his persecutors in order to reach the city, so that he arrived with nothing but his religion. The same report is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās with a group of his companions, who ransomed themselves from the people of the sanctuary with their property.

al-Ālūsī keeps further occasions: a raiding party that was cut off, and the plain duty of commanding good and forbidding evil. Because the sources differ over the occasion, the reader is shown that the verse is wider than any one of the reports. The man who gives his life for the pleasure of God is described in every age, and the reports are windows on the same quality.

**THE PLEASURE THAT WAS SOUGHT**

The aim of the exchange is named at the beginning: the pleasure of God. as-Saʿdī keeps the aim as the point of the sentence, since a man may risk his life for spoil, for a name or for a tribe, and this man risks it for what pleases his Lord.

Because the aim is named rather than the reward, the reader is shown the rank of such a person. The bargain is not a calculation of profit but a preference of the One who gives over everything given, and the verse lets the reader measure his own aims against it.

**THE GRACE THAT MADE IT POSSIBLE**

The verse closes with the quality that explains the whole: ***“And Allah is Ever Gracious to ˹His˺ servants”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the grace as the first cause of the sale, since the man who sold his life did not begin the bargain himself. The willingness was given to him before he gave anything.

The same closing is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as a statement of compassion towards those who were killed for their faith. Because the verse ends with the grace of God rather than with the courage of the man, the reader is shown where the credit of a sacrifice belongs.

The Book names the purchase in a later passage, (9:111 — **“Allah has indeed purchased from the believers their lives and wealth in exchange for Paradise”**), so that the reader sees the sale of this verse as one side of a bargain the Book states in full. The warning against the other kind of man stands earlier in this chapter, (2:206), where the refusal of a plain word is answered with the fire.

The lesson also reaches a reader who gives generously from his money and holds his time, his comfort and his name in a closed hand. The verse gives him a man who gave the whole of what he had and asked for nothing but the pleasure of God, and it asks him which part of his own life is still in the shop.

The case is like a merchant who is offered a partnership in a mine and sells his stall to buy the share. His neighbours think he has lost his mind, the mine opens, and the man who kept his stall spends the season selling to the miners.

---

## Verse 2:208

> O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Surely he is your sworn enemy

**THE ENTRY THAT IS COMPLETE**

The verse addresses the community with a demand about the whole of its religion: ***“O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the last word of the command as a word for all together, and keeps the earliest reports on it: enter the religion in its entirety, every part of it, with nothing left outside.

al-Jalālayn keeps the occasion in a group of the believers who had kept the practices of the religion they came from. They observed the Sabbath and avoided the meat of the camel after they had embraced Islam, and the verse ordered them into the whole of the religion they had entered.

**THE WORD WITH TWO READINGS**

The two readings of this word are kept by al-Baghawī, one with a vowel that gives the sense of peace and one that gives the sense of submission, and he notes that the two readings meet in the same meaning. Because the community had already believed, the reader is shown that the order concerns the depth of an entry already begun rather than the first step of it. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense in a plain form: come all of you to the prescriptions of the religion.

Because the command is given to believers, the reader is shown that the entry into the religion is not finished by a single act. The address is to people who had already believed, and the order is to hand over the rest of the household of the self after the door has been opened.

**THE STEPS THAT ARE NOT FOLLOWED**

The command then has a second half: ***“and do not follow Satan’s footsteps.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the danger as the religion taken in parts. The man who follows his own desire takes the commands that suit him and leaves the rest, and the verse closes that door by naming the enemy who lays the trail.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as a warning in both directions. Sincere devotion may overshoot into a practice that the law never set, and slackness may leave a part of the law untaken; the verse orders the believer into the whole of the religion and out of the trails that lead away from it.

**THE ENEMY WITHOUT A DISGUISE**

The sentence ends with the reason: ***“Surely he is your sworn enemy”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the hostility as one that is plainly declared, so that no believer is excused for treating the steps as harmless. Because the enemy is named at the end of the command, the reader is shown that the trail is not a path but a trap. Since the danger is attached to a step rather than to a doctrine, the reader is taught that a whole religion can be left one small habit at a time.

The Book gives the same order to the whole of humanity in an earlier verse of the chapter, (2:168 — **“do not follow Satan’s footsteps”**), and repeats the warning that he is a sworn enemy. A further passage states the path that the feet were meant to walk, (6:153 — **“So follow it and do not follow other ways”**), so that the reader has the road and the trail set side by side.

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps the fasts, pays the alms and leaves a part of the law untouched because the people around him do not touch it. The verse gives him an order to enter the whole house and an enemy to watch at the threshold, and it asks him which room he has kept locked.

The case is like a family that moves into a house and boards up one room because it reminds them of the previous owner. The house is theirs, the room is theirs, and the damp in the wall behind their own bed comes from the door they never opened.

---

## Verse 2:209

> If you falter after receiving the clear proofs, then know that Allah is indeed Almighty, All-Wise

**THE SLIP THAT IS NAMED**

The verse states the cost of a return: ***“If you falter after receiving the clear proofs”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the faltering as the missing of the truth and the leaving of the religion after it had become clear, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the origin of the expression in the slipping of a foot.

The same image is kept by al-Ālūsī with the note that the word is used of opinions and beliefs as well as of steps. Because the image is taken from walking, the reader is shown the kind of failure the verse describes. The man had been on a road; the verse does not speak of a man who never found it.

**THE PROOFS THAT HAD COME**

The proofs are named in the sentence itself: the clear signs that had come to them. al-Ālūsī keeps them as the arguments that establish the truth, and keeps the other reading in which they are the verses of the Book that speak of it.

as-Saʿdī keeps the warning as the sharper for that reason. The one who leaves a religion he never understood is a stranger to the truth; the one who leaves after the proofs have arrived has stepped off a road he had seen.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse then names what such a person will find: ***“then know that Allah is indeed Almighty, All-Wise”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the power that nothing can prevent from taking its answer and the second as the wisdom in the answer itself.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same pair and notes that the overpowering is placed before the wisdom, so that the reader does not mistake patience for weakness. Because the two names stand together, the reader is shown that the reply to a denial is neither blind nor late. Since the sentence gives the warning while the feet are still on the road, the reader is shown that the guidance itself works by naming the ground before the step is taken.

**THE WARNING THAT IS ALSO A MERCY**

Because the sentence is addressed to a community that had believed, the reader is shown that the warning itself is part of the guidance. Since the proofs are named in the same line as the slip, the reader is taught that the two arrive together and the choice is made between them. The verse does not wait for the fall to name the ground; it names it while the feet are still on the road.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the passage as the closing of the command to enter the religion completely, since a command gains its weight from the warning attached to it. The Book describes the same reversal in the verse that follows, (2:210), where the matter is settled in a moment, and the reader is shown what the waiting of the deniers finally meets.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been convinced of a duty for years and has arranged his affairs around not performing it. The verse gives him a picture of a foot lifted and set down in the wrong place, and it asks him how long he can keep the road in view and the step in the wrong direction.

The case is like a driver who is warned at the last turning before the bridge and drives past the sign because the road looked wider. The bridge is behind him by a mile and the next crossing is a day away.

---

## Verse 2:210

> Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels? ˹If He did˺, then the matter would be settled ˹at once˺. And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺

**THE WAITING NAMED**

The verse asks a question with the force of a refusal: ***“Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels?”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the waiting as the expectation of the deniers, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the question as a denial rather than a request for information.

al-Ālūsī keeps the pronoun open between the deniers, the people of the Book and the men described earlier in the passage, and notes that each reading fits the sentence. Because the question is put in the form of a wait, the reader is shown the strange position of a person who has been given proofs and asks for a spectacle.

**THE COMING THAT IS NOT LIKE OURS**

The coming is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the coming of God on the day of judgement without any manner that can be described. al-Jalālayn keeps it as the coming of His command, and notes the passages where the coming of God is named in the same way.

Because the sentence names the shade of clouds and the angels, the reader is shown that the scene is the end of the world rather than a sign in the market. The people who asked for a proof are offered the last event of the creation, and the offer is a rebuke rather than an answer.

**THE MATTER SETTLED**

The verse then states the outcome of such a coming: ***“˹If He did˺, then the matter would be settled ˹at once˺.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the settling as the day of recompense with all its terrors, when the case of every person is closed and no argument remains.

The same sense is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās in the picture of the two groups already separated, the people of the garden in the garden and the people of the fire in the fire. Because the settling is named as a single moment, the reader is shown that the wait of the deniers is not a period of grace but a delay of the inevitable.

**THE RETURN OF ALL MATTERS**

The verse closes with a general sentence: ***“And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the answer to every dispute of the passage, so that the matters that people leave unsettled are gathered to the One who settles them.

al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading and notes that the return is a return to a judge who has not delegated the case. Because the last sentence is stated without a condition, the reader is shown that the return does not depend on a person's willingness to be judged. Since the settling is named as a single moment, the reader is shown that the whole argument of the passage rests on a meeting that no one will miss.

The Book sets the same scene in the passage of the shaking, (2:214), where the help of God is named near, and the reader sees the two answers of the waiting. A further verse keeps the return of matters to the Lord alone, (2:216), so that no reader imagines the case closed in this world.

The lesson also reaches a reader who says that he would believe if a sign were shown to him personally, as though the creation were a shop with a counter. The verse gives him a question about the clouds and the angels and asks him what kind of proof he is actually waiting for. Because the answer is the day when the matter is settled, the reader is shown that the request for a private sign is a request to delay.

The case is like a passenger who refuses to board until the captain comes to his house to explain the route. The ship leaves at the hour printed on the ticket, and the man standing on the quay is the only one who thinks the schedule was changed.

---

## Verse 2:211

> Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them. And whoever trades Allah’s favour—after receiving it—˹for disbelief˺ should know that Allah is indeed severe in punishment

**THE QUESTION PUT TO THEM**

The verse turns the argument to an old community: ***“Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the command as an order to the Prophet ﷺ to put the question to them, and al-Ālūsī keeps its purpose as a rebuke rather than a request for information.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the grammar of the command and the reading of the verb, and notes that the question is addressed to a people whose history was known to them. Because the question asks for a number rather than a reply, the reader is shown that the evidence against them is their own record.

**THE SIGNS COUNTED**

al-Jalālayn keeps the clear signs as the parting of the sea, the sending down of the food from the sky, and the like. The same phrase is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās in a broader range: how often the commands and the prohibitions came to them, and how long they were honoured with the religion in the time of their prophet.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same history as an example for the community of the city, since the people of the Book had been given proofs and had turned against the messenger who came after. Because the signs are counted rather than described, the reader is shown that the fault was not a lack of evidence.

**THE TRADE OF A FAVOUR**

The sentence then names the offence: ***“And whoever trades Allah’s favour—after receiving it—˹for disbelief˺”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the exchange as the giving away of a gift for a price that ruins the seller, and notes that the favour is called a favour because it is the reach of the hand of God.

The trade is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as the exchange of the religion for something else, and al-Ālūsī keeps the same sense with the note that the trade is made with open eyes. Because the sentence says after receiving it, the reader is shown that the fault belongs to the one who had the gift in his hand.

**THE SEVERE ANSWER**

The verse closes with the name that answers the trade: ***“should know that Allah is indeed severe in punishment”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the severity as the strength of the answer and al-Ālūsī keeps it as the power that no one escapes. Because the warning is given to a community with a long history, the reader is shown that the severity is not a threat over a single mistake. Since the favour was received before it was traded, the reader is shown that the account is kept against a person who had every means of knowing.

The Book puts the same severity in the verse that follows, (2:212 — **“Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit”**), so that the reader sees the gift and the account held by the same hand. A further passage states the law of the earlier community in a single line, (2:211), and the reader is invited to compare it with the report of the signs.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been given a truth in his youth and has traded it for the approval of a group. The verse gives him a ledger with one entry and asks him what price he received. Because the signs are counted by the Giver and not by the receiver, the reader is shown that no one has been given so little that he can plead ignorance.

The case is like an heir who sells a piece of family land for a season of easy living. The money is spent before the year ends, the land is fenced by a stranger, and the man explains to his children how the sale was forced on him.

---

## Verse 2:212

> The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and they mock the believers. Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them on the Day of Judgment. And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit

**THE LIFE THAT WAS ADORNED**

The verse opens with a picture of the other side of the city: ***“The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the adorning as the love of the passing life placed in their hearts, so that they are content with it and busy with its pleasures.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same sense and notes that the adornment is real and not a figure of speech, since the world was made beautiful in their eyes. Because the sentence says the life was adorned for them rather than by them, the reader is shown that the attachment grew in them before it was chosen.

**THE MOCKERY OF THE POOR**

The sentence then names what the attachment produced: ***“and they mock the believers.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the mockery as the laughter of the wealthy at the poverty of the first believers, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading with the names of the poor companions of the Prophet ﷺ left in their state.

as-Saʿdī keeps the mockery as the fruit of the adornment. The man who measures by wealth sees the poor believer as a failure, and the measure itself is the blindness the sentence describes. Because the mockery is attached to the adorning in one sentence, the reader is shown that the two things grow from one root.

**THE RANK REVERSED**

The verse then states the reversal: ***“Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them on the Day of Judgment.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the mindfulness as the guarding against the denial that the mockers live in, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the sentence as the answer of the passage to the laughter of the rich.

Because the comparison is placed on the day of judgement rather than in the market, the reader is shown that the account is not settled by the ledger of this world. Since the mockery is named as the fruit of the adornment, the reader is shown that a wrong measure of wealth turns into a wrong measure of people. The ranking is named as the reward of a quality and not of a fortune, and the reader is left to ask which ladder he is climbing.

**THE PROVISION WITHOUT LIMIT**

The verse closes with a sentence that answers the mockery at its root: ***“And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit”***. The provision is kept by Ibn Kathīr as the gift that is not measured out by the merit of the receiver, so that a poor man may be rich in what cannot be spent.

as-Saʿdī keeps the same reading and notes that the sentence is placed after the reversal on purpose. The mockers counted their wealth as proof of favour, while the hand of God gives without a ledger and the true measure is the state of the heart. Because the sentence follows a reversal of rank, the reader is shown that the provision of this world is not a certificate of standing.

The Book states the same reversal in the passage of the tables of the earlier community, (2:211 — **“Allah is indeed severe in punishment”**), so that the reader sees the wealth of a denier and the punishment of a denier in one frame. A further verse keeps the guidance in the hand of God alone, (2:213 — **“Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path”**), and the reader is shown that the two gifts of this verse and the next belong to one Giver.

The lesson also reaches a reader who measures his neighbours by the cars in their driveways and his own worth by the same count. The verse gives him a ranking that is announced on another day and a provision that is given without limit, and it asks him which scale he uses when he looks at a poor man who prays.

The case is like a man who laughs at a labourer for carrying water while he sits beside a well he has paid to dig. When the well dries up in the summer, the labourer's route to the spring is the only one left, and the man with the empty well is the one who asks for a cup.

---

## Verse 2:213

> Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺. Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes. And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy. Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes. And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path

**THE ONE COMMUNITY**

The verse reaches back to the beginning of the human story: ***“Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the disagreement of the early readers over the state of that community, one group reading it as a people united on the guidance and another as a people united on the same error. He keeps the reports on both sides and notes that the sentence is the introduction to the sending of the prophets.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the plain reading that the people were on one religion, and keeps the report that the reference is to the children of Adam at the covenant. as-Saʿdī keeps the same reading with a fuller picture: the community was on the guidance for generations after their prophet, and when they differed in the religion God raised the messengers to settle the difference.

**THE PROPHETS SENT AS BEARERS**

The sentence then names the answer of God to the division: ***“Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners”***. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the two roles as the news of the garden for the one who believes and the warning of the fire for the one who refuses, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair in the same order.

The sending is kept by Ibn Kathīr as the beginning of the line of the messengers, and he notes that the verse gathers the whole institution in one sentence. Because the messengers are named by their function rather than by their names, the reader is shown that the office is older than any particular scripture and wider than any one people.

**THE BOOK THAT JUDGES**

What was sent with them is named next: ***“and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the Book as the judgement that was sent down to settle the disagreements, and keeps the phrase in truth as the guarantee of the ruling itself.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the sentence as the statement of a pattern that runs through history: the revelation comes to settle a dispute, and the dispute reopens around the revelation itself. Because the judging is named as the purpose of the Book, the reader is shown what the scripture was sent to do in a community that had already lost its way.

**THE JEALOUSY THAT DIVIDED THEM**

The next sentence turns to the receivers: ***“And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy.”*** Ibn Kathīr keeps the dispute as the quarrelling of the people of the Book among themselves over the Book they had been given, and keeps the motive named at the end.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same reading and notes that the fault is sharper because the proofs had already arrived. The quarrel was not a search for the truth but a contest over position, and the reader is shown that a community can lose its book while carrying it.

**THE GUIDANCE GIVEN BY GRACE**

The verse then names the way out of the confusion: ***“Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes.”*** Ibn Kathīr keeps the guidance as the act of God for a people who could not have found the truth by their own reasoning, and keeps the grace as the reason named in the sentence itself.

The same sense is kept by as-Saʿdī, with the note that the guidance is attached to belief rather than to birth or to learning. Because the sentence names grace rather than merit, the reader is shown that the settle argument of history has an answer he does not own.

**THE PATH AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a general sentence: ***“And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the path as the road of the truth that leads to the garden, and keeps the choice of the guide in the hand of God.

The closing is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān as the comfort of the community of the city, since the disagreements of the older communities are answered by a guidance given in the present. Because the last sentence names a path rather than a party, the reader is shown that the aim of the whole passage is a walk rather than a debate.

The Book gives the same account of the sending in the chapter of the family of ʿImrān, (3:19), and names the path again in the verse of the prayer of the community, (1:6), so that the reader hears the last words of this verse as an echo of the daily prayer.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has watched a community divide over a fine point and has decided to keep out of every question. The verse gives him a history in which the dispute is named as jealousy and the guidance as grace, and it asks him which of the two he is carrying into his own argument. Because the guidance is promised to those who believe, the reader is shown that neutrality is not the same thing as faith.

The case is like an inheritance divided among brothers who each hire a lawyer to read the same will. The will is read aloud in the court, the estate is spent on the reading, and the only one who leaves with his share is the brother who never hired anyone.

---

## Verse 2:214

> Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, “When will Allah’s help come?” Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near

**THE QUESTION ABOUT THE PRICE**

The verse puts the community in front of its own expectation: ***“Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you?”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the question as the statement of a law that does not change, that the one who carries the religion will be tried in it.

al-Ṭabarī keeps the question as a rebuke to a community that wanted the reward without the road, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports on the occasion of the verse. Because the question is addressed to believers, the reader is shown that the trial is not a punishment but a stage of the journey.

**THE AFFLICTION THAT WAS NAMED**

The verse then lists what came upon the earlier communities: ***“They were afflicted with suffering and adversity”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as poverty and the second as illness and pain, so that the trial takes both the purse and the body. The same pair is kept by Ibn Kathīr in the reports of the earlier nations.

The same stages are kept by as-Saʿdī: the loss of the means, then the loss of health, and then the fear. Because the loss is described as something done to them rather than chosen by them, the reader is shown that the trial of the believer may arrive without any act of his own.

**THE SHAKING THAT REACHED THE PROPHET**

The verse then goes further: ***“and were so ˹violently˺ shaken”***. al-Baghawī keeps the occasion in the siege when the community was pressed by hunger, cold and fear, and keeps the line of the Book where the hearts reached the throats. al-Ālūsī keeps the same report and adds the other battle named as the occasion.

The sentence then reaches its peak: ***“that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, “When will Allah’s help come?””*** Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the report that the question was on the lips of the believers around their prophet, and notes that the question was a plea and not a doubt. Because the cry is placed in the verse itself, the reader is shown that the strain of the road had touched even the best of the community.

**THE ANSWER THAT IS NEAR**

The verse closes with the reply: ***“Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the promise that victory comes after the trial and not before it, and keeps the note that the nearness is measured by the help rather than by the calendar.

The verse is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān as a comfort for the community of the city and for every community after it, since the account of the earlier believers is written down for the ones who come later. Because the last word of the verse is nearness, the reader is shown what the question of the sufferers was worth.

The Book states the same law in the words of the verse of trial, (2:155 — **“We will certainly test you”**), so that the reader sees the promise of testing given before the events. A further verse keeps the duty of the fight with the same comfort, (2:216 — **“Allah knows and you do not know”**), and the two passages together show that the servant is not told the schedule.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has served a good cause for years and has begun to ask when the effort will be answered. The verse gives him a cry from the companions of the Prophet ﷺ and a promise that the help is near, and it asks him what he expected the road to be like. Because the question of the sufferers is written in the Book without blame, the reader is shown that the complaint of the tired is not the same thing as the denial of the enemy.

The case is like a father who takes his son up a mountain by a path he has used for years. The boy asks three times how much further, and the father answers each time for the same reason: the top is not far, and the boy has never been there before.

---

## Verse 2:215

> They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say, “Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers. Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.”

**THE QUESTION ABOUT SPENDING**

The verse records a question about the use of money: ***“They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the questioner as an elderly man of wealth who asked the Prophet ﷺ what he should give and to whom, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same report with the same two parts.

al-Jalālayn keeps the same occasion and notes that the question was about both the thing given and the person who receives it. Because the answer names the recipients rather than the amount, the reader is shown which half of the question the Book treats as the more important.

**THE ORDER OF THE CLAIMS**

The answer is given in a list: ***“Say,”*** ***“Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the order as the order of the rights, since the parents hold the first claim and the near relations come after them according to the closeness of the tie.

The same list is kept by Ibn Kathīr, with the note that the verse was revealed about voluntary giving, so that the reader learns the order of his charity before the obligations of the estate were laid down. Because the near relatives are named before the strangers, the reader is shown that the alms of a man begin at his own door.

**THE GOOD THAT IS KNOWN**

The verse then closes with a sentence about the giver: ***“Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.”*** Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the promise that no gift is lost, whether or not the people hear of it, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same note in a shorter form.

The confidence of the sentence is kept by as-Saʿdī as the reason a believer gives without publicity, since the record is kept by the One who needs no witness. Because the praise of the people is not mentioned in the promise, the reader is shown what kind of fame the verse is offering.

The Book describes the righteous in the same terms in the verse of the qualities, (2:177 — **“who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor”**), so that the reader sees the list of this verse used as a portrait of a life. A further passage keeps the same concern for the poor in the chapter of the cave, (18:1), and the reader is shown how often the Book returns to the purse of the believer.

The lesson also reaches a reader who gives generously to a distant cause and lets his own relatives ask a stranger for help. The verse gives him a list that begins with the two people who carried him and asks where his money goes first. Because the closing sentence names the knowledge of God rather than the thanks of the poor, the reader is taught to give for the record that matters.

The case is like a man who sends a parcel to a village he has never seen and forgets that his brother lives in the next street with an empty fridge. The parcel arrives, the photograph of the delivery is framed, and the brother eats at a neighbour's table.

---

## Verse 2:216

> Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it. Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you and like something which is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know

**THE DUTY WRITTEN DOWN**

The verse states an obligation that the community had not wanted: ***“Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the opening as the laying down of a duty, and keeps the reports on the people addressed by it.

al-Ālūsī keeps the two ways the duty falls: an obligation on each person when the enemy has entered the land, and a duty on the community as a whole when the enemy is still in his own country. as-Saʿdī keeps the sequence of the passage, since the community had been ordered to hold back while it was weak and was ordered to fight after it had gathered strength in the city.

**THE DISLIKE NAMED**

The sentence names the reluctance of the community in the same breath: ***“though you dislike it.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the dislike as the natural shrinking of a soul from hardship, and notes that the obligation was laid down despite it rather than because of a change in feeling.

The same sense is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās in plainer words, that the duty was heavy on them. Because the reluctance is named in the verse and not left to the reader to notice, the reader is shown that the command does not depend on the mood of the one who receives it.

**THE REVERSAL OF LIKES**

The verse then widens the lesson: ***“Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you”*** ***“and like something which is bad for you.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the example in the fight itself: the believer dislikes it, and in it there is the reward of the one who falls and the spoil of the one who lives. as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as a law of the self, since the soul leans towards rest and away from the work that builds.

Because the sentence is stated as a possibility and not as a rule about war, the reader is shown its reach into every part of a life. The appointment he dreads and the comfort he prefers may hold the two ends of the same story, and the verse says so without naming the outcome.

**THE KNOWLEDGE AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with the distinction between two kinds of knowing: ***“Allah knows and you do not know”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the reason the command is to be obeyed without waiting for the plan to be explained, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same note in the same order.

The verse is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān as the reply to every objection raised by a temperament against a duty, since the objection rests on a knowledge that the objector does not have. Because the last word of the verse is a confession of ignorance, the reader is shown where the argument ends.

The Book gives the same account of the price of the road in the verse of trial, (2:214 — **“They were afflicted with suffering and adversity”**), so that the reader sees the community tested before it was made responsible for the fight. A further passage keeps the duty of the wealthy beside the duty of the fighter, (2:215), and the two verses together show the two hands of the same community.

The lesson also reaches a reader who refuses a hard duty because the people around him have decided that the times do not require it. The verse gives him a command written down before his feelings were consulted and a knowledge that is held by another, and it asks him on what basis he has made his own assessment. Because the dislike of the community is recorded in the verse and not condemned in it, the reader is shown that a heavy heart is permitted while the duty is performed.

The case is like a patient who argues with his doctor about the operation he dreads and wins the argument. The pain is dulled for a season, the illness is not, and he returns to the same room with the same question and less time.

---

## Verse 2:217

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

**THE QUESTION AFTER THE RAID**

The verse opens with a question that had become an accusation: ***“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months.”*** The occasion is kept by several of the ten. A small party had been sent out under the command of one of the men of the community, and in the course of it a man of the enemy was killed. Because the quarrel turned on the date of the killing rather than on the killing itself, the reader is shown how a community can be trapped by a calendar. The community counted the day as the last of one of the permitted months, and the enemy counted it as a day of the sacred month of Rajab. The killing became the talk of the city.

The narrative is kept in full by al-Baghawī, with the date of the sending and the names of the travellers, and by al-Jalālayn in a shorter form. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sequence and adds that the men had been sent to watch a caravan rather than to fight. Because the questioners were hostile, the reader is shown that the verse answers an accusation as well as a doubt.

**THE SIN THAT IS NAMED**

The answer begins by naming the offence: ***“Say,”*** ***“Fighting during these months is a great sin.”*** The reading is kept by al-Ṭabarī, who notes that the offence is stated plainly rather than excused. The community was not told that the killing was lawful; it was told that the matter was grave.

The number of the months is kept in a report that al-Ṭabarī records in more than one line. ʿUthmān asked on the pulpit about the month named in this verse, and a line of the Table Spread was recited back to him which counts the months of the year as twelve with four that are sacred. Because the calendar is fixed in another passage, the reader is shown that the offence named here is measured by a rule that was older than the quarrel. as-Saʿdī keeps the discussion of the ten over whether the prohibition of fighting in those months still stands, and keeps the two readings side by side: the majority hold that the command to fight the association of partners everywhere came later and set the earlier rule aside, while others hold that the prohibition was never lifted and that only the beginning of a fight is barred, not the defence of a community under attack.

**THE FOUR OFFENCES AND THE TWO WEIGHTS**

The verse then sets a heavier weight on the other side: ***“But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah.”*** The list is kept by al-Ṭabarī in the same order and by al-Qurṭubī with a long treatment of its rulings. The four things named are the turning of people away from the religion, the denial of God, the barring of the sanctuary and the driving out of its people.

The comparison closes the sentence: ***“For persecution is far worse than killing.”*** The word is kept by several of the ten as the testing of a believer in his faith until he is turned from it. al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that the man killed in the raid had been watching the community, and that the greater harm was the persecution that was driving the believers from their homes. Because the passage weighs two offences rather than defending either one, the reader is shown how the Quran teaches a scale.

**THE WAR THAT WILL NOT STOP**

The verse then states what the other side had decided: ***“And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can.”*** The sentence is read by al-Ṭabarī as a description of the people of the sanctuary, whose aim was to bring the community back from its religion.

The condition at the end of the sentence is kept in the same reading: the enemy would do it if the power were in their hands. Because the verse describes an intention rather than an event, the reader is shown why the community was told to prepare. The quarrel was not about a single caravan; it was about the survival of the faith of the travellers.

**THE ONE WHO TURNS BACK**

The last sentences turn the matter to the believer: ***“And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the work of such a person is lost, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same note with the warning that the loss is total.

The verse closes with the end that follows: ***“It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that the community feared for the men of the raiding party, and keeps the ruling that the fear was answered by the verse that follows. Because the passage ends with the loss of a person who leaves the faith rather than with the fate of an enemy, the reader is shown where the real danger of the moment lay.

**WHAT THE PASSAGE SETTLES**

The Book states the same rule about persecution in the verse of the return, (2:191 — **“For persecution is far worse than killing”**), so that the reader sees the sentence used twice in the same chapter as a standard rather than a phrase. A further passage counts the months of the year and names the four that are sacred, (9:36 — **“the number of months ordained by Allah is twelve”**), and the reader of the two together is shown that the calendar of the fight is held by God.

The lesson also reaches a reader who weighs his own small fault against a large wrong done to him and finds his own case lighter in both scales. The verse gives him a rule in which the offence he committed is named and the offence against him is measured beside it. Because the answer begins with his own fault, the reader is shown that the passage was written for the community rather than for its enemies.

The case is like a man whose neighbour has blocked the only road to his shop for a year, and who breaks a fence in a month when building is forbidden. The fence is the offence and the road is the harm, and the court that hears the case orders the road opened before it fines either man.

---

## Verse 2:218

> Surely those who have believed, emigrated, and struggled in the Way of Allah—they can hope for Allah’s mercy. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**THE PARTY THAT ASKED ABOUT ITS REWARD**

The verse answers a question that came from the men who had been sent out: ***“Surely those who have believed”*** ***“emigrated, and struggled in the Way of Allah”***. The report is kept by al-Baghawī and al-Jalālayn, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps it in the plainest form: the men asked whether their journey counted as a campaign and whether they would be rewarded.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same occasion with the note that the party feared the sin of a killing in the sacred month and did not expect any wage at all. Because the words came down over a case of fear, the reader is shown that the mercy named here was meant to settle a doubt rather than to reward a triumph.

**THE THREE WORKS IN ONE BREATH**

The verse gathers three things: the faith, the leaving of the homeland, and the struggle. al-Ṭabarī keeps the emigrating as the leaving of the dwellings of the association of partners and the moving away from their neighbourhoods. as-Saʿdī keeps the three as the title of felicity, and keeps the order in which they are named: a man believes, then he leaves what he loves for the sake of God, then he spends his strength in the path.

Because the three are named as one description of one people, the reader is shown that the works of the religion belong together. The man who believes without leaving his ease, and the man who leaves without the struggle of the self, are both told what the caravan of this verse was made of.

**THE HOPE THAT IS NAMED**

The sentence then states the outcome: ***“they can hope for Allah’s mercy.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the hope as the cautious expectation of a thing that is great, and notes that the sentence was a promise to the very men whose case had been doubtful. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading with the note that the mercy includes the reward they had asked about.

Because the hope is named rather than the certainty, the reader is shown the rank of the travellers. Since the three works are named as one description, the reader is taught that the promise is not earned by a single act. Since the hope is attached to three works rather than to a feeling, the reader is taught that the promise belongs to the road and not to the mood. They had left their homes for a land they did not know, and the Book promised them a mercy they would ask for each day rather than a wage that would be counted in their hands.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with the pair that had answered the fear of the party: ***“And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the forgiveness as the covering of the deed they feared, and keeps the mercy as the gift that followed it. al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair in the same order.

Because the names are attached to the description of the travellers rather than to their question, the reader is shown what kind of people the promise is addressed to. The verse was revealed over a doubt of men who had left their homes, and it closes on the two names that answer a doubt.
