The Book sets the same promise for the men of the march in a later chapter, (9:111 — **“Allah has indeed purchased from the believers their lives and wealth in exchange for Paradise”**), so that the reader sees the hope of this verse as the small edge of a bargain the Book states in full. The warning of the passage before this one stands over the same travellers, (2:217 — **“For persecution is far worse than killing”**), and the two together show a community that is promised mercy and warned in the same breath.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has given something up for the sake of his religion and has begun to ask whether it was worth the price. The verse gives him a sentence with the three works in it and a hope that is named by God. Because the promise is attached to works he can still perform, the reader is shown that the road is open to the one who has not yet left anything.

The case is like a family that sells a house in the capital to open a clinic in a village where there was none. For two years nobody thanks them and the ledger shows a loss, and the first child who is carried through the door alive settles the question they had stopped asking.

---

## Verse 2:219

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.” They ˹also˺ ask you ˹O Prophet˺ what they should donate. Say, “Whatever you can spare.” This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect

**THE QUESTION AND THE ANSWER IN STAGES**

The verse opens with a question about two old companions of a household: ***“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the community had already been divided over them, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the sequence of the rulings that came down one after another, this verse among them.

The answer is given in a single sentence: ***“Say,”*** ***“There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the reading that the benefit is the pleasure of the drink and the gain of the game, and al-Ṭabarī keeps the same note in his own words. Because the verse names a benefit without calling it good, the reader is shown the difference between a thing that helps and a thing that is right.

**THE SCALE THAT IS STATED**

The last words of the answer weigh the two sides: ***“but the evil outweighs the benefit.”*** Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the plain statement that the harm of the two is greater than their use, and notes that the community was expected to follow the weight rather than the pleasure.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings that grew from the verse: the drink that covers the mind is forbidden whatever its name or its make, and the game that takes wealth by chance stands with it. Because the first answer did not forbid the two outright, the reader is shown how a community was trained by a ruling that named the evil before it removed the thing.

**THE SECOND QUESTION OF THE SAME PASSAGE**

The verse then adds another question: ***“They ˹also˺ ask you ˹O Prophet˺ what they should donate.”*** The question is kept by al-Ṭabarī as a question about the measure as well as the kind, and the answer is given at once: ***“Say,”*** ***“Whatever you can spare.”***

The word is kept by al-Ṭabarī as the surplus that remains over the need of the household, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same sense with the note that the giving of the surplus came before the alms were fixed by measure. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that a man gives what he can do without. Because the two questions stand in one verse, the reader is shown that the Book treats the purse and the habits of the self as one subject. Maʿārif al-Qurʾan keeps the sequence of the three rulings on the drink, from the scale of this verse to the command to shun it, so that the reader sees a community trained by stages rather than by a single blow.

**THE CLEARING AND THE REFLECTION**

The verse closes with a sentence that is repeated through this stretch: ***“This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the clarity as the mark of the passage, since the rulings arrive one by one and each is stated in plain words. al-Jalālayn keeps the reflection as the duty that follows an explanation.

Because the closing word is reflection rather than obedience, the reader is shown what kind of community the passage is building. The answer about wine had left a scale in their hands, and the Book expected them to weigh with it before the next ruling came.

The Book states the end of the matter in a later passage, (5:90 — **“Intoxicants, gambling, idols, and drawing lots for decisions are all evil of Satan’s handiwork”**), where the two things are named as the work of an enemy, and the reader sees the stair that begins with the scale of this verse. A further passage keeps the giving of what a man loves among the marks of the righteous, (2:177 — **“who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor”**), so that the two answers of this verse are held together.

The lesson also reaches a reader who can name the harm of a habit and keeps it because he can also name its pleasure. The verse gives him a scale with the harm written on the heavier side and leaves the weighing to him. Because the sentence closes on reflection, the reader is taught that a scale in the hand is worth more than a ruling he has not yet applied.

The case is like a fisherman who counts the fish he catches with a net that also brings up the young of the year. He knows the price of the catch and the cost of the empty season to come, and the choice he makes in the boat decides whether there is a catch next year.

---

## Verse 2:220

> upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you ˹O Prophet˺ concerning orphans. Say, “Improving their condition is best. And if you partner with them, they are bonded with you ˹in faith˺. And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good. Had Allah willed, He could have made it difficult for you. Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

**THE REFLECTION THAT SPANS TWO WORLDS**

The verse opens with a phrase that finishes the sentence before it: ***“upon this world and the Hereafter.”*** The first words of the verse are kept by al-Ṭabarī as the completion of the command to reflect, so that the thinking of the community is meant to run over both the account of this life and what follows it.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the same attachment and notes that the two worlds are named together because the rulings of the passage concern both. A man who weighs his gain in the market by the harm of the next life is the person the verse is describing. Because the phrase is not a new sentence, the reader is shown that the questions of the passage were answered inside a single argument.

**THE FEAR OF THE GUARDIANS**

The verse then turns to another question: ***“And they ask you ˹O Prophet˺ concerning orphans.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the occasion in the command that had come down before it, which warned the guardians against taking the property of the fatherless. The community took the warning so hard that they separated the food and the drink of the orphan from their own, and the hardship became a burden.

Al-Ṭabarī keeps the same report and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plainest form of it: the guardians were afraid to mix anything of the orphan with their own, and the verse came down to relieve them. Because the fear of the community was greater than the command itself, the reader is shown how a ruling is completed by a mercy.

**THE BEST AND THE PARTNERSHIP**

The answer is given in two halves: ***“Say,”*** ***“Improving their condition is best.”*** The word is kept by al-Ṭabarī as the setting right of the property and the affairs of the orphan, and al-Jalālayn keeps the simple sense of the good that is done for him.

The second half opens the household: ***“And if you partner with them, they are bonded with you ˹in faith˺.”*** Al-Ṭabarī keeps the phrase as a statement that the orphans are kin in the religion, so that the sharing of a table and a loaf is a partnership and not a theft. Because the door is left open after the best course is named, the reader is shown that the strict rule and the practical life were meant to stand together.

**THE INTENTION THAT IS WEIGHED**

The verse then states what God sees: ***“And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good.”*** Ibn Kathīr keeps the sentence as the answer to the guardians who had quarrelled over the mixing of the wealth, and notes that the deed is judged by the purpose behind it. as-Saʿdī keeps the same reading and adds that the two intents are known to God whether or not the neighbours can see them.

Because the sentence names the intention rather than the act, the reader is shown where the chapter locates the difference between a guardian and a thief. Two men may eat at the same table and sign the same account, and the record of the One who knows separates them.

**THE NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a sentence that keeps the door wide: ***“Had Allah willed, He could have made it difficult for you.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, and notes that the burden was lightened by the hand of the same Lord who could have tightened it. The two names follow: ***“Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”***

al-Ālūsī keeps the pair as the reason the ruling is what it is: the power could have made the matter hard, and the wisdom chose the way that keeps the guardian and the ward in one house. Because the verse closes on the two names rather than on the ruling, the reader is shown that the mercy of the ruling is itself part of the wisdom.

The Book commands the guarding of the orphan in a short line of the forenoon, (93:9 — **“do not oppress the orphan”**), where the warning is stated without the machinery of an estate, and the reader of the two passages is shown that the subject is older than the question. The rule of the wealth is stated in the chapter of the women, (4:2 — **“Give orphans their wealth”**), so that the guardian of this verse is a trustee in a system that was already laid down.

The lesson also reaches a reader who shares his table with a child of another father and finds himself counting the mouthfuls. The verse gives him a partner in the household and a ruling that weighs the intention rather than the plate. Because the orphans are named as partners in the faith, the reader is shown that the account is kept in a register that has nothing to do with the size of the estate.

The case is like two men who buy a boat together and keep a ledger of every litre of fuel. The ledger says one owes the other a small sum, and the catch they would not have made alone settles the debt in a single morning on the water.

---

## Verse 2:221

> Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe; for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you. And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you. They invite ˹you˺ to the Fire while Allah invites ˹you˺ to Paradise and forgiveness by His grace. He makes His revelations clear to the people so perhaps they will be mindful

**THE TWO COMMANDS IN ONE RULING**

The verse lays down a wall around the household: ***“Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe”*** The same rule is stated later for the other side of the marriage, and the reports place the revelation in the houses of the community rather than among its enemies.

al-Ṭabarī keeps the two commands in one ruling, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that the question had come from the men of the city who were drawn to women of the association of partners for their beauty. Because the command is stated for both sides of a marriage, the reader is shown that the verse is a law about the house itself rather than a licence for one party.

**THE BETTER AND THE FREE**

The verse supports the rule with a scale: ***“for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you.”*** Faith is weighed here against rank and beauty, and the same scale is used in the next sentence for the other side of the house: ***“And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe”*** ***“until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you.”***

al-Ālūsī keeps the discussion of the ten over the women of the Book, and keeps the reading in which this verse is general while the later passage allows the chaste women of those who were given the Book. as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as the answer to a calculation that many a family makes in the open, when it weighs the poor believer against the rich stranger.

**THE PLEASANT LOOK**

The clause that meets the reader at his own door is repeated in both halves: ***“for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you.”*** The same words are used of the men, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the note that the phrase was placed there because the pull of the eye had been the reason for the question.

Because the attraction is named rather than denied, the reader is shown that the Book speaks to the person who is looking and answers him in his own language. Since the measure set is the faith of a person, the reader is taught where the scale of a household is held. The measure it leaves him is the faith of the person beside him and nothing else in the ledger.

**THE TWO INVITATIONS**

The verse then names the direction of each way: ***“They invite ˹you˺ to the Fire while Allah invites ˹you˺ to Paradise and forgiveness by His grace.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as two invitations to two houses, and notes that a marriage is a choice of the road that the two people will walk together.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the same image and adds that the invitation of the first side is made by conduct rather than by speech. Because the two invitations stand in one sentence, the reader is shown what a household becomes in the long run: a company that walks the couple towards one of the two ends.

**THE CLOSING THAT SPEAKS TO THE PEOPLE**

The verse ends with the sentence that closes several passages of this stretch: ***“He makes His revelations clear to the people so perhaps they will be mindful”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sense that the clarity is the mercy of a Lord who does not leave a household in the dark.

The Book permits the chaste women of the people of the Book in a later passage, (5:5 — **“chaste women of those given the Scripture before you”**), so that the reader knows that the wall of this verse is drawn around the association of partners rather than around every stranger. A further passage keeps the promise to the one who keeps the command for the sake of God, (65:2 — **“And whoever is mindful of Allah, He will make a way out for them”**), and the reader is shown what the restraint of this verse is worth.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been told to consider a proposal by a family and is being asked to weigh the income, the house and the looks. The verse gives him a ledger with one line at the top and asks him what the house will be like when the income has changed. Because the invitation of each side is stated plainly, the reader is taught that the decision of a marriage is a decision about a road.

The case is like a family that buys a plot because the road to it looks wide and new, and never asks where the road leads when it leaves the town. The house is built, the traffic arrives, and the family spends its evenings listening to the lorries of a route they never chose.

---

## Verse 2:222

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about menstruation. Say, “Beware of its harm! So keep away, and do not have intercourse with your wives during their monthly cycles until they are purified. When they purify themselves, then you may approach them in the manner specified by Allah. Surely Allah loves those who always turn to Him in repentance and those who purify themselves.”

**THE QUESTION THAT FOLLOWED AN OLD PRACTICE**

The verse records a question on a subject the community had inherited from two directions: ***“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about menstruation.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports on the occasion, and al-Baghawī keeps the same reports with the names of the men who came asking.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the practice of the earlier community, which had kept away from the woman entirely during her days and had made her food and her bed separate. The community of the city had taken some of that habit, and the question was asked to settle it. Because the answer names a harm rather than a custom, the reader is shown that the ruling was given for the body.

**THE HARM NAMED**

The first words of the answer are short: ***“Say,”*** ***“Beware of its harm!”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the order that follows as a command about the place rather than about the person, and keeps the practice reported from the household of the Prophet ﷺ, where the wife was asked to wrap herself before she lay beside him. al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading in a short form.

The clause that follows is stated in plain words: ***“So keep away, and do not have intercourse with your wives during their monthly cycles until they are purified.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the command as the forbidding of one act, and notes that the eating, the sleeping and the company were left open. Because the verse restricts the command to the act, the reader is shown that the earlier practice had gone past the harm it feared.

**THE APPROACH AND THE MANNER**

The verse then opens the way again: ***“When they purify themselves, then you may approach them in the manner specified by Allah.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the difference of the ten over the word for the purification, whether it means the washing of the whole body. He keeps the reports that the community had asked about the manner from another direction, and that the answer sent them back to the place the law had made lawful.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the phrase as the lawful manner of the approach, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading. Because the manner is named as something specified rather than invented, the reader is shown that the verse leaves nothing of the matter to the fashion of the household.

**THE TWO QUALITIES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a sentence that names two kinds of people: ***“Surely Allah loves those who always turn to Him in repentance and those who purify themselves.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the first as the returning of the one who has gone past a limit, and the second as the cleanliness of the body and the character.

al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair and the same order, and notes that the sentence was placed after a ruling about the body. Because the closing sentence speaks of the heart and the skin in one breath, the reader is shown that the religion treats the two as one subject.

The Book states the same care for the body in the command of the fast, (2:187 — **“Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques”**), where the limit is drawn by the same hand that opens the way here. A further passage returns to the same subject with the command of the prayer, (4:1 — **“Be mindful of Allah”**), so that the reader is shown how often the Book joins the rights of the body to the rights of the Lord.

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps away from a wife in her days with a disgust that the law never asked of him. The verse gives him a limit and a door in the same sentence, and it asks him whether the harm he fears is the harm the Lord named. Because the answer opens with the harm rather than the habit, the reader is taught that the ruling was given to protect a person and not to punish her.

The case is like a household that shuts a room for a week every month because a rumour said the air was bad. The doctor opens the window, names the one thing to avoid, and the family finds that the rest of the room was always safe.

---

## Verse 2:223

> Your wives are like farmland for you, so approach them ˹consensually˺ as you please. And send forth something good for yourselves. Be mindful of Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good news to the believers

**THE IMAGE OF THE TILTH**

The verse answers a quarrel with an image: ***“Your wives are like farmland for you”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the tilth as the place where the seed is planted and the crop is expected, and keeps the reports that the sentence answered a claim of the Jews of the city about the manner of the approach.

al-Baghawī keeps the same occasion and the same report about the claim that a child would be born with a defect. The verse answers a superstition with a picture of a field. Because the image is taken from farming, the reader is shown that the matter belongs to the body and its fruit rather than to the habits of the neighbours.

**THE APPROACH LEFT OPEN**

The verse then gives the freedom within the law: ***“so approach them ˹consensually˺ as you please.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as the permission of the lawful place in any manner the couple agree on, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same reading with the note that the permission excludes what the law has forbidden.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the report that the men of the helpers and the men of the city had quarrelled over the question, and that the verse settled it. Because the permission is stated in the plural, the reader is shown that the agreement of the two people is part of the matter and not a concession granted to one.

**THE GOOD SENT FORWARD**

The verse then turns the picture towards the account: ***“And send forth something good for yourselves.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the good is the seeking of a child, and the reports that it is the remembrance of God before the act. al-Jalālayn keeps the second reading in a short form.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the reading of the good deed and the intention that a person sends forward to be met later. Because the sentence stands between a permission and a meeting, the reader is shown that the private act has a public account. Since the good is sent forward rather than kept, the reader is taught that the ledger of a household is written in advance. What is sent forward from the bed is met on another day.

**THE MEETING AND THE NEWS**

The verse closes with two sentences: ***“Be mindful of Allah, and know that you will meet Him.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the meeting as the standing before the Lord on the day of the account, and as-Saʿdī keeps the mindfulness as the guard that keeps the couple inside the law in the first place.

The last words turn to the community: ***“And give good news to the believers”***. The good news is kept by Ibn Kathīr as the promise of the garden for the one who keeps the commands, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading with the note that the sentence was placed at the end of a ruling about the household.

The Book returns to the same picture of the field in a later passage, (4:1), and states the same meeting in the closing of the spouses' duty elsewhere, (4:1 — **“Be mindful of Allah”**), so that the reader of the two passages is shown that the household has a ledger of its own.

The lesson also reaches a reader who separates his religion from the hours of his house and keeps the two lives in different rooms. The verse gives him a sentence about meeting God in the middle of a permission, and it asks him what he intends to carry to that meeting from the bed he shares. Because the good news is addressed to believers rather than to ascetics, the reader is shown that the married life is one of the places where faith is kept. Since the sentence about the meeting follows the permission, the reader is taught that the hours of the household are counted among the acts that are seen.

The case is like a farmer who sows his field with a mixture of seed and thistle because the sack was open in the barn. The harvest is his own, the thistles come up with the wheat, and the field he had planned to leave to his children is the field he has to clear.

---

## Verse 2:224

> Do not use Allah’s Name in your oaths as an excuse for not doing good, not guarding against evil, or not making peace between people. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE OATH USED AS A WALL**

The verse forbids a habit that had grown among good people: ***“Do not use Allah’s Name in your oaths as an excuse”*** ***“for not doing good, not guarding against evil,”*** ***“or not making peace between people.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the sentence came down about a man who had sworn not to keep the ties of his family or not to set a matter right between two parties.

al-Baghawī keeps the report of the oath of a father in the community against the visits of a relative, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reports with the ruling that follows from them. Because the verse addresses itself to the good rather than to the wicked, the reader is shown that a vow can be the instrument of a family quarrel.

**THE THREE GOOD THINGS NAMED**

Three acts are named as the ones an oath may not block: the doing of good, the guarding against evil and the making of peace. as-Saʿdī keeps the first as the general duty of the good deed, the second as the guard against the forbidden, and the third as the settlement between people, which he treats as the greatest of them.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same three and notes the reason for their naming: a person who swears against the visits of his kin has already chosen the evil he meant to avoid. Because the verse lists the three as one command, the reader is shown that the family tie and the settlement are not favours a person may withdraw by an oath.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse closes with a pair that reaches the intention: ***“And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the hearing of the words of the oath and the second as the knowledge of the purpose behind it. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same pair and the same order.

Because the two names are placed after the command, the reader is shown that the words of a man are not measured by their sound. Since the hearing and the knowledge are named together, the reader is taught that no excuse survives the record of the intention. A promise to do nothing is heard by the One who knows what the promiser wanted, and the verse closes on the record of both the words and the aim.

The two kinds of oaths are ruled on in the next sentence of the same passage, (2:225), and the penalty of a deliberate oath is set out in the chapter of the table, (5:89). The same subject returns in a later passage, (2:225 — **“Allah will not hold you accountable for unintentional oaths”**), and the penalty for a deliberate oath is named in the chapter of the table, (5:89 — **“The penalty for a broken oath is to feed ten poor people from what you normally feed your own family”**). The reader of the two passages is shown that the law opens a way out of a vow rather than leaving it as a wall.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has promised his family that he will never again set foot in his brother's house. The verse gives him a command that the name of God is not an instrument for a grudge, and it asks him where the oath ends and the spite begins. Because the two names at the close describe the One who hears the words and knows the hearts, the reader is taught that the matter is judged on the side that the oath was made to protect. Since the three acts are duties rather than favours, the reader is shown that no vow can cancel a right that belongs to another person. Because the sentence is addressed to the good, the reader is taught that the danger of an oath lies in the hands of the person who keeps it. Since the name of God is the thing being used, the reader is shown how a private quarrel can be dressed in the highest authority a person knows.

The case is like a man who swears before his children that he will never lend the neighbour his ladder, and then finds the neighbour's roof in flames. The ladder is his, the oath is his, and the whole street watches him decide which of the two was really sacred.

---

## Verse 2:225

> Allah will not hold you accountable for unintentional oaths, but for what you intended in your hearts. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing

**THE TWO KINDS OF OATH**

The verse divides the oaths of a man into two kinds: ***“Allah will not hold you accountable for unintentional oaths,”*** ***“but for what you intended in your hearts.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the first as the careless word that slips into a conversation, and keeps the reports of the community that the tongue says by God yes and by God no without meaning it.

al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading in a short form, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports of the companions on what such a word includes. Because the first kind is named as the one that carries no account, the reader is shown that the law weighs the heart rather than the sound.

**THE INTENTION THAT IS WEIGHED**

The second half of the sentence is the part that matters: what the heart intended when the oath was spoken. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading and notes that the deliberate vow is the one that binds a man to the promise he made with his purpose.

as-Saʿdī keeps the intention as the turning point of the whole subject, since a word that was meant stands as a debt and a word that was not meant falls away. Because the verse joins the two in one sentence, the reader is shown that no oath can be judged by the words alone; the record of the mind is read with it.

**THE TWO NAMES AND THE TEMPER OF THE RULING**

The verse closes with the pair that holds the whole subject: ***“And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the covering of the slip and the second as the patience that does not hurry the answer. al-Ālūsī keeps the same pair and notes that the patience is the reason a community is not destroyed for its careless words.

Because the two names follow a ruling about speech, the reader is shown the temper of the law. Since the patience of the Lord is named in the same sentence as the forgiveness, the reader is taught that the mercy of a ruling is part of its meaning. A person may speak a hundred oaths in a month and be asked about none of them, and the patience of the Lord is the ground under that mercy.

The Book rules on the broken deliberate oath in the chapter of the table, (5:89 — **“The penalty for a broken oath is to feed ten poor people from what you normally feed your own family”**), and the sentence before this one forbids the use of the name of God as a wall against good, (2:224). The reader of the two passages is shown that the Book treats the vow as a matter of purpose from its first line to its last.

The lesson also reaches a reader who says by God in every second sentence and then wonders why his promises have no weight in his own house. The verse gives him a distinction between a sound and a decision, and it asks him how many of his oaths his heart ever signed. Because the closing name is the Forbearing, the reader is taught that the mercy of God is not the licence of the tongue. Since the account of an oath is kept by the One who knows the intention, the reader is shown that the careless word and the sworn promise are read in the same book.

The case is like a man who keeps a book of the debts owed to him and the debts he owes, and who writes the second column in pencil because nobody reads it. The debts are collected from him one by one, and the pencil marks are honoured by the day he has to answer.

---

## Verse 2:226

> Those who swear not to have intercourse with their wives must wait for four months. If they change their mind, then Allah is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**THE OATH OF SEPARATION**

The verse takes up a habit that the people of the days before Islam had used as a divorce: ***“Those who swear not to have intercourse with their wives”*** ***“must wait for four months.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that a man would swear against his wife and leave her hanging between a marriage and a separation, and the verse set a limit to the waiting.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports and the rulings that grew from them, and al-Jalālayn keeps the measure of the four months as the term in which the wife cannot be abandoned without a decision. Because the verse gives a term rather than a ruling of its own, the reader is shown that the law was protecting the woman from an oath that had no end.

**THE FOUR MONTHS AND WHAT FOLLOWS**

The waiting is named in the sentence itself, and the ten differ over what falls at its close. al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that a man who has sworn must return to his wife or separate from her by a divorce, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the rulings on the patience of the wife and her rights during the term.

The plain sense is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās, that the term is the boundary of the oath, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same reading with the note that the law was made to force a decision. Because the verse names a term of four months and no more, the reader is shown that the door out of the quarrel was left open the whole time.

**THE CHANGE OF MIND**

The verse then allows the return: ***“If they change their mind, then Allah is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the change of mind as the returning to the wife after the oath, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the return requires an expiation for the broken oath and a settling of the matter.

as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as an invitation to the better way, and notes that the door of the mercy is named at the very place where a man has been wronged by his own promise. Because the change of mind is named before the punishment, the reader is shown which of the two ends the law prefers.

**THE HOUSEKEEPING OF A RULING**

The passage is kept by al-Ālūsī as part of the long treatment of the household in this chapter, since the oaths come after the inheritance, the marriage and the nursing of the children. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same place for it and notes that the whole stretch was sent to guard the weak side of a house.

Because the sentence ends on the two names, the reader is shown that the whole matter of the oath is left inside the mercy of the Lord. Since a term of four months was set for a quarrel inside a house, the reader is taught that the law cares for the side that cannot speak for itself. A family quarrel is settled by a term, a door and a name, and the verse closes with the gentler of the two names.

The Book orders the waiting of the divorced wife in the chapter of the divorce, (65:2 — **“And whoever is mindful of Allah, He will make a way out for them”**), and states the retracting of divorce twice in the same passage of this chapter, (2:229 — **“Divorce may be retracted twice”**), so that the reader sees the oath of this verse and the divorce of the law standing side by side. The household is given a way out in both.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has stopped speaking to his wife and counts the days of the silence as if the silence were the stronger position. The verse gives him four months and a door, and it asks him what he is waiting for. Because the two names at the close describe a Lord who forgives the broken promise and is merciful to the one who returns, the reader is taught that the way back is open from the first day of the quarrel.

The case is like a man who quarrels with his brother and swears never to enter his shop again, and then stands in the street for a year watching the door. The shop is open every day, the brother is behind the counter, and the only thing that keeps the man outside is a sentence he said aloud and never meant.

---

## Verse 2:227

> But if they settle on divorce, then Allah is indeed All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE OATH THAT ENDS AT A DECISION**

The sentence closes the law of the oath and leaves the man at a door: ***“But if they settle on divorce”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the reading that the settling is the finish of the oath by a decision rather than by the return. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same sense with the term of the four months standing behind it.

The reports that a man who let the four months pass without returning to his wife was held to the separation are kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the note that the waiting of those months made the separation an accomplished one rather than a new start is kept by al-Ālūsī. Because the sentence turns on a resolve rather than on a word, the reader is shown that the law waited for the man's own choice to arrive at a decision. Since the four months are given to the woman, the reader sees where a delay falls hardest.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE END OF THE TERM**

The closing names are the same pair that ends the earlier ruling: ***“then Allah is indeed All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. al-Ālūsī keeps the first as the hearing of the oath the man had spoken. And the second as the knowledge of what he wanted when he spoke it. Because the oath was the thing that began the matter, the reader is shown why the two names return at the point where it ends.

al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading in a short form, and as-Saʿdī keeps the note that the pair stands as a warning to the man who swears lightly and then lets the months decide for him. The two names are a ledger of the words and of the purpose behind them. Because an oath is heard as a sound and judged as an aim, the reader is taught to weigh what he swears by what he wants.

**WHAT A FOURTH MONTH SETTLES**

The ten differ over what a man owes when the four months have passed and he has neither returned nor pronounced a divorce. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the separation then stands, while al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the months themselves worked the separation. So that the man is left with the keeping of a new contract if he wants her back.

The same reading, with the note that the law was made for the wife, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, since a woman held by an oath has no term to count and no judge to ask. Because the verse gives the decision to the man and the waiting to the woman, the reader is shown how the Book balances the hand that holds the oath with the side that suffers it.

The waiting of the divorced wife is fixed in a later passage of this chapter, (2:228 — **“Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles”**), where the same care for the household is set out in greater detail. A further passage teaches the reader what the patience of a woman is worth before God, (65:2 — **“And whoever is mindful of Allah, He will make a way out for them”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has sworn in the heat of an argument and now counts the quiet as a victory. The verse gives him four months and a decision, and it asks him what he means to do with the fourth. Because the names at the close are Hearing and Knowing, the reader is taught that the oath was never the secret he thought it was.

The case is like a man who ties a rope across his own doorway and tells himself the house is guarded. The rope is his, the door is his, and every visitor who turns away in that season is a guest he invited once.

---

## Verse 2:228

> Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺. It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands reserve the right to take them back within that period if they desire reconciliation. Women have rights similar to those of men equitably, although men have a degree ˹of responsibility˺ above them. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**THE WAITING THAT BELONGS TO THE WOMAN**

The verse opens with a command that gives a term its own owner: ***“Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can re-marry˺.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports on the difference between the two readings of the term. For its part, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the long dispute of the ten over whether the count is of the monthly course or of the clean interval between the courses.

The same dispute with the names of those who held each view is kept by al-Baghawī, and the summary that the count is a matter of the law rather than of the body alone is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the waiting is placed at the start of the verse, the reader is shown that the law begins with the side that carries the consequence of the marriage.

**THE HIDDEN THING IN THE WOMB**

The next sentence forbids a silence that would harm another: ***“It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs,”*** and the ground of the command is named after it: ***“if they ˹truly˺ believe in Allah”*** ***“and the Last Day.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the sense that the concealment covers the child as well as the course. In the same way, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading in a plain form.

The reports of the community on a woman who hid the state of her body to hurry a marriage are kept by al-Ṭabarī. And the point that the fear of God in this verse is asked of a person in a private room with no witness is kept by as-Saʿdī. Because the command is tied to faith rather than to a court, the reader is shown where the law expects the truth to be kept.

**THE RIGHT OF RETURN AND ITS TERM**

The verse then grants the husband a door while the months run: ***“And their husbands reserve the right to take them back within”*** ***“that period if they desire reconciliation.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings on the kind of divorce meant here. On this point, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading with the note that the return needs no new contract while the months stand.

al-Ālūsī keeps the note that the right belongs to the husband in the revocable divorce, and as-Saʿdī keeps the condition of the sentence: the return has to be for a settlement rather than for a grudge. Because the door is granted with a condition, the reader is shown that a return made to harm the woman is a return the law will not count.

**THE RIGHTS, THE DEGREE AND THE TWO NAMES**

The verse then states the balance of the house: ***“Women have rights similar to those of men equitably”*** ***“although men have a degree ˹of responsibility˺ above them.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the degree as the duty of the man to carry the cost and the decision. Alongside that, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same reading with the note that the degree is a service rather than a rank.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain sense that the rights are equal while the duty differs, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the reports that the degree is about the spending and the guarding of the family. Because the sentence puts the similar rights before the degree, the reader is shown that the difference is meant for the house rather than for the scale of a person. The pair at the close is read by al-Jalālayn as the power that guards the house and the wisdom that orders it: ***“And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise”***.

The waiting of the widow and the waiting of the expectant mother are set out later in the same passage, (65:1 — **“then divorce them with concern for their waiting period”**). And the case of the woman whose age hides the count is fixed in the same chapter, (65:4 — **“their waiting period is three months”**). The reader of the three passages sees one subject handled from three sides.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has convinced himself that the end of a marriage releases him from every duty towards the woman he lived with. The verse gives him a season of waiting, a rule against hiding, a right of return with a condition and a duty of spending, and it asks him which of the four he plans to honour. Because the two closing names are the Almighty and the All-Wise, the reader is taught that the arrangement of the house was made by the One who knows what the two people need.

The case is like two partners who divide a business and agree that neither will open the books of the firm for three months, so that the customers can choose where to take their trade. The agreement protects the reputation of the shop, and it protects the partner who has no keys to the till.

---

## Verse 2:229

> Divorce may be retracted twice, then the husband must retain ˹his wife˺ with honour or separate ˹from her˺ with grace. It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry given to their wives, unless the couple fears not being able to keep within the limits of Allah. So if you fear they will not be able to keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame if the wife compensates the husband to obtain divorce. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers

**THE TWO THAT REMAIN A MARRIAGE**

The verse begins with a count: ***“Divorce may be retracted twice”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the reading that the number is the limit of the revocable kind. For its part, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the report of how the people of the days before Islam divorced without end and took their wives back only to harm them.

The same report, with the story of the man who let his wife reach the end of the waiting and then took her back again, is kept by al-Baghawī. And the point that the two allowed pronouncements were set as a boundary rather than as a habit is kept by as-Saʿdī. Because the sentence counts the pronouncements, the reader is shown that the Book was answering a practice rather than describing a freedom.

**THE HONOUR AND THE GRACE**

The verse then puts the two roads of the third moment side by side: ***“then the husband must retain ˹his wife˺ with honour”*** ***“or separate ˹from her˺ with grace.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the first as the keeping that gives the wife her rights and the second as the release that leaves no debt and no reproach, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair in a short form.

The sense that the honour is shown in the treatment and the grace in the release is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same reading, with the note that the two roads close off the third of a house kept on the edge, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the law names only two ends, the reader is shown what a half-marriage is worth in the judgment of the Book.

**THE DOWRY THAT MAY NOT BE TAKEN BACK**

The next sentence turns to the wealth of the wife: ***“It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry given to their wives”***. al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings on the gifts a husband may not reclaim. On this point, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading with the note that the dowry became the property of the wife on the day it was given.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reason in the verse itself: the dowry is the price of a contract that the man chose to enter and then chose to leave, and the loss belongs to the one who broke what he built. Because the sentence guards the purse of the woman, the reader is shown that the law protects the side that leaves the room with less.

**THE WIFE WHO BUYS HER RELEASE**

The verse then opens a door that the ten discuss at length: ***“unless the couple fears not being able to keep within the limits of Allah.”*** ***“So if you fear they will not be able to keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame”*** ***“if the wife compensates the husband to obtain divorce.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the report of the first woman in the community who came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked for a separation, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings that grew from it.

al-Ālūsī keeps the condition that the fear has to be of the limits and not of the temper, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading with the note that the compensation is a price agreed between the two. Because the fear of the limits is the ground named here, the reader is shown that a separation bought for a grudge stands outside the permission.

**THE LIMITS AND THE WRONGDOERS**

The verse closes on the limits: ***“These are the limits set by Allah, so do not transgress them.”*** ***“And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the limits are the rules set out before them. Alongside that, And as-Saʿdī keeps the note that the wrong is measured by the crossing rather than by the feeling.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the transgression is the taking of what was forbidden in the same passage. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the warning that the words at the close are a fence around everything above them. Because the sentence names the wrongdoers at the end of a law about the house, the reader is shown that the private quarrel is judged on the same page as the public crime.

The rights of the woman in a separation are guarded in a later passage, (4:19 — **“It is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will”**). And the two roads of the verse are repeated in the next stretch of this chapter, (2:231 — **“either retain them honourably or let them go honourably”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps a wife in the house because leaving would cost him money, and who calls the arrangement patience. The verse gives him a price for the door and names the two ways of honour, and it asks him which of them he is living in. Because the closing sentence calls the crosser of the limits a wrongdoer, the reader is taught that a marriage held by force is outside the law he claims to follow.

The case is like a man who keeps a shop open for years with a partner he no longer greets, because dissolving the business would mean splitting the shelves. The shelves are counted once, the stock is divided once, and the years of standing behind the same counter are counted by neither of them.

---

## Verse 2:230

> So if a husband divorces his wife ˹three times˺, then it is not lawful for him to remarry her until after she has married another man and then is divorced. Then it is permissible for them to reunite, as long as they feel they are able to maintain the limits of Allah. These are the limits set by Allah, which He makes clear for people of knowledge

**THE THIRD TIME**

The verse takes up the case on the far side of the count that was set before it: ***“So if a husband divorces his wife ˹three times˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the reading that the third pronouncement closes the door of the revocable kind. In the same way, And al-Baghawī keeps the same sense with the reports of the people of the days before Islam who divorced their wives without a limit.

The plain reading that the third is the one that ends the marriage is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās, and the rulings on the pronouncements that follow one another in a single sitting are kept by al-Qurṭubī. Because the woman becomes lawful again only after another marriage, the reader is shown that the door of return was left to a new contract rather than to a new oath. Since the condition names a second marriage and not only a paper, the reader sees that an arrangement of convenience is not a marriage.

**THE OTHER MAN AND THE SECOND SEPARATION**

The verse then sets the condition: ***“then it is not lawful for him to remarry her”*** ***“until after she has married another man”*** ***“and then is divorced.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the condition that the second marriage has to be a real one, entered for its own sake. In the same vein, And al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading with the note that the union has to be completed.

The reports of the community on the arrangements people made to hurry a first husband back are kept by al-Ālūsī. And the same warnings, with the note that such a marriage is a curse on the three of them, are kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the condition stands between the two, the reader is shown that the law refuses to be used as a gate kept by a hired hand.

**THE PERMISSION AND ITS CONDITION**

The verse then allows a new beginning: ***“Then it is permissible”*** ***“for them to reunite”*** ***“as long as they feel they are able to maintain the limits of Allah.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the thought that the feelings here are the knowledge of the two. Alongside that, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the words make the two the judges of their own house.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the permission is a mercy for a couple whose first years were spent in quarrels and who have learned what the limits are. Here too, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that the knowledge of the limits is the condition of the return. Because the condition is knowledge rather than certainty of the future, the reader is shown that the law asks the couple to be honest rather than to be sure.

**THE CLEAR LIMITS AND THE PEOPLE OF KNOWLEDGE**

The verse closes with a sentence that points at the whole passage: ***“These are the limits set by Allah”*** ***“which He makes clear”*** ***“for people of knowledge”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sense that the clarity belongs to those who will carry it, as knowledge without practice is no knowledge, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading in a short form.

al-Baghawī keeps the note that the whole passage was sent down after the community had emptied the marriage of its terms. For its part, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that the plain words are the mercy of a law that never leaves a matter dark. Because the closing sentence speaks of knowing rather than of hearing, the reader is shown that the three divorces were never meant to be a wall but a teaching.

The count of the two pronouncements is stated just before, (2:229 — **“Divorce may be retracted twice”**). And the prevention of a return is forbidden in the same stretch of the chapter, (2:232 — **“do not prevent them from re-marrying their ex-husbands”**), so the reader sees the door left ajar at each step.

The lesson also reaches a reader who treats the three pronouncements as a threat he can hold over his wife and take back as often as he likes. The verse shows him the far side of the third time, where the house he broke is a house another man may build. And it asks him how much of his own life he is willing to spend on a sentence. Because the sentence at the close names the people of knowledge, the reader is taught that the man who understood the passage and still used it as a lever has understood nothing. Since the third divorce is the only one that cannot be taken back, the reader sees that the law leaves him no room to repeat himself.

The case is like a man who tears the trunk of a young tree across with a rope so that the branch will grow in a chosen direction, and who returns each month to tear it a little further. The tree keeps growing, the bark keeps opening, and the shape he wanted is the only thing on the plot that was never his to keep.

---

## Verse 2:231

> When you divorce women and they have ˹almost˺ reached the end of their waiting period, either retain them honourably or let them go honourably. But do not retain them ˹only˺ to harm them ˹or˺ to take advantage ˹of them˺. Whoever does that surely wrongs his own soul. Do not take Allah’s revelations lightly. Remember Allah’s favours upon you as well as the Book and wisdom He has sent down for your guidance. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**THE HOUR WHEN THE TERM RUNS OUT**

The verse begins at the edge of the waiting: ***“When you divorce women”*** ***“and they have ˹almost˺ reached the end of their waiting period, either retain them honourably”*** ***“or let them go honourably.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the sentence was sent down about a man who took his wife back at the last hour only to divorce her again. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same reports with the names of the houses they were told about.

The ruling that a return made at the very end of the waiting is valid. And that the intention behind it is what the verse is guarding, is kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the same pair of roads is kept by al-Jalālayn in a short form. Because the command is given at the last minute of the term, the reader is shown that the law watched the exact point where a woman's hope turns back on her.

**THE RETURN THAT HARMS**

The verse then forbids the return made as a punishment: ***“But do not retain them ˹only˺ to harm them ˹or˺ to take advantage ˹of them˺.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the harm as the returning for the sake of keeping the woman in suspense. Here too, And al-Ālūsī keeps the reports of the ten on what the advantage means when a man keeps a wife to inherit her wealth or to hold her against another marriage.

The plain sense that the harm is anything done outside the law is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās, and the same reading, with the note that the inner purpose is made a part of the ruling, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the Book judges a return by its reason, the reader is shown that the outward form of a marriage can stand over a hidden intention.

**THE SOUL THAT IS WRONGED**

The sentence that follows is one of the heaviest in the passage: ***“Whoever does that surely wrongs his own soul.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the wrong falls on the one who chose it. For its part, And al-Jalālayn keeps the same with the note that the wife is not the only one damaged by such a house.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the report that a man who harmed his wife during the waiting was made to stand before the law with the words of the verse read to him. In the same way, And as-Saʿdī keeps the point that a hidden harm is a harm a person has done to himself first. Because the sentence turns the damage inward, the reader is shown that the Lord does not need to send anyone after the offender.

**THE FAVOURS THAT MAY NOT BE TAKEN LIGHTLY**

The verse then turns on the man's own history: ***“Do not take Allah’s revelations lightly.”*** ***“Remember Allah’s favours upon you”*** ***“as well as the Book”*** ***“and wisdom He has sent down”*** ***“for your guidance.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the favours as the guidance itself. In the same vein, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the reading that the warning covers both the neglect of the rules and the misuse of them.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the Book and the wisdom are the two things given to the community. On this point, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that a house built on the warning of the Lord cannot be used against the people of the Lord. Because the sentence is placed after the forbidden return, the reader is shown what such conduct treats lightly.

**THE MINDFULNESS AND THE KNOWLEDGE**

The verse reaches its close on a pair of commands: ***“Be mindful of Allah”*** ***“and know that Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the guard over the intention and the second as the knowledge that reaches the hidden rooms. Alongside that, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading in a short form.

as-Saʿdī keeps the closing pair as the whole answer of the passage, since the fear of God inside a private quarrel is what stands between a family and a long cruelty. Because the verse ends with knowledge rather than with a punishment, the reader is shown that the law trusts him with a matter no court could ever see.

The two roads of the verse are set out in the earlier ruling, (2:229 — **“It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry”**). And the rights of the woman in a house are guarded again in the chapter of the women, (4:19 — **“It is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps his wife in the house so that no other man may have her, and who calls that keeping a family. The verse gives him two honourable doors and forbids the third way, and it asks him what he is holding and why. Because the close of the verse speaks of the favours and the Book, the reader is taught that a marriage is one of the places where a person shows what he has done with what he was given.

The case is like a man who parks his car across a neighbour's gate for the night and tells himself he is only keeping the space. The gate opens once in the morning, the neighbour's day begins late, and the space he kept was never the one he needed.

---

## Verse 2:232

> When you have divorced women and they have reached the end of their waiting period, do not prevent them from re-marrying their ex-husbands if they come to an honourable agreement. This is enjoined on whoever has faith in Allah and the Last Day. This is purer and more dignifying for you. Allah knows and you do not know

**THE GUARDIAN WHO STANDS IN THE WAY**

The verse turns from the husband to the family around the woman: ***“When you have divorced women”*** ***“and they have reached the end of their waiting period, do not prevent them from re-marrying their ex-husbands”*** ***“if they come to an honourable agreement.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the sentence came down about a guardian in the community who refused his relative the return to the man she had married. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same report with the name of the house it was told about.

The rulings that followed are kept by al-Qurṭubī: a guardian has no authority to refuse a marriage the woman wants and the contract makes lawful. The same reading is kept by al-Jalālayn, with the note that the address is to the men of the family. Because the verse speaks to those who are not the two parties, the reader is shown how far the law reaches into a house.

**THE HONOURABLE TERMS**

The condition of the sentence is set in its own words: the return has to be ***“if they come to an honourable agreement.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the agreement as a new contract with a dowry and two willing parties. In the same way, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the honourable part covers the manner as well as the terms.

The plain reading that the agreement is made between the man and the woman is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the reports of those who held that a refusal was a harm done to a relative for the sake of an old quarrel, is kept by al-Ālūsī. Because the verse ties the permission to the terms, the reader is shown that the door it opens is not a licence but a settlement.

**THE FAITH IN THE SENTENCE**

The verse then lifts the command to the level of belief: ***“This is enjoined on whoever has faith in Allah”*** ***“and the Last Day.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the warning belongs to those who accept the teaching. On this point, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading with the note that a man who blocks a lawful marriage has not understood what he claims to believe.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain form of the sentence, and as-Saʿdī keeps the note that the verse joins the rights of two people to the confession of the tongue. Because the command is tied to the two articles of faith, the reader is shown that the treatment of a woman in a family is part of the religion and not of its margins.

**THE PURER AND THE MORE DIGNIFYING**

The verse then tells the community what its own interest is: ***“This is purer”*** ***“and more dignifying for you.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the purity as the keeping away from the harm that grows out of a blocked marriage. Alongside that, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that a family which lets its women choose keeps its own name clean.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the reading that the dignity is for both the guardian and the woman, since the whole street sees what was done. Here too, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that a reputation is spent by the same hands that guard it. Because the interest of the guardian is named beside the right of the woman, the reader is shown how the Book argues.

**THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE TWO SIDES**

The verse closes on a line that is repeated across the chapter: ***“Allah knows”*** ***“and you do not know”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the knowledge as the Lord's grasp of what is best for the two. For its part, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that a guardian argues from his own pride while the verse argues from the outcome.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the words leave the matter in the hands of the One who sees the end, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same reading in a short form. Because the sentence follows the words about purity and dignity, the reader is shown that the family that trusts the judgment of God finds its own standing in the end.

The roads of the release are set out in the sentence before this one, (2:231 — **“either retain them honourably or let them go honourably”**). And the rights of the woman are guarded in the chapter of the women, (4:19 — **“It is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who refuses a marriage for his sister because the man is poor and the family has a name to keep. The verse gives him a command, a condition and a sentence about knowledge, and it asks him whose name was being kept in the first place. Because the close speaks of the knowledge of God, the reader is taught that the man who blocks what he cannot see is working against the only eye that can.

The case is like a household that locks the gate of the courtyard at sunset to keep the family safe, and then finds that the children have learned to climb the wall. The gate is as strong as it ever was, and the wall is the place where the family now meets.

---

## Verse 2:233

> ˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. If you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**THE NURSING THAT BELONGS TO THE CHILD**

The verse follows the separated parents into the room where the infant is kept: ***“˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring”*** ***“for two whole years”*** ***“for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the command is phrased as a statement of what the law has established rather than as a request. So that the duty of the mother is settled where the two have parted.

The rulings on the woman who is asked to nurse a child she did not bear, and on the child whose mother refuses, are kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the same measure of the two years, with the note that the words cover the full time, is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the child's need is named before the parents' quarrel, the reader is shown where the Book places the centre of the house.

**THE FATHER'S BREAD AND CLOTHING**

The next sentence turns to the one who carries the cost: ***“The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance”*** ***“and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the sense that the nursing mother is owed the like of what she would have had in the marriage. Alongside that, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the food and the dress are measured by the standing of the two.

The reason is kept by as-Saʿdī: a woman who gives her body to the child cannot earn in the market, so the law puts her maintenance on the shoulder of the father. Because the duty is attached to the child rather than to the marriage, the reader is shown that the divorce does not end the obligations the child created.

**THE CHARGE THAT NO ONE CAN BEAR**

The verse then sets a ceiling on the whole arrangement: ***“No one will be charged with more than they can bear.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the same sentence as the answer of the law to a man or a woman who has no more to give, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading in a short form.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings that a father whose means are small pays what he has, and that a mother may not be pressed beyond her strength. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence is the ground of the whole passage. Because a limit is named inside the command, the reader is shown that the law is made for the people who have to carry it.

**THE MOTHER AND THE FATHER WHO MUST NOT SUFFER**

The verse then speaks to those around the child: ***“No mother”*** ***“or father should be made to suffer”*** ***“for their child.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sense that the child may not be used as a lever, since neither parent may be hurt through the child or pressed by means of it.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the harm forbids a father from withholding the costs to punish the mother, and a mother from refusing the child to punish the father. For its part, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the reports of the community on the quarrels that reached the courts of the city. Because the sentence stands in the middle of the passage, the reader is shown what the law feared most in a broken house.

**THE HEIRS AND THE NEW ARRANGEMENTS**

The verse then carries the duty down the line: ***“The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the duty passes to those who inherit from a father who dies while the child is still nursing. In the same way, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading with the note that the child's right does not die with the man.

The verse then allows two changes by consent: ***“But if both sides decide”*** ***“after mutual consultation and consent”*** ***“to wean a child”*** ***“then there is no blame on them.”*** ***“If you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible”*** ***“as long as you pay fairly.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the two clauses as the door left open for a family that finds a better way. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the consultation is the condition and not the courtesy.

**THE CLOSE ON SIGHT**

The verse ends with the two names: ***“Be mindful of Allah”*** ***“and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the first as the guard over the share that each side owes. And the second as the knowledge of the small things done in a room where only the child is watching, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair in a short form.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the reading that the sight of God covers the father who pays with a grudge and the mother who nurses with a reproach. So that the account of the child is kept by the One who sees both. Because the verse closes on the watching of God rather than on a fine, the reader is shown that the law leaves the family with a witness it cannot lose.

The burden that no soul carries beyond its strength is stated in the closing of the chapter, (2:286 — **“Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford”**). And the duty of children towards their parents is set out in another chapter, (31:14 — **“and We have commanded people to ˹honour˺ their parents”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who uses his child as a message to his former wife, and who counts the missed visits as points won in an argument. The verse gives him a nursing mother with her food and her dress, a father with his capacity, and a command that neither be made to suffer, and it asks him which of the three he has been reading. Because the closing name is the All-Seeing, the reader is taught that the small cruelties of a broken house are the ones most carefully written.

The case is like two people carrying a heavy table down a narrow staircase and arguing about who is holding it wrong. The table is the same table, the staircase is the same staircase, and the dent in the wall belongs to both of them.

---

## Verse 2:234

> As for those of you who die and leave widows behind, let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days. When they have reached the end of this period, then you are not accountable for what they decide for themselves in a reasonable manner. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**THE WIFE WHO IS LEFT BEHIND**

The verse turns from the divorce to the death: ***“As for those of you”*** ***“who die and leave widows behind, let them observe a waiting period of four months”*** ***“and ten days.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports on the count of the days and on the moment the months begin. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the names of the companions who were asked about it.

The long treatment of the questions that grew from the sentence, from the woman whose husband dies before the marriage is complete to the woman who is already carrying a child, is kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the plain measure of the months is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the verse speaks of the widow with a gentleness no law could compel, the reader is shown the place the Book gives to a wife who has lost her partner.

**THE WISDOM OF THE FOUR MONTHS**

The verse does not explain its own measure, and the ten supply the reason: ***“let them observe a waiting period of four months”*** ***“and ten days.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the note that the four months are the time in which a child becomes known. In the same vein, And al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the ten days were added to complete the count.

The same sense that the months protect the line of the dead man is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the note that the waiting covers both the right of the child and the respect of the marriage is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the law waited long enough for the truth of the body to appear, the reader is shown that the waiting is a mercy before it is a restriction. Since the count is fixed by the month and not by the feeling, the reader sees that the mourning of a widow is given a shape she can carry.

**THE FREEDOM AT THE END OF THE TERM**

The verse then releases the woman: ***“When they have reached the end of this period”*** ***“then you are not accountable”*** ***“for what they decide”*** ***“for themselves in a reasonable manner.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the address as the guardians and the family around her. Alongside that, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings that after the waiting she may marry whom she chooses on lawful terms.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the sense that the reasonable manner is the lawful marriage and not a way of spending the estate, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same reading in a short form. Because the sentence takes the case out of the hands of the family, the reader is shown that the law returns to the widow the command of her own life.

**THE AWARENESS OF WHAT PEOPLE DO**

The verse closes with a name that reaches the family: ***“And Allah is All-Aware of what you do”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the awareness as the knowledge of the intentions behind the arrangements made while the months run. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the verse ends on the deeds rather than on the words.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the closing line is a warning to a family that would hurry a widow or a man who would press her. For its part, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same reading with the remark that no court watches the months of mourning. Because the verse ends on the awareness of God, the reader is shown where the law keeps the matters that have no witnesses. Since the sentence addresses the family rather than the widow, the reader sees where the pressure in such a house usually comes from.

The waiting of the divorced woman is set out earlier in the chapter, (2:228 — **“Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles”**). And the provision of a year is stated in the verse that follows, (2:240 — **“a year’s maintenance”**), so the reader sees the two kinds of waiting side by side.

The lesson also reaches a reader who speaks about the widow of a neighbour with the ease of a man discussing a business. The verse gives him a term, a rule about what she may decide and a name that watches the street, and it asks him how he would speak if the room were his own. Because the closing name is the All-Aware, the reader is taught that the dignity of a widow is a duty that has no receipt to show.

The case is like a family that plants a tree in the yard when a father dies and then argues about who may cut it. The tree grows while they argue, and the shade it gives in the summer is shared by all the voices in the courtyard.

---

## Verse 2:235

> There is no blame on you for subtly showing interest in ˹divorced or widowed˺ women or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in your hearts. Allah knows that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺. But do not make a secret commitment with them—you can only show interest in them appropriately. Do not commit to the bond of marriage until the waiting period expires. Know that Allah is aware of what is in your hearts, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing

**THE HINT THAT IS NO CRIME**

The verse opens a narrow door for the man who has heard of a waiting woman: ***“There is no blame on you”*** ***“for subtly showing interest in ˹divorced or widowed˺ women”*** ***“or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in your hearts.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports of the community on what a hint sounds like. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same reports with the words the companions advised to use.

The rulings on the difference between a hint and a request are kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the same, with the note that the words of the speaker must leave the door of a refusal open, is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the sentence acquits the man of the thought and forbids the bargain, the reader is shown how finely the law reads a conversation.

**THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE LOOKING MAN**

The verse then names what the Lord already knows: ***“Allah knows”*** ***“that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sense that the desire itself is no fault, since the law was made for people who hope. On this point, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the verse teaches the reader to name his intention honestly.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the heart's plan is known before the tongue forms a sentence. Alongside that, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the acquittal of the first clause is a mercy, because the man who is told to wait is a man with a closed door in front of him. Because the knowledge of God is named before the prohibition, the reader is shown what the two-sided mercy of the passage is.

**THE SECRET COMMITMENT**

The command then follows: ***“But do not make a secret commitment with them”*** ***“you can only show interest in them appropriately.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports on the kind of promise that is meant. Here too, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the forbidden thing is a contract hidden from the family.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain form of the sentence, and as-Saʿdī keeps the note that an appointment with a waiting woman is a harm to her as well as to her family, however quietly it is made. Because the Book permits the hint and forbids the appointment, the reader is shown that the law guards the honour of the woman in the eyes of the street.

**THE EXPIRY AND THE FEAR**

The verse then fixes the boundary: ***“Do not commit to the bond of marriage”*** ***“until the waiting period expires.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the sense that the knot may not be tied while another man's term is still running. For its part, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings on a marriage made in that time and what follows it.
