Then the verse turns inward: ***“Know”*** ***“that Allah is aware of what is in your hearts”*** ***“so beware of Him.”*** Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the first as the knowledge of the intention and the second as the caution that grows out of it. In the same way, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading in a short form. Because the warning is tied to the heart rather than to the hand, the reader is shown where the law places the beginning of a crime.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with a gentler pair than its warning suggests: ***“And know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the covering of the thought and the second as the patience that gives the man time to wait. In the same vein, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same pair with the note that the verse ends where it began, a man whose hope is understood and a door that will open in its season.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the reading that the patience of the Lord is the reason a man who fell into a hurried promise is not cut off for it. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the two names follow a ruling about the heart's secrets. Because the verse ends on the forbearance of the Lord after forbidding the secret, the reader is shown that the law both closes a door and holds it shut with patience.

The waiting of the widow is fixed in the verse before this one, (2:234 — **“let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days”**). And the terms of the settlement are guarded earlier in the chapter, (2:231 — **“either retain them honourably or let them go honourably”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who sends a friend to sound out a widow's family while the months still run, and who thinks that a message carried by another mouth is no message. The verse gives him a hint, an appointment and a term, and it asks him which of the three he is spending. Because the close names the Forgiving and the Forbearing, the reader is taught that the waiting he thinks is waste is the season in which his own intention is grown.

The case is like a man who waits outside a shop while it is being rebuilt and tells the craftsmen what he intends to buy the day it opens. The shop opens on its own day, the man is at the door with his money, and the only thing the waiting cost him was the price he did not pay for a broken window.

---

## Verse 2:236

> There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the dowry is settled. But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation—the rich according to his means and the poor according to his. A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers

**THE DIVORCE BEFORE THE NIGHT**

The verse takes up the shortest of marriages: ***“There is no blame”*** ***“if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated”*** ***“or the dowry is settled.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports on the two cases the sentence joined, the marriage not yet entered and the dowry not yet named. Here too, And al-Baghawī keeps the same reading with the plain sense that no waiting period falls on a woman who was not entered.

The rulings on a dowry mentioned in the contract but not yet paid are kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the same, with the note that the word for the marriage here covers the whole contract, is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the Book allows the separation, the reader is shown that a bond which was never consummated is not treated as a broken house.

**THE GIFT THAT REPLACES THE DOWRY**

The verse then commands a kindness in place of the dowry: ***“But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the sense that the gift is a mark of respect for a woman who was ready to marry and is now sent home. For its part, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the word for it carries the meaning of joy given to another.

al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports of the companions on what was given in such cases, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the plain reading that the gift is a duty rather than a favour. Because the verse answers a dismissal with a present, the reader is shown the tone the law wanted between people who do not go on together. Since no dowry was settled in this case, the reader sees that the gift is not a share but a courtesy.

**THE RICH AND THE POOR**

The verse then scales the gift: ***“the rich according to his means”*** ***“and the poor according to his.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings on the measure of the compensation. In the same way, And al-Jalālayn keeps the same with the note that the law does not fix a sum for the whole community.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the standing of the man and the standing of the woman are both considered. In the same vein, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the small gift of the poor man is as acceptable as the large gift of the rich. Because the verse measures the duty by the purse, the reader is shown that the law asks no one beyond his means. Since the small gift is named beside the large one, the reader sees that the law measures the intention and not the sum.

**WHO CARRIES THE DUTY**

The verse closes by naming who carries the duty: ***“A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers”***. al-Baghawī keeps the good-doers as those who do what they do well. On this point, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence puts the gift among the marks of a person's religion.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the obligation falls on those who fear God in the small matters. Alongside that, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same reading with the remark that a man may divorce lawfully and still be a poor example of the law. Because the verse ends on the doers of good rather than on a penalty, the reader is shown where the Book places the true measure of a separation. Since the duty is named without a figure, the reader is taught that the generosity of a man is left to his own sense of honour.

The half of the dowry in the case of a named sum is set out in the next verse, (2:237 — **“pay half of the dowry”**). And the duty of kindness between those who part is guarded in the same stretch, (2:229 — **“Divorce may be retracted twice”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who tells himself that a marriage which never happened leaves nothing behind it and nobody owed. The verse gives him a compensation, a measure and a duty, and it asks him what he wants to be known as in a street that watched the engagement. Because the closing sentence names the good-doers, the reader is taught that the manner of a parting is the part of the story that is remembered.

The case is like two families who prepare a wedding and then call it off a week before, and one of them returns every plate it borrowed. The plates go back clean, the guests go home, and the two families still nod to each other across the market for the next twenty years.

---

## Verse 2:237

> And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry, pay half of the dowry, unless the wife graciously waives it or the husband graciously pays in full. Graciousness is closer to righteousness. And do not forget kindness among yourselves. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**THE DOWRY NAMED AND THE MARRIAGE NOT ENTERED**

The verse takes the case that was left open in the sentence before it: ***“And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage”*** ***“but after deciding on a dowry, pay half of the dowry,”*** The reading that the half is owed, because the contract was completed and the marriage was not, is kept by al-Ṭabarī. And the same, with the note that the woman keeps the half and returns the other, is kept by al-Baghawī.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the long discussion of the ten over whether the sentence abrogated the rule that gave the whole gift, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain measure of one half. Because the verse fixes a fraction rather than leaving the matter to the temper of the man, the reader is shown that the Book settles what people would otherwise argue about for years.

**THE WIFE WHO GIVES UP HER SHARE**

The sentence then opens two ways out: ***“unless the wife graciously waives it”*** ***“or the husband graciously pays in full.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the first as the wife's gift of her half to a man she now leaves. And the second as his gift of the whole where the law only asked a half.

The plain reading that the two doors are the generosity of each side is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the note that the law left the better way to those who want it, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the two waivers are named after the rule, the reader is shown that the law prefers a settlement to a sum.

**THE WAIVER THAT GOES BEYOND THE DUTY**

The verse then names the goal of the whole arrangement: ***“Graciousness is closer to righteousness.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the generous act stands nearer to the fear of God than the exact payment. On this point, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that a man may be right in the money and wrong in the manner.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain form of the sentence, and as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the verse is teaching the community to leave a parting with its kindness intact. Because the sentence measures a payment by its nearness to God, the reader is shown that a lawful claim can still be a poor way of using the law.

**THE KINDNESS THAT MUST NOT BE FORGOTTEN**

The penultimate sentence is a general instruction inside a private case: ***“And do not forget kindness among yourselves.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the kindness as the good word and the small gift that no contract mentions. Alongside that, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the command covers the whole of life rather than the matter at hand.

The plain sense that forgetting the kindness is what turns a separation into a war is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās, and the same reading is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān in a short form. Because the verse speaks to a whole community in the middle of a rule about a marriage, the reader is shown how far a private affair reaches.

**THE SIGHT OF GOD OVER THE PARTING**

The verse closes with its witness: ***“Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the sight as the knowledge of how the half was paid and how the waiver was offered. Here too, And al-Jalālayn keeps the same pair of words in a short form.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the reading that the sentence is placed over the parting because the parting is where people are least watched and least kind. For its part, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that no court would ever learn whether the kindness was given. Because the verse ends on the sight of the Lord, the reader is shown the only witness such a matter ever has.

The half of the dowry and the two waivers are matched by the rule of the gift before the dowry is named, (2:236 — **“But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation”**). And the two ways of honour in a separation are set out earlier, (2:229 — **“Divorce may be retracted twice”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has counted his rights to the last coin and intends to keep the last word as well. The verse gives him a half, a waiver and a sentence about nearness to God, and it asks him which of the three he would like to be known for. Because the closing words name the eye that misses nothing, the reader is taught that the money and the kindness are written on the same line.

The case is like two men who dissolve a partnership in a shop and split the stock down the middle; one of them leaves the coffee machine as a gift. The machine was never in the books, the coffee is drunk by the man who stayed, and the street remembers the morning it was carried in.

---

## Verse 2:238

> Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers—especially the middle prayer—and stand in true devotion to Allah

**THE COMMAND THAT HOLDS THE ORDER TOGETHER**

The verse cuts across a long passage about marriage and money with a single command: ***“Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers”***. The sense that the guarding is the keeping of the prayers at their times and within their conditions is kept by al-Ṭabarī. And the same, with the note that the command calls for the steady watch of a shepherd, is kept by al-Baghawī.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that the command came down in a season of fighting, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain list of the five. Because the verse stands between the laws of the house and the rules of the field, the reader is shown that the pillar the community is built on is not the law of the family but the prayer.

**THE ONE PRAYER SINGLED OUT**

The verse singles out one of the five: ***“especially the middle prayer”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the long report of the difference among the companions over which prayer the middle one is, from the dawn to the night, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same discussion with its proofs.

as-Saʿdī keeps the report of the afternoon as the one chosen by the majority, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the note that the middle is singled out because of the danger of losing it. Because the ten keep a whole table of opinions about one word, the reader is shown how carefully a wording of the Book is read by the people of learning.

**THE STANDING IN DEVOTION**

The verse closes with the posture of the body: ***“and stand in true devotion to Allah”***. al-Baghawī keeps the standing as the body before the Lord and the devotion as the heart inside the body. On this point, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the two are named together so that neither is left alone.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading that the standing is the place of the prayer, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that a standing without the heart is a form the verse refuses. Because the verse adds the devotion to the standing, the reader is shown that the law of the prayer is kept in two places at once.

**THE REPORTS THAT CAME WITH THE VERSE**

A report is kept by al-Ṭabarī from the community that the prayer had been made heavy on the first Muslims and that the command was sent when attention wandered from it. al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the reading of one of the companions who recited the sentence with the name of the middle prayer in it.

The discussion of the ten over the reading that named the prayer outright is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, and the plain text as it stands in the codex of the community is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. Because the verse teaches the community to hold its order at the centre, the reader is shown what the scholars were careful to preserve.

**THE DEVOTION THAT KEEPS A COMMUNITY UPRIGHT**

The prayer is named as the thing that holds a person back from the wrong, and another passage of the Book says it plainly, (29:45 — **“Indeed, ˹genuine˺ prayer should deter ˹one˺ from indecency and wickedness”**). The remembrance is named as the purpose in the chapter of the prophets, (20:14 — **“and establish prayer for My remembrance”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader whose days are packed with claims about the rights of a house and no room for the five prayers. The verse gives him a command that stands at the head of the whole stretch, and it asks him which of his duties he would keep if he could keep only one. Because the sentence is placed among the laws of the family, the reader is taught that the household is held up by the prayer before it is held up by the contract.

The case is like a family that argues for a year about the plan of the house and never pours the foundation. The bricks are stacked in the yard, the drawings are on the wall, and the first rain of the winter finds the plot bare.

---

## Verse 2:239

> If you are in danger, pray on foot or while riding. But when you are safe, ˹take time to˺ remember Allah for teaching you what you did not know

**THE PRAYER IN THE HOUR OF FEAR**

The verse follows the command of guarding the prayers with the case that would break them: ***“If you are in danger, pray on foot”*** ***“or while riding.”*** The reports on the fear meant here, the fear of an enemy and of a beast and of a flood, are kept by al-Ṭabarī. And the same list, with the plain rule that the prayer is not left even then, is kept by al-Baghawī.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings on the shortened prayer and the prayer facing away from the direction of the House, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same with the note that the word for foot is used of a man walking. Because the verse lowers the posture and keeps the prayer, the reader is shown what the Book will not allow to be dropped.

**THE TWO POSTURES THAT REPLACE THE STANDING**

The two postures are named rather than described in full: ***“pray on foot”*** ***“or while riding.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sense that the rider may pray facing the way his mount carries him. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the direction of the House is not asked of a man in flight.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the report that the community prayed in that manner in the days of the fighting, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the rule covers the traveller and the man in retreat. Because the law bends the form and keeps the act, the reader is shown the difference between the letter of the prayer and its place in a life.

**THE SAFETY AND THE REMEMBRANCE**

The verse then lifts the ease again: ***“But”*** ***“when you are safe, ˹take time to˺ remember Allah”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the remembrance as the prayer in its full form with its bowing and its direction. For its part, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same reading with the note that the sentence returns the community to the ordinary order.

The plain form of the sentence, with the permission in the danger and the command in the safety, is kept by al-Jalālayn. And the point that the two states of a person are answered by two forms of one act is kept by as-Saʿdī. Because the safety is named after the fear, the reader is shown that the law never forgot the garden behind the battle.

**THE TEACHING THAT DESERVES THE THANKS**

The verse closes on the reason for the command: ***“for teaching you what you did not know”***. al-Baghawī keeps the teaching as the guidance itself, the times of the prayer, the direction and the rules of the fear. In the same vein, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the community had no way of knowing any of it before.

al-Ālūsī keeps the reading that the sentence makes the whole law a gift and the prayer a payment of thanks, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that the command stands where the gratitude should stand. Because the verse ends with knowledge rather than with fear, the reader is shown what the prayer is answering.

The remembrance of God in every posture is commanded in another chapter, (4:103 — **“remember Allah—whether you are standing, sitting, or lying down”**). And the same remembrance is joined to the prayer in the chapter of the prophets, (20:14 — **“and establish prayer for My remembrance”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who leaves the prayer when his day becomes hard and tells himself that God understands his pressure. The verse gives him a shortened form for the danger and a full order for the safety, and it asks him which of the two he is living in. Because the closing words speak of what he was taught, the reader is taught that the prayer is the receipt for a gift he did not pay for.

The case is like a man who keeps a letter from his father in his pocket on the road and reads it again at every stop, and who at last arrives home and finds the writer waiting at the door. The letter was never the point of the journey, and the journey was never the point of the letter.

---

## Verse 2:240

> Those of you who die leaving widows should bequeath for them a year’s maintenance without forcing them out. But if they choose to leave, you are not accountable for what they reasonably decide for themselves. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**THE BEQUEST BEFORE THE DEATH**

The verse returns to the house of the dying man: ***“Those of you who die leaving widows should bequeath”*** ***“for them a year’s maintenance without forcing them out.”*** The report that the sentence was sent down about the men who left their wives in the houses of the family with no provision is kept by al-Ṭabarī. And the same, with the note that the will was a duty before the estate was divided, is kept by al-Baghawī.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings on the share of the widow in the estate and on the sentence that fixed her part, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the year and the house. Because the verse puts a house and a year's bread in the hands of a man who is about to leave, the reader is shown what the Book asks of a person at the end of his life.

**THE TWO SENTENCES AND THE ONE HOUSE**

The ten keep a long discussion of how this sentence stands beside the earlier rule that gave the widow four months and ten days: ***“for them a year’s maintenance without forcing them out.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the year was the earlier command and that the fixed share of the estate came later.

The reading that the two rules do not conflict, since the waiting is one thing and the maintenance another, is kept by as-Saʿdī. And the same, with the note that the Book may add a kindness without taking back a right, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the two rules are read together by the ten, the reader is shown how a community reads its own book rather than one sentence at a time.

**THE WOMAN WHO CHOOSES TO LEAVE**

The verse then releases her from the house: ***“But if they choose to leave, you are not accountable”*** ***“for what they reasonably decide”*** ***“for themselves.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the sense that the widow may go out after the waiting and marry. And that the family carries no blame for what she then does in a lawful manner.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the choice belongs to her, and as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that her decision is named before the duties of anyone else. Because the Book gives the widow the last word about her own house, the reader is shown the place of a woman in the law of the family.

**THE TWO NAMES THAT CLOSE THE PASSAGE**

The verse ends with the same pair that closed the law of the waiting: ***“And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the power that carries out the promise of the provision and the second as the wisdom that arranged the shares. In the same way, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading in a short form.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the pair as the answer to a family that would argue about a widow's bread, since the One who set the duty is able to see it kept and wise in what He set. Because the sentence closes the stretch about the household, the reader is shown that the whole passage was arranged by the same hand that ends it.

The four months and the ten days are commanded before this verse, (2:234 — **“let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days”**). And the waiting of the woman who is not able to count the months is fixed in another chapter, (65:4 — **“their waiting period is three months”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who writes a will in his last week and forgets the woman who nursed him through his illness. The verse gives her a year, a house and the command that she not be pushed out, and it asks the testator what he thinks he is leaving behind. Because the close names the Almighty and the All-Wise, the reader is taught that a bequest is a matter of power and of wisdom before it is a matter of paper.

The case is like a farmer who knows the winter is coming and plants his last field anyway, so that the people who eat from his land will have bread after he has gone. The field is his for one more season, and the harvest is theirs for as long as they can remember his name.

---

## Verse 2:241

> Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced women—a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺

**THE PROVISION THAT STANDS ON ITS OWN**

The verse gathers the cases that were spread through the passage into one command: ***“Reasonable provisions must be made”*** ***“for divorced women”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the reading that the sentence covers every woman who is separated, whether the marriage was entered or not, so that no divorce leaves a woman with nothing.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the difference of the ten over the kind of parting that carries the duty, and al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence was repeated after the detailed rules to close the gaps between them. Because the verse speaks in the plural, the reader is shown that the matter belongs to the community rather than to the conscience of one man. Since the sentence follows the detailed cases, the reader sees that the law closes its own gaps rather than leaving them to chance.

**THE DUTY THAT IS LAID ON THE MINDFUL**

The one who carries it is then named: ***“a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the mindfulness as the fear that makes a person keep a duty no court would check. On this point, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the quality of the people who do this without being watched is what the sentence names.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the duty falls on those who fear the Lord in the small matters of a house. Alongside that, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same reading with the remark that the sentence makes the treatment of a divorced woman a mark of a person's religion. Because the verse ends on the mind of the giver rather than on the sum, the reader is shown where the law places the real cost.

**THE GAP THE SENTENCE FILLS**

The note that the command follows a list of cases is kept by al-Ṭabarī, since the list would leave a woman outside every rule without the general sentence: ***“Reasonable provisions must be made”*** ***“for divorced women”***. The same is kept by Ibn Kathīr with the note that the Book closes its laws with a command wide enough to carry the odd case.

The reading that the provision is measured by the means of the man and the standing of the woman is kept by al-Ālūsī, and the same is kept by al-Jalālayn in a short form. Because the sentence is general and the cases were particular, the reader is shown how the Book protects the people who do not fit the examples.

**THE REASON THE BOOK ENDINGS MATTER**

The verse is the ending of the whole stretch about marriage, and the next verse names the purpose of such endings: (2:242 — **“This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you”**). The duty of kindness between people who part is guarded earlier in the same passage, (2:229 — **“Divorce may be retracted twice”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has paid every sum the law demanded and left his former wife to arrange her own life in silence. The verse gives her a provision and puts the duty on the mindful, and it asks him which list he wants his name to be on. Because the sentence joins the money to the fear of God, the reader is taught that the last payment of a marriage is made to the Lord rather than to the woman.

The case is like a household that moves out of a rented flat and scrubs the floors before the keys go back, though no clause in the lease asks for it. The next family walks into a clean house, and the landlord tells the story for years.

---

## Verse 2:242

> This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will understand

**THE SENTENCE THAT CLOSES A STRETCH OF LAW**

The verse is a seal on the whole passage of the household: ***“This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you”***. The sense that the clarity is the explaining of the rules that were sent before it is kept by al-Ṭabarī. And the same, with the note that the sentence points back at the waiting periods, the dowries and the provisions, is kept by al-Baghawī.

The reading that the words stand as a sign of the mercy of the lawgiver is kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain form of the sentence is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the verse gathers a long and difficult passage into one line, the reader is shown what this Book has been doing all along. Since the sentence looks back at the rules rather than forward to a new one, the reader sees that the law takes stock of itself.

**THE GOAL THAT IS NAMED AT THE END**

The verse then names what the explanation is for: ***“so perhaps you will understand”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the understanding as the act of a person who reads a rule and grasps what it is protecting. For its part, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the words are a hope rather than a description.

The plain sense that the sentence asks the community to take the laws as a lesson rather than as a burden is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same reading, with the note that a person may know a rule and still not understand it, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the verse ends on understanding, the reader is shown that the passage is not finished until it changes the way he looks at a house. Since the hope is placed on the reader rather than on the lawgiver, the reader is taught that the rules were written to be lived and not only to be kept.

**THE CLARITY THAT IS NOT MERELY INFORMATION**

The note that the explanation in this Book comes with a purpose is kept by al-Ālūsī, since the rules were given to build a community rather than to fill a page: ***“This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the same with the note that the word for the revealing carries the sense of making a thing plain.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the reading that the clarity is a favour and the understanding is the answer, and as-Saʿdī keeps the same in a short form. Because the sentence is used at the end of the passage about women, the reader is shown how the Book asks to be read.

**THE READING THAT LEAVES A PERSON DIFFERENT**

The verse closes the stretch before the next one turns to a story of a people who fled their homes, (2:243 — **“Allah said to them”**). And the same call to understanding is made at the end of the rules of the fast, (2:187). The reader who keeps the two endings side by side sees a book that explains and then waits to be understood.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has learned the rules of the household as a list of permissions and refusals. The verse gives him a sentence about clarity and a hope about understanding, and it asks him what he has understood of the family he lives in. Because the verse speaks of understanding rather than of obeying, the reader is taught that a rule known by heart and not by mind is a wall that keeps nobody warm. Since the hope of the sentence is placed on the reader, the reader sees that the law leaves room for him to arrive at its meaning late. Because the passage that closes here was about women and houses, the reader is shown that the Book means the family to be understood and not only administered.

The case is like a father who explains to his sons why a field is left unsown for a season, and who finds in the spring that one of them has understood and the others have only obeyed. The field produces for the one who listened, and the father's words were never only about the field.

---

## Verse 2:243

> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of death? Allah said to them, “Die!” then He gave them life. Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful

**THE TOWN THAT EMPTIED ITSELF**

The verse opens a window on a people of the past: ***“Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those”*** ***“who fled their homes in the thousands”*** ***“for fear of death?”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the flight was from a plague. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same report with the note that the houses were left standing and the streets empty.

The reading that the seeing here is the seeing of the heart rather than of the eye, since the story is known from the reports rather than from the road, is kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the same, with the count of the thousands left open, is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the verse asks a question rather than telling a tale, the reader is shown that the story is brought forward to be thought about.

**THE FEAR THAT DROVE A WHOLE TOWN OUT**

The reason for the flight is named in the verse itself: ***“for fear of death?”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sense that the people who ran from the plague were running from the decree that had already reached them. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that no door keeps out what is written.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the reports that the numbers given for the crowd were four thousand and more, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the count is left to the reports rather than to the reader's guess. Because the flight is named with its motive, the reader is shown what a person does when the fear of death sits in his house.

**THE WORD THAT CAME UPON THEM**

The verse then states the answer of the Lord without a battle: ***“Allah said to them, “Die!””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the whole crowd died where they stood. So that the roads were left with the bodies of the people who had run from the plague.

The discussion of the ten over the manner of the death is kept by al-Ālūsī, and the plain sense that the command was given to the living is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the verse answers the flight with a single word, the reader is shown how short the distance is between a person and his end.

**THE LIFE THAT CAME AFTER**

The sentence turns at once: ***“then He gave them life.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the reports that a prophet of that people prayed over them. And that the crowd rose again and lived out their years in the houses they had left, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the revival was a sign for the people who were still there.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the people were shown the power of the One they had fled from, since the death they feared came from Him and the life they wanted came from Him too. Because the sentence joins the dying and the living in three words, the reader is shown what the Book means when the Lord is named over both.

**THE BOUNTY AND THE INGRATITUDE**

The verse closes on two sentences about the human family: ***“Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity”*** ***“but most people are ungrateful”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the bounty as the gifts that keep coming even after people turn their backs. In the same vein, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the note that the ingratitude is the fault of the many rather than of the few.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the point that the story was brought into this chapter for the community that was being taught to fight, so that the fear of death would not keep them from the field. Because the verse ends on ingratitude, the reader is shown what the flight really was.

The story of the towns that were left empty is told again in the chapter of the cave, (2:259 — **“Allah said”**). And the lesson of a test in battle is drawn from the two armies in another chapter, (3:13 — **“one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has spent his years avoiding every risk that might shorten his life. The verse gives him a crowd of thousands who ran and a word that found them all, and it asks him what the running was for. Because the close names the bounty and the ingratitude in one breath, the reader is taught that the life a person guards is the gift he did not buy.

The case is like a village that builds a wall on the side of the river because that is where the last flood came through, and leaves the door on the hill open. The water arrives from the hill in the spring, and the wall on the river is the only part of the story the neighbours remember.

---

## Verse 2:244

> Fight in the cause of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE COMMAND THAT FOLLOWS THE STORY**

The verse is short and stands directly after the crowd that fled: ***“Fight in the cause of Allah”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the command as an address to the community of the Prophet ﷺ. Alongside that, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that the sentence follows the tale of the crowd so that the example would be understood.

al-Baghawī keeps the reading that the fighting is in the way of the religion rather than for a banner, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same in a short form. Because the command stands where a story of flight has just ended, the reader is shown that the two are meant to be read together.

**THE COST THAT THE FIGHTING ASKS**

The ten keep the note that the verse does not name wealth. And that they read the fighting of this verse with the spending that the next verses praise: ***“Fight in the cause of Allah”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the sense that the fight stands only with two things, the body and the wealth, since an army without provision is a crowd.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same reading with the note that the community is taught to bring both to the field. For its part, And al-Ālūsī keeps the remark that the command was placed in the middle of the chapter of the household so that a man would know what his money is for. Because the sentence is short, the reader is shown how much the ten found inside it.

**THE TWO NAMES THAT CLOSE THE COMMAND**

The verse then joins the command to a reminder: ***“and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the first as the hearing of the words a man speaks on the road to the field. And the second as the knowledge of what he intended when he set out.

The same pair is kept by Ibn Kathīr with the note that the two names are a warning against a fight that is carried on for the sake of the spoil. And the plain reading is kept by al-Jalālayn in a short form. Because the command ends on the hearing and the knowing, the reader is shown that the deed is judged by the purpose that sent it out.

**WHY THE TWO NAMES STAND HERE**

The verse is one of the places where the Book joins a heavy duty to the names of God, and the same pair closes the command of the prayer elsewhere in the chapter, (2:238 — **“Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers”**). The lesson of the field is drawn out again where the Book speaks of the two armies, (3:13 — **“one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who gives his money to a cause and expects the world to record the gift. The verse gives him a hearing and a knowledge that precede his own account of himself, and it asks him who the fight was for. Because the sentence names the One who hears before the One who knows, the reader is taught that the words of a man on the road are counted with his deeds. Since the fighting is named as a duty rather than a choice, the reader sees that the field is one of the places where a person's words are tested.

The case is like a man who repairs the roof of the mosque in his own street and tells everyone he meets that nobody else lifted a hand. The roof keeps the rain out for twenty years, and the story of the repairs is told in the market with his name attached to it.

---

## Verse 2:245

> Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over? It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases and increases ˹wealth˺. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned

**THE QUESTION THAT IS AN INVITATION**

The verse puts the command of the field aside for a moment and asks a question: ***“Who will lend to Allah a good loan”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the loan is the spending of a person on the path of the religion. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the question is asked in the form of an invitation rather than of a doubt.

The readings of the ten on the word for the loan are kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the same, with the remark that the sentence speaks of a loan because the giver keeps his right to the return, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the verse asks who will come forward, the reader is shown that the Book invites rather than commands in this matter.

**THE LOAN THAT IS GOOD**

The condition of the loan is in its own words: ***“a good loan”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the good as the wealth that is earned lawfully and given freely. Here too, And al-Jalālayn keeps the same with the note that the pure intention belongs to the goodness of the gift.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the loan is given for the sake of God and with nothing else in the heart. For its part, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that a gift made for a name is no loan to the Lord. Because the goodness is asked of the giver as well as of the gift, the reader is shown where the law of charity begins.

**THE MULTIPLICATION AND THE HANDS THAT HOLD WEALTH**

The verse answers the giver with a promise: ***“which Allah will multiply many times over?”*** ***“It is Allah ˹alone˺”*** ***“who decreases and increases ˹wealth˺.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the multiplication as the many times that the Book explains elsewhere as seven hundred. In the same way, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the reports of the community on what the giver receives.

as-Saʿdī keeps the second sentence as the ground of the first, since the One who holds the increase and the decrease is able to return the loan many times over. In the same vein, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the wealth of a person moves in a hand that is not his own. Because the holding of wealth is named after the promise, the reader is shown what the promise rests on.

**THE RETURN THAT NO ONE MISSES**

The verse closes with the line that ends many passages of the chapter: ***“And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the return as the gathering of every person before the Lord. On this point, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the giver and the hoarder will stand in the same place.

The reading that the sentence warns the man who cannot bring himself to lend is kept by al-Baghawī. And the same, with the note that a person who is returning to his Lord cannot lose what he sent ahead, is kept by as-Saʿdī. Because the verse ends on the return, the reader is shown that the ledger of a life is closed in another place.

The same invitation is made with the same words in the chapter of the mutual disregard, (64:17 — **“If you lend to Allah a good loan, He will multiply it for you”**). And the figure of the multiplication is drawn out in the parable of the grain, (2:261 — **“The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who counts every gift he has made and wonders when the return will appear in his account. The verse gives him a loan, a promise and a return, and it asks him where he thinks the increase is kept. Because the hands that decrease and increase are named before the gathering at the end, the reader is taught that the wealth he holds is already on its way somewhere. Since the question is addressed to a person rather than to a crowd, the reader sees that the invitation stands open in every generation.

The case is like a merchant who leaves his goods in the hands of a partner while he travels, and who spends the journey worrying about the stock. The goods are sold at a price he never asked for, and the worry was the only part of the trip that was his.

---

## Verse 2:246

> Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses? They said to one of their prophets, “Appoint for us a king, ˹and˺ we will fight in the cause of Allah.” He said, “Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?” They replied, “How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah, while we were driven out of our homes and ˹separated from˺ our children?” But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except for a few of them. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers

**THE CHIEFS WHO ASKED FOR A KING**

The verse opens the long story that will carry the rest of the chapter: ***“Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses?”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the chiefs were the men of weight and standing among that people. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the word for them carries the sense of the gathered heads of a tribe.

The discussion of the ten over the moment of the asking, whether it was long after Moses or in the days of the kings, is kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the plain reading that the prophet they spoke to was raised among them is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the verse addresses the community of the Prophet ﷺ with a scene from another people, the reader is shown that the Book teaches by example.

**THE REQUEST AND THE PROMISE**

The chiefs speak plainly: ***“They said to one of their prophets, “Appoint”*** ***“for us a king, ˹and˺ we will fight in the cause of Allah.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the people had lost their land and their standing and wanted a leader to gather them again. In the same vein, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the request was for the rule of a king rather than for a crown.

The name of the prophet they came to is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās as Samuel, and the report that the king who was given to them was Saul is kept by the ten. Because the request names the fight and not the spoil, the reader is shown how a people speak when they have been beaten down and want their place back.

**THE QUESTION THAT TESTED THEM**

The answer comes as a question: ***“He said,”*** ***“Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that he had read their resolve and doubted it. On this point, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the prophet spoke from his knowledge of what the people had done before.

The question is kept by as-Saʿdī as a warning rather than a refusal. And the same, with the remark that a leader who has seen a people run does not hand them a sword at once, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the question was answered by their own flight later, the reader is shown how the Book prepares a lesson in advance.

**THE CLAIM AND THE PROMISE OF THE CHIEFS**

The chiefs answer with their history: ***“They replied, “How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah”*** ***“while we were driven out of our homes”*** ***“and ˹separated from˺ our children?””*** al-Baghawī keeps the reports on the lands they had lost. Here too, And al-Jalālayn keeps the plain sense that they spoke of what had been taken from them.

al-Ālūsī keeps the reading that the chiefs spoke for the whole people and promised what an army promises in the first hour, and as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that their words were honest when they were said. Because the verse keeps their promise in full voice, the reader is shown that the Book does not accuse them of lying at that moment.

**THE FIELD WHERE THE PROMISE ENDED**

The story closes on the deed: ***“But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except”*** ***“for a few of them.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the disobedient were the many and the steadfast the few. For its part, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the flight was the answer the prophet had feared.

The point that the story is told in this chapter to teach the community that the words of a crowd are not the deeds of a crowd is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. And the plain reading of the few is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the sentence names the few without naming them, the reader is shown where the praise of the Book goes.

**THE RECORD THAT MISSES NO ONE**

The verse ends with a line that reaches all the way back to the promise: ***“And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the knowledge as the record of the promise and the flight in the same book. In the same vein, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the note that the wrong is the breaking of a word that was given freely.

al-Ālūsī keeps the reading that the sentence covers the men who broke the promise as well as the leaders who sent them. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the remark that the flight of the many did not cancel the promise of the few. Because the verse ends on knowledge rather than on a punishment, the reader is shown the patience that gives a people time to become what they promised.

The test with the river and the few who stayed will be told in the verses that follow, (2:249 — **“Allah will test you with a river”**). And the lesson of the two armies that met is drawn in another chapter, (3:13 — **“one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who promises in the assembly what he does not intend to carry into the street. The verse gives him a crowd in the thousands, a prophet who asked twice and a field where the promise ended, and it asks him which of the two days of a promise he lives in. Because the close speaks of a knowledge that misses neither the words nor the running, the reader is taught that the pledge of a person is already in a book he cannot edit. Since the few who stood are named without their names, the reader sees that the Book remembers the deed before the man.

The case is like a village that signs a paper to rebuild the canal together in the dry season. And then finds that the water is low in every house and the tools are locked in the sheds when the work begins. The canal is cleared by four men in the end, and the water reaches the fields of the whole village the next spring.

---

## Verse 2:247

> Their prophet told them, “Allah has appointed Saul to be your king.” They protested, “How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches?” He replied, “Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature. Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.”

**THE KING THAT WAS GIVEN**

The verse answers the request of the chiefs with a name they had not considered: ***“Their prophet told them, “Allah has appointed Saul to be your king.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the man given to them was not of the house of the kings. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the prophet had asked for a king and was answered with one.

The reports that describe the trade of the man before the crown are kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain sense that the appointment came from God rather than from a vote of the chiefs is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the sentence reports an appointment and not an election, the reader is shown how the answer to a prayer may arrive in a shape the askers did not expect.

**THE OBJECTION OF THE CHIEFS**

The chiefs answer at once: ***“They protested, “How can he be our king”*** ***“when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he”*** ***“and he has not been blessed with vast riches?””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the report that the man had no wealth and no royal line. So that the objection was made of the two things a people usually weigh.

al-Ālūsī keeps the sense that the chiefs measured the matter with the measure of a market, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the lineage and the purse were the whole of their argument. Because the objection is kept in the Book word for word, the reader is shown how a community talks when the choice was made for it.

**THE ANSWER OF THE PROPHET**

The reply is stated in three parts: ***“He replied, “Allah has chosen him over you”*** ***“and blessed him with knowledge”*** ***“and stature.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the knowledge as the understanding of the affairs of a people and the stature as the strength of the body for a field of war, since a king of those days led in person.

as-Saʿdī keeps the same pair with the note that the two gifts are the equipment of the office rather than the ornaments of the man. In the same vein, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the choice of God stands above the claims of a family. Because the answer names what a king needs rather than what a people admire, the reader is shown where the Book places the worth of a leader.

**THE KINGDOM THAT IS GIVEN AND THE TWO NAMES**

The verse then states the whole matter as a rule: ***“Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills.”*** ***“And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the first as the freedom of the Lord in his gifts. And the second as the knowledge that reaches the hidden merits of a man.

The same pair is kept by Ibn Kathīr with the note that the sentence answers both halves of the objection, the family and the purse, since the One who holds the kingdom is able to give it to a man of no house. And the plain form of the two names is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the verse closes on the bounty and the knowledge, the reader is shown that a gift and a judgement are never separated in the hand that gives.

The coming of the ark is promised as the sign of the appointment in the verse that follows, (2:248 — **“the Ark will come to you”**). And the same freedom in the giving of a kingdom is seen in the story of the two armies, (3:13 — **“one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been passed over for a post in his own town because his family is small and his purse is light. The verse gives him a king taken from the trades, a kingdom that is given rather than earned, and two reasons from God rather than from men, and it asks him which ledger he reads when he measures a person. Because the close names the Bountiful and the Knowing, the reader is taught that the worth of the man is hidden in the hand that made him.

The case is like a village that needs a new keeper for the communal well and chooses the man who carries the heaviest buckets, though he owns no land and speaks in a slow voice. The well is kept for thirty years, and the village remembers the year they argued about the man before they remembered the water.

---

## Verse 2:248

> Their prophet further told them, “The sign of Saul’s kingship is that the Ark will come to you—containing reassurance from your Lord and relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron, which will be carried by the angels. Surely in this is a sign for you, if you ˹truly˺ believe.”

**THE SIGN THEY ASKED FOR**

The chiefs had demanded a proof of the appointment, and the man of God gave them one they already knew: ***“Their prophet further told them, “The sign of Saul’s kingship is that the Ark will come to you—”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the ark had been taken from that people in an earlier war. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that its return was the thing they had given up hoping for.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports on the shape of the chest and the gold of its covering, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain sense that the sign was the return of what they had lost. Because the proof was built from their own history, the reader is shown how the Book answers a stubborn people with the one thing they could not argue about.

**THE REASSURANCE INSIDE**

The contents are then named: ***“containing reassurance from your Lord”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the long discussion of the ten over what the reassurance is, from a mercy of the Lord to the presence of the heart at the meeting with Him. In the same way, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the word for it carries the sense of a calm that settles in a person.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the ark carried a comfort for the people who feared. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that a chest can hold no power of its own, since the power is named as coming from God. Because the sentence names the Lord as the source, the reader is shown that the object was never the point. Since the sign was promised to a people who had asked for one, the reader sees that the proof was given in the shape of their own history.

**THE RELICS OF THE TWO HOUSES**

The verse then names what remained in the chest: ***“and relics of the family of Moses”*** ***“and the family of Aaron”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the relics were of the things left by the two brothers, from the staff to the fragments of the tablets. On this point, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the note that the two houses are named because the guidance of that people had come through them.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the relics in a short form, and as-Saʿdī keeps the note that a people who had lost the ark had also lost the memory of what was in it. Because the Book names the families of the two prophets, the reader is shown what a community keeps when it keeps its history.

**THE CARRIERS AND THE FAITH**

The arrival of the ark is then described: ***“which will be carried by the angels”***. al-Baghawī keeps the reports that the people saw it travelling between the sky and the earth. Alongside that, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that the sight settled the argument in a day.

The verse then joins the sign to the faith of the watchers: ***“Surely in this is a sign for you”*** ***“if you ˹truly˺ believe.””*** Ibn Kathīr keeps the sense that a sign is read by the people who are ready to read it. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the same sight is a wonder to one man and a lesson to another. Because the verse ends on the faith of the reader, the reader is shown where the value of a sign is decided.

The test by the river is set out in the verse after this one, (2:249 — **“Allah will test you with a river”**). And the answer of the few who trusted is kept in their prayer at the field, (2:250 — **“Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has lost a good thing and decided that God has finished with him and his house. The verse gives him a chest returned to a people who had given it up, and it asks him what he would do if the lost thing came back carried by hands he could not see. Because the close names the belief of the watcher, the reader is taught that the mercy often arrives before the faith that reads it.

The case is like a family that loses its father's ring in a flood and finds it years later in the silt of the garden. The ring is the same ring, the ground is the same ground, and the year it was found is remembered as the year the family began to speak to one another again.

---

## Verse 2:249

> When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned: “Allah will test you with a river. So whoever drinks ˹his fill˺ from it is not with me, and whoever does not taste it—except a sip from the hollow of his hands—is definitely with me.” They all drank ˹their fill˺ except for a few! When he and the ˹remaining˺ faithful with him crossed the river, they said, “Now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors.” But those ˹believers˺ who were certain they would meet Allah reasoned, “How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah! And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast.”

**THE ARMY ON THE ROAD**

The verse opens on the march: ***“When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned:”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the king took his men out of the holy city on a hot day and that they asked him for water on the way. In the same way, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the journey was made across a dry land.

The reading that the going forth was the beginning of the test is kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain route of the march is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the verse places the test on the road rather than at the battle, the reader is shown where a leader finds out what his men are made of.

**THE RIVER THAT SIFTED THE ARMY**

The warning is stated in the words of the king: ***“Allah will test you with a river.”*** ***“So whoever drinks ˹his fill˺ from it is not with me”*** ***“and whoever does not taste it”*** ***“except a sip from the hollow of his hands”*** ***“is definitely with me.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the command as a test of obedience rather than of thirst. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that water was lawful and the obedience was the point.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that a man who could not hold himself from a river would not hold himself in a field. On this point, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that the small allowance left in the hollow of a hand was the mercy inside the test. Because the permission was left open in a measure a person could carry, the reader is shown that the law of the trial was not meant to break anyone.

**THE MANY WHO DRANK AND THE FEW WHO HELD**

The verse then reports the result: ***“They all drank ˹their fill˺ except”*** ***“for a few!”*** ***“When he and the ˹remaining˺ faithful with him crossed the river,”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the crossing was made by a small company. Alongside that, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the note that the number of those who held back was small.

The point that the crowd which left the city was not the army which crossed the river is kept by as-Saʿdī, and the plain reading of the few is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the few are named without a number, the reader is shown what a test does to a crowd.

**THE FEAR AT THE RIVERBANK**

The verse then gives the words of the shaken: ***“they said, “Now we are no match”*** ***“for Goliath and his warriors.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the report that the speaker was a company of the men who had crossed and had counted the enemy. Here too, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that the fear was a human reading of the numbers.

The reading that the words came from the men whose hearts were still tied to the arithmetic of the field is kept by Ibn Kathīr. And the same, with the note that the sentence was placed there to show the difference between the two groups inside one army, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the Book keeps the frightened words without condemning them at once, the reader is shown how gently the story leads a reader to the lesson.

**THE REASONING OF THE FEW WHO KNEW**

The answer comes from the other company: ***“But those ˹believers˺ who were certain they would meet Allah reasoned,”*** ***“How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah!”*** ***“And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the certainty of the meeting with God as the ground of the courage, since a man who expects to stand before his Lord does not count the enemy twice. In the same way, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the reasoning is put in the mouth of the few so that the many would hear it.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain sense of the history they remembered, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence is a law of the field rather than a tale of the past. Because the verse ends on the steadfast, the reader is shown what the victory was made of before it was won.

The prayer of the two companies before the battle is kept in the verse that follows, (2:250 — **“Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance”**), and the two armies are described again in another chapter, (3:13 — **“one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has counted the numbers in his own quarrel and decided that nothing can be done. The verse gives him a river, a crowd that drank and a few who crossed, and it asks him which company he would have been standing in that morning. Because the close names the steadfast as the ones with God, the reader is taught that the strength of a person is measured before the battle and not after it.

The case is like a caravan that sets out on a hard road where the rule is one cup of water at each well, and half the travellers drink from the skins they were told to carry unopened. The wells are still ahead of them, the road is still long, and the ones who arrive are the ones who trusted the instruction more than the thirst.

---

## Verse 2:250

> When they advanced to face Goliath and his warriors, they prayed, “Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, make our steps firm, and give us victory over the disbelieving people.”

**THE FIELD WHERE THE TWO LINES MET**

The verse brings the two armies into sight of each other: ***“When they advanced to face Goliath and his warriors,”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the small company came out of the defile and stood in the open ground. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the enemy was drawn up in ranks.

The reports on the size of the army of the enemy and on the man who led it are kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain sense that the meeting was in the open is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the enemy chief is named before the prayer, the reader is shown what the men were looking at when they spoke.

**THE PRAYER OF THE FEW**

The verse then gives the prayer in three requests: ***“they prayed, “Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance,”*** ***“make our steps firm,”*** ***“and give us victory over the disbelieving people.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the first as the patience that keeps a man in his place. And the second as the steadiness of the feet in the charge.

as-Saʿdī keeps the order of the three as the order of the need, since the courage of the heart comes before the firmness of the body and the victory stands after both. Alongside that, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the men asked for the means rather than for the end. Because the prayer begins with the inner strength, the reader is shown what these men knew about a battle.

**THE STEPS THAT HAD TO HOLD**

The middle request is the shortest and the hardest: ***“make our steps firm”***. al-Baghawī keeps the reading that the feet of a soldier carry the whole man. So that a wavering step ends a line, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same in a short form.

The plain sense that the request was made of God, because no man can promise his own feet, is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the note that the words are the mark of a person who has understood that his body is not his own, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the prayer asks for the steadiness of the body as a gift, the reader is shown where a believer puts his confidence before a hard hour.

**THE VICTORY THAT IS ASKED OF GOD**

The third request is the one a soldier is expected to make: ***“and give us victory over the disbelieving people.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the asking is for the triumph of the truth rather than for the pride of the winners. In the same way, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the enemy is named by its disbelief and not by its tribe.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the men asked for the victory as a mercy for the people of the truth. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that the prayer was answered in a way none of them could have planned. Because the request names the people rather than the man, the reader is shown what the little company was fighting for.

The answer to the prayer is kept in the verse that follows, (2:251 — **“So they defeated them by Allah’s Will”**). And the men are remembered with the steadfast in the same story, (2:249 — **“And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who stands before a hard task and asks only for the result. The verse gives him three requests in the order of a battle, the heart and the feet before the crown, and it asks him which of the three he has been praying for. Because the men who prayed were the ones who had kept their hands from the river, the reader is taught that a prayer of this kind is made by a person who has already obeyed.

The case is like a farmer who asks the sky for rain in the morning and spends the afternoon digging the channel through which it will run. The rain comes, the channel carries it to the roots, and the field that is watered is the one with the trench.

---

## Verse 2:251

> So they defeated them by Allah’s Will, and David killed Goliath. And Allah blessed David with kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed. Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another, corruption would have dominated the earth, but Allah is Gracious to all

**THE VICTORY THAT WAS GIVEN**

The verse answers the prayer of the small company: ***“So they defeated them by Allah’s Will,”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the routing is credited to the permission of the Lord rather than to the arm of the men. Alongside that, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence follows the prayer so that the cause would be plain.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports on the battle as it was fought, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the defeat. Because the victory is named with its permission, the reader is shown where the Book puts the credit for a rout.

**THE SHEPHERD AND THE GIANT**

The verse then names the deed that turned the day: ***“and David killed Goliath.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the young man came to the field with a sling and that he was not one of the soldiers of rank. Here too, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the giant had called the men of the other army out for days.

The plain sense that the killer of the enemy chief was a boy from the flocks is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the note that the Book names the deed in four words because the whole lesson lies in it, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the verse names a sling and a kingdom in one sentence, the reader is shown what the hand of God does with small means.

**THE KINGDOM AND THE WISDOM**

The verse then turns to what the young man received: ***“And Allah blessed David with kingship”*** ***“and wisdom and taught him what He willed.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the kingdom as the rule over that people after the death of Saul. And the wisdom as the understanding that decides a case by the truth.

as-Saʿdī keeps the pair as the two gifts of a ruler, the crown and the mind. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the teaching named at the end is the revelation given to a prophet who would be a king. Because the verse puts the shepherd in the palace in one line, the reader is shown how quickly the Lord may raise a person.

**THE ORDER THAT HOLDS A WORLD TOGETHER**

The verse then states a law that reaches beyond the field: ***“Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another, corruption would have dominated the earth,”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the checking of one people by another is the wall that keeps a land from being overrun by the wicked. On this point, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the sentence covers the standing armies of every age.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the balance among the nations is a mercy of God for the ordinary people who farm and trade. Alongside that, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the word for corruption covers both the ruin of property and the ruin of religion. Because the earth is named rather than a single battle, the reader is shown how wide the Book makes a single charge.

**THE GRACE THAT REACHES EVERYONE**

The verse ends on a name that holds the whole passage: ***“but Allah is Gracious to all”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the grace as the favour shown to the whole creation, since the order of a land is a kindness even to those who never thank anyone for it. Here too, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence closes a story of a battle with a word about mercy.

The reading that the grace names the patience of the Lord with a world that would otherwise be left to its strong men is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, and the same is kept by al-Qurṭubī in a short form. Because the verse ends on the grace rather than on the victory, the reader is shown what the Book wants him to take out of the field.

The story of the two armies is closed with a sentence about the signs, (2:252 — **“And you are truly one of the messengers”**), where the Book calls the whole narrative a proof of the message. And the same law of the repelling of peoples is stated in the chapter of the pilgrimage, (22:40 — **“Had Allah not repelled”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who believes that his own strength is the only wall between his house and the world. The verse gives him a small company, a sling that ended a giant, a crown given to a shepherd and a mercy that holds the nations apart. And it asks him who is keeping the world from falling while he sleeps. Because the close names the grace that reaches all, the reader is taught that the quiet street he lives in is one of the gifts he never paid for.

The case is like a town that raises a small guard on the bridge because the river beyond it is full of rival traders, and that sleeps behind the guard for a hundred years. The bridge is guarded by men, and the peace it keeps is the mercy of a Lord who checks one people with another.

---

## Verse 2:252

> These are Allah’s revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. And you are truly one of the messengers

**THE STORY THAT IS A REVELATION**

The verse seals the long narrative of the chiefs and the field: ***“These are Allah’s revelations”*** ***“which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth.”*** The sense that the whole passage was sent down to be recited as it stands is kept by al-Ṭabarī. And the same, with the note that the sentence gathers the tales of the people of Israel into the message itself, is kept by al-Baghawī.

The reading that the truth named at the end covers both the history and the lesson is kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain form of the sentence is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because a story of ancient wars is called a revelation, the reader is shown that the Book does not tell a tale for its own sake.

**THE PROPHETHOOD THAT THE STORY PROVES**

The verse then turns to the messenger who receives it: ***“And you are truly one of the messengers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as an answer to the people of the city who had asked for a proof of the message. On this point, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the reports on the question that led to it.

The reading that the stories of the prophets are among the proofs of the one who is told them is kept by as-Saʿdī, since no man of the desert tells the affairs of a people of old in that order without a teacher. And the same, with the note that the chapter was defending the messenger as well as guiding the community, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the verse links the narrative to the office, the reader is shown what the Book means by a sign.

**THE TALES THAT COME IN ONE VOICE**

al-Ālūsī keeps the note that the same hand arranged the story of the crowd that fled, the ark, the river and the giant, and that the arrangement is the proof rather than the wonders inside it: ***“These are Allah’s revelations”***. The same is kept by Ibn Kathīr with the remark that the Book tells the stories of the two houses with the ease of a man describing his own street.

The plain reading that the plural of the revelations covers the whole passage is kept by al-Jalālayn, and the same is kept by as-Saʿdī in a short form. Because the whole stretch is called a revelation rather than a report, the reader is shown how the Book holds its history and its law in one voice.

**THE MESSENGER WHO IS NAMED ONE OF MANY**

The verse places the messenger in a line rather than on a throne: one of the messengers. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the point that the sentence honours him with the company of the prophets who came before him, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that the next verse begins the account of their ranks.

The plain sense that the messenger stands in the same rank as the men named in the verses around him is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the remark that the community was taught to honour all of them without dividing them, is kept by al-Baghawī. Because the sentence names him as one of a company, the reader is shown the humility that the Book builds into the highest office.

The ranks of the messengers are opened in the verse that follows, (2:253), and the greatest of the revelations of that chapter is named a little later, (2:255).

The lesson also reaches a reader who reads the old stories as curiosities and turns the page. The verse gives him a whole narrative called a revelation and a messenger called one of the messengers, and it asks him what he has done with what he has read. Because the sentence ends on the truth of the recitation, the reader is taught that a story in this Book is a message with an address on it. Since the whole passage was recited to a messenger rather than written for a library, the reader sees that the lesson of the story is meant for the one who hears it.

The case is like a man who reads the letters his grandfather wrote from a war he never saw, and who finds his own name in the last line of the third page. The battles are old, the ink is brown, and the letter is addressed to him.

---

## Verse 2:253

> We have chosen some of those messengers above others. Allah spoke directly to some, and raised some high in rank. To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. If Allah had willed, succeeding generations would not have fought ˹among themselves˺ after receiving the clear proofs. But they differed—some believed while others disbelieved. Yet if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another. But Allah does what He wills

**THE RANKS AMONG THE MESSENGERS**

The verse opens the subject of the ranks: ***“We have chosen some of those messengers above others.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the preferring is a gift of the Lord rather than a step earned by a man. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the messengers share one message and differ in what each was given.

The discussion of the ten over the meaning of the preferring, whether it lies in the miracles or in the degrees of the world to come, is kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the plain reading that the difference is in the gifts rather than in the truth they carried is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the choice is named before the gifts, the reader is shown where the honour of a prophet begins.

**THE ONE WHO WAS SPOKEN TO**

The verse then names the first of the gifts: ***“Allah spoke directly to some,”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the one meant is Moses, whose speech with the Lord gave him the title of the one who was spoken to. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the favour was given without an intermediary.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the speech is a favour named beside the other favours. On this point, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the remark that a man is raised by what he is given rather than by what he claims. Because the speech is named before the ranks, the reader is shown what the greatest of the distinctions in that list was.

**THE RAISED RANKS AND THE TWO GIFTS TO JESUS**

The verse then moves from the speech to the degrees: ***“and raised some high in rank.”*** ***“To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs”*** ***“and supported him with the holy spirit.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the degrees as the stations of the prophets. And the clear proofs as the signs that answered the people of his time.

The reading that the mother of Jesus is named so that his human line would be plain beside the signs given to him is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. And the same, with the note that the holy spirit is the angel who carried the revelation, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the gifts of the two prophets are placed in one sentence, the reader is shown how the Book honours its messengers without dividing their message.
