**THE DIFFERENCE THAT CAME AFTER THE PROOFS**

The verse then turns to the people who received the truth: ***“If Allah had willed, succeeding generations would not have fought ˹among themselves˺ after receiving the clear proofs.”*** ***“But they differed”*** ***“some believed while others disbelieved.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the fighting came from the choice of the people rather than from a failure of the proof. For its part, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that the argument of a man is not the argument of a sign.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the sentence comforts the messenger by showing him that the people of the prophets before him did the same with their proofs. In the same way, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that the Book speaks of generations rather than of a single city. Because the proof is named before the quarrel, the reader is shown where the responsibility of a people begins.

**THE WILL THAT SETTLES THE MATTER**

The verse closes on a sentence that ends the argument about the will of God: ***“Yet if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another.”*** ***“But Allah does what He wills”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the answer to the question of why the truth did not make everyone one people, and the second as the whole ground of the answer.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the two sentences put the matter back into the hands of the Lord. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the verse teaches the community not to demand of the truth that no one refuse it. Because the verse repeats the will twice and ends there, the reader is shown where the Book wants the discussion to stop.

The spending that follows from belief is commanded in the next verse, (2:254 — **“before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining”**). And the same clear proofs given to Jesus are remembered in another chapter of the Book, (2:253).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has become bitter because his family did not accept what he knows to be true. The verse gives him generations who fought by a choice rather than by a knowledge, and it asks him whether the quarrel of other people is his to settle. Because the close puts the matter in the will of the Lord, the reader is taught that a man is asked for the plain word and not for the outcome of it.

The case is like a teacher who spends a year explaining one chapter to a class and finds in the examination that half of them heard the words and half of them heard the lesson. The bell rings, the papers go home, and the year of teaching is the same year for the whole room.

---

## Verse 2:254

> O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession. Those who disbelieve are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers

**THE COMMAND TO SPEND**

The verse addresses the community directly: ***“O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that the command covers the duty that is owed and the gift that is offered above it. Alongside that, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the wealth was named as a provision so that the giver would remember its source.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports of the community on whether the sentence means the alms that are obligatory, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading that the command is general. Because the verse reminds the giver that the wealth was provided, the reader is shown how the Book asks for a share of a gift.

**THE DAY THAT LEAVES NO ROOM FOR A DEAL**

The verse then names the reason for the haste: ***“before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining,”*** ***“friendship, or intercession.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the bargaining as the trade that can still be made in this life. And the friendship as the patron who might speak for a man, and the intercession as the appeal that others may make.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the three things named are the three ways a person finds help in the world. For its part, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the verse takes all three away so that a man would spend while the ways are open. Because the Book lists what will be missing rather than what will be found, the reader is shown how the warning works.

**THE WRONGDOERS WHO KEPT THEIR WEALTH**

The verse closes with a sentence that names the opposite of the giver: ***“Those who disbelieve are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the plain sense that the disbelief here is the refusal that shows itself in the closed hand. In the same way, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the note that the verse connects the creed to the money.

The reading that the word for the wrongdoers covers the one who withholds what God has ordered him to give is kept by al-Ālūsī. And the same, with the remark that the sentence comes after the command so that the reader would weigh the two together, is kept by al-Baghawī. Because the hoarder is called a wrongdoer, the reader is shown where the Book places stinginess in the scale.

**THE PATH FROM DOCTRINE TO THE PURSE**

The earlier command of the fighting stands a little above this verse, (2:244 — **“Fight in the cause of Allah”**), and the greatest verse of the chapter follows it, (2:255). The reader of the three together sees a chapter that moves from the field to the purse and from the purse to the seat of the Lord.

The lesson also reaches a reader who intends to settle his accounts with his Lord when he has a little more capital. The verse gives him a day with no bargaining and no intercession, and it asks him when he thinks the open market will close. Because the sentence about the wrongdoers follows the command so closely, the reader is taught that the belief in the heart reaches the hand in the end.

The case is like a traveller who plans to buy the tickets for the whole family at the border because the queue at home is long. The gates close in the evening, the queue at the border is longer, and the money in his pocket buys nothing after the last bell.

---

## Verse 2:255

> Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission? He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them, but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺. His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him. For He is the Most High, the Greatest

**THE VERSE THAT STANDS ABOVE THE REST**

The chapter arrives at the sentence the community has recited at its worst moments: ***“Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the long reports on the words of the two names, that the Ever-Living is the One whose life has no beginning and no end. And the All-Sustaining the One upon whom every other thing stands.

The report that this verse is the greatest of the Book is kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the same, with the note that the greatness lies in what it gathers of the knowledge of God rather than in its length, is kept by as-Saʿdī. Because the community was taught to recite it at night and after the prayers, the reader is shown what a short passage may carry.

**THE SLEEP THAT NEVER COMES**

The verse then clears away every weakness of the creature: ***“Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the two words as the lesser and the greater kind of rest. So that the sentence leaves no state in which the Lord is absent from His creation.

The reports of the community on a man who asked about the night and was answered with this line are kept by al-Baghawī. And the same, with the note that a person who is sure of the sentence sleeps better than the man who asked, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the Book denies the two states in one breath, the reader is shown what the word of the Lord over the world must mean.

**THE OWNERSHIP THAT COVERS THE WORLD**

The verse then names the extent of the possession: ***“To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens”*** ***“and whatever is on the earth.”*** al-Jalālayn keeps the plain sense that the ownership covers every thing and every person. In the same way, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the note that the sentence is placed beside the denial of sleep so that a man would know who watches a world that no eye can hold.

**THE INTERCESSION THAT NEEDS A LEAVE**

The verse raises a question in the middle of its declarations: ***“Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission?”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sense that no advocate stands at the court of the Lord without his case being allowed. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence answers a people who held that their leaders would plead for them.

The reading that the question is a denial in the form of an asking is kept by Ibn Kathīr. And the same, with the remark that the sentence prepares the reader for the day when no advocate may speak uninvited, is kept by as-Saʿdī. Because the verse named the intercession in the sentence before it, the reader is shown how the Book explains its own warning.

**THE KNOWLEDGE THAT ONLY HE HOLDS**

The verse then states what the creatures may know of the matter: ***“He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them”*** ***“and what is behind them”*** ***“but no one can grasp any of His knowledge”*** ***“except what He wills ˹to reveal˺.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the two directions as the past and the future. So that the knowledge of a person is a window opened by the Lord rather than a light of his own.

**THE THRONE THAT CARRIES THE TWO**

The verse then reaches the throne itself: ***“His Seat encompasses the heavens”*** ***“and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him.”*** al-Ālūsī keeps the reports of the community on the meaning of the Seat. And the note that the ten were careful in this place, since they spoke of what the words carry and stopped at what the words leave. Because the Book ends the sentence on the preservation that does not tire, the reader is shown what the throne is not.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the two sides, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence is the answer of the Book to a mind that wants to weigh the Lord with its own measure. Because the permission stands at the end of the knowledge, the reader is shown that the door of learning is held in the same hand as the door of mercy.

**THE TWO NAMES THAT CLOSE THE THRONE**

The verse ends on a short and heavy line: ***“For He is the Most High, the Greatest”***. al-Baghawī keeps the height as the distance between the Lord and every measure of the creatures. And the greatness as the sum of the two names, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that the verse that began with the unity ends with the majesty.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the two names close the passage as the seal on everything stated before them. In the same way, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the remark that a reader who has finished the verse should find nothing in himself that needs to be argued with. Because the sentence stands after the description of the throne, the reader is shown where the Book puts the end of a lesson about God.

The warning about the intercession is repeated with its day in the verse before this one, (2:254 — **“before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining”**). And the call of a messenger who was sent to the whole world comes in another chapter, (2:252 — **“And you are truly one of the messengers”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who cannot sleep because he has measured his troubles against his own strength. The verse gives him a Lord who does not doze, a throne that covers the sky and the ground. And a knowledge that is opened by permission, and it asks him whose keeping he is relying on when he shuts his eyes. Because the close names the Most High and the Greatest, the reader is taught that the night watch is kept by the One who never kept it in a hurry.

The case is like a caravan that crosses a country where the guards of the road change every few miles, and one night the travellers learn that the whole route lies inside the lands of a single lord. The tents are pitched in the open, the horses are untied, and nobody in the caravan sleeps badly after the letter is read.

---

## Verse 2:256

> Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE SENTENCE THAT OPENS THE DOOR OF BELIEF**

The verse follows the throne verse with a declaration about the road to faith: ***“Let there be no compulsion in religion,”*** The reports that the sentence was sent down about a man of the helpers whose children had been brought up in another faith are kept by al-Ṭabarī. And the same, with the note that the community was told to leave the matter to the message rather than to the hand, is kept by al-Baghawī.

The long discussion of the ten over the reach of the sentence, whether it covers the people of the Book or every person, is kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the plain reading that faith is not to be forced is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the command is stated as a fact rather than as a prohibition, the reader is shown how firmly the Book closed the door on compulsion.

**THE ROAD THAT IS PLAIN**

The verse then gives its reason: ***“for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sense that the way of guidance has been made clear enough for a person to walk it by his own sight. For its part, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that a road which can be seen needs no pushing.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the proofs have been spread out, so that a person who refuses does so against what he can see. In the same way, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that the sentence turns the matter into a question of honesty rather than of power. Because the Book answers the command with the clarity of the road, the reader is shown what the community is asked to trust.

**THE HANDHOLD THAT DOES NOT BREAK**

The verse then describes the believer's act: ***“So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah”*** ***“has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the renouncing as the turning away from every rival claimed beside the Lord. And the handhold as the hold that a man keeps in a place where the ground gives way.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the reading that the handhold is named as unfailing because the One who is held does not let go. On this point, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the grasp is made by a hand that would otherwise have nothing to hold in a hard season. Because the verse pairs a denial with a trust in one sentence, the reader is shown what belief asks of a person.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with the pair that closes so many of the rulings of the chapter: ***“And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the hearing of the confession of a man and the second as the knowledge of what his heart meant by it. Alongside that, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the two names are placed where compulsion would otherwise have been used.

as-Saʿdī keeps the pair as the reason no one needs to force a neighbour, since the One who hears the words is the One who knows what is inside the speaker. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that a confession made under pressure is no confession at all. Because the sentence speaks of hearing and knowing rather than of seeing and punishing, the reader is shown who is asked to judge a faith.

The spending of the community is commanded just before this verse, (2:254 — **“before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining”**). And the Lord who keeps the heavens and the earth is named in the verse before it, (2:255).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been told that his people's faith is a matter for the family's honour rather than for the heart. The verse gives him a command against compulsion, a plain road and a handhold that holds, and it asks him what he would be protecting if he forced a mind into a shape it did not choose. Because the close names the One who hears and knows, the reader is taught that the faith of a person is a trust between him and his Lord.

The case is like a father who buys his son a shop in the market and finds in the spring that the boy has left it locked to work with the boats at the harbour. The shop stands open in the records of the town, and the work at the boats is the only trade that ever paid the household.

---

## Verse 2:257

> Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light. As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods who lead them out of light and into darkness. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**THE ONE WHO KEEPS THE BELIEVERS**

The verse answers the sentence about the handhold with a promise about the hand that holds it: ***“Allah is the Guardian of the believers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the guarding as the help and the care of the One who takes the affairs of a person into his own charge. In the same way, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the guarding covers the help, the love and the management of a life.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports of the community on the meaning of the word, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that faith is the greatest blessing a person can be handed. Because the sentence stands right after the verse that named the firm handhold, the reader is shown whose hand is holding.

**THE ROAD OUT OF THE DARKNESS**

The verse then names the work of the Guardian: ***“He brings them out of darkness”*** ***“and into light.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the darkness as the many kinds of error and the light as the guidance that gathers a person to the truth. In the same vein, And al-Jalālayn keeps the same with the note that the move is named as a bringing out rather than as a walking away.

The plain sense that the believers were taken out of a companionship of error into a companionship of faith is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the note that the plural of the darkness is kept in the Arabic while the light is named once, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the road is described as a road between two houses, the reader is shown what a change of belief does to a life.

**THE GUARDIANS OF THE OTHER SIDE**

The verse then turns to the other company: ***“As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods”*** ***“who lead them out of light”*** ***“and into darkness.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the leading as the pull of the false objects of worship that a people take up instead of the Lord. Alongside that, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the light they left is the natural knowledge of the Creator that every person carries.

The reading that the guardians of that company are the very things they chose is kept by as-Saʿdī, since a person is led by what he loves. And the same, with the remark that the road goes in both directions and the choice decides the direction, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the Book sets the two companies side by side, the reader is shown that no one stands still in this matter.

**THE FIRE THAT HAS NO END**

The verse closes on the end of the second road: ***“It is they who will be the residents of the Fire.”*** ***“They will be there forever”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the residency as the dwelling that has no term. For its part, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the sentence is placed at the end of the road so that the reader would see where the path leads before he takes a step on it.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the words, and al-Baghawī keeps the same with the remark that the light and the darkness are named before the fire, since a person is asked to see the way before he is told its end. Because the close speaks of a dwelling rather than of a punishment, the reader is shown how long the Book makes a choice last.

The same two roads are named in the chapter of the cattle, where the Book speaks of those who were in darkness and were brought into light by their Lord. And the close of the chapter calls the believers to ask for mercy on the day of the return, (2:286 — **“You are our ˹only˺ Guardian”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who thinks of his faith as a private opinion that costs him nothing either way. The verse gives him a Guardian, a road out of darkness and a warning about a dwelling without an end, and it asks him who is leading him by the hand he never looks at. Because the sentence says the believers are brought out rather than that they climbed out, the reader is taught that the strength to leave a dark place was never his own.

The case is like a man who is shown two roads out of a valley at dusk; one climbs towards a village with lamps in it, and the other falls away into a plain with no light at all. The roads were cut by other feet long before he came, and the only thing that belongs to him is the choice of the one he takes.

---

## Verse 2:258

> Are you ˹O Prophet˺ not aware of the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because Allah had granted him kingship? ˹Remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord is the One Who has power to give life and cause death.” He argued, “I too have the power to give life and cause death.” Abraham challenged ˹him˺, “Allah causes the sun to rise from the east. So make it rise from the west.” And so the disbeliever was dumbstruck. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people

**THE KING WHO ARGUED WITH A SHEPHERD**

The verse opens a scene from the life of the friend of God: ***“Are you ˹O Prophet˺ not aware of the one”*** ***“who argued with Abraham about his Lord”*** ***“because Allah had granted him kingship?”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the man was a king of the land of Babylon who held the rule of a great people. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the crown was the thing that made him speak.

The plain reading that the argument was about the existence and the power of the Lord rather than about a law is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the note that a man with a kingdom finds it hard to hear of a King above him, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the cause is named as the kingship, the reader is shown what a gift can do to the mind of the one who receives it.

**THE FIRST ANSWER OF ABRAHAM**

The verse then gives the opening move: ***“˹Remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord is the One”*** ***“Who has power to give life”*** ***“and cause death.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the argument as the power of the Lord over the thing no king can control, since a crown cannot hold a soul in a body, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same in a short form.

The reading that the friend of God chose the clearest sign of the Creator, the life that comes and goes without any hand of a ruler, is kept by as-Saʿdī. And the same, with the note that the answer was meant for a mind that had asked for a proof rather than for a fight, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the argument begins with the body, the reader is shown how the Book meets a person where he lives.

**THE CLAIM OF THE KING**

The verse then reports the answer of the king: ***“He argued, “I too have the power to give life”*** ***“and cause death.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the man called two captives and ordered one to be killed and the other released. So that the claim was made with an act rather than with a proof, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that a word play can pass for an argument at a court.

The reading that the king was measuring the giving of life by the granting of a pardon is kept by al-Ālūsī. And the same, with the remark that the man had not understood what he had been asked, is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. Because the Book keeps the claim without a comment at this point, the reader is shown how a false proof is allowed to stand until the light of the next sentence falls on it.

**THE SUN THAT SETTLED THE MATTER**

The verse then gives the argument that could not be twisted: ***“Abraham challenged ˹him˺, “Allah causes the sun to rise from the east.”*** ***“So make it rise from the west.””*** ***“And so the disbeliever was dumbstruck.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the closing of the case, since a king holds a court and does not hold the sky. In the same way, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the friend of God moved from the argument of the body to the argument of the heavens.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the point that the men of learning take from the verse the value of a proof that cannot be argued with, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the sunrise. Because the answer is a command rather than a reply, the reader is shown how a debate ends when the matter is put in the open.

**THE GUIDANCE THAT IS WITHHELD**

The verse closes on a sentence about that king and every man like him: ***“And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people”***. al-Qurṭubī keeps the guidance as the showing of the way. And keeps the reports that the man who argued was left to his own mind after he had closed it, and al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the wrong here is the wrong done to the truth.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the reading that the sentence stands as a warning to a person who argues for a position because he holds it rather than because it is true. On this point, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the remark that the verse ends on the fate of a kingdom that had all the proofs and none of the hearing. Because the close speaks of a people rather than of a single king, the reader is shown that a court is not the only place where such an argument is lost.

The argument from the rising of the sun is kept beside another scene of a proof in the chapter of the cattle. And the same mercy that keeps a believer's road lit is asked for at the close of this chapter, (2:286 — **“You are our ˹only˺ Guardian”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been given a position of authority in his trade and has begun to think that his rank settles his arguments. The verse gives him a king with a throne and a friend of God with a sunrise, and it asks him which of the two would stand if the sky were asked to move. Because the close names the wrongdoers as the ones left without guidance, the reader is taught that the greatest loss of a powerful man is the hearing he no longer has.

The case is like two men arguing over the height of a wall in a courtyard, and one of them asks the other to hold back the tide with his hand. The tide comes in every evening, the wall is measured in the morning, and the man who spoke of the sea never spoke of the wall again.

---

## Verse 2:259

> Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. He wondered, “How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?” So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years then brought him back to life. Allah asked, “How long have you remained ˹in this state˺?” He replied, “Perhaps a day or part of a day.” Allah said, “No! You have remained here for a hundred years! Just look at your food and drink—they have not spoiled. ˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey! And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign for humanity. And look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh!” When this was made clear to him, he declared, “˹Now˺ I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything.”

**THE MAN ON THE ROAD TO A DEAD CITY**

The verse opens another scene of a proof: ***“Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one”*** ***“who passed by a city”*** ***“which was in ruins.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the city was the ruined house of the holy place that a conqueror had left in rubble. Here too, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the roofs had fallen onto the walls.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the differences of the ten over the man, whether he was a prophet or a man of the righteous who rode a donkey with a flask of juice and a basket of figs, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the ruined city. Because the ruins are named before the question, the reader is shown what the man was looking at when the doubt came.

**THE QUESTION AND THE DEATH**

The verse then gives the thought and the answer: ***“He wondered, “How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?””*** ***“So Allah caused him to die”*** ***“for a hundred years”*** ***“then brought him back to life.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the death as the answer of the Lord to the asking of a heart. For its part, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the question was one of wonder rather than of denial.

The reading that the man was shown the thing he had asked about inside his own body is kept by as-Saʿdī, since the death of a man is the destruction of a city in one frame. And the same, with the remark that the lesson was given in a hundred years rather than in a sentence, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the Lord answered a question with an experience, the reader is shown how the Book teaches a mind that will not be argued with.

**THE QUESTION OF THE HOURS**

The verse then reports the first words of the man after the waking: ***“Allah asked, “How long have you remained ˹in this state˺?””*** ***“He replied, “Perhaps a day”*** ***“or part of a day.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reply as the estimate of a man who had gone to sleep in the morning and woken in the same light. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the food at his hand was still fresh.

The plain reading that the man answered from what his senses told him is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the remark that a body which had lain a century is judged by the eyes of the waker, is kept by as-Saʿdī. Because the Book keeps the wrong estimate without a rebuke at that point, the reader is shown how gently the lesson is built.

**THE FOOD, THE DONKEY AND THE BONES**

The verse then opens the scene to the man's own eyes: ***“Allah said, “No!”*** ***“You have remained here”*** ***“for a hundred years!”*** ***“Just look at your food”*** ***“and drink they have not spoiled.”*** ***“˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey!”*** ***“And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign”*** ***“for humanity.”*** ***“And look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together”*** ***“then clothe them with flesh!””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the keeping of the food as the proof that the years had passed outside the man while his provisions stood still. Alongside that, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the donkey was the second proof and the sign was the third.

The reading that the man was made a sign for the people of his town as well as for himself is kept by al-Ālūsī, since he walked back among them with a story no one could deny. And the plain reading of the bones is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the proofs are given in the order of the man's own life, the reader is shown what the Lord does with a question asked in the dust of a ruin.

**THE CONFESSION AT THE END**

The verse closes on the words of the man: ***“When this was made clear to him, he declared, “˹Now˺ I know”*** ***“that Allah is Most Capable of everything.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the knowing as the certainty that had been asked of him. For its part, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the man had asked for a sight and was given a certainty.

The plain sense that the words close the matter for the rest of his life is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the remark that the story is told so that a reader who wonders about the raising of the dead would find the answer already given, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the verse ends on the power of the Lord rather than on the man, the reader is shown where the story was leading all along. The townsmen who saw the rider come back with a fresh basket in his hand were given a proof that walked among them. And the report of what they saw was carried by the same road for the people who came after them. A proof that a person can touch with his fingers asks less of a mind than a sentence read from a page, and the Book chose the harder way for a doubt that had settled in a heart. The food in the hand of a sleeper is the plainest argument against the thought that time dissolves everything a person owns, because the basket had stood where the years had not. And the man who ate from it carried the answer in his own bag for the rest of the road.

The raising of the dead is argued from the same power in the scene of the birds, (2:260 — **“Show me how you give life to the dead”**). And the same hand is named over the earth and the heavens in the verse about the possession of all things, (2:284 — **“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who stands in front of a thing that has been broken for years and asks how it could ever be put right. The verse gives him a city in ruins, a man who slept a century and a donkey that was gathered from its bones. And it asks him what part of his own life he thinks is beyond the hand that kept the food fresh. Because the close names a power over everything, the reader is taught that the ruin he sees is a picture of the hour before the rebuilding and not of the end.

The case is like a farmer who finds a dry field in the month of the drought and tells himself that nothing will grow there again. He sleeps through the season, wakes in the spring of the following year, and finds a green line along the ditch where the seed had fallen from his own sack. The ditch was watered by no one, the season was the same season, and the seed had been lying there since the day he gave up.

---

## Verse 2:260

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord! Show me how you give life to the dead.” Allah responded, “Do you not believe?” Abraham replied, “Yes I do, but just so my heart can be reassured.” Allah said, “Then bring four birds, train them to come to you, ˹then cut them into pieces,˺ and scatter them on different hilltops. Then call them back, they will fly to you in haste. And ˹so you will˺ know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

**THE REQUEST OF THE FRIEND OF GOD**

The verse opens the third of the scenes with the asking of Abraham: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord!”*** ***“Show me how you give life to the dead.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the friend of God asked for a sight with his own eyes. In the same way, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the asking came from a heart that wanted more than a report.

The long discussion of the ten over whether such a question could come from a doubt is kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain reading that the request was for a showing rather than for a proof is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the Book praises the man in other places as a believer of long standing, the reader is shown that the asking was not the beginning of his faith.

**THE QUESTION OF THE LORD**

The verse then gives the answer: ***“Allah responded, “Do you not believe?””*** ***“Abraham replied, “Yes I do”*** ***“but just so my heart can be reassured.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the question as a kindness rather than a reproach, since it gave the man room to explain himself. In the same vein, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the reports of the community on the difference between knowing and seeing.

The plain reading that belief and reassurance are two stations is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the note that the reply of the friend of God has become a saying for every believer who wants his heart settled, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the verse separates the confession from the assurance, the reader is shown that the two are not enemies.

**THE FOUR BIRDS**

The verse then gives the answer in an act: ***“Allah said, “Then bring four birds, train them to come to you, ˹then cut them into pieces,˺”*** ***“and scatter them on different hilltops.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports of the ten on the kinds of the four birds and on the parts that were mixed. Alongside that, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the hills were chosen so that the parts could not be gathered by any hand.

The reading that the exercise was made with the man's own hands, so that the proof would be carried by the fingers that had cut and scattered, is kept by as-Saʿdī. And the same, with the remark that the keeping of the heads in his hand was the finishing touch of the lesson, is kept by al-Ālūsī. Because the Lord answered a request for sight with a command to work, the reader is shown what the Book does with a heart that wants a sign.

**THE CALL AND THE RETURN**

The verse then states the promise: ***“Then call them back, they will fly to you in haste.”*** ***“And ˹so you will˺ know”*** ***“that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the calling as the voice of the man whose own hands had done the scattering. For its part, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the birds came to the man who had cut them and not to the hill where they had lain.

The plain reading that the parts flew together at the call is kept by al-Jalālayn. And the point that the knowing named at the end is the certainty that a person carries in his chest after he has seen the work is kept by as-Saʿdī. Because the verse ends on the two names, the reader is shown that the power and the wisdom that raised the birds are the same pair that keeps his own affairs.

The scene of the man who was made a sign for a town stands just before this one, (2:259 — **“And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign”**). And the same power over the dead is stated in the closing of the chapter, (2:284 — **“And Allah is Most Capable of everything”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been told about the raising of the dead all his life and finds that the words have not reached his heart. The verse gives him a friend of God asking for a sight, four birds in his own two hands and a call that brought them back, and it asks him what he wants his own certainty to be built on. Because the close names the Almighty and the All-Wise, the reader is taught that the Lord who raised the birds is the Lord who arranges the seasons of a single heart.

The case is like a child who is told by his father that the seed in the ground will come up as wheat, and who digs a hole every week to check. The father gives him a pot, a seed and a windowsill, and the boy waters his own plant until the day it can be seen from the door.

---

## Verse 2:261

> The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts into seven ears, each bearing one hundred grains. And Allah multiplies ˹the reward even more˺ to whoever He wills. For Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing

**THE GRAIN THAT BECOMES A FIELD**

The verse opens a set of parables about spending: ***“The example of those”*** ***“who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is”*** ***“that of a grain”*** ***“that sprouts into seven ears, each bearing one hundred grains.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the grain as the seed of the farmer's field and the ears as the reward that comes from a single act. Alongside that, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the number is named so that a reader would count it.

The plain reading of the seven ears is kept by al-Jalālayn, and the same, with the note that the Book takes a picture from the work of the people it addresses, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the parable is drawn from farming, the reader is shown how the Book teaches a community that lives by the soil. Since the ears are named with their number, the reader sees that the promise is meant to be counted and not only admired.

**THE MULTIPLICATION THAT HAS NO FIGURE**

The verse then opens the number beyond the count: ***“And Allah multiplies ˹the reward even more˺ to whoever He wills.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as the answer to a giver who might think the seven hundred is the ceiling. Here too, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the reports that the multiplication may reach a number no eye has seen.

The plain reading that the increase is in the hand of the Lord rather than in the weight of the gift is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the note that a small gift from a poor man may be multiplied beyond the great gift of a rich one, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the measure is left open, the reader is shown that the Book refuses to put a ceiling on generosity. Since the multiplication is tied to the will of the Lord, the reader is taught that the return is a gift rather than a wage.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends on a pair that explains how such a return is possible: ***“For Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing”***. al-Baghawī keeps the first as the wealth that never runs out. And the second as the knowledge of what each giver intended when he gave.

The same pair is kept by al-Jalālayn in a short form. And the reading that the two names answer the two fears of a giver, the fear that the wealth will be lost and the fear that the gift will not be noticed, is kept by al-Ālūsī. Because the verse closes on the knowledge of the One who sees the seed, the reader is shown who is keeping the account.

The same picture of the seed that becomes many is used in the chapter of the cattle. And the giving that follows this verse is described with its wrong way in the next one, (2:262 — **“do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who counts what he puts into a cause as money that has left his hand for good. The verse gives him a seed, seven ears and a hundred grains in each, and it asks him whether he has ever seen a farmer refuse to sow because the ground would swallow the seed. Because the close names the Bountiful and the Knowing, the reader is taught that no gift is lost and no intention is missed.

The case is like a man who plants a single row of maize at the edge of his plot because the rest of the field is rented to another. The row becomes a hedge, the hedge feeds his family for a month, and the neighbour who rented the field asks him for seed the following year.

---

## Verse 2:262

> Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah and do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity or hurtful words—they will get their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**THE GIVING THAT KEEPS ITS MANNER**

The people whose gift stands are then named: ***“Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah”*** ***“and do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity”*** ***“or hurtful words”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the reminder as the counting of a favour done to a person. And the hurt as the word that makes the receiver feel small in front of others.

The reports that the sentence came down about men of the community who had given much and then talked of it in the market are kept by al-Baghawī. And the same, with the rulings that followed on the giving that is announced, is kept by al-Qurṭubī. Because the verse joins the gift and the manner in one sentence, the reader is shown that the hand and the tongue are counted in the same ledger.

**THE REWARD THAT IS KEPT**

The verse then names what such givers receive: ***“they will get their reward from their Lord”***. The sentence is kept by al-Jalālayn as the promise that the account is held by the One who saw the gift and heard what was said of it afterwards. And the same is kept by as-Saʿdī with the note that the reward is named as coming from the Lord so that no one would look for it in the thanks of a person.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the reward stands whether or not the receiver ever thanked the giver. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that a gift which is mentioned afterwards is paid in the market rather than in the garden. Because the promise is made in the name of the Lord, the reader is shown where the true wage of a gift is kept.

**THE FEAR AND THE GRIEF THAT ARE LIFTED**

The verse closes on a pair that is repeated across the passage: ***“and there will be no fear”*** ***“for them, nor will they grieve”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the fear as the dread of what is coming and the grief as the pain over what has gone. So that the two words cover the whole of a person's life.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the same pair with the note that the sentence is placed after a promise of reward so that the reader would know that the gift has not left him poorer in his peace. Alongside that, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that a giver who expects a return from people carries both the fear and the grief with him. Because the verse removes both from the giver, the reader is shown what sincerity buys in this world before the next.

The same promise of a reward with the Lord is made to the givers in the verse that follows, (2:274 — **“their reward is with their Lord”**). And the manner of the giving is described in the parable of the garden, (2:265 — **“that of a garden on a fertile hill”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has helped a relative through a hard year and cannot stop mentioning the help at every gathering. The verse gives him a gift, a silence after it and a reward kept by his Lord, and it asks him which of the two payments he would rather have. Because the close removes the fear and the grief from the giver, the reader is taught that the remark made after a gift costs him more than the money did. Since the reward is kept by the Lord and not by the receiver, the reader sees that the silence of a giver is part of his deed.

The case is like a man who pays the school fees of his brother's children and then tells the story at every wedding in the family for ten years. The children finish their schooling, the story is worn thin by the telling, and the brother's table is the one place where the man is never seated at ease.

---

## Verse 2:263

> Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Most Forbearing

**THE WORDS THAT STAND ABOVE THE COIN**

The verse puts two small things above one great one: ***“Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the kind word as the answer a poor man receives when he is turned away. And the forgiveness as the covering of his asking rather than a rebuke for it.

The same is kept by al-Qurṭubī with the reports that the sentence came down about the men who gave and then made the receiver feel the weight of the gift. And the plain comparison is kept by al-Jalālayn in a short form. Because the Book weighs a kind answer against a sum and finds the answer the weightier of the two, the reader is shown how the scale of the religion works. Since the comparison is stated plainly, the reader sees that the Book does not measure a deed by its size alone.

**THE GIFT THAT COSTS MORE THAN IT GIVES**

The sentence names the harm that can follow a gift: ***“charity followed by injury”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the injury as the word that undoes the good of the gift. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the Book treats the receiver's dignity as part of the gift itself.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that a man who keeps his coin and answers with a kind word has done better than the man who pays and then wounds. On this point, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the two words of the verse are the ones a poor man carries home with him. Because the harm is named as following the gift, the reader is shown how close a good deed stands to a bad one.

**THE TWO NAMES THAT CLOSE THE SCALE**

The verse ends on the pair that explains why the harm never touches the Lord: ***“And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Most Forbearing”***. al-Baghawī keeps the first as the freedom of the Lord from needing the gift of any person. And the second as the patience that does not hurry to answer the man who spoils his own gift.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same pair with the note that the patience of the Lord is the reason a giver is given time to see what he has done, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading in a short form. Because the verse ends on the sufficiency of the Lord, the reader is shown that the gift was never a service done to God.

The kind word is joined to the same patience of the Lord in the verse about the giving that is spoiled, (2:264 — **“Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺”**). And the good word is asked of the believers in another chapter, where the Book sets the manner of a person beside his faith.

The lesson also reaches a reader who has nothing to give and thinks that he has therefore nothing to offer at all. The verse gives him a kind word, a forgiveness and a place above the coin, and it asks him who told him that a poor man's hands are the only part of him that counts. Because the close names the Self-Sufficient, the reader is taught that the Lord of the worlds asks for the kind answer of a person because that answer is what the person is. Since the coin never reaches the Lord of the worlds, the reader sees that a gift is measured by the manner it is wrapped in.

The case is like a woman at a well who has no bucket of her own and greets every traveller as he fills his; she carries nothing home, and the whole village remembers the morning with her in it.

---

## Verse 2:264

> O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words, like those who donate their wealth just to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. Their example is that of a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain—leaving it just a bare stone. Such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity. Allah does not guide ˹such˺ disbelieving people

**THE COMMAND AGAINST A RUINED GIFT**

The verse addresses the community directly: ***“O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺”*** ***“or hurtful words, like those”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the wasting as the emptying of the deed until nothing of it remains. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the image is that of a vessel with a hole in it.

The rulings that follow about a gift which is spoiled after it was given are kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain sense that the reward is cancelled by what is said afterwards is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the verse is addressed to believers, the reader is shown that the danger lies in the practice of the good and not only of the wicked.

**THE GIVER WHO LOOKS FOR PRAISE**

The verse then describes the people it compares them with: ***“who donate their wealth just to show off”*** ***“and do not believe in Allah”*** ***“or the Last Day.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the showing off as the gift given for the eye of the crowd rather than for the eye of the Lord. In the same way, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the sentence puts the show and the disbelief in one line because they grow from the same root.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that a person who does not believe in the last accounting has nothing to give for except the praise of the people in front of him. In the same vein, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the verse teaches the community where a loud giver is standing. Because the Book names the motive rather than the amount, the reader is shown what is being weighed in a gift.

**THE ROCK AND THE RAIN**

The verse then gives its picture: ***“Their example is”*** ***“that of a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain”*** ***“leaving it just a bare stone.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the thin soil as the appearance of a good deed laid over a heart with no root in it. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the rain was the very thing that made the seed grow in the other parable of this passage.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the washing away, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that the two parables of the passage stand side by side so that a reader would compare the fertile ground with the stone. Because the picture ends with the soil gone, the reader is shown what a deed looks like when its reason is missing.

**THE REWARD THAT CANNOT BE KEPT**

The verse then states the result: ***“Such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity.”*** ***“Allah does not guide ˹such˺ disbelieving people”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the inability as the loss of the thing that was in their hands for a day. Alongside that, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the note that the reward was never theirs to keep because the intention behind it was borrowed from the crowd.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the closing sentence as a warning that reaches every giver, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the guidance withheld here is the guidance that would have shown an insincere man his own heart. Because the verse ends on the guidance of the Lord, the reader is shown that the cure for a spoiled gift begins long before the gift.

The parable of the fertile hill is given right after this verse, (2:265 — **“that of a garden on a fertile hill”**). And the two kinds of giving are drawn together in the closing verses of the passage, (2:272 — **“Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who gives to the mosque in the month of the festival and makes sure that his name is read out with the list. The verse gives him a rock, a thin layer of soil and a heavy rain, and it asks him what remains of his gift when the rain has passed through the street. Because the close names the people who cannot keep their own reward, the reader is taught that a deed needs a reason deeper than the ground it fell on.

The case is like a man who paints the front of a house he does not own because the street will see it from the road. The paint holds for one season, the wood underneath goes on rotting, and the owner of the house returns in the spring to a wall of flakes.

---

## Verse 2:265

> And the example of those who donate their wealth, seeking Allah’s pleasure and believing the reward is certain, is that of a garden on a fertile hill: when heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce. If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**THE GARDEN ON THE RISING GROUND**

The verse answers the rock with a garden: ***“And the example of those”*** ***“who donate their wealth, seeking Allah’s pleasure”*** ***“and believing the reward is certain, is”*** ***“that of a garden on a fertile hill”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the hill as the raised ground that catches the water and holds it. And the certainty as the firm belief that the gift returns.

The same is kept by al-Baghawī with the note that the two conditions of the sentence are the very two things missing in the giver of the rock, the pleasure of the Lord and the belief in the return. And the plain image of the garden is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the parables stand one after the other, the reader is shown what makes the same seed live in one place and die in another. Since the ground is named as fertile, the reader sees that the difference lies in the soil and not in the rain.

**THE RAIN AND THE DRIZZLE**

The verse then shows the garden in two seasons: ***“when heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce.”*** ***“If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the heavy rain as the season of plenty in which a giver doubles his gift. And the drizzle as the thin year in which a little is enough for the same ground.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reading that the garden is fruitful in either weather. Alongside that, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that the sentence comforts a reader whose means are small, since the drizzle is named as sufficient for a heart that is rooted. Because the picture does not depend on the weather alone, the reader is shown where the strength of a deed lives. Since the small rain is named as sufficient, the reader is taught that a good ground has no bad season.

**THE SIGHT THAT MEASURES THE GIVING**

The verse closes with the name that reaches into the intention: ***“And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sight as the knowledge of what each giver meant by his gift. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence is placed at the end of two parables so that a reader would weigh his own intention rather than another man's gift.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the name, and al-Baghawī keeps the same with the remark that the one who sees the deed is able to tell the good ground from the stone. Because the verse ends on the sight of the Lord, the reader is shown that the whole difference between the two parables lies where no eye of a person can look. Since the two givers may act alike in the street, the reader sees that the division between them is made in a place the market cannot see.

The rock that loses its soil is described just before this verse, (2:264 — **“leaving it just a bare stone”**). And the same pair of reward and fear is promised to the sincere givers, (2:274 — **“and there will be no fear”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who gives less than a neighbour and takes that as a verdict on his own deed. The verse gives him a heavy rain and a drizzle over the same ground, and it asks him which of the two the garden was waiting for. Because the close names the One who sees what people do, the reader is taught that the size of the gift belongs to the purse and the worth of it belongs to the heart.

The case is like two plots on a hillside, one watered by the channel and the other left to the rain. The channel dries up in a hard year, the rain still comes, and the two fields are green in the same month.

---

## Verse 2:266

> Would any of you wish to have a garden with palm trees, grapevines, and all kinds of fruits with rivers flowing underneath and as they grow very old with dependent children, a fiery whirlwind hits the garden, burning it all up? This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will reflect

**THE GARDEN OF A LIFETIME**

The verse asks a question that gathers the whole picture of the passage: ***“Would any of you wish to have a garden with palm trees, grapevines”*** ***“and all kinds of fruits with rivers flowing underneath”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the garden as the plantation of a man who has laboured for years. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the trees named are the ones a household of that land lived on.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain image of the rivers, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the question is put to every reader rather than to one man, since the wish in it is a common wish. Because a scene of plenty is built before the fire is named, the reader is shown how the Book makes a person want a thing before it takes it away.

**THE OLD AGE AND THE CHILDREN**

The verse then adds the two things that make the loss unbearable: ***“and as they grow very old with dependent children, a fiery whirlwind hits the garden, burning it all up?”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the whirlwind as the fire carried on a wind that passes over the trees. And the dependants as the children who have no other support.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the old man with small children is the picture of a person whose good deeds are needed most on the last of his days. Alongside that, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the burnt garden of a poor family is one of the heaviest losses a person may carry. Because the age and the fire stand in one line, the reader is shown what it costs to lose a lifetime's work at the hour of need. Since the children are named as dependants, the reader sees that the loss of the garden is the loss of a household's bread.

**THE SENTENCE THAT ASKS FOR THOUGHT**

The verse then names its own purpose: ***“This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you”*** ***“so perhaps you will reflect”***. The clarity is kept by al-Qurṭubī as the teaching given in pictures, since a mind holds an image better than a rule. And the same is kept by Ibn Kathīr with the note that the closing call to reflect is what the whole passage was building towards.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the question was left for the reader to answer in his own heart. For its part, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the remark that a person who has answered it honestly has already understood the two parables of the garden and the rock. Because the verse ends with a call to think rather than with a command, the reader is shown how the Book leaves a lesson standing in front of a person.

The contrast of the two gardens is stated in the verse before this one, (2:265 — **“If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient”**). And the same call to reflection closes the passage of the spending, (2:272 — **“and you will not be wronged”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has built his whole standing on one good deed of his youth and has not looked at it in years. The verse gives him a flourishing garden, an old age and a fire in one night, and it asks him what he would have left if the wind turned before the morning. Because the close asks him to reflect rather than to weep, the reader is taught that the question is a warning given early enough to be used. Since the garden is described before the fire, the reader sees that the loss was drawn for him in full before he was asked to answer.

The case is like a man who plants a grove in the year his first child is born and waters it every dry season until his hair is white. The fire comes on the evening after his youngest son's wedding, and the only thing that survives is the line of the ditch he dug with his own hands.

---

## Verse 2:267

> O believers! Donate from the best of what you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth. Do not pick out worthless things for donation, which you yourselves would only accept with closed eyes. And know that Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy

**THE COMMAND TO GIVE FROM THE BEST**

The verse opens the next stretch of the passage about giving: ***“O believers! Donate from the best of what you have earned”*** ***“and of what We have produced”*** ***“for you from the earth.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the earning as the profit of trade and craft and the produce as the harvest of the field. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the two halves cover the wealth of a town and of a farm.

The reports that the sentence came down about men of the community who set aside the poor dates and the broken fruit for the charity are kept by al-Qurṭubī. And the plain reading of the good things is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the best is named rather than the surplus, the reader is shown what kind of gift the Book is asking for. Since the wealth is described as earned and grown, the reader sees that the command covers the work of the hand and the yield of the soil.

**THE THINGS THAT WOULD BE REFUSED**

The verse then forbids the other way: ***“Do not pick out worthless things”*** ***“for donation, which you yourselves would only accept with closed eyes.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the closed eyes as the picture of a man who takes a bad thing because he has no choice. Here too, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the sentence puts the giver in the place of the receiver for a moment.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that a person who would not take a thing for his own household should not send it to the house of the Lord. For its part, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the plain sense that the poor are the guests of the community and not its bin. Because the gift is measured by what the giver would accept himself, the reader is shown the standard the Book uses for a charity. Since the receiver is placed in the seat of the giver for one sentence, the reader is taught that the poor are the neighbours of the giver and not his strangers.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends on a pair that answers the whole command: ***“And know that Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy”***. al-Baghawī keeps the first as the freedom of the Lord from needing any gift. And the second as the praise that belongs to Him whether or not a person gives.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the same pair with the note that the two names close the door on the thought that a bad gift is better than none, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading in a short form. Because the close names the sufficiency of the Lord, the reader is shown that the charity is the need of the giver rather than of the One who is given to. Since the praise belongs to the Lord in either case, the reader sees that a bad gift takes nothing from the glory of the Giver of all.

The giving of the best is joined to the promise of the reward in the verses that follow, (2:272 — **“Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full”**). And the parable of the good ground is drawn in the verse before this one, (2:265 — **“that of a garden on a fertile hill”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who clears a shelf of things his own family will not use and calls the pile a donation. The verse gives him the earning of his hands, the produce of the earth and a closed eye in front of his own gift. And it asks him what the receiver would say if he could see the house the sack came from. Because the close names the Self-Sufficient and the Praiseworthy, the reader is taught that the Lord of the worlds accepts a gift for its worth and not for its weight.

The case is like a man who is invited to a wedding and takes the fruit from the bottom of the basket at his door, where the flies have been. The hosts put the dish out with the others, and the guests pass it on to the next table without lifting the cloth.

---

## Verse 2:268

> The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty and bids you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺, while Allah promises you forgiveness and ˹great˺ bounties from Him. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing

**THE TWO VOICES AT THE PURSE**

The verse sets two speakers in front of a person with money: ***“The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty”*** ***“and bids you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the threat as the fear planted in a heart that the giving will leave a family hungry. Here too, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the shameful deed named here is the holding back of what is owed.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports of the community on the way the whisper works on a person at the hour of the gift, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain pair of the threat and the promise. Because the verse puts the two voices side by side, the reader is shown that the argument for giving and the argument for keeping are both heard inside one chest.

**THE PROMISE FROM THE OTHER SIDE**

The verse then gives the answer: ***“while Allah promises you forgiveness”*** ***“and ˹great˺ bounties from Him.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the forgiveness as the covering of the sins of a giver and the bounties as the provision that comes back in a form no one expected. For its part, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the two promises answer the two fears, the fear of loss and the fear of want.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading that the promise of the Lord stands against the threat of the whisperer. In the same way, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that a person weighs the two voices by the standing of the one who speaks. Because the forgiving and the giving stand in one sentence, the reader is shown what a closed hand is really refusing. Since the whisper is answered with a promise rather than with a warning, the reader sees that the Book argues with a frightened person by giving him something better to fear losing.

**THE TWO NAMES AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends with the pair that seals the promise: ***“And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the wealth that is never reduced by giving. And the second as the knowledge of the struggle inside the person who is deciding.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same pair with the note that the knowledge is named because the fear of poverty is a hidden thing that no neighbour can see, and al-Baghawī keeps the same in a short form. Because the close names the One who knows the whisper, the reader is shown that the argument was never as private as it felt.

The same promise of forgiveness and bounty is kept in the verse about the good Loan, (2:245 — **“Who will lend to Allah a good loan”**). And the giving that is spoiled by a word is treated in the verses just above this one, (2:264 — **“O believers! Do not waste your charity”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has heard the argument about his old age in his own head every time he opens his purse. The verse gives him a threat and a promise, an enemy who speaks of poverty and a Lord who speaks of forgiveness, and it asks him whose voice he has been calling the voice of reason. Because the close names the One who knows what is in the chest, the reader is taught that the whisper is answered by a promise and not by a debate. Since the two names at the end speak of wealth and of knowledge, the reader sees that the argument is settled in two places he cannot see.

The case is like a man who keeps his grain behind a locked door because a neighbour once told him that the winter would be long. The winter passes, the grain goes mouldy in the dark, and the neighbour who borrowed from him in the spring is the one who carries his harvest to the market.

---

## Verse 2:269

> Allah grants wisdom to whoever He wills. And whoever is granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege. But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason

**THE GIFT THAT IS NOT EARNED**

The greatest of the things a person may be given is then named: ***“Allah grants wisdom to whoever He wills.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the wisdom as the understanding of the religion and the right judgement in the affairs of a life. Here too, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence makes the gift an act of the Lord rather than a fruit of study.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading that the giving is by the will of the Lord. For its part, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the reminder comes in the middle of the verses about money so that a reader would know what is worth more than wealth. Because the will is named before the gift, the reader is shown where the road to understanding starts. Since the giving is left open to whoever the Lord chooses, the reader sees that no family and no school holds the key to it.

**THE PRIVILEGE THAT IS CALLED GREAT**

The verse then names the worth of the gift: ***“And whoever is granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the privilege as the good that no wealth can buy. In the same way, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the sentence puts a gift of the mind above the gifts of the hand.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that a person who can tell the better from the worse in his own affairs has been handed the ground of every other good. In the same vein, And Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same with the plain sense that the privilege is the wisdom itself. Because the gift is called a privilege rather than a reward, the reader is shown that it was never owed to anyone. Since the privilege is named as great, the reader sees that the Book measures it against the wealth of the whole passage.

**THE PEOPLE OF REASON WHO TAKE THE REMINDER**

The verse closes with a sentence about who hears it: ***“But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason”***. The reason is kept by al-Ālūsī as the mind that follows a proof where it leads rather than where the person wants it to go. And the same is kept by al-Baghawī with the note that the reminder is offered to everyone and taken by a few.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the close, and as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the remark that the people of reason are named last so that a reader would ask himself which company he stands in. Because the close names the mind of the hearer, the reader is shown that the road to wisdom passes through a listening heart. Since the reminder is named as the thing taken, the reader is taught that the wisdom of a person is shown in what he does with a warning.

The gift of understanding is asked for in the prayer of the end of the chapter, (2:286 — **“Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us”**). And the wisdom that comes from the Lord is named beside the Book in another passage of the chapter, (2:231 — **“Remember Allah’s favours upon you”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who reads the books of his trade for years and finds that his decisions in his own house have not improved. The verse gives him a gift that is asked for rather than bought, a privilege above wealth and a company of people who can hear a reminder. And it asks him how often he has asked for the first of the three. Because the close names the people of reason, the reader is taught that the mind which takes a warning is the mind that was given the warning as a gift.

The case is like two men who inherit the same shop, one of whom spends his evenings at the account books and the other at the door watching the street. The second learns what the customers want before the first has finished his first column, and the shop of the second is the one that is still open.

---

## Verse 2:270

> Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely known to Allah. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers

**THE GIFT AND THE VOW THAT ARE KNOWN**

The verse gathers the two kinds of giving that a person may keep to himself: ***“Whatever charities you give”*** ***“or vows you make are surely known to Allah.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the charity as the gift of the hand and the vow as the promise a person binds himself to for the sake of God. In the same way, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence covers the small gift and the private promise in one word.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the two, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence answers a person who wonders whether a hidden gift counts at all. Because the knowledge of the Lord is named rather than a reward, the reader is shown that the account of a private deed is kept before the deed is paid.

**THE DEEDS THAT HAVE NO WITNESS BUT ONE**

The two acts that often leave no trace among people are then named: ***“Whatever charities you give”*** ***“or vows you make”***. The reading that the knowledge of the Lord makes the smallest gift as visible in the account as the largest is kept by as-Saʿdī. And the same, with the remark that a vow made in a quiet room is a debt registered in a book no hand can tear, is kept by al-Ālūsī.

The plain sense that a person who has promised God a thing is held to it whether or not anyone heard is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the note that the sentence comforts the giver whose charity is known only to the poor man at his door, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the deeds are named as known, the reader is shown what the fear of a hidden slip and the hope of a hidden gift both rest on. Since the two acts are joined in one sentence, the reader sees that the hand and the tongue are read from the same page.

**THE WRONGDOERS AND THE HELPERS THEY LACK**

The verse closes with a warning that reaches those who keep what they promised: ***“And the wrongdoers will have no helpers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the helpers as the family and the friends who might speak for a man in the day of the account. Alongside that, And al-Jalālayn keeps the plain sense that no company will stand with the one who withheld the truth.

al-Baghawī keeps the reading that the helper is denied because the one who wrongs others gathers no friends who will pay for him. Here too, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the closing line is placed after a sentence about charity so that the reader would see the two roads of wealth. Because the verse ends on the absence of help, the reader is shown the last state of a person who keeps everything for himself. Since the sentence is short and stands alone, the reader sees that the Book leaves the thought to settle on its own.

The gifts that are given openly and in secret are weighed in the verse that follows, (2:271 — **“but to give to the poor privately is better”**). And the reward of the giving is named in the same passage, (2:274 — **“their reward is with their Lord”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has made a promise to God in a hard night and has been looking for a way to forget it quietly. The verse gives him a register that holds both the gift and the vow, and it asks him who he thinks is keeping the second column. Because the close names the wrongdoers as those who have no helpers, the reader is taught that the friends a person gathers in the world are the ones who stay away when the account is read. Since the helpers are named as absent rather than as unwilling, the reader sees that the loss of a wrongdoer is complete before anyone thinks about refusing him.

The case is like a man who borrows a sum from a friend and then gives the friend a wide berth for years. The debt stands in the friend's book all along, and the man is never seen in the market without looking over his shoulder.

---

## Verse 2:271

> To give charity publicly is good, but to give to the poor privately is better for you, and will absolve you of your sins. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**THE GIFT IN THE OPEN**

The verse allows the first way: ***“To give charity publicly is good”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the permission of the open gift, since it stirs others to follow and it shows the good example of a giver. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the permission is given without a reproach.

The reports of the community on the two kinds of giving. And the opinion that the open gift is the obligatory one and the secret gift the free one, are kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain reading of the permission is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the verse permits the open gift before it praises the hidden one, the reader is shown how carefully the Book treats the practice of a community.

**THE GIFT IN THE DARK**

The verse then weighs the two: ***“but to give to the poor privately is better”*** ***“for you, and will absolve you of your sins.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the private gift as the safer way for the giver, since no eye is there to share in the deed. And the covering of the sins as the mercy that follows such a gift.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the private gift protects the dignity of the poor man as well as the sincerity of the rich one. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the poor are named in the sentence because their feelings are part of the deed. Because the poor are named before the reward, the reader is shown what the Book places first in a charity.
