Since the private gift is called better for the giver, the reader sees that the mercy of a charity runs in both directions at once.

**THE NAME THAT WATCHES THE STREET**

The verse ends with the awareness that reaches the outer deed: ***“And Allah is All-Aware of what you do”***. Ibn Kathīr keeps the awareness as the knowledge of the gift and of the hand that gave it, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the close.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that the sentence is placed after both ways so that a reader would know that neither the loud gift nor the quiet one is hidden from the One who counts them, and as-Saʿdī keeps the same in a short form. Because the verse ends on the awareness of the Lord, the reader is shown where the two ways are finally weighed. Since the permission is given to the open gift, the reader is taught that no way of giving was ever closed to a sincere hand.

The open and the secret gift are joined to the promise of the reward in the verse above, (2:270 — **“Whatever charities you give”**). And the manner of the giving is guarded in the passage just before it, (2:264 — **“Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who gives in the open because he wants his neighbours to know that he is not a miser. The verse gives him a permission and a better road in one sentence, and it asks him what his gift would look like if the room were empty. Because the close names the One who is aware, the reader is taught that the quiet gift is the one with only one witness, and that witness is the reason it was given.

The case is like a man who leaves a bag of rice at his neighbour's door before the dawn prayer and walks away without knocking. The neighbour never learns who left it, and the man finds that he sleeps better on the nights when nobody says his name.

---

## Verse 2:272

> You are not responsible for people’s guidance ˹O Prophet˺—it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills. Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is for your own good—as long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah. Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full, and you will not be wronged

**THE BURDEN THAT IS LIFTED FROM THE MESSENGER**

The verse answers a worry the giver carries: ***“You are not responsible”*** ***“for people’s guidance ˹O Prophet˺”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the report that the sentence came down when some of the community were slow to give to the families of the unbelievers of the city, since the reward was thought to belong to the believers alone. In the same vein, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the name of the house it was told about.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that the givers had been told to keep their charity inside the community. And the answer of the verse that the turning of a heart belongs to the Lord, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the sentence. Because the verse lifts a burden from the messenger, the reader is shown what a person may and may not carry for another.

**THE GUIDANCE THAT BELONGS TO THE LORD**

The verse states the ground of the sentence: ***“it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the guidance is a gift of the Lord rather than a result of a coin. So that a giver would not weigh his charity by the change he sees, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence frees a person from a task he was never given.

The plain sense that the messenger carried the word and the Lord carried the hearts is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the remark that the verse is a comfort for every believer who has spent on a relative who did not change, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the duty is separated from the outcome, the reader is shown the limits of what one man can do for another. Since the guidance is named as the gift of the Lord, the reader sees that a change of heart is not the wage of a coin.

**THE GIFT THAT RETURNS TO THE GIVER**

The verse then turns to the purse: ***“Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is”*** ***“for your own good”*** ***“as long as you do”*** ***“so seeking the pleasure of Allah. Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full”*** ***“and you will not be wronged”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the condition as the purity of the aim. And the return as the reward the giver meets in the hand of the Lord.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the benefit of a charity comes back to the giver before it reaches the receiver. In the same way, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the sentence secures the gift from loss, whether the poor man thanks him or not. Because the gain is named as the giver's own, the reader is shown what a person is really buying with his coin. Since the return is promised in full, the reader sees that no gift is a loss and no receiver is a burden.

**THE FULL PAYMENT AND THE WRONG THAT IS LIFTED**

The verse closes on a promise without a measure: ***“Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full”*** ***“and you will not be wronged”***. al-Baghawī keeps the full payment as the return that loses nothing of the gift, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the close.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the wrong named here is the reduction of a reward, and as-Saʿdī keeps the same in a short form. Because the verse ends on the justice of the Lord, the reader is shown that the fear of a lost gift was never grounded in the first place.

The same return is promised to the spenders in the verse before this one, (2:271 — **“but to give to the poor privately is better”**). And the reward that is kept with the Lord is named again in the same passage, (2:274 — **“their reward is with their Lord”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has paid for the schooling of a nephew and has watched the boy drift away from the mosque. The verse gives him the word of guidance, the will of the Lord and a payment that comes back in full, and it asks him which of the three he was really working for. Because the close promises that no gift is reduced, the reader is taught that a charity is measured by the hand that gives and not by the life it changes.

The case is like a man who plants a tree at the edge of a road he does not own and never learns who eats the fruit. The tree stands for fifty years, the shade falls on the travellers of three generations, and the planter's name is on nothing but the soil.

---

## Verse 2:273

> ˹Charity is˺ for the needy who are too engaged in the cause of Allah to move about in the land ˹for work˺. Those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not in need ˹of charity˺ because they do not beg. You can recognize them by their appearance. They do not beg people persistently. Whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah

**THE POOR WHOSE WORK KEEPS THEM FROM THE ROAD**

The people a charity is meant for are then named: ***“˹Charity is˺ for the needy”*** ***“who are too engaged in the cause of Allah to move about in the land ˹for work˺.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the reports that the sentence came down about the men of the bench, the strangers of the city who had given themselves to the learning of the Book. Alongside that, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that their days were spent in the mosque and their nights on the benches of it.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the long discussion of the ten over the kind of poverty meant here, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading that these men could not take a trade because they were occupied. Because the reason for the poverty is named rather than the poverty itself, the reader is shown that the Book knows why a man might have nothing. Since the men are described as occupied rather than as idle, the reader sees that the community was asked to carry those who were carrying its learning.

**THE RICH LOOK OF A POOR MAN**

The verse then describes the ignorance of the neighbours: ***“Those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not in need ˹of charity˺”*** ***“because they do not beg.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that a poor man who keeps his quiet is mistaken for a man with enough. Here too, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the verse teaches the community to look past the asking hand.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that a person who does not beg is often left out of the charity of his own street. For its part, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the remark that the men of the bench were spared no meal by the community once it understood. Because the mistake is named before the cure, the reader is shown how the Book turns a neighbour's eye towards the truth of a house.

**THE SIGN THAT CAN BE SEEN**

The verse then gives the mark: ***“You can recognize them by their appearance.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the appearance as the paleness of a face and the worn cloth on a body. And the note of the ten that the walking and the manner of a man tell his story to anyone who looks with attention.

The same is kept by al-Ālūsī with the remark that the verse does not ask a believer to be a judge of hearts but to use the eyes he has. And the plain reading of the sign is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the Book gives a visible mark for a hidden need, the reader is shown that the duty of the neighbour is meant to be possible.

**THE ASKING THAT STOPS SHORT**

The verse then names the manner of these poor: ***“They do not beg people persistently.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as the mark of a person who asks once and then holds his peace. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the reports that the men of the bench would take what was given without complaint and would refuse to press any household twice.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the plain reading that the verse honours the pride of the poor rather than condemning it. Alongside that, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the community was taught to give before a man reaches the point of asking. Because the manner is named beside the need, the reader is shown what the quiet of a poor man costs him.

**THE GIFT THAT IS KNOWN TO THE LORD**

The verse closes with the sentence that reaches every charitable hand: ***“Whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah”***. al-Qurṭubī keeps the knowledge as the pledge that no gift of a man to a stranger is lost, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the close.

The same is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās with the note that the sentence ends on the knowledge of the Lord because the giver may never learn where his coin went. And the same is kept by as-Saʿdī in a short form. Because the verse ends on the knowledge of the Lord, the reader is shown that the quiet of a poor man and the quiet of a giver are both written in the same book.

The people whose poverty is not seen are remembered with the neighbours of the giver in the verse about the open and private gift, (2:271 — **“but to give to the poor privately is better”**). And the same company is promised abundance in the chapter of the night, where the Book speaks of the guest who came and was turned away.

The lesson also reaches a reader who gives at the door of a man whose car is old and whose clothes are clean. The verse gives him a poor man with no asking hand, a face that can be read and a gift that reaches its owner in the account. And it asks him how many such men he has walked past in his own street. Because the close names the One who knows every charity, the reader is taught that the merit of a gift does not depend on the address it reaches.

The case is like a neighbour who sits on his step every evening reading an old book while the other men of the street come home with their tools. Nobody in the street suspects that his cupboard has been empty for a week, and the family that feeds him once a month is the only one that ever learns his name.

---

## Verse 2:274

> Those who spend their wealth in charity day and night, secretly and openly—their reward is with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**THE GIVING THAT HAS NO HOUR**

The verse gathers the givers of every hour and every manner: ***“Those who spend their wealth in charity day”*** ***“and night, secretly and openly”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the two pairs as the times of the giving and the ways of it. So that no giver is left outside the promise, and al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence covers the small gift of the night as well as the open gift of the market.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that the verse came down for the men of the community who gave by day and by night, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the four words. Because the verse names no amount and no hour, the reader is shown how wide a promise can be made.

**THE REWARD THAT IS KEPT WITH THE LORD**

The verse then names what such givers hold: ***“their reward is with their Lord”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the sentence as the pledge that the return of a gift is kept in a hand that never runs dry. Alongside that, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the reward is named as being with the Lord so that no giver would look for it at the door of the man he fed.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the gift may bring no thanks in this world and lose nothing of its worth. Here too, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the remark that the sentence is set in the middle of the parables so that a reader would weigh it against the loss of a spoiled deed. Because the verse places the reward outside the street, the reader is shown where the account of a silent giver is kept.

**THE FEAR AND THE GRIEF THAT DO NOT REACH THEM**

The verse closes on the pair that has closed the earlier promise: ***“and there will be no fear”*** ***“for them, nor will they grieve”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the safety of the giver on the day of the account and the second as his freedom from regret over what he gave, and al-Baghawī keeps the same in a short form.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that no giver ever grieves over a gift that was taken by the Lord. For its part, And as-Saʿdī keeps the point that the two words cover the whole of a life, this world and the next. Because the verse ends on the two pains a person fears, the reader is shown what the charity of a night is worth.

The same promise was made to the givers who keep their tongues quiet, (2:262 — **“they will get their reward from their Lord”**). And the reward of the quiet giver was named with the knowledge of the Lord, (2:273 — **“Whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been told that a charity must be planned in the month of the accounts and given with a public hand. The verse gives him a night and a day, a secret and an open gift, and it asks him which of the four he has been leaving out of his ledger. Because the close removes the fear and the grief from such givers, the reader is taught that the generosity of a person ends where his regret begins and not where his purse does.

The case is like a woman who keeps a bowl of coins by her door and drops one in it on her way out and another on her way back in. The bowl fills slowly through the year, the neighbours who watch her never see the whole sum, and the orphans of the street eat through the winter without knowing where the bread comes from.

---

## Verse 2:275

> Those who consume interest will stand ˹on Judgment Day˺ like those driven to madness by Satan’s touch. That is because they say, “Trade is no different than interest.” But Allah has permitted trading and forbidden interest. Whoever refrains—after having received warning from their Lord—may keep their previous gains, and their case is left to Allah. As for those who persist, it is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**THE STANDING OF THE TAKERS OF INTEREST**

The verse opens the section on the wealth that grows on a debt: ***“Those who consume interest will stand ˹on Judgment Day˺ like those driven to madness by Satan’s touch.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the standing as the rising of the resurrection. And the picture as a man who cannot keep his feet and falls back each time he tries to stand.

al-Baghawī keeps the same with the reports of the community on the manner of that rising, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the long treatment of the rulings of interest that follows from this verse. Because the Book pictures the taker of interest as a man out of his own control, the reader is shown what the Book thinks of wealth that grows without work or risk.

**THE CLAIM THAT TRADE IS THE SAME**

The verse then gives the argument of the takers: ***“That is because they say, “Trade is no different than interest.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the claim as the reasoning of a man who compared the profit of a sale with the profit of a loan, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain form of their words.

The reading that the people of the days before Islam had made the two alike in their minds, since both bring a gain, is kept by as-Saʿdī. And the same, with the note that the Book answers the claim not by comparing the two profits but by naming the law, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the verse keeps the argument of the other side in its own words, the reader is shown that the Book is not afraid of the reasoning it answers.

**WHAT IS PERMITTED AND WHAT IS FORBIDDEN**

The verse then states the rule: ***“But Allah has permitted trading”*** ***“and forbidden interest.”*** al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings that grew from the two sentences. Here too, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the permission of trade and the ban on interest stand side by side so that no one would confuse the two.

The plain sense that the difference is made by the law rather than by the market is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. And the same, with the remark that the trade of a man carries work, risk and a sold good, while the loan carries none of them, is kept by Ibn Kathīr. Because the two are named in one line, the reader is shown how closely the forbidden thing resembles the permitted one. Since the difference is set by the law rather than by the market, the reader sees that a trader's own reasoning cannot be his guide.

**THE ONE WHO STOPS AND THE ONE WHO GOES ON**

The verse then divides the takers into two: ***“Whoever refrains”*** ***“after having received warning from their Lord”*** ***“may keep their previous gains”*** ***“and their case is left to Allah.”*** ***“As for those who persist, it is they”*** ***“who will be the residents of the Fire.”*** ***“They will be there forever”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the keeping of the past gains as the mercy shown to a man who was taken in the practice before the rule reached him. In the same way, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the door of the return is left open by the sentence.

al-Ālūsī keeps the reading that the persistence named at the end is the refusal that comes after the knowledge. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that the two ends of the verse are the two ends of a life, the stopping and the going on. Because the verse puts the mercy before the warning, the reader is shown what the Book prefers.

The ban on the practice is repeated in the commands that follow, (2:278 — **“and give up outstanding interest”**). And the mercy of the Lord over the past is named again in the promise to the givers, (2:274 — **“their reward is with their Lord”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has arranged his income so that a sum of money works for him without any trade behind it. The verse gives him a man stumbling on the day of the rising, an argument that the Book answers with a law and two doors at the close. And it asks him which of the two doors he is walking towards. Because the close names the fire for the man who goes on, the reader is taught that the danger of a practice is measured by what it does to the person who keeps it.

The case is like a farmer who lends his neighbour a sack of seed in the spring on the condition that he takes back a sack and a half in the harvest. The rain fails, the neighbour's crop is thin, and the farmer spends the winter arguing about a debt that was never in the ground with him.

---

## Verse 2:276

> Allah has made interest fruitless and charity fruitful. And Allah does not like any ungrateful evildoer

**THE TWO KINDS OF GROWTH**

The verse sets two forms of increase side by side: ***“Allah has made interest fruitless”*** ***“and charity fruitful.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the futility as the loss of the blessing on a wealth that grew on a debt. And the fruitfulness as the mark that the Lord puts on a gift.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports of the community on the man who lends at interest and finds his wealth thinner in the end, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain pair of the two sentences. Because the Book uses the picture of a plant for both, the reader is shown that the two kinds of wealth are judged by what they produce in the hand of the Lord.

**THE WEALTH THAT LOOKS LARGE**

The verse does not say the money disappears: ***“Allah has made interest fruitless”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the sum may grow in the counting while the blessing is taken from it. So that a man with a full purse may be a poor man in his own house.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the loss is in the account of the Lord rather than in the ledger of the market. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence explains the doom of the previous verse in a quieter way. Because the futility is named without being described, the reader is shown how much the Book leaves to a thinking mind. Since the two kinds of growth are set side by side, the reader sees that the choice between them is put in front of him every day.

**THE GIFT THAT MULTIPLIES**

The second half of the sentence gives the other growth: ***“and charity fruitful”***. al-Baghawī keeps the fruitfulness as the increase that the Lord writes into a gift. On this point, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that a small gift of a poor man may be written as a mountain in the account.

The plain reading that the two sentences together are the whole argument of the section on wealth is kept by Ibn Kathīr, and the same is kept by al-Jalālayn in a short form. Because the verse puts the two in one breath, the reader is shown that every purse is either working for its owner or against him.

**THE NAME THAT CLOSES THE SECTION**

The verse ends with the sentence about the character of the practice: ***“And Allah does not like any ungrateful evildoer”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the ungrateful as the man who received his wealth from the hand of the Lord and then used it in the way the Lord forbade. Alongside that, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the disbelief of a person shows first in his treatment of the weak.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the close, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that the sentence is placed after the two kinds of growth so that a reader would see how a man becomes ungrateful. Because the verse ends on what the Lord does not like, the reader is shown that the matter is a question of gratitude before it is a question of money.

The pair of the two growths is carried on in the command that follows the section, (2:278 — **“O believers! Fear Allah”**), and the reward of the fruitful charity is named in the passage above, (2:274 — **“their reward is with their Lord”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who compares the interest on his savings with the gifts he gives and finds that the first column is the thicker one. The verse gives him a growth that is taken away and a growth that is kept, and it asks him which of the two ledgers his children would rather inherit. Because the close names the ungrateful, the reader is taught that the man who forgets where his wealth came from is already spending a gift he did not earn.

The case is like two fields in the same plain, one of them rented out for a fixed sum every season without the owner lifting a hand. And the other worked by the owner himself; the rented field is bare in the year the tenant leaves, and the worked field feeds the family that planted it.

---

## Verse 2:277

> Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**THE FOUR MARKS OF THE COMPANY**

The verse gathers the believers under four marks: ***“Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer”*** ***“and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the four as the belief of the heart, the work of the hands, the prayer of the body and the giving of the purse. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the verse places the four in one company.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the list, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the verse stands after the section on interest so that the reader would see the two kinds of person side by side. Because the marks begin with the heart and end with the purse, the reader is shown the whole route a belief takes through a life.

**THE REWARD THAT IS NAMED AFTER THE MARKS**

The verse then promises the return: ***“will receive their reward from their Lord”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the reward is named as coming from the Lord because the four works are done for Him rather than for a market. In the same way, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the verse is the answer to the section on the wealth that grows on a debt.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the four works are the description of the community that the Book is building. In the same vein, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that the marks are given in the order of a person's day, from the belief in the morning to the giving in the evening. Because the reward is named after the marks, the reader is shown what the Book counts as a life. Since the four works are gathered in one sentence, the reader sees that no single deed stands alone as the whole of a faith.

**THE TWO PAINS THAT ARE LIFTED**

The verse closes with the pair that has closed the promises of the passage: ***“and there will be no fear”*** ***“for them, nor will they grieve”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the first as the safety of the day of the account and the second as the freedom from regret over the years that were spent, and al-Baghawī keeps the same in a short form.

as-Saʿdī keeps the point that a person who has spent his life between the four works has nothing to dread in front of him and nothing to mourn behind him. On this point, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the two words close the whole treatment of wealth in this chapter. Because the verse ends on the two pains, the reader is shown what the four marks buy in this world before the next.

The same four works are named in the closing of the chapter, where the believers pray for pardon, (2:286 — **“Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us”**). And the giving of the alms-tax is joined to the prayer in the chapter of the prophets, (20:14 — **“and establish prayer for My remembrance”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been looking for a single deed large enough to settle his whole account. The verse gives him four works that fit into one ordinary day, and it asks him which of the four he has left to the side. Because the close removes the fear and the grief from such people, the reader is taught that the peace of a life is built out of small things done on ordinary mornings.

The case is like a household that opens its shutters at dawn, sweeps the yard, keeps its prayers and sets aside a share of the day's bread for a neighbour. Nothing in the house is remarkable, and the family is the one the whole street calls when it needs a hand.

---

## Verse 2:278

> O believers! Fear Allah, and give up outstanding interest if you are ˹true˺ believers

**THE COMMAND THAT CLOSES THE DEBATE**

The verse addresses the community with a command and a condition: ***“O believers! Fear Allah”*** ***“and give up outstanding interest”*** ***“if you are ˹true˺ believers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the fear as the guard over the heart that makes a person leave a profit he has already counted. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the command was sent to the men of the city who had sums still owed to them.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings that a Muslim who owed or was owed such a sum was told to surrender the increase and keep only the principal, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the sentence. Because the command is tied to the confession of belief, the reader is shown that the matter is not a matter of trade but of faith. Since the address is made to the whole community, the reader sees that the practice was never the business of a few moneylenders.

**THE SUMS THAT ARE STILL OUT**

What is to be left is then named: ***“and give up outstanding interest”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the command covers the increase still owed on a running debt rather than the increase already taken in the past, since the previous verse left the past to the mercy of the Lord.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that a man with a hand in such a contract was asked to lift it. In the same way, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence was the hardest of the commands for the traders of that city. Because the sums still owed are named, the reader is shown how practical the Book is in the way it dismantles a practice.

**THE CONDITION THAT WEIGHS THE COMMAND**

The verse closes on the words that put the command inside the creed: ***“if you are ˹true˺ believers”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the condition as the proof that the surrender of the profit is the mark of a faith that reaches the purse. In the same vein, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the sentence leaves no room for the man who keeps the creed and the practice together.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the close, and as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the remark that the verse is written as an address from start to finish, since a command about wealth reaches a person at his counter. Because the close speaks of belief, the reader is shown that the last word on the matter belongs to the heart. Since the fear of God is named before the giving up, the reader sees the order in which a person is asked to move.

The warning that follows the command is given in the next verse, (2:279 — **“then beware of a war with Allah”**). And the mercy left for the past is named in the verse above, (2:275 — **“may keep their previous gains”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has a small sum of interest owed to him and tells himself that the amount is too small to matter. The verse gives him a command, a condition and a closing word about belief, and it asks him what he would do if the sum were ten times larger. Because the verse ties the giving up to the sincerity of a faith, the reader is taught that the size of the sum is a matter for the ledger and the obedience is a matter for the heart.

The case is like a man who has agreed to take a basket of fruit from his neighbour's tree at the end of the season in return for a loan he made in the spring. The season comes, the fruit is at the door, and the man stands in his yard deciding whether to carry the basket back over the wall.

---

## Verse 2:279

> If you do not, then beware of a war with Allah and His Messenger! But if you repent, you may retain your principal—neither inflicting nor suffering harm

**THE WARNING OF A WAR**

The verse follows the command with the heaviest warning of the passage: ***“If you do not”*** ***“then beware of a war with Allah”*** ***“and His Messenger!”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the warning as the declaration of a war that the community was to carry against the practice. Here too, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the reports that the men of the city took the sentence seriously enough to give up their claims.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings that a ruler of the community was to make the practice the business of the state rather than the quarrel of two men, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the warning. Because a war is named rather than a fine, the reader is shown that this matter stands in a class of its own among the sins. Since the war is declared by the Lord and His messenger together, the reader sees that the community itself is asked to take the side of the weak.

**THE REPENTANCE THAT KEEPS THE CAPITAL**

The verse then opens the door: ***“But if you repent, you may retain your principal”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the repentance as the turning away from the practice. And the capital as the sum that belongs to the lender whatever the law says about the increase.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the man who turns back keeps the wealth he lent and loses only the profit that grew on it. In the same way, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the sentence protects the wealth of the lender while it protects the borrower from the increase. Because the principal is named rather than a punishment, the reader is shown how carefully the Book divides the two.

**THE BALANCE THAT DOES NOT LEAN**

The verse closes on the two sides of the contract: ***“neither inflicting nor suffering harm”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the first as the harm of the lender who takes more than he gave. And the second as the harm of the borrower who withholds what he owes, and al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the sentence puts the two parties on one scale.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the close, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the remark that the rule of the Book in the matter of a debt is the return of the like, since the lender gains nothing and the borrower loses nothing beyond what he took. Because the two harms stand at the close, the reader is shown what a just contract is meant to leave behind. Since the borrower is named as the one who may suffer, the reader sees that the Book is guarding the side that has no power in the bargain. Since the capital is protected for the lender and the increase is taken from him, the reader sees that the Book refuses to mend one wrong with another.

The command that shows the way out of the practice is given just above this verse, (2:278 — **“and give up outstanding interest”**). And the patience owed to a man in difficulty is commanded in the verse that follows, (2:280 — **“postpone it until a time of ease”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been told that a warning about a war can only mean the swords of a battlefield. The verse gives him a declaration, a door of return and a balance with two pans. And it asks him what kind of war the Book is threatening when the dispute is between a rich man and a man who cannot pay. Because the close names the two harms, the reader is taught that the community's answer to the practice is the protection of the weak and not the punishment of the poor.

The case is like a man who has taken a load of goods on trust and finds in the market that the price has fallen. The seller wants the old figure, the buyer has only the new one, and the whole street waits to see whether the two men will settle or go to the judge.

---

## Verse 2:280

> If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt, postpone it until a time of ease. And if you waive it as an act of charity, it will be better for you, if only you knew

**THE DEBTOR WHO CANNOT PAY**

The verse turns from the lender's profit to the borrower's burden: ***“If it is difficult”*** ***“for someone to repay a debt, postpone it”*** ***“until a time of ease.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the difficulty as the poverty that leaves a man with nothing over his family's bread. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the postponement is owed to a man whose case is known and not only claimed.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the rulings on the man who has a little property and the man who has none, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain command of the waiting. Because the lender is asked to wait rather than to forgive, the reader is shown how the Book leads a person from the easy duty to the greater one. Since the postponement is owed to the man whose case is known, the reader sees that the community is expected to know its own poor.

**THE SLACK THAT BECOMES A GIFT**

The verse then names the better road: ***“And if you waive it”*** ***“as an act of charity, it will be better”*** ***“for you, if only you knew”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the waiver as the surrender of the debt itself. In the same way, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the sentence moves the lender from the patience of a creditor to the open hand of a giver.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the debt of a poor man is one of the best places for a charity. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the remark that the Book weighs the two roads for the lender rather than for the debtor. Because the waiver is named as better rather than as permitted, the reader is shown what the Book would choose for a man with a claim. Since the lender keeps his right in either case, the reader sees that the Book asks for a gift and never for an injustice.

**THE KNOWLEDGE THAT WOULD SETTLE THE MATTER**

The verse ends on a phrase that calls the reader to weigh it himself: ***“if only you knew”***. al-Baghawī keeps the words as the invitation to think about the reward that the Lord writes for such a giver, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the close.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the sentence leaves the choice in the hands of the lender without taking away any of his right. On this point, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the remark that a man who was told the value of a charity would spend his days looking for debtors. Because the close speaks of what a person knows, the reader is shown that the whole question is one of understanding. Since the choice is left in the hand of the lender, the reader sees that the Book prefers a gift that was decided freely. Because a man weighs a debt against a reward that no ledger holds, the reader is taught that the arithmetic of the market cannot settle this account.

The postponement of the debt is joined to the command of the purchases in the debt verse that follows, (2:282 — **“When you contract a loan”**). And the mercy shown to the poor is named with the reward of the givers, (2:274 — **“their reward is with their Lord”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been chasing a man for a small sum for two years and finds that the chase has cost him more than the sum. The verse gives him a waiting and a waiver, a reward for the second and a claim he may keep, and it asks him which of the two he would rather carry into the day of the account. Because the close says that a knowing man would do it, the reader is taught that the obstacle was never the money but the arithmetic he uses.

The case is like a man whose tenant cannot pay the last month of the rent after a season of illness. The landlord lets the month go and keeps the tenant for another five years, and the empty room he was afraid of standing vacant is filled with another family the same week.

---

## Verse 2:281

> Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done, and none will be wronged

**THE DAY THAT GATHERS EVERY ACCOUNT**

The verse closes the long treatment of wealth with a command about the day: ***“Be mindful of the Day”*** ***“when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah”***. al-Ṭabarī keeps the mindfulness as the guard that a person keeps over his dealings because he knows where they will be read. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the return is named as a gathering rather than as a journey.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports that the verse was among the last to come down, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the return. Because the sentence is placed after the rules about interest and debts, the reader is shown what the Book wanted a trader to carry into his shop.

**THE PAYMENT THAT REACHES EVERY SOUL**

The verse then states the account: ***“then every soul will be paid in full”*** ***“for what it has done”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the payment as the exact meeting of a person with the work of his own hands. In the same way, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the payment covers the coins that were counted and the words that were spoken over a man in difficulty.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that every soul is paid for its own deeds and not for the deeds of a family. In the same vein, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the remark that the sentence puts the small wrong of a dishonest contract beside the great crimes of a life. Because the payment is named as full, the reader is shown that nothing of a loan or a gift will be left out of the reckoning.

**THE WRONG THAT NO ONE SUFFERS**

The verse ends with the sentence that guards the justice of the day: ***“and none will be wronged”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the words as the promise that no soul is asked for more than it did, and al-Baghawī keeps the same in a short form.

al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the sentence is placed after the payment so that no reader would think the account leans against him. On this point, And as-Saʿdī keeps the point that the man who was wronged in this world will find the wrong recorded in his favour. Because the verse ends on the justice of the Lord, the reader is shown where the debts that were never paid in the market are settled.

The same day is named in the command about the debts of the rich, (2:280 — **“postpone it until a time of ease”**). And the same justice is stated in the closing verse of the chapter, (2:286 — **“Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has settled a matter with a poor man by a clever reading of a contract. The verse gives him a day, a full payment and a promise that no one is wronged, and it asks him whose signature he thinks is holding the paper. Because the close removes the wrong from the account, the reader is taught that the man who gains by a trick will meet the loss in another court. Since the day is named before the payment and the payment before the promise, the reader sees the order in which the Book wants a person to think about his dealings.

The case is like a dealer who weighs his sacks with a stone in the pan and counts the difference as his profit for a year. The stone is found in the pan one morning by his own son, and every customer he cheated is standing at the door before the evening.

---

## Verse 2:282

> O believers! When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing. Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties. The scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write. They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt. If the debtor is incompetent, weak, or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate for them with justice. Call upon two of your men to witness. If two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice will witness—so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her. The witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned. You must not be against writing ˹contracts˺ for a fixed period—whether the sum is small or great. This is more just ˹for you˺ in the sight of Allah, and more convenient to establish evidence and remove doubts. However, if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves, then there is no need for you to record it, but call upon witnesses when a deal is finalized. Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses. If you do, then you have gravely exceeded ˹your limits˺. Be mindful of Allah, for Allah ˹is the One Who˺ teaches you. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**THE LONGEST COMMAND IN THE BOOK**

The verse opens with the address and the case: ***“O believers! When you contract a loan”*** ***“for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the writing as the record that protects both parties from a quarrel later. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence covers the trading of a debt as well as a plain loan.

The long treatment of the ten over the meaning of the contract meant here. And over the wisdom of a written record in the dealings of a community, is kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain reading of the command is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the Book writes a rule for the paperwork of a market, the reader is shown how far the law reaches into the ordinary business of a town.

**THE SCRIBE AND THE JUSTICE HE OWES**

The verse then turns to the one who writes: ***“Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties.”*** ***“The scribe should not refuse to write”*** ***“as Allah has taught them to write.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the justice as the exact record without a leaning to either side. And the teaching as the skill that was given to the writer, so that the sentence asks him to pay for it with the service of his hand.

The reading that the ability to write is a gift that carries a duty is kept by as-Saʿdī. And the same, with the note that the community was told to keep its own records rather than to leave the matter to memory, is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān. Because the scribe is asked to work without payment in this verse, the reader is shown what a shared skill owes to a community.

**THE WORDS OF THE DEBTOR AND THE GUARDIAN**

The verse then fixes whose words go into the record: ***“They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind”*** ***“and not defrauding the debt.”*** ***“If the debtor is incompetent, weak”*** ***“or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate”*** ***“for them with justice.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the dictation as the right of the man who carries the debt, since he is the one who will answer for it. Alongside that, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the note that the guardian stands in the place of a person who cannot speak for himself.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the record follows the debtor so that no lender would write a larger sum into the paper. Here too, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the remark that the guardian who dictates is held to the same justice as the debtor himself. Because the weak and the unable are named, the reader is shown that the law of the contract was made for the people who are usually left out of one.

**THE WITNESSES AND THE TWO WOMEN**

The verse then commands the witnessing: ***“Call upon two of your men to witness.”*** ***“If two men cannot be found”*** ***“then one man and two women of your choice will witness”*** ***“so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her.”*** ***“The witnesses must not refuse”*** ***“when they are summoned.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the pairing as the wisdom of the community for the matter of recall. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the reports of the ten on the differences of people in the keeping of a testimony.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the duty of a witness is owed to the community, since a right that has no witness is a right that dies, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the numbers. Because the reminder of one woman to another is named, the reader is shown what the concern of the Book for an ordinary memory is worth.

**THE SMALL SUM AND THE LARGE**

The verse then forbids the leaving out of the small matters: ***“You must not be against writing ˹contracts˺”*** ***“for a fixed period whether the sum is small”*** ***“or great.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the answer of a person who thinks a small debt too light for a paper. In the same way, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the rulings that grew from the words.

The reading that the habit of a written record is kept by the small contracts as much as by the great ones is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, since a market learns its habits from its usual trade. And the same is kept by Ibn Kathīr with the note that the two sizes are named so that no borrower would be ashamed to write a little. Because the small is named before the great in one line, the reader is shown that the Book counts the two alike.

**THE JUSTICE OF THE RECORD AND THE EVIDENCE**

The verse then gives the reason for the command: ***“This is more just ˹for you˺ in the sight of Allah”*** ***“and more convenient to establish evidence”*** ***“and remove doubts.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the justice as the fairness of a written agreement and the removal of doubts as the end of the quarrels that devour a community. On this point, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the sentence is the wisdom behind the whole verse.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that a written paper settles a matter before two men have to stand in front of a judge. Alongside that, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that the doubts named here are the doubts of the two parties about each other. Because the peace a paper brings is named, the reader is shown how the Book builds the trust of a market out of a habit.

**THE IMMEDIATE SALE AND THE WITNESSES**

The verse then gives the exception: ***“However”*** ***“if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves”*** ***“then there is no need”*** ***“for you to record it”*** ***“but call upon witnesses”*** ***“when a deal is finalized.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the exception as the allowance made for a sale completed in the market, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the words.

as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that even the small sale is asked to have its witnesses, since a record is the harder duty and a witness the easier one. Here too, And al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the rulings on the hand-to-hand trade of the town. Because the verse lightens the paper and keeps the witness, the reader is shown how the law carries a community by steps.

**THE WRONG DONE TO THE SCRIBE AND THE WITNESS**

The verse then guards the men who serve the two duties: ***“Let no harm come to the scribe”*** ***“or witnesses.”*** ***“If you do”*** ***“then you have gravely exceeded ˹your limits˺.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the harm as the loss of a day's work or the pressing of a writer and a witness beyond what they owe. For its part, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the sentence protects the weak man who is asked to serve a rich one.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the reading that a community which punishes its own writers and witnesses will soon have none. In the same way, And al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that the crossing of the limits named at the end is the wrong done to a volunteer. Because the two who serve without a wage are named, the reader is shown what the law thinks of the people who carry its own machinery.

**THE CLOSE ON TEACHING AND KNOWLEDGE**

The verse closes on the two names that hold the whole passage: ***“Be mindful of Allah”*** ***“for Allah ˹is the One Who˺ teaches you.”*** ***“And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things”***. al-Jalālayn keeps the teaching as the very rules that were given in the verse. So that the command is paid for by the One who taught it, and al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the knowledge named at the end reaches every hidden term of a contract.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the reports of the community on the value of the verse. On this point, And as-Saʿdī keeps the reading that the Book ends a page of rules about paper and witnesses with the two names that no clerk can hold in a file. Because the verse ends on knowledge, the reader is shown who the witness of every private agreement is.

The justice of the day of the account is named in the verse just before this one, (2:281 — **“and none will be wronged”**). And the same care for the weak man is commanded in the verse about buying on trust, (2:280 — **“postpone it until a time of ease”**).

The wisdom of the passage is drawn out by al-Qurṭubī, who keeps the note that a paper protects the lender from a denial and the borrower from a demand. So that neither party needs to suspect the other, and by al-Baghawī, who keeps the same with the remark that the Book made the record a duty of the religion rather than a habit of the merchants. The two readings belong together, because the paper serves the lender who fears a loss and the borrower who fears an unfair claim, and neither of them is asked to trust a memory. Since the long verse covers the writer, the debtor, the guardian, the witnesses and the small sum as well as the great, the reader is shown that no part of a market was left outside the teaching. A community that writes its contracts is a community whose quarrels are settled at the desk instead of at the gate. And the habit travels from the desk into the household, where a family that writes its agreements keeps its peace.

The lesson also reaches a trader who keeps his agreements in his head because the men he deals with are his friends. The verse gives him a writer, a paper, two witnesses and a rule that the small sum is written like the great one. And it asks him what his friendships would look like if the market turned and every memory grew short. Because the close names the knowledge of the Lord over all things, the reader is taught that the paper is written for the day when a friend becomes a litigant. The paper is a mercy for the honest, since it frees a man from being doubted by his own brother.

The case is like two neighbours who divide a field between their houses by a line of stones that only they can remember, and whose children argue about the line twenty years after the two men have died. The stones are moved by the plough of a stranger, and the friendship of the fathers is spent in a court by sons who never quarrelled while they were alive.

---

## Verse 2:283

> If you are on a journey and a scribe cannot be found, then a security can be taken. If you trust one another, then ˹there is no need for a security, but˺ the debtor should honour this trust ˹by repaying the debt˺—and let them fear Allah, their Lord. And do not conceal the testimony, for whoever conceals it, their hearts are indeed sinful. And Allah ˹fully˺ knows what you do

**THE PLEDGE ON THE ROAD**

The verse gives the rule for the case where the paper is out of reach: ***“If you are on a journey”*** ***“and a scribe cannot be found”*** ***“then a security can be taken.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the security as a pledge held in the hand of the lender until the debt is paid. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence was sent for the traders who met on the roads between the towns.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the long treatment of the rulings on the pledge, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the journey. Because the Book provides for a case that would look impossible on a road, the reader is shown how carefully the law of the market was built.

**THE TRUST THAT TAKES THE PLACE OF A PAPER**

The verse then names the better way: ***“If you trust one another”*** ***“then ˹there is no need for a security, but˺ the debtor should honour this trust ˹by repaying the debt˺”*** ***“and let them fear Allah, their Lord.”*** as-Saʿdī keeps the trust as the honesty of a borrower who was given the goods on his word. Alongside that, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the fear of the Lord is named where no witness and no paper stand.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that a man who is trusted with a debt carries the claim in his own chest. Here too, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the remark that the sentence makes the honesty of a borrower a matter between him and his Lord. Because the fear of the Lord is named at the exact place where the world cannot see, the reader is shown what the Book counts as a strong man.

**THE TESTIMONY THAT MAY NOT BE HIDDEN**

The verse then guards the witness: ***“And do not conceal the testimony”*** ***“for whoever conceals it, their hearts are”*** ***“indeed sinful.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the hiding as the silence of a man who saw a contract and is asked about it later. For its part, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the sentence covers the witness of a right as well as the witness of a crime.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the words, and al-Ālūsī keeps the same with the remark that the sin is placed in the heart first, since the tongue hides what the man already knows. Because the verse speaks of a hidden act rather than of a public one, the reader is shown how the Book treats the wrongs that a court would never find.

**THE KNOWLEDGE AT THE CLOSE**

The verse ends on the name that reaches the chest of the silent witness: ***“And Allah ˹fully˺ knows what you do”***. as-Saʿdī keeps the knowledge as the record of the spoken word and of the word that was swallowed, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the plain reading of the close.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the same with the note that the sentence was placed after the command so that no witness would think his silence a private matter, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same in a short form. Because the verse ends on the knowledge of the Lord, the reader is shown that the court of the heart has no appeal.

The writing of the contract is commanded in the verse before this one, (2:282 — **“When you contract a loan”**). And the payment of every soul on the day of the account is stated in the verse above it, (2:281 — **“then every soul will be paid in full”**).

The lesson also reaches a man who witnessed a loan between two relatives and has said nothing for years because both men are still alive. The verse gives him a trust, a pledge and a testimony that may not be hidden, and it asks him what he would say if the matter were read out in front of the family. Because the close names the knowledge of the Lord, the reader is taught that the silence of a witness is a choice made in front of a witness who never forgets. A word spoken at the right hour is often the whole difference between a family that settles and a family that divides.

The case is like a man travelling with a neighbour's goods on his camel and no paper between them. The goods are delivered, the man carries the trust home in his chest for a month, and the neighbour waits at the gate with the sum counted before either of them says a word.

---

## Verse 2:284

> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Whether you reveal what is in your hearts or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE OWNERSHIP THAT COVERS EVERYTHING**

The verse opens the closing movement of the chapter with a declaration of possession: ***“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens”*** ***“and whatever is on the earth.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the ground of the account that follows, since the One who owns a thing may ask about the use of it. On this point, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the two halves of the sentence leave nothing outside the ownership.

al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the two words, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the verse answers the thought of a person who hides a matter in his chest and believes it belongs to him alone. Because the declaration comes first, the reader is shown what gives the Book its right to ask.

**THE SECRET THAT COMES INTO THE OPEN**

The verse then states the reach of the account: ***“Whether you reveal what is in your hearts”*** ***“or conceal it, Allah will call you to account”*** ***“for it.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the revealing and the concealing as the two states of a thought. So that no intention is left outside the reckoning, and al-Qurṭubī keeps the long treatment of the ten over what this accounting covers.

The reading that the account of the inner life is followed by the mercy named in the next sentence is kept by as-Saʿdī, since the Book does not leave a person alone with the fear raised in the sentence before. And the plain sense that the heart is a place the Lord reads like the street is kept by Ibn ʿAbbās. Because the hidden heart is named before the judgment, the reader is shown how the Book treats the inside of a person. The order of the two sentences is a mercy, and it teaches a reader to look at his own thoughts with the same patience the Book shows him.

**THE FORGIVENESS AND THE PUNISHMENT IN ONE SENTENCE**

The verse then names the two ends: ***“He forgives whoever He wills”*** ***“and punishes whoever He wills.”*** al-Baghawī keeps the two as the mercy and the justice of the One who is free in both. For its part, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the note that the sequence of the two sentences teaches a person to stand between hope and fear.

al-Ālūsī keeps the reading that the will named here is not a caprice but the will of the One who knows the hearts he is judging, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the pair. Because the verse leaves both doors open, the reader is shown why the community was taught to ask for pardon in the verses that follow.

**THE CAPACITY THAT CLOSES THE VERSE**

The verse ends on the name that holds the whole passage: ***“And Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. The capacity is kept by as-Saʿdī as the power that will carry out the account that was declared. And the same is kept by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān with the note that the sentence is placed last because it answers the doubt of the man who wonders how a hidden thought could ever be brought to a court.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain reading of the close, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same in a short form. Because the verse ends on the power of the Lord, the reader is shown that the account of the hearts is not a threat that an ordinary court could ever carry out.

The faith of the messenger and the community is declared in the verse that follows, (2:285 — **“The Messenger ˹firmly˺ believes”**). And the same capacity over the raising of the dead was stated in the story of the man who slept a hundred years, (2:259 — **“that Allah is Most Capable of everything”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who keeps a careful account of his public deeds and lets his heart run as it likes in private. The verse gives him the ownership of the heavens and the earth, the revealing and the concealing, and the two doors of forgiveness and punishment, and it asks him which part of his life he thinks is not being written. Because the close names the power over everything, the reader is taught that the Lord who owns the sky is the Lord who reads the thought that never reached the tongue.

The case is like a man who keeps his shop in good order for the customers and his store-room stacked with spoiled goods. The door of the shop is swept every morning, the store-room is opened once a year, and the smell that greets him at that door is the one thing in the building nobody else had to mention.

---

## Verse 2:285

> The Messenger ˹firmly˺ believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. They ˹all˺ believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers. ˹They proclaim,˺ “We make no distinction between any of His messengers.” And they say, “We hear and obey. ˹We seek˺ Your forgiveness, our Lord! And to You ˹alone˺ is the final return.”

**THE MESSENGER AND THE COMMUNITY IN ONE LINE**

The verse joins the messenger to the people: ***“The Messenger ˹firmly˺ believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord”*** ***“and so do the believers.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the answer to the account that was announced in the verse before it, since the community was told how the message was received. Alongside that, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the two parties stand together in one belief.

al-Qurṭubī keeps the reports of the community on the merit of this verse and its neighbour, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the two clauses. Because the message came to a messenger and was carried by a people, the reader is shown that the religion was never the possession of one man.

**THE FOUR ARTICLES IN ONE SENTENCE**

The four articles of the belief are then gathered: ***“They ˹all˺ believe in Allah, His angels, His Books”*** ***“and His messengers.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the four as the short form of the whole creed. Here too, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the Books and the messengers are named together so that no one would take one of them and leave the rest.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that belief in the messengers of the Lord is part of the belief in the Lord. For its part, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the remark that the sentence is placed at the close of the chapter because it gathers its whole teaching. Because the four articles are named in one line, the reader is shown what a person accepts when he accepts the message.

**THE DECLARATION ABOUT THE MESSENGERS**

The verse then gives the words of the community: ***“˹They proclaim,˺ “We make no distinction between any of His messengers.””*** al-Ālūsī keeps the sentence as the refusal of the community to honour one messenger by dishonouring another. In the same way, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the words answer the practice of the earlier communities that took some of their prophets and rejected the rest.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the plain reading that the declaration covers the belief in the message of every one of them, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same in a short form. Because the sentence is given in the first person of the community, the reader is shown how a confession is meant to be spoken.

**THE HEARING, THE OBEDIENCE AND THE RETURN**

The verse closes with the words that gather the whole of a life: ***“And they say, “We hear”*** ***“and obey. ˹We seek˺ Your forgiveness, our Lord!”*** ***“And to You ˹alone˺ is the final return.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the hearing as the acceptance of the command before the doing of it. And the obedience as the work that follows, so that the two words are the whole of the religion in a short form.

as-Saʿdī keeps the asking of forgiveness as the answer of a community that knows it will fall short. On this point, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the note that the return named at the end is the reason a person obeys at all. Because the verse ends on the return to the Lord, the reader is shown where the obedience of a person is finally delivered.

The prayer that follows this verse carries the same confession in the words of a request, (2:286 — **“Our Lord! Do not punish us”**), and the same belief in the Books and the messengers was named among the marks of the mindful in the opening of the chapter, (2:4 — **“and have sure faith in the Hereafter”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been taught to prefer one part of the message and to shut his ear to the rest. The verse gives him four articles in one sentence and a confession that makes no distinction among the messengers, and it asks him which of the four he has been leaving out. Because the close names the return to the Lord, the reader is taught that the whole of a life is a hearing followed by an obedience and a journey home.

The case is like a family that receives a number of letters from a father who is away and reads only the one that speaks of the money. The letters are kept in the same drawer, and the instructions about the land are the ones that were never opened.

---

## Verse 2:286

> Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford. All good will be for its own benefit, and all evil will be to its own loss. ˹The believers pray,˺ “Our Lord! Do not punish us if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord! Do not place a burden on us like the one you placed on those before us. Our Lord! Do not burden us with what we cannot bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our ˹only˺ Guardian. So grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”

**THE BURDEN THAT IS MEASURED TO THE BEARER**

The chapter closes with a sentence of relief after a long stretch of law: ***“Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the sentence as the answer to the fear that the verse before it had raised in the community, since the account of the hearts had seemed heavier than any person could carry. Here too, And al-Baghawī keeps the same with the note that the relief stands at the end of the chapter as its seal.

The long treatment of the ten over what the sentence lifts from the community is kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain reading of the measure is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the Book closes a chapter of commands with a sentence about capacity, the reader is shown what kind of law this is.

**THE GOOD AND THE EVIL THAT BELONG TO THE DOER**

The verse then states the ownership of the deed: ***“All good will be”*** ***“for its own benefit”*** ***“and all evil will be to its own loss.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the pair as the rule that a person carries his own deed and no other's. For its part, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the two sentences answer the person who fears that his good is spent on another.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the plain sense that the deed of a soul returns to the soul. In the same way, And Ibn Kathīr keeps the same with the remark that the sentence follows the law of the burden so that no one would think the account moves to a stranger. Because the gain and the loss stand in one breath, the reader is shown how the Book puts a whole life into two clauses. Since the measure of the burden is named in the first sentence, the reader sees that the two clauses after it are the comfort of a person who knows his own limits.

**THE THREE PRAYERS OF THE BELIEVERS**

The verse then gives the prayers of the community: ***“˹The believers pray,˺ “Our Lord!”*** ***“Do not punish us”*** ***“if we forget or make a mistake.”*** ***“Our Lord!”*** ***“Do not place a burden on us like the one you placed on those before us.”*** ***“Our Lord!”*** ***“Do not burden us with what we cannot bear.”*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the three as the requests of a community that has read its own weakness. In the same vein, And Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the same with the reports that the words were taught to the believers as a form of asking.

The note that the earlier communities were burdened with heavy duties, and that this community asked to be spared the like, is kept by al-Qurṭubī, and the plain reading of the three prayers is kept by al-Jalālayn. Because the requests begin with a slip and end with the limit of strength, the reader is shown the order in which a person learns to know himself.

**THE PARDON, THE MERCY AND THE VICTORY**

The verse then gathers the last requests: ***“Pardon us, forgive us”*** ***“and have mercy on us. You are our ˹only˺ Guardian.”*** ***“So grant us victory over the disbelieving people.””*** al-Ṭabarī keeps the pardon as the covering of a deed that is known, the forgiveness as the wiping of it away and the mercy as the kindness that follows a person after both. On this point, And as-Saʿdī keeps the same with the note that the three words move a soul from its worst state to its best.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the guardian as the one who takes charge of the community in every matter, and al-Jalālayn keeps the plain reading of the close. Because the verse ends with a request for victory after a request for mercy, the reader is shown what the community was asking for as the chapter closed.

The sentence of relief is the seal on the long chapter, and the same measure of a soul is stated in the chapter of the cattle, where the Book declares that no soul is charged beyond its scope. And the same return to the Lord was named in the confession just above, (2:285 — **“And to You ˹alone˺ is the final return.”**).

The lesson also reaches a reader who has been carrying the fear that the commands of the Book were made for someone stronger than himself. The verse gives him a measure, a deed that belongs to its doer and three prayers that he may say out loud, and it asks him what he would ask for first if the three were put in his hand. Because the close of the chapter is a prayer for pardon, mercy and victory, the reader is taught that a servant of the Lord is meant to finish his reading on his knees and not on his feet.

The case is like a man who is asked to carry a load up a hill and is met at the bottom by the owner of the load, who measures the sack against his frame and takes a third of it out before the climb. The hill is the same hill, the load is the same load, and the man reaches the top on his own feet.
